He also saw its limits. The narrower the question, the less closely it matches real life, as when a model assumes hydrocarbon fuels are infinite. Because economic variables can only be isolated in theory, the method reveals tendencies, not absolutes. In highly interconnected systems, changing one variable changes all the others, so holding the rest constant is impossible in reality.

  <!-- nature-econ-105 -->

- **Economic models: simple maps of a messy economy**

  Economies are shaped by many things at once: decisions, resource limits, environmental and geographical constraints, laws and chance. An economic model cuts through that tangle. It is a simplified, often mathematical, picture of an economic process, built from a set of variables and the relationships between them. Models help forecast economic activity, propose and justify policy, and plan inside firms and centrally planned economies. Some predict only the direction of change, such as buyers wanting less when a price rises, and are often drawn as simple two-dimensional graphs. Most rest on unrealistic assumptions, such as perfect information or frictionless markets. Some leave out important issues such as externalities. Their forecasts can be far apart. In the late 1980s the Brookings Institution compared 12 leading macroeconomic models and found they gave significantly different answers to the same shocks. Like weather forecasts, economic forecasts fail because models cannot capture full detail and are sensitive to small changes in their equations.

  <!-- nature-econ-152 -->

- **Preferences: how people rank their options**

  Taste and need, not price, availability or income, decide what a person wants most. In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted. Most models of decision-making share one basic principle, transitivity: anyone who prefers A to B and B to C should prefer A to C. An ordering that is both transitive and complete is called rational, and people who follow one are called rational agents. Real people do not always behave this way. Their preferences can form cycles with no best choice. Most economic models assume preferences stay stable, an assumption long disputed outside the school described in Neoclassical economics: the mainstream's core. In fact preferences shift with new technology and social influence, as when friends at lunch shift each other's food choices. Ragnar Frisch built the first mathematical model of preferences for demand and utility theory in 1926.

  <!-- nature-econ-141 -->

- **Indifference curves: mapping equal satisfaction**

  An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining every combination of two goods that a consumer likes equally well. A set of these curves for one person is an indifference map, read like contour lines: curves further out mean more satisfaction. Their downward slope expresses a willingness to give up some of one good for more of the other. They usually bow in toward the origin, the corner of the graph where both amounts are zero. The slope at any point is the rate at which the consumer will make that swap (see The marginal rate of substitution: what you would swap). The best affordable choice lies where an indifference curve just touches the line of what the consumer can afford. Edgeworth set out the mathematics in 1881, Pareto first drew the curves in 1906, and Hicks and Allen popularized them in the 1930s. Not everyone accepts them. Hovenkamp argued that people value what they own more than what they could buy, so they have no indifference curve at all. Courts, he said, should ask what people would accept to give something up.

  <!-- nature-econ-125 -->

- **Complementary goods: things that go together**

  Razors have been sold cheaply as loss leaders, priced low on purpose to raise demand for the blades. Complementary goods are goods used together, so one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular. Cars and gasoline, phones and phone service, and printers and cartridges are everyday pairs. When the price of one falls, people want more of its partner, a link measured by Cross elasticity of demand: how one price moves another good, which is negative for such pairs. A perfect complement must be used with its partner, like left and right shoes, and its indifference curve forms a right angle. The bond need not run both ways. A game needs a console, but a console does not need that particular game.

  <!-- nature-econ-108 -->

- **Ordinal utility: ranking without measuring**

  If George prefers A to B and B to C, any set of numbers that keeps that order describes his preferences equally well. The numbers themselves mean nothing. This is ordinal utility: it ranks a person's options in order of preference, saying which is better but not by how much. The alternative, Cardinal utility: measuring how much better, treats the size of the gaps between options as meaningful too. Vilfredo Pareto introduced the ordinal concept in 1906. It turned out to be enough. All of the theory of how consumers choose under certainty can be written in ordinal terms, and usually is. Preferences can be drawn as indifference curves, with curves further from the origin meaning higher utility. For a utility function to exist at all, preferences must be complete, so that any two options can be compared. They must also be transitive: if A beats B and B beats C, A beats C.

  <!-- nature-econ-139 -->

- **Positive and normative: what is versus what ought to be**

  "More government spending would lower unemployment" and "milk should cost $6 a gallon so dairy farmers live better" sound like the same kind of claim. They are not. Positive economics describes and explains how the economy works, so the first statement can in principle be checked against evidence. Normative economics says what people or societies ought to do, so the second rests on value judgments. John Neville Keynes called the first the science of "what is" and the second the study of "what ought to be," and his definitions became standard in teaching. In 1932 Lionel Robbins argued economics should study how to reach given ends with limited resources, not judge which ends to pursue. Some normative work aims to be objective: Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses seeks the best decision given stated assumptions about value. Ecological economists argue economics is unavoidably normative. The line itself is disputed. Philosophers such as Hilary Putnam doubt that facts and values can be fully separated. Caplan and Miller argue that many supposed disagreements over values are really about facts.

  <!-- nature-econ-140 -->

- **Trade-offs: more of one thing means less of another**

  A full container must lose some items before it can take any more. That is a trade-off in its simplest form: a choice in which you accept less of one thing in return for more of another. Limits of many kinds create trade-offs, even simple physics. Investing shows one clearly. Stocks offer higher potential returns with more risk, while bonds are safer but pay less. Economists express a trade-off as the cost of the most preferred alternative given up, explored in Opportunity cost: the price of the road not taken. They often draw it as a frontier of the best possible combinations, such as the limit on how much of two goods an economy can make. Nature brings its own versions. In environmental management, funding under REDD+: paying countries to keep their forests faces trade-offs among biodiversity conservation, carbon storage and fair distribution, since maximizing one reduces the other two. More broadly, the tension between prosperity for all and environmental conservation makes trade-offs necessary in sustainability.

  <!-- nature-econ-099 -->

- **Opportunity cost: the price of the road not taken**

  An hour away from work to buy $200 of office supplies costs more than $200. Someone who earns $25 an hour also gives up $25 of earnings. The $200 is paid out of pocket; the lost $25 is hidden but just as real. Together they show opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up when limited resources force you to pick one option over others. Put simply, it is the benefit you would have had from your second-best choice. The idea expresses the link between scarcity and choice, and its aim is the efficient use of scarce resources. It counts every cost of a decision, visible and hidden, and is not limited to money. Lost time, pleasure or any useful benefit counts too. One kind of cost is left out. Money already spent and unrecoverable should not sway present or future decisions (see Sunk costs: what is spent is spent). The concept also explains trade. A party that can produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others holds the edge described in Comparative advantage: why the best at everything still trades. Governments face the same arithmetic: $840 billion spent on a war cannot fund healthcare, education or tax cuts.

  <!-- nature-econ-095 -->

- **Rational choice: people as careful calculators**

  Economists often explain behavior by asking a simple question: what would a rational person do, weighing the same costs and benefits? That is rational choice modeling. It assumes people can rank and weigh their options, so they choose by balancing costs against benefits. Their preferences are taken to be complete and transitive, and a decision counts as rational if it follows logically from them. Early neoclassical economists such as Jevons assumed people choose to maximize their happiness, or utility. The model can even show how individually rational people reach collectively irrational outcomes. Its critics are many. Herbert Simon argued that people's reasoning has limits (Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough), so they often settle for a good-enough decision (Satisficing: stopping at good enough). Research in behavioral psychology has challenged the theory and produced an alternative, Prospect theory: how people really weigh risk. Others argue that people often act from habit, impulse or emotion rather than calculation. Economists, psychologists and sociologists have long disputed both its assumptions and its predictions.

  <!-- nature-econ-098 -->

- **The budget constraint: what your money can buy**

  Income draws a hard edge around every shopping list. A budget constraint is the full set of combinations of things a person can afford with their income at current prices. With two goods it becomes a straight line, the budget line, which shows the trade-off between them. Its slope is the ratio of the two prices. That ratio is the opportunity cost of one more unit of one good, measured in units of the other. Paired with indifference curves, the budget constraint is the basic tool for analyzing how consumers choose. The best affordable bundle usually lies where an indifference curve just touches the budget line. Real budgets are rarely so tidy. Taxes, subsidies, quantity discounts and welfare benefits can bend the line or put kinks in it. The idea applies to time as well. In labor economics the wage acts as the price of leisure, because one more hour off costs one hour's wage.

  <!-- nature-econ-102 -->

- **Consumer choice: how preferences become spending**

  Every shopping trip is, in theory, a small problem in getting the most for your money. Consumer choice theory is the part of microeconomics that explains how people's preferences shape what they spend and how much they demand. Its central assumption is that consumers maximize utility subject to their budget constraint, choosing the best bundle they can afford. Preferences are drawn as indifference curves, each showing bundles that leave the consumer equally satisfied. In practice, income, culture, product information and psychological factors all affect how people value goods. The theory makes one neat prediction: every price change splits into two parts, explained in The income effect: richer or poorer, you buy differently and The substitution effect: switching to what got cheaper. Behavioral economists criticize the theory because consumers often rely on rough shortcuts that ignore some information (Heuristics: the mind's shortcuts). People also let money already spent sway them, like traveling through a storm to use a concert ticket.

  <!-- nature-econ-110 -->

- **The substitution effect: switching to what got cheaper**

  When one good gets cheaper relative to another, buyers shift toward it. The substitution effect is that change in what a consumer buys, caused purely by the change in relative prices. Any price change can be split into this effect and a second one, The income effect: richer or poorer, you buy differently, which comes from the change in purchasing power. On a graph, the substitution effect is a move along the original indifference curve, while the second effect is the move to a different curve. John Hicks and R. G. D. Allen introduced the idea to English readers in 1934, building on Pareto. They reached conclusions that Eugen Slutsky had found in 1915. A related measure, defined by Hicks and by Joan Robinson, tracks how the mix of inputs used shifts as their relative prices change.

  <!-- nature-econ-147 -->

- **The utility maximization problem: the best you can afford**

  In the textbook picture, every consumer solves the same puzzle. The utility maximization problem describes how a consumer chooses the most preferred bundle of goods they can afford with limited income at given prices. It assumes the consumer can rank every possible bundle by the utility it gives. Solving it gives a systematic account of what consumers buy and how that changes when income or prices change. The limit reflects scarcity, and money is not the only one: consumers may also face time constraints and budgets spread over time. One result is tidy. If all prices and income rise at the same rate, the affordable set and the best choice stay the same. Real consumers fall short. Lacking time or information, they sometimes pick bundles that do not maximize utility. The problem was first developed by the utilitarian philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

  <!-- nature-econ-150 -->

- **Market structure: from many sellers to just one**

  How prices form in a market depends on its structure. That means how many firms sell in it, how alike their products are and how easily firms can enter or leave. At one extreme sits Perfect competition: the textbook ideal market. Many small firms sell identical products and are price takers, unable to set their own price, which drives prices down to the cost of making one more unit. In Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different, many firms sell slightly different products, as with restaurants, cereal and clothing. Next comes Oligopoly: a market run by a few, where a few firms dominate. They may collude and form price-raising alliances (Cartels: rivals who agree not to compete). At the other extreme is Monopoly: the market with one seller, a single supplier, which tends to charge higher prices and produce below the socially best level. The buyer's side has its own extreme, Monopsony: the market with one buyer, with only one buyer. A mining company that is the only employer in an isolated town is an example, and it can set wages low.

  <!-- nature-econ-137 -->

- **Thinking at the margin: one more unit at a time**

  Economic decisions, in theory, are made one extra unit at a time. In economics, the margin is the current level of consumption or production. Marginal concepts describe what happens with one small change in that quantity rather than with the total. Whether to get one more unit depends on the benefit of that unit. A consumer keeps buying until the benefit of one more unit equals its market price. A firm facing a competitive market price keeps producing until one more unit would cost more than it sells for. These ideas form the basis of price theory and predict how much people buy and sell. Neoclassical analysis often assumes goods can be divided endlessly, so a marginal change can be infinitely small. Strictly, the smallest relevant step may be quite large. Marginal thinking matters for nature too. Economists generally agree on one rule for regulating emissions efficiently. Every polluter should face the full marginal social cost of its actions. Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits uses the same logic, letting reductions happen first where cutting emissions is cheapest.

  <!-- nature-econ-128 -->

- **Marginal utility: the value of the next piece**

  Economists care less about the whole box of chocolates than about the next piece. Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction a person gets from consuming one more unit of a good or service. In economics, marginal means a small change from some starting level. Marginal utility can be positive, negative or zero. Negative means each extra unit does more harm than good. The concept underpins marginal analysis, which compares the extra benefits of an activity with its extra costs. Since utility is hard to measure directly, economists rank options by watching what people actually choose. The idea grew out of an old puzzle: how are prices set? Economists developed marginal utility while trying to explain it, and Daniel Bernoulli published the first clear statement of the theory in 1738. Critics note that people may not optimize as the theory assumes, and that utility varies between people and over time.

  <!-- nature-econ-091 -->

- **The marginal rate of substitution: what you would swap**

  Suppose a consumer would give up 2 units of one good to get 1 more unit of another, and feel exactly as satisfied. That swap rate, 2, is the marginal rate of substitution. Graphically it is the slope of an indifference curve at a given bundle, taken as a positive number, so it differs at each point on the curve. It also equals the marginal utility of the first good divided by the marginal utility of the second. A law of diminishing marginal rate of substitution follows. The more of one good a consumer already has, the less of the other they will give up for an extra unit. Two rules follow. Utility is highest when spending is split so that the marginal utility per unit of money is equal for every good. And two people keep trading as long as their swap rates differ. Once the rates are equal, no further exchange can benefit both.

  <!-- nature-econ-129 -->

- **Marginalism: why diamonds cost more than water**

  Water keeps people alive, yet diamonds cost more. Marginalism resolves the puzzle. It is the economic theory that explains differences in the value of goods by their marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit. Water has greater total utility, but a diamond has greater marginal utility. Behind this sits a law, also called Gossen's First Law, that each added unit brings less extra benefit than the one before (see Diminishing marginal utility: why the twentieth candy disappoints). Marginalism explains prices through the meeting of buyers and sellers: buyers want less and sellers offer more as the price rises. Following Alfred Marshall, marginalists also explained costs by the extra output each added input produces. At the most general level, the extra cost of one more unit is an opportunity cost, though the term usually means the extra money spent. Marginalism is an integral part of mainstream economic theory.

  <!-- nature-econ-131 -->

- **Neoclassical economics: the mainstream's core**

  The dominant approach to microeconomics takes its name from Thorstein Veblen, who coined the term in 1900. Neoclassical economics explains production, consumption and prices through Supply and demand: the model behind prices, driven by people maximizing utility and firms maximizing profit. Three assumptions hold it up. People have rational preferences. Individuals maximize utility and firms maximize profits. And people act independently with full information. In this view a good's value comes from its marginal utility to the user, unlike Classical economics: Smith, Ricardo, Malthus and Mill and Marxian economics, which use the labor theory of value. The approach developed in the 1870s and replaced the classical school as the mainstream. Its break with the classical school is often dated to Jevons and Menger in 1871 and Walras in 1874–1877. From the 1950s, combined with Keynes's ideas, it formed the neoclassical synthesis that dominated mainstream economics. Although it favors markets, it accepts that externalities, a form of market failure, can stop markets from producing socially desirable outcomes. Under suitable assumptions, though, flexible prices allow every welfare-improving trade, so markets left free yield an optimum of social welfare.

  <!-- nature-hist-023 -->

- **Criticisms of neoclassical economics: the case against the mainstream**

  Thorstein Veblen mocked the neoclassical view of a person as "a lightning calculator of pleasures and pains." He was far from alone. Marxist, behavioral, Austrian, post-Keynesian, institutionalist and other schools each break with neoclassical economics, and insiders such as Joseph Stiglitz criticize it too. The main target is its assumption of rational, self-interested, fully informed people. Behavioral economists study how real decisions differ from that picture. Hayek argued that by assuming full information, its equilibrium models assume away the real problem: discovering knowledge spread among many people. Critics also say it carries a normative bias while claiming to be value-free, and they call for more pluralistic teaching. Because it holds that market exchange usually allocates goods best, critics charge that it promotes commodification, turning things into goods for sale, and privatization. Defenders reply that it is also the main tool for judging how policies affect inequality. Schools still disagree over whether its assumptions and mathematical methods are sound, and whether modern mainstream models have moved beyond it.

  <!-- nature-econ-155 -->

- **Four types of goods: who can be excluded, who competes**

  Can people be kept from using something, and does one person's use leave less for others? Economists sort goods into four types by those two questions. Food and clothing answer yes to both: they are Private goods: yours to keep, and gone once used. Cinemas and cable television can exclude people, but one viewer does not use them up, which makes them Club goods: members only, but no one else loses. Air and national defense pass neither test. They are Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few, and mainstream economists accept that markets under-provide them. The fourth type matters most for nature. Common-pool resources: hard to fence, easy to deplete, such as fish and timber, are rival but hard to exclude people from. Without clear ownership rules (Property rights: the rules of who owns what), they may be overfished. Forests, water systems, fisheries and the global atmosphere all fall in this group, and all are vital to human survival. The scheme took its modern form in 1977. Elinor and Vincent Ostrom treated both tests as matters of degree and added that shared kind as a fourth type.

  <!-- nature-econ-121 -->

- **Goods and services: things and activities**

  A restaurant sells both: the food on the plate and the service at the table. Goods are usually tangible items such as pens or pears, while services are activities other people provide, such as teaching or haircuts. Most products fall somewhere between pure goods and pure services. Producing, distributing and consuming them underpins all economic activity and trade. Adam Smith drew a sharper line. He counted only work that produced material goods as productive and treated services as unproductive.

  <!-- nature-econ-122 -->

- **Diminishing marginal utility: why the twentieth candy disappoints**

  Three pieces of candy beat two, but the twentieth adds little beyond the nineteenth and may even make things worse. That is the law of diminishing marginal utility: each extra unit of something consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before. It shows up in the concave shape of most utility functions, curves that rise ever more slowly. The law helps explain the value of goods and why people prefer having things sooner. Bernoulli and Cramer concluded that money itself becomes less desirable as more of it accumulates. The dislike of gambles (Risk aversion: why a sure thing often wins) is mainly attributed to this decreasing marginal utility.

  <!-- nature-econ-092 -->

- **Substitute goods: when one can replace another**

  Coca-Cola and Pepsi are close substitutes, because both meet the same wish for a cola drink. Substitute goods are goods that can replace each other, so cheaper prices for one reduce demand for the other. When the price of a good rises, demand for its substitutes rises, a positive link measured by Cross elasticity of demand: how one price moves another good. A perfect substitute can be used in exactly the same way as the good it replaces, and its indifference curves are straight lines. Buyers then choose purely on price and will not buy the dearer one at all. Someone who sees Coca-Cola and Pepsi Max as perfect substitutes would be happy spending the whole budget on either. Imperfect substitutes are not traded one-for-one, because many buyers prefer one brand over the other. And as a consumer accumulates more of one good, they will pay less for each extra unit of its substitute.

  <!-- nature-econ-411 -->

- **Normal goods: buying more as income rises**

  A normal good is one that people buy more of when their income rises, unlike the opposite case covered in Inferior goods: buying less as income rises. Whether a good counts as normal comes from observation, not from the good itself. The same car can be normal for middle-income buyers and inferior for rich ones. Economists measure the response with Income elasticity of demand: what richer people buy: the percentage change in quantity bought divided by the percentage change in income. For a normal good it lies between zero and one, while luxuries score above one. When income rises, more of a normal good is wanted at every price.

  <!-- nature-econ-138 -->

- **Free goods: when there is enough for everyone**

  A free sample is not a free good. A free good is one that is not scarce, so it is available in any quantity with no opportunity cost to society. Something given away at zero price still used scarce resources in its making. Older textbooks offered seawater and air as examples, plentiful enough for everyone to have as much as they want. Ideas and works that can be copied at almost no cost are free goods too, but patents and copyright make some of them scarce to reward their creators. The label can mislead. Treating water as a free good has been blamed for underpricing 98% of water.

  <!-- nature-econ-118 -->

- **The economic problem: what, how and for whom**

  Every economy must answer three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. Together they form the economic problem. Because resources are scarce, producing more of one good means taking resources away from others. Production is efficient only if no reallocation could make more of one good without making less of another. Economies answer the questions by custom, by central command or, in economies that mix the two, by both market signals and government directives. Paul Samuelson argued that prices in competitive markets answer all three questions at once. Keynes saw something deeper underneath. He called the struggle for subsistence the most pressing problem not only of humanity but of all life.

  <!-- nature-econ-115 -->

- **Cardinal utility: measuring how much better**

  Ordinal utility can say that two ice creams beat one, but not by how much. Cardinal utility goes further. It treats satisfaction as something that can be measured with numbers, so the size of the differences between options means something. A utility function counts as cardinal or ordinal depending on whether it says anything beyond the ranking, such as how strong a preference is. Daniel Bernoulli used a cardinal utility of money, based on logarithms, to resolve The St. Petersburg paradox: an infinite prize nobody pays for. The approach seems to assume that absolute levels of satisfaction exist, so gains can be compared across situations.

  <!-- nature-econ-101 -->

- **Marshallian demand: what a consumer buys at given prices**

  A Marshallian demand function gives how much of a good a consumer buys, depending on its price, their income and the prices of other goods. It solves the utility maximization problem. It is also called uncompensated demand, because a price rise is not offset by extra income, unlike the version in Hicksian demand: holding satisfaction fixed. If all prices and income rise by the same factor, the quantities bought stay the same. When people favor mixes (Convex preferences: why mixes beat extremes) and prices are positive, there is a single best bundle.

  <!-- nature-econ-133 -->

- **Convex preferences: why mixes beat extremes**

  Convex preferences are preferences in which averages are liked better than extremes, so a person prefers a mix of goods to a lot of just one. The idea roughly matches diminishing marginal utility without needing a utility function. With strictly convex preferences, the average of two equally liked bundles beats either one, so indifference curves bow in toward the origin. Perfect substitutes mark the boundary case. Their indifference curves are straight lines, and the average gives the same utility.

  <!-- nature-econ-142 -->

- **Bads: things people pay to be rid of**

  Usually money and goods move in opposite directions. With garbage they travel together: a household pays a collector to take it away. Garbage is a bad, the opposite of a good: something with negative value, such as waste, that its owner will pay to be rid of. A bad lowers a consumer's overall welfare, and in effect the garbage has a price below zero.

  <!-- nature-econ-120 -->

- **Explicit costs: money out the door**

  Wages, rent, overheads and materials share one feature: each involves handing over money. An explicit cost is a direct, out-of-pocket cost of an action, paid in cash or by handing over resources. Explicit costs always have a money value and involve a transfer of money, such as paying employees. They show up in a firm's financial statements. Hidden costs, the subject of Implicit costs: the income you quietly give up, are never recorded in the accounts.

  <!-- nature-econ-096 -->

- **Compensating variation: the payment that undoes a price change**

  When a price rises, how much money would make a person whole again? Compensating variation is the amount that would leave someone exactly as well off after a price change as before, measured at the new prices. John Hicks introduced the measure in 1939. It can be read as what a planner must pay a consumer, after the change, to compensate them. The same logic underlies Kaldor–Hicks efficiency: could the winners pay off the losers, where a policy passes if winners could compensate losers, even if they never do. Its mirror image is Equivalent variation: a price change in money terms.

  <!-- nature-econ-107 -->

- **Budgets across time: borrowing and saving**

  A budget does not stop at the end of the month. An intertemporal budget constraint links what a person can consume in different periods through borrowing and saving at a rate of interest. Borrowing now raises present consumption at the cost of less consumption later, and saving does the reverse. Behavioral economists add a twist (Present bias: why now beats later): people give extra weight to consumption now over consumption later.

  <!-- nature-econ-103 -->

- **Soft budget constraints: when rescue is always coming**

  A firm that expects to be rescued behaves differently from one that does not. A soft budget constraint exists when an organization expects an outside body, usually a government, to cover its losses if it gets into financial trouble. Hungarian economist János Kornai introduced the term in the late 1970s to study state-owned firms in centrally planned economies. Expecting bailouts, those firms invested too much, saved too little on costs and lobbied for more resources, contributing to chronic shortages. The expectation of rescue also breeds the problem explored in Moral hazard: taking risks someone else pays for, as with too-big-to-fail banks.

  <!-- nature-econ-104 -->

- **The expenditure minimization problem: satisfaction at least cost**

  Turn the consumer's usual question around, from how much satisfaction a budget can buy to how little a goal costs. The expenditure minimization problem asks how little money a consumer needs to reach a given level of satisfaction at current prices. It is the mirror image, or dual, of the utility maximization problem. Its answer comes in two parts. The expenditure function gives the minimum money needed, and the demand function in Hicksian demand: holding satisfaction fixed gives the cheapest bundle that reaches the target.

  <!-- nature-econ-117 -->

- **Hicksian demand: holding satisfaction fixed**

  A Hicksian, or compensated, demand function gives how much of a good a person buys when their satisfaction is held fixed and they spend as little as possible. It shows how demand responds to a price change if income is adjusted to keep the person on the same indifference curve. That isolates the substitution effect. It comes from the expenditure minimization problem, while Marshallian demand comes from the utility maximization problem. Marshallian demand is easier to observe directly, and the two are linked by The Slutsky equation: splitting a price change in two.

  <!-- nature-econ-123 -->

- **Equivalent variation: a price change in money terms**

  Equivalent variation is the change in a person's wealth that would affect their welfare as much as a given price change would. John Hicks introduced it in 1939, together with compensating variation. The difference is the yardstick: equivalent variation values the welfare change at the old prices, compensating variation at the new ones. It is the most common modern measure of a taxpayer's loss from a distorting tax. The gap between that welfare loss and the revenue collected is the tax's pure waste, explained in Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets.

  <!-- nature-econ-116 -->

- **What is economics? From wealth to scarce means**

  Economics began life as political economy, stretching the Greek idea of household management to the running of a state. Its definition has kept moving ever since. In 1803 Jean-Baptiste Say called it the science of producing, distributing and consuming wealth. In 1890 Alfred Marshall called it the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, tied to the material requisites of well-being. In 1932 Lionel Robbins defined it as the study of human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses. His version is perhaps the most commonly accepted today.

  <!-- nature-econ-112 -->

- **Factors of production: land, labor and capital**

  Every good and service is made from inputs. Economists call them factors of production, and the classic trio is land, labor and capital. How much of each is used determines output, through a relationship explored in The production function: from inputs to output. One common list adds a fourth basic factor, the entrepreneur. Land, labor and capital are primary factors: they help production without becoming part of the product or being much changed by it. Materials and energy are secondary, because they come from the primary ones. The list has a history. The 18th-century French physiocrats held that a nation's wealth came only from land and agriculture. Adam Smith and David Ricardo saw the parts of a price as payments for land (rent), labor (wages) and capital. The list still draws fire. Some economists, such as Robert Ayres and the metabolism of industry and Benjamin Warr, fault orthodox economics for overlooking resources from nature and the decline of resource capital.

  <!-- nature-econ-086 -->

- **Capital: goods made to make other goods**

  A chocolate bar is a consumer good; the machine that makes it is capital. Capital means durable goods that people have produced and then use to make further goods and services, like the machinery in a factory. Unlike raw materials or energy, it is not used up in one round of production. It gives productive services over many cycles. Economists treat capital as a factor of production alongside labor and land, a classification dating from the classical economists. Unlike land and resources that cannot be renewed, capital can be produced or increased. Producing goods that are not consumed straight away, but used to make other goods, is called investment or capital accumulation. A nation's capital stock includes buildings, equipment, software and inventories, and modern usage also counts non-physical assets.

  <!-- nature-econ-083 -->

- **Land: every gift of nature, not just the ground**

  To an economist, a geostationary orbit counts as land. So do particular locations, mineral deposits, forests, stocks of fish, air quality and parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. In economics, land means every naturally occurring resource, not just the ground itself. It is one of the three classic factors of production, alongside capital and labor. Resources from nature underlie the production of every good, including capital goods. Income earned from owning or controlling them is called rent. Land's role was argued over at length by the classical economists but became minor in 20th-century neoclassical economics. Its weight has not shrunk. In the UK, land makes up 51% of the country's total net worth. Because nobody created land, it has no original owner. Rival claims to locations and mineral deposits have fed many civil wars and revolutions.

  <!-- nature-econ-082 -->

- **Economic systems: who owns, who decides**

  Scarcity forces every society to answer the same questions: what to produce, how to produce it and who gets what is produced. An economic system is the way a society organizes the production, allocation and distribution of goods and services to answer them. Systems are usually classed along two lines: who owns the means of production, and whether resources are allocated through markets or planning. Private ownership with markets is market capitalism. Public or cooperative ownership with planning is a socialist planned economy. Public ownership with markets is market socialism. Sorted by how they allocate resources, systems include market, mixed, planned, traditional, subsistence and gift economies. Capitalism combines private ownership of the means of production with markets to coordinate the economy. History has tested the alternatives. By the 1990s most communist states had ended or reformed their centrally planned economies, moving toward markets.

  <!-- nature-econ-153 -->

- **Diminishing returns: when more hands add less**

  Put more workers on a factory floor with fixed machines and space, and output first more than doubles. Then it rises in proportion. Eventually each new worker adds less and less as people get in each other's way. This is diminishing returns: the fall in extra output gained as more of one input is added while all other inputs stay fixed. It is also called diminishing marginal productivity. Output stays positive, but output per unit of input falls, and so does efficiency. The idea has deep roots in farming. In 1815 Ricardo, Malthus, West and Torrens applied it to land rent, drawing on English agriculture after the Napoleonic Wars. Diminishing returns mean rising costs, both for the next unit and on average. They also explain the bowed-out shape of the limit on what an economy can produce (The production-possibility frontier: what an economy can make). Technological or managerial innovation can reduce or remove them. Modern versions also hold other outputs equal, since one process can make co-products, such as a factory producing more goods and more CO2.

  <!-- nature-econ-113 -->

- **The production-possibility frontier: what an economy can make**

  In one example, 10 more packets of butter cost 5 guns when little butter is made, but 50 guns when butter output is near its maximum. A production-possibility frontier is a graph showing every combination of two outputs an economy can make when all its resources are used fully and efficiently. It illustrates scarcity, opportunity cost and efficiency: more of one good means moving resources away from another. A point on the curve is efficient. A point inside means resources are wasted or idle, and a point beyond is impossible with current resources and technology. The curve usually bows outward because opportunity cost rises, as resources less suited to a good are moved into it. It shifts outward when labor or capital grow or technology improves, which is how an economy grows. It shifts inward if the labor force shrinks, raw materials run out, or a natural, military or ecological disaster destroys productive capacity. Being on the frontier is not everything: market failures such as externalities can lead an efficient economy to produce the wrong mix of goods.

  <!-- nature-econ-143 -->

- **The labor theory of value: worth measured in work**

  For Adam Smith and David Ricardo, the long-run "natural price" of a good came back to labor. The labor theory of value holds that a good's economic value is set by the total socially necessary labor needed to produce it. Smith tied value to the labor a good could command in exchange. Ricardo tied it to the quantity of labor embodied in making it. In its simplest form, a product's final value is the value of the labor time plus the value of the tools, materials and power used, called constant capital. Marx built on it to construct his theory of surplus value, which holds that profit comes from the unpaid labor of workers, taken by capitalists. Today the theory is usually associated with Marxism. From the late 19th century, mainstream neoclassical economics largely replaced it with the theory of marginal utility. Critics from the Austrian School and neo-Ricardian economics still dispute it, especially over the "transformation problem" of turning values into prices.

  <!-- nature-econ-130 -->

- **Institutional economics: the rules shape the game**

  Markets are not simply given. Institutional economics sees them as the result of complex interactions between institutions, such as firms, states, laws and shared rules of behavior. It studies how those institutions, and their evolution, shape economic behavior. Instead of assuming stable preferences, rationality and equilibrium, it focuses on learning, limited reasoning and evolution. Its name traces to a 1919 article by Walton H. Hamilton. In the early 20th century it was central to American economics through Thorstein Veblen, Wesley Mitchell and John R. Commons. Veblen's The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899) analyzed how people consume conspicuously to display success. Later, a newer school (New institutional economics: the rules behind the market) tried to bring the approach into the mainstream through theories of Property rights: the rules of who owns what, information and Transaction costs: the price of making a deal. The older tradition continues today as a leading heterodox approach, one outside the mainstream.

  <!-- nature-econ-157 -->

- **Mixed economies: markets with a government hand**

  Most market-oriented economies today, including the United States, are mixed economies. A mixed economy combines features of capitalism, such as private businesses, with features of socialism, such as government-run services. The blend can mean markets with planning, markets with state intervention, or private with public enterprise. John Maynard Keynes advocated one version. In it, private ownership and profit-seeking stay dominant, but markets are regulated. Governments use taxing, spending and control of money to fight booms, busts, unemployment and inequality. They also provide education, healthcare, infrastructure, environmental protection and management of public lands. The Nordic countries, with their extensive welfare states, belong here too. China, Norway, Singapore and Vietnam run large state-owned sectors alongside large private ones. Because real economies rarely match an ideal, mixed economies are usually described as leaning toward private or public ownership. Some reject the idea entirely. Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek and orthodox Marxists argue no lasting mixture is possible, since either markets or planning must drive the economy.

  <!-- nature-econ-154 -->

- **The subjective theory of value: worth in the eye of the beholder**

  A collectable car or comic book can gain value long after it was made, through age, personal attachment, cultural meaning or scarcity. The subjective theory of value explains why. It holds that a good's value is set by the people buying or selling it. No property of the good, and no labor that went into it, decides it. It broke away from the labor theory of value during the The Marginal Revolution: three thinkers, one idea. Jevons, Walras and Menger created its modern version independently and almost at the same time in the late 19th century. One consequence is striking. Because trades are voluntary, both sides value what they receive more than what they give, so trade itself can create value. The theory also helps explain why non-essential goods can be worth more than essential ones. Alfred Marshall combined both views. Prices, he said, depend on objective production costs on the sellers' side and on buyers' subjective utility.

  <!-- nature-econ-146 -->

- **Matter, energy and design: an ecological view of production**

  Ecological economists replace land, labor and capital with three different factors: matter, energy and design intelligence. The point is to make production obey physical limits. Matter can be recycled but never created or destroyed, so there is an upper limit on how much can be withdrawn and used. Energy loses its usefulness over time, as when electricity running a machine turns into heat. Once matter and energy are used at their maximum sustainable rates, only better design can raise output per unit. This underlies a central claim of the field: infinite growth is impossible.

  <!-- nature-econ-087 -->

- **Entrepreneurship: a fourth factor of production?**

  Land, labor and capital do not organize themselves. Entrepreneurship, the work of combining them to make a profit, is sometimes counted as a fourth factor of production. Some authors added it in the first half of the 20th century, and it became standard in the post-war neoclassical synthesis. Many economists today instead treat Human capital: the skills people carry to work as the fourth factor, with entrepreneurship as one form of it. Others have proposed energy, the value of social ties, or cultural heritage.

  <!-- nature-econ-088 -->

- **Fixed and circulating capital: what lasts and what is used up**

  Adam Smith split capital into two kinds. Fixed capital, such as machines and storage buildings, is not used up in making a product. Circulating capital, such as raw materials and intermediate products, is. Smith also made clear that capital is a stock, an amount that exists at a point in time. Marx later drew a different line. His constant capital is spending on machinery and plant, while variable capital is spending on labor power, which he saw as the only source of surplus value.

  <!-- nature-econ-085 -->

- **Types of capital: from money to nature**

  Capital is not only machines. Economists divide it into several kinds, including financial, social, instructional, human, public and natural capital. One kind, Financial capital: the money that buys the machines, is traded in financial markets, and its market value rests on expected revenues and risk rather than on money invested in the past. Another, Human capital: the skills people carry to work, broadly combines social, instructional and individual human talent. Public capital covers government-owned infrastructure such as highways, water treatment, electric grids, hospitals and schools. Natural capital is the world's stock of resources from nature, and some of it gives people free goods and services called ecosystem services.

  <!-- nature-econ-084 -->

- **The Marginal Revolution: three thinkers, one idea**

  In 1871 two economists in different countries published the same new idea. In England, Jevons argued in The Theory of Political Economy that value depends entirely on utility. In Austria, Carl Menger presented the theory in his Principles of Economics. Walras followed in Switzerland in 1874. This spread of marginal utility theory in the 1870s is called the Marginal Revolution. A second generation, including Alfred Marshall, Böhm-Bawerk, Wieser and Pareto, carried the ideas into the mainstream. Over the 20th century a large literature grew on the conflict between marginalism and the labor theory of value.

  <!-- nature-econ-094 -->

- **Absolute advantage: simply being better at it**

  Suppose the UK needs fewer hours to make cloth and Portugal fewer to make wine. By specializing and trading, both end up with more of each good. That is absolute advantage at work: the ability of a person, firm or country to produce a good or service more efficiently than others. Adam Smith first described it in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. Arguing against Mercantilism: the race to hoard gold, he said all nations could gain from free trade and specialization. Yet a party can lack an absolute advantage in anything and still gain from trade, through the principle covered in Comparative advantage: why the best at everything still trades.

  <!-- nature-econ-151 -->

- **Comparative advantage: why the best at everything still trades**

  Even a country that is better at producing everything gains by trading. That is the principle of comparative advantage, and it holds for people and firms as well as countries. Gains are greatest when each party specializes in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and trades for the rest. This differs from absolute advantage, which is about being more productive overall. David Ricardo developed the classical theory in 1817, using the example of Portugal and England producing wine and cloth. He wrote amid the debate over Britain's 1815 Corn Laws, which taxed imported grain to protect landowners. In 1930 Gottfried Haberler restated the idea in terms of opportunity cost, measuring a good's value in forgone units of another good. The principle describes what specialization and trade would bring, not a strict prediction of behavior. Critics such as James K. Galbraith argue that countries locked into agriculture stay poor, because farming depends on land, a finite resource. Others dispute that comparative advantage justifies free trade, pointing to strategic trade policy and global value chains.

  <!-- nature-econ-106 -->

- **The marginal rate of transformation: the cost of switching output**

  The marginal rate of transformation is the slope of the production-possibility frontier. It measures how much of one good must be given up to make one more unit of another. It is also called the marginal opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other. If the slope at a point is 2, making one more packet of butter means giving up 2 guns. The rate also marks the efficient ideal described in Pareto efficiency: when no one can gain without someone losing, reached when it equals every consumer's marginal rate of substitution.

  <!-- nature-econ-144 -->

- **The Marxist case against marginalism**

  Marxist economists rejected marginalism. They held to the labor theory of value and argued that prices cannot be explained by individual preferences alone. Ernest Mandel argued that marginalism ignored production and explained, at best, short-term price swings rather than stable long-run prices. Maurice Dobb pointed to money: marginalist prices depend on the distribution of income, since people's ability to express preferences depends on their spending power. Oskar Lange and Michał Kalecki, in the Marxian tradition, tried to combine it with marginalism and neoclassical economics. Marxist and mainstream economists still disagree over whether marginal utility or labor explains value.

  <!-- nature-econ-132 -->

- **Implicit costs: the income you quietly give up**

  A firm sits on land it bought for $50 a century ago. The land could now rent for $10,000 a month. The $10,000 is a real cost of staying put; the $50 should be ignored. That forgone rent is an implicit cost: the opportunity cost of using something you already own. It is the opposite of an explicit cost, which is paid directly, and it also covers income given up by choosing not to work. Implicit costs make up the gap between Economic profit: better than the alternatives? and accounting profit, so the first is never more than the second.

  <!-- nature-econ-124 -->

- **Economic cost: counting what you pass up**

  An accountant and an economist can look at the same decision and see different costs. Economic cost is the total value of everything given up for a course of action, including the opportunities passed over. Counting opportunity cost is what separates it from accounting cost. Economists use it to compare how wise one course of action is against another. Some costs change with output, while others come from assets that do not vary with production. The extra cost of producing one more unit gets its own entry, Marginal cost: the price of one more unit.

  <!-- nature-econ-114 -->

- **Sunk costs: what is spent is spent**

  A company plans a factory expected to cost $100 million and yield $120 million. After $30 million is spent, the value projection falls to $65 million. Should it finish? Finishing would cost $70 million more to get $65 million, so it should walk away. If the projection had fallen only to $75 million, continuing would be rational. In both cases the $30 million already spent plays no part. It is a sunk cost: money, time or effort already spent that cannot be recovered. It contrasts with prospective costs, future costs that can still be avoided by acting. Standard economic theory holds that only future costs matter to a rational decision, a rule called the bygones principle or marginal principle. Everyday life is less disciplined. People often let past spending, for example on repairing a car or a house, shape their future decisions.

  <!-- nature-econ-148 -->

- **Fixed and variable costs: what changes with output**

  Rent, salaries and utility bills arrive whatever a firm produces. Such costs are fixed: they do not change with output. Raw materials, delivery and production supplies are variable, rising and falling with output. In the short run, a firm's whole cost bill equals the fixed part plus the variable part. The line between the two depends on time. Over a few months most costs are fixed, but over 10 years most become variable, as workers and machines can be changed.

  <!-- nature-econ-135 -->

- **Economic profit: better than the alternatives?**

  A new business can show $10,000 of accounting profit and still have an economic profit of −$30,000. The gap is opportunity cost. Economic profit is revenue minus all costs, including opportunity costs, whereas accounting profit counts only the measurable costs of running a business. When economic profit is zero, revenue covers every explicit and implicit cost, and there is no reason to move resources elsewhere. That break-even point is Normal profit: just enough to stay in business. So economic profit does not show whether a decision makes money. It shows whether the decision is wiser than the alternatives.

  <!-- nature-econ-097 -->

- **The cost-of-production theory of value: price as the sum of costs**

  Add up the wages, profit and rent that went into a good, Adam Smith said, and you have its natural price. That is the cost-of-production theory of value: a thing's price is set by the full cost of the resources used to make it. The costs can include any factor of production, such as labor, capital or land, plus taxes. Smith, its best-known proponent, held that market prices can stray from the natural price in the short term. The theory works best when expanding all inputs expands output in proportion, and when only one factor of production is not itself produced.

  <!-- nature-econ-136 -->

- **The sunk cost fallacy: throwing good money after bad**

  Managers told they had made an earlier poor investment put in an average of $12.97 million more. Those told someone else had made it put in $9.43 million. The difference is the sunk cost fallacy: the tendency to keep going with something because of what has already been invested, even when stopping would be better. It is "throwing good money after bad" instead of "cutting one's losses." Managers of many US utility companies were found overly reluctant to end economically unviable nuclear plant projects. Behavioral economists link the fallacy to the way choices are framed, overoptimism, a sense of personal responsibility and the wish not to appear wasteful.

  <!-- nature-econ-149 -->

- **Inferior goods: buying less as income rises**

  Potatoes behave as an inferior good in the Andes but are a high-prestige food in Bangladesh. An inferior good is one that people buy less of as their income rises; normal goods are the opposite. Examples include subcompact economy cars, public transit, payday lending, second-hand clothes and cheap food. The label reflects affordability, not quality, and the same good can be normal for one group and inferior for another.

  <!-- nature-econ-126 -->

- **The income effect: richer or poorer, you buy differently**

  When a good gets cheaper, its buyers become a little richer. The income effect is the change in how much of a good people buy when their real income, or purchasing power, changes. With prices fixed, a change in income shifts the budget line in parallel: outward when income rises, inward when it falls. People buy more of a normal good as income rises and less of an inferior good. So a price cut lets the consumer buy more of that good or of others, depending on which kind it is. Together with the substitution effect, the income effect makes up the full effect of a price change.

  <!-- nature-econ-111 -->

- **Giffen goods: when a higher price means buying more**

  A Giffen good breaks the usual rule of buying: it is a rare kind of inferior good that people buy more of when its price rises. It must take up so much of a person's spending that a price rise makes them poorer and pushes them to buy even more of it. The idea is named after Sir Robert Giffen. The classic story has Irish families in the Great Famine buying more potatoes as prices rose, cutting back on meat and vegetables. Yet potatoes were not in fact Giffen goods then. Economists disagree on whether Giffen goods exist in real markets.

  <!-- nature-econ-389 -->

- **The Slutsky equation: splitting a price change in two**

  The Slutsky equation splits the change in demand caused by a price change into a substitution effect and an income effect. It links ordinary (Marshallian) demand to compensated (Hicksian) demand, which holds utility fixed. The substitution effect is always negative, because indifference curves slope downward. The sign of the income effect depends on the good. The substitution effect cannot be seen directly, but it can be calculated from the two observable terms. The equation also explains Giffen goods. There a strong income effect outweighs the substitution effect, and the usual rule that higher prices cut buying fails.

  <!-- nature-econ-145 -->

### Markets, prices and surplus

A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information, and a price is the sum both sides will accept. On one side stands demand, the quantity people are willing and able to buy at various prices. On the other stands supply, the amount sellers are willing and able to offer. The basic model of supply and demand says the price moves until those two amounts match, a balance economists call equilibrium. This chapter follows that model from the law of demand to elasticity, rivalry among sellers and the free market.

- **Markets: where buyers meet sellers**

  Markets range from one building's food market to a city's housing market, a whole country, or worldwide trades such as diamonds. A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information. Each exchange, with or without money, is called a transaction. Most markets rely on sellers swapping goods or labor for buyers' money rather than on barter. A market can arise more or less on its own or be built on purpose. Economists see it as a coordinating mechanism: it uses prices to pass information among firms, households and individuals, and that use of prices is its defining feature. By letting tradeable things be valued and priced, markets spread resources around a society. Some markets are even created by regulation to tackle side effects such as pollution, for example markets in pollution permits. Markets can also go wrong. When a market's equilibrium is not efficient, economists say a market failure has occurred, though government fixes can fail too. A seller or buyer with the power to sway prices (Market power: the ability to set your own price) can distort them, which lowers welfare and efficiency.

  <!-- nature-econ-342 -->

- **Price: where buyers and sellers agree**

  In April 2020 the price of West Texas Intermediate crude oil for May delivery turned negative for the first time, at -$37.63 a barrel. That strange day tests the definition of a price. A price is the amount of money buyers are willing and able to pay for a good or service, and that sellers are willing to accept. Prices are shaped by production costs, by supply and by demand. A single seller may set them, or market conditions may impose them. Price theory says that in a market left free, the price settles where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded. Price and cost are different things. Price is what the buyer pays, while cost of production is the seller's own spending on making the product. Milton Friedman named five functions of prices, among them passing on information, giving incentives to produce what is valued, and rationing fixed supplies among consumers. Prices also posed an old puzzle. Adam Smith's diamond–water paradox asks why diamonds cost more than water, though water is essential to life and diamonds are mere ornament. Carl Menger's theory of marginal utility was offered as one answer.

  <!-- nature-econ-356 -->

- **Willingness to pay: the most you would hand over**

  People will pay more for the same soft drink at a luxury resort than at a beach bar or a local shop. Willingness to pay is the highest price at which a person will definitely buy one unit of something, and as the soft drink shows, it depends on context. It matches the standard economic idea of a consumer's reservation price, though some researchers treat it as a range. The idea has a long public history. Jules Dupuit argued that a bridge, road or canal is worth the sum of what its users would pay. Adding up their willingness to pay, he said, measures its social benefit. Today, Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses does the same, turning hard-to-price impacts into money, though the amounts are often hard to estimate. For nature, survey methods such as Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey simply ask people what they would pay for an ecosystem or one of its services. A related measure, The value of a statistical life, estimates how much people would pay to lower their risk of dying, and is used to cost deaths from air pollution. One wrinkle runs through all of this. People's maximum willingness to pay for an object is typically lower than the least they would accept to give it up once they own it.

  <!-- nature-econ-344 -->

- **Demand: wanting something and being able to pay**

  Demand is not the same as desire. In economics it means both wanting something and being able to pay for it. Demand is the quantity of a good that people are willing and able to buy at various prices over a given period. It is a flow, measured per unit of time, not a single purchase. The most important influence is the good's own price. Normally, the lower the price, the more people buy. Demand also depends on the prices of complements and substitutes, income, tastes, expectations, population size, climate and government policy. Expectations matter more than they might seem. If consumers expect a price rise, they buy more now to avoid paying more later. Goods with no substitutes, such as insulin, have nearly perfectly inelastic demand: price barely changes how much is bought. Not everyone accepts demand as the goal. E. F. Schumacher, who named natural capital challenged the idea that meeting demand is the purpose of economic activity, separating wise demands for genuine needs from unwise ones.

  <!-- nature-econ-369 -->

- **Supply: what sellers will offer**

  Farmers, factories and workers looking for jobs all answer the same question: how much will they offer at a given price? Supply is the amount of something that producers, workers or other sellers are willing and able to offer for sale. It is usually drawn as a supply curve, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal, for one seller or a whole market. Supply depends on the good's own price, the prices of related goods, production costs, technology and sellers' expectations. These work in two different ways. A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the curve. A change in anything else shifts the whole curve, as when a costlier ingredient shifts it left. Behind the curve sits cost. A firm's short-run supply curve traces its extra cost per unit (Marginal cost: the price of one more unit) above the point where it would shut down. The market supply curve adds up what all firms would supply at each price. Where there are no externalities, the curve shows the social cost of each extra unit. It has limits, too. A supply curve exists only under Perfect competition: the textbook ideal market. A lone seller has none, because it picks price and quantity together.

  <!-- nature-econ-412 -->

- **Supply and demand: the model behind prices**

  In the fourteenth century the scholar Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that when desire for goods rises while availability falls, the price rises. Modern economics made that insight its theoretical foundation: the model of supply and demand. It explains how a market sets prices. The price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer, and the equilibrium is the price and quantity where the two curves cross. Each curve has a logic. Consumers buy another unit as long as its value to them is more than its price, so the buyers' curve slopes downward. When many small firms compete, supply follows the extra cost of each unit: firms produce more as long as that cost is below the market price. Augustin Cournot first drew the buyers' curve in 1838, Fleeming Jenkin added the sellers' curve in 1870, and Alfred Marshall popularized both in 1890. The model reaches beyond goods. Workers supply labor, businesses demand it, and the equilibrium price is the wage rate. Where a single seller or buyer can sway prices, other models fit better. Critics question the model itself. Sraffa doubted the consistency of supply curves drawn for a single market. Post-Keynesians argue it fails to explain prices that firms set by adding a mark-up to their costs.

  <!-- nature-econ-360 -->

- **Equilibrium: when the market stops moving**

  Economists borrowed equilibrium from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes. Economic equilibrium is a state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so prices and quantities stop changing. In a market equilibrium, rivalry among sellers sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce. That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes. Pull the price away and forces push it back. A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down. A price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up. When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium moves. Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behavior is consistent, no agent wants to change its behavior, and the outcome comes from a stable dynamic process. Balance is not the same as good. Paul Samuelson and others warn that a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve. During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved, because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford. Some economists also challenge the classical view that markets left alone always clear, pointing to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.

  <!-- nature-econ-335 -->

- **The law of demand: higher price, fewer buyers**

  Charles Davenant stated it in 1699: all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls. This is the law of demand. It says only which way quantity moves when price changes, not by how much. Alfred Marshall drew it as a graph and joined it with supply in his Principles of Economics in 1890. The graph, covered in The demand curve: buying at every price, puts quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical, and it slopes downward. A price change moves buyers along that curve. Changes in the number of buyers, income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations shift the whole curve. Together with its partner on the sellers' side (The law of supply: higher price, more for sale), the law fixes the equilibrium price and quantity. It has exceptions: Giffen goods, status goods (Veblen goods: when a high price is the point), necessities, and cases where buyers expect prices to keep changing.

  <!-- nature-econ-388 -->

- **Free markets: prices without government steering**

  To classical economists such as Adam Smith, a free market meant one free of privilege, exclusive selling rights and artificial scarcities. Today the term means an economic system without government steering. Prices of goods and services are set by the supply and demand of buyers and sellers. Its supporters contrast it with a regulated market, where government steps into supply and demand through taxes or rules. A free market does not demand rivalry among sellers as such, but it does demand that new sellers be free to enter. Free markets are usually linked with capitalism, but they have also featured in some forms of market socialism. In practice governments usually step in to cut harms such as planet-warming emissions, sometimes by using markets, as in carbon trading. The arguments run both ways. Critics say real free markets drift toward price-fixing and dominant single sellers, and unequal bargaining power, which led to measures such as US antitrust law. Coase, Friedman, von Mises and Hayek replied that markets can absorb or adjust to supposed market failures.

  <!-- nature-econ-378 -->

- **Elasticity: how strongly one thing responds to another**

  If buyers' elasticity for a good is −2, a 10% price rise cuts the quantity they buy by 20%. Elasticity measures how much one economic variable responds to a change in another: the percentage change in one divided by the percentage change in the other. The main kinds track how buying responds to price and to income, how selling responds to price, and how buying one good responds to another good's price. Elasticity helps explain who bears indirect taxes and how welfare is split among consumers, producers and government. It also guides pricing. Seller revenue is highest at unit elasticity, so a firm should raise its price when demand is inelastic and cut it when demand is elastic. Time is arguably the biggest influence on supply: the longer suppliers have to respond, the more supply changes. Goods made from scarce resources from nature, such as gasoline, respond poorly, so rising demand drives their prices up. Alfred Marshall first described price elasticity informally in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

  <!-- nature-econ-374 -->

- **The demand curve: buying at every price**

  A demand curve is a graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price. Price goes on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal. It can show one consumer's demand or, added up across everyone, a whole market's. It normally slopes down because of the law of demand. Exceptions include status goods (Veblen goods: when a high price is the point), Giffen goods and speculative bubbles. The curve moves in two ways. A price change moves buyers along it, while a change in anything else, such as income, related goods' prices, population or expectations, shifts the whole curve. When incomes rise, demand for normal goods shifts out and demand for inferior goods shifts in. If hamburgers get dearer, demand for chicken, a substitute, shifts out, while demand for ketchup, a complement, shifts in. One practical snag remains. Demand curves are estimated statistically from past data, yet only one point on the curve can be observed at any one time.

  <!-- nature-econ-371 -->

- **Competition: the contest for customers**

  In 1776 Adam Smith described competition as steering productive resources to their most valued uses and encouraging efficiency. Competition is the contest among firms for customers and limited resources, fought with price, product, promotion and place. It arises from scarcity: there is never enough to satisfy every human want. Classical economists held that it pushes firms to develop new products and technologies, giving consumers more choice and better goods. More choice usually means lower prices than when one or a few firms dominate. How much competition a market has depends on the number of firms, barriers to entry, information and access to resources. Share and foreign-exchange markets are usually seen as close to perfect, while real estate is a very imperfect market. For a few goods, having many firms is itself inefficient, because competition duplicates costs that do not vary with output; Natural monopoly: when one supplier is cheapest covers these cases. Economists still debate how relevant the textbook ideal of Perfect competition: the textbook ideal market is to real markets, and whether it should serve as the benchmark.

  <!-- nature-econ-363 -->

- **Price elasticity of demand: how buyers react to price**

  Suppose a price rises $5 from $100 and sales fall 20 tons from 200 tons. Quantity drops 10% while price rises 5%, so the price elasticity of demand is −2. That number measures how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price. Demand is inelastic when the elasticity is below one in absolute value and elastic when it is above one. Close substitutes make demand more elastic. Necessities such as insulin, and broad categories such as food in general, are less elastic. Elasticity also grows with time: after a lasting fuel price rise, more people switch to carpooling or public transport. For inelastic goods a price rise increases revenue, while for elastic goods it lowers revenue. Revenue peaks where elasticity is exactly one. The measure also predicts who bears a tax. With perfectly inelastic demand consumers pay all of it; with perfectly elastic demand firms pay all of it. Alfred Marshall is credited with defining it in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

  <!-- nature-econ-358 -->

- **The invisible hand: self-interest serving the public**

  Adam Smith used the phrase just once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and once in The Wealth of Nations. He wrote of "an" invisible hand, never "the." It became his most famous metaphor: the way free markets can lead self-interested people to benefit the public without meaning to. In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about free trade. Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularized the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve. The idea is a central justification for the hands-off thinking behind neoclassical economics. Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there. With externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution, which is why environmental economics deals largely with market failures. Stiglitz, Piketty and others argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good. Scholars also disagree about what Smith himself meant.

  <!-- nature-econ-387 -->

- **Income elasticity of demand: what richer people buy**

  As people grow richer, their spending on food grows more slowly than their income, an observation called Engel's law. Income elasticity of demand measures this kind of response: how strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income. It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income. If a 10% rise in income lifts demand by 20%, it is 2.0. Normal goods score positive and inferior goods negative; below 1 marks a necessity and above 1 a luxury. Food as a whole lies between zero and one. Estimates for gasoline in developed economies range from 0.66 to 1.26. Elasticities for food and energy tend to fall as incomes rise: for cereals, from 0.62 in Tanzania to 0.05 in the United States. As economies get richer, spending shifts toward services, which need fewer commodities to produce. The pattern matters for nature. Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.

  <!-- nature-econ-385 -->

- **Comparative statics: before-and-after snapshots**

  Comparative statics compares two economic outcomes, one before and one after a change in some outside factor, once the economy has settled into its new equilibrium. It compares the two snapshots but does not study the path between them. Economists use it to study changes in supply and demand in one market, and changes in government taxing, spending or money policy for a whole economy. The method had been drawn in graphs since at least the 1870s; John R. Hicks (1939) and Paul A. Samuelson (1947) formalized it. Results usually come from a linear approximation of the equilibrium equations, which assumes the equilibrium is stable. Because of that approximation, they hold only for very small changes. For models of steady growth, the counterpart is comparative dynamics. Two mathematical results support the method. The envelope theorem describes how the value of an optimal solution changes with a parameter. Claude Berge's 1963 maximum theorem describes when the optimal solution varies continuously with the parameters.

  <!-- nature-econ-463 -->

- **Price signals: what a price tells people**

  When a product runs short and its price rises, people pay more attention to it and produce more of it.
