Dense canopies typically score about 0.3 to 0.8, while bare soils give around 0.1 to 0.2. Researchers studying Great Plains rangeland developed it to correct for the changing sun angle, and its earliest reported use was in 1973 by Rouse and colleagues. Farmers use it to assess crop health, spot stress before it is visible and predict yields. Falling NDVI can signal drought, deforestation or degraded land. It has limits: it keeps only part of the original spectral information and is affected by the atmosphere, sensors, soil and snow.

  <!-- nature-es-069 -->

- **Spatial analysis: asking where**

  As far back as at least 1,400 BC, Egyptian surveyors measured taxable plots with ropes, an early root of spatial analysis. Today it is the set of formal techniques that study things through their location, shape and geographic arrangement, drawing especially on spatial statistics. In a narrower sense it is geospatial analysis, usually done with GIS software. It was developed for ecology, geology and epidemiology and now reaches forests and water, disaster risk and climate adaptation. Basic operations include stacking maps and buffering, which marks areas within a set distance of features such as roads or rivers. Gravity models estimate flows of people, materials or information between places. Its most fundamental problem is defining where the things being studied are located. Another trap is the ecological fallacy: drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregated data.

  <!-- nature-es-073 -->

- **Species distribution models: predicting where life lives**

  Where will a species live when the climate shifts? Species distribution modeling uses ecological models and environmental data, most often climate, to predict where a species lives across space and time. It can project a future range under climate change, a past range, or where an invasive species might spread. Its main use is conservation: finding highly suitable habitat to prioritize sites for protection and restoration. It also helps identify climate refugia, places likely to stay suitable as the climate changes. Correlative models fit a species' observed range to environmental conditions. They are quick but describe only where the species actually lives now, and they extrapolate poorly. Mechanistic models use its physiology to work out where it could survive, handling shifting ranges better but needing much data. MaxEnt, the most widely used method, works from presence-only records even when few exist. Remote sensing and GIS have greatly expanded the data available.

  <!-- nature-es-076 -->

- **Land change models: forecasting the face of the Earth**

  In 2011 a study in western Mexico ran two outwardly similar land change models and got considerably different results. That is a fair warning about a powerful tool. Land change models describe, project and explain how land cover and the human uses of land change over time. They help explain how people have changed Earth's surface and will change it, guiding decisions from a single plot to whole regions. The method applies landscape ecology and is a key part of land change science. Approaches include machine-learning models trained on past land cover, cellular models that compare neighboring areas, economic supply-and-demand models, agent-based models and hybrids. The model should fit the goal: agents for questions about policy and actors, machine learning and cellular models for spotting patterns. Practitioners use them to explore the effects of policies on water, food, urbanization and more. All carry irreducible uncertainty, and the further ahead they project, the more uncertain they become.

  <!-- nature-es-066 -->

- **Active and passive sensors**

  Remote sensing instruments come in two classes. Passive sensors record energy an object reflects or emits, most often reflected sunlight; cameras, radiometers and spectrometers are common examples. Active sensors send out their own energy and measure what comes back. Radar and Lidar: measuring the world with laser light are active systems that time a pulse's return to find the distance to a target.

  <!-- nature-es-058 -->

- **Lidar: measuring the world with laser light**

  A 2024 lidar study found that England has 390,000 km of hedgerows. Lidar measures distance by shining a laser at a surface and timing how long the reflected light takes to return. As an active sensor, it supplies its own light and uses the speed of light to turn return time into distance. From an aircraft it can map terrain at 30-centimeter resolution or better. In forests it measures tree heights and crown widths and estimates canopy volume, biomass and carbon density.

  <!-- nature-es-068 -->

- **False-color images: seeing the invisible**

  A false-color composite is an image in which wavelengths are shown in colors other than their true ones, to reveal patterns the eye cannot normally see. It is made by changing which parts of the spectrum are displayed as red, green and blue. Pseudocolor works differently: it maps a single band onto a new color scale, a trick that also works for temperature or elevation.

  <!-- nature-es-060 -->

- **Raster and vector: two ways to store a map**

  Mapped things are usually treated either as discrete objects, like a house or road, or as continuous fields, like rainfall or population density. A GIS traditionally stores them in two ways: as raster images made of cells, or as vector points, lines and polygons. It can convert between them, for example by tracing lines around same-class cells of a satellite image to make vector shapes. Point clouds are a newer hybrid that pair three-dimensional points with color values.

  <!-- nature-es-052 -->

- **How sharp is a satellite's eye?**

  Landsat records seven bands of light; the Hyperion sensor resolves 220, from 0.4 to 2.5 μm. That difference is spectral resolution, one of four ways to describe remote sensing data. Spatial resolution is pixel size, typically squares from 1 to 1,000 metres on a side. Radiometric resolution is how many intensity levels a sensor can tell apart, typically 8 to 14 bits, or 256 up to 16,384 shades per band. Temporal resolution is how often a satellite or plane passes over, which matters for tracking deforestation over time.

  <!-- nature-es-059 -->

- **Map overlay: stacking maps to find answers**

  Map overlay combines several spatial datasets of the same area into a new one, like stacking maps of one region on top of each other. Overlays work like Venn diagrams: a union keeps everything from both inputs, while an intersect keeps only where they overlap. With rasters, overlay uses map algebra, a function that combines each layer's cell values and can weight some inputs more than others. In 1983 Dana Tomlin coined 'cartographic modeling' for producing and analyzing several thematic layers of the same area.

  <!-- nature-es-053 -->

- **Choosing the best site with GIS**

  Finding the best place to restore a habitat means juggling many criteria at once. GIS multi-criteria decision analysis compares alternative places against several criteria together. Decision rules combine the criteria so the alternatives can be ranked or prioritized. The method may cut the cost and time of finding potential restoration sites.

  <!-- nature-es-055 -->

- **Spatial interpolation: filling in the gaps between samples**

  Measurements taken at one place closely resemble those taken nearby. That tendency justifies spatial interpolation: building a continuous surface, usually a raster, by predicting values between measured sample points. Geostatistics, the branch of statistics for continuous spatial data, models these correlations to predict values at unmeasured places. Methods include inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines, Thiessen polygons and trend surfaces.

  <!-- nature-es-054 -->

- **Bayesian networks: reasoning backward from evidence**

  A doctor sees symptoms and must work back to the likely disease. A Bayesian network does this kind of reasoning. It is a probability model that shows a set of variables and how they depend on each other, drawn as a diagram of arrows with no loops. Each node is a variable and each arrow a direct dependency. The network applies Bayes' theorem automatically, updating beliefs about unobserved variables as evidence comes in. Ecologists have used such networks to explore where ecological regime shifts are likely.

  <!-- nature-es-062 -->

- **Causal loop diagrams: drawing the feedback**

  More buyers of a product mean stronger word of mouth, which brings more buyers. A causal loop diagram maps loops like that: a simple drawing of a system's parts and how they affect each other. Reinforcing loops amplify change, while counteracting loops push back. Double slashes on an arrow mark a significant delay between cause and effect. The diagram supports qualitative analysis. For numbers, it is turned into a stock and flow diagram and simulated on a computer.

  <!-- nature-es-078 -->

- **Edges and ecotones: life at the borders**

  Where a forest gives way to grassland, a new kind of place appears. An ecotone is the transition zone where two ecological communities meet. It keeps traits of both neighbors and often holds species found in neither. Ecotones can be natural, like a lakeshore, or made by people, like a field cleared from forest. Fencerows, forest-to-marsh transitions and riparian zones along rivers are classic examples. An edge is the part of an ecosystem near its border, where neighboring patches make conditions differ from the interior, often changing which species live there.

  <!-- nature-es-048 -->

- **Patches, corridors and matrix: the parts of a landscape**

  Landscape ecologists read land as a mosaic. A patch is a fairly uniform area that differs from its surroundings. Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides. The matrix is the well-connected background system that holds them. Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is: a forest with fewer open gaps is better connected. Patches change and fluctuate over time, a process called patch dynamics.

  <!-- nature-es-047 -->

- **Fragmentation: when the landscape breaks apart**

  Landscape fragmentation is the breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller, separate pieces. Repeated random clearing, natural or human, can splinter continuous cover into isolated patches. The change is not gradual. Once cleared area passes a critical level, a landscape flips from connected to disconnected. Metapopulation models, which treat scattered groups as linked populations, gave conservation biologists a tool to judge whether populations can survive this.

  <!-- nature-es-049 -->

- **Lotka and Volterra: the dance of predator and prey**

  After fishing in the Adriatic was cut back during the First World War, fish and shark numbers swung in puzzling ways. Vito Volterra built a model to explain them in 1926, a year after Alfred Lotka developed the same idea. The Lotka–Volterra model is a pair of equations, one for prey and one for its predator, describing how their numbers rise and fall together. Its parameters are the prey's growth rate, the predation rate, the predator's assimilation efficiency and the predator's death rate. It is not unchallenged: supporters of the rival Arditi–Ginzburg model argue the field data reject it.

  <!-- nature-es-064 -->

- **i-Tree: putting a value on every tree**

  How much is a city's tree canopy worth? A suite of US Forest Service software called i-Tree tries to answer. It measures and values the services trees provide in cities and the countryside. It quantifies services such as pollution removal, carbon storage and rainwater runoff avoided. Some tools work up from ground inventories of trees, others down from remote sensing data. Urban foresters use it to turn a forest's structure into ecosystem services and economic value. It began in 2002 as a sample survey that simulated a full urban tree inventory.

  <!-- nature-es-065 -->

- **Participatory GIS: maps made by the people who live there**

  Participatory GIS puts mapping tools in the hands of local people, so their own knowledge shapes planning decisions. It combines sketch maps, 3D models, aerial photos, satellite images and GPS to turn what people know about places into maps for discussion. Its aim is to empower marginalized groups and protect traditional knowledge by leaving control of sensitive maps with their makers. Uses range from neighborhood planning to managing forests, water and wildlife. Practitioners still debate top-down against bottom-up approaches, and critics ask who really gets access to the technology.

  <!-- nature-es-070 -->

- **InVEST: free software for mapping nature's value**

  InVEST is used in more than 185 countries to map valuable ecological resources and weigh trade-offs in land and water use. The name stands for Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs. It is free, open-source software from the Natural Capital Project for mapping and valuing ecosystem services, with 20+ models covering land, freshwater, marine, coastal and urban settings. Users steer investments toward both conservation and development. Alongside the ARIES project and the Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, it is one of several tools that help businesses value services. Its developer works with governments, banks, companies and communities to bring nature's values into decisions.

  <!-- nature-es-080 -->

- **The modifiable areal unit problem: same data, different answers**

  Draw a population density map using state boundaries, then redraw it using county boundaries, and the results differ radically. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, a source of statistical bias. Results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions. Totals, rates and densities all depend on both the shape and the size of the units chosen.

  <!-- nature-es-075 -->

- **Spatial autocorrelation: near things are related**

  Values at nearby locations tend to be related, positively or negatively. This spatial autocorrelation breaks the independence that standard statistics assume. Regressions that ignore it can give unstable estimates and unreliable significance tests. Spatial regression models capture it, and it can also be read as useful information rather than a nuisance. Classic measures include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

  <!-- nature-es-074 -->

- **Testing a land change model against reality**

  A model can look brilliant by cheating. Calibrating it with data from after its first time period can make it seem far more accurate than it really is. Land change model validation guards against this by comparing a model's processes or predicted maps with what really happened. Pattern validation often uses three maps: the real maps at two dates and the simulated second map. Pixels are sorted into hits, misses, false alarms and similar classes. The Figure of Merit turns these into one percentage for the overlap between real and simulated change.

  <!-- nature-es-067 -->

- **Runoff curve numbers: how much rain runs off**

  A paved parking lot has a curve number of 98; open space in good condition on sandy soil has 39. The runoff curve number is an empirical figure used in hydrology to predict how much rainfall runs straight off the land rather than soaking in. It ranges from 30 to 100; higher numbers mean more runoff. It depends on the soil and on how land is used and treated. Soils fall into four groups, from A, deep sands that soak water up fast, to D, clays and shallow soils that absorb it very slowly.

  <!-- nature-es-071 -->

## Valuing nature

Water keeps people alive, yet diamonds cost far more. That old puzzle opens this part of the course, which asks what it means to say nature has value. Economists separate a thing's usefulness from the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Philosophers ask a different question: is nature good only as a means to human ends, or good in itself? Between the belief that humans are the most important beings on the planet and the view that every living thing has equal worth lies a wide range of positions, and societies turn out to value the non-human world in several ways at once.

### Kinds of value

Some things are very useful and trade for little; others are nearly useless and trade for a fortune. This chapter starts with that gap between usefulness and exchange. It then turns to philosophy, which separates what is good as a means from what is good as an end in itself. From there come rival views of humanity's place: one centered on people, one on all living things, one on nature as a whole, and one that trusts technology to solve environmental problems. Along the way the chapter sorts the ways societies see importance in the non-human world, as useful, as valuable in itself, and through relationships with it.

- **Use value: what a thing is good for**

  Gold can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor. Each of those is a use, and together they make up its use value: the features that let a thing satisfy a human want or need. The idea comes from classical and Marxist economics. Adam Smith noticed that use and price can part company. Diamonds have little use but fetch a great deal in trade, while water is very useful yet cheap. For Marx, every commodity, a good made to be traded, is both a use value and an Exchange value: what a thing trades for: the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Not every useful thing can become a commodity. It must be tradable, its ownership must pass securely from one person to another, and there must be real demand. Later, marginalist economics traced use value to the Marginal utility: the value of the next piece consumers find in a good. Critics of turning nature into commodities still draw on Marx's double idea.

  <!-- nature-val-058 -->

- **Exchange value: what a thing trades for**

  Marx gave every commodity four attributes: use value, exchange value, value and price. Exchange value is the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods. It is not the same as the money price, which only roughly matches it. Behind both, Marx held, lies value itself, set by the socially necessary labor time needed to produce a good: the work it typically takes. Modern neoclassical economics, the mainstream school, no longer treats exchange value as a separate idea. For it, exchange value is simply the market price, the subject of Price: where buyers and sellers agree. Before anything can be traded at all, certain conditions must hold: secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand. Critics of turning nature into commodities see a danger here. Expressing every kind of worth through a single exchange value puts very different things on one scale.

  <!-- nature-val-068 -->

- **Environmental philosophy: do rivers have rights?**

  Do rivers have rights? Questions like that belong to environmental philosophy, the branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it. It emerged as a branch of its own in the 1970s. Its early figures include Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Richard Routley, Arne Næss and J. Baird Callicott. A major debate of the 1970s and 80s asked whether nature has value in itself or only as a means to human ends. On one side stood nature-centered views, including Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness; on the other stood human-centered ones. Another debate asks whether wilderness really exists, or whether, as William Cronon suggested, it is a cultural construct with colonial overtones. Today the field also takes up environmental activism, Environmental justice: who lives next to the dump?, climate change and the using up of finite resources.

  <!-- nature-val-065 -->

- **The paradox of value: why diamonds outprice water**

  Nothing is more useful than water, Adam Smith observed, yet it will buy scarcely anything. Diamonds are far less useful and cost much more. This is the paradox of value, also called the diamond–water paradox. Smith is its classic presenter, though the puzzle appears as early as Plato's Euthydemus. Smith split 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', the ideas now called use value and exchange value. The most useful things, he noted, often have little exchange value. Supporters of the labor theory of value had one answer: price reflects the toil of acquiring a good. Marginalists had another. They separated total utility from Marginal utility: the value of the next piece. Water is so plentiful that one more unit adds little, while scarce diamonds add more. Böhm-Bawerk's farmer with five sacks of grain shows the logic: he values the last sack by its least important use, feeding pigeons. Change the setting and the paradox flips. A person dying of thirst in a desert would pay more for water than for diamonds.

  <!-- nature-val-070 -->

- **Good as a means, or good in itself**

  A hammer and a washing machine are valuable for what they do. Their value is instrumental: they are good as a means to an end. Happiness and pleasure are different. They are usually thought valuable for their own sake, the kind of worth explored in Intrinsic value: worth for its own sake. The sociologist Max Weber coined the terms. Not everyone accepts the split. John Dewey thought belief in value for its own sake was a mistake, and treated instrumental judgment as the only way to coordinate behavior well. J. Fagg Foster treated sustainability as a synonym for instrumental value, since success must never be short term.

  <!-- nature-val-057 -->

- **Anthropocentrism: putting humans at the center**

  In 1906 J. Howard Moore argued that Darwin's theory of common descent had 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism. The idea has proved hard to kill. Anthropocentrism is the belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet. In this view humans stand apart from nature and above it, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use. Nature's value becomes instrumental, a means to human ends. Environmental ethics: arguments for protecting nature often treats this outlook as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere, the living envelope of the planet. Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism, the male-centered outlook, in feminist theory. Its defenders answer that the real problem is only shallow anthropocentrism. A sound long-term view, they argue, would keep the environment suitable for humans. William Grey called for an enriched idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views. Environmental philosophers still dispute who is right: whether human-centered thinking itself causes ecological harm, or only its shallow, short-term form. Religion enters the argument too. The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify the view, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation. Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks instead of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.

  <!-- nature-val-059 -->

- **Intrinsic value: worth for its own sake**

  The Zoological Society of London warns that insect decline means a double loss. Species lose their instrumental value, and their intrinsic value as well. Intrinsic value, in ethics, is the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else. Instrumental value, by contrast, comes from a thing's relation to some other valued thing. Every major ethical theory treats something as intrinsically valuable. Virtue ethics points to flourishing; consequentialists, who judge acts by their results, point to pleasure. Some conservation biologists argue that nature has intrinsic value independent of its usefulness to people. Arne Næss's Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness, coined in 1972, gave all non-human beings this kind of worth. Whether absolute intrinsic value exists at all is debated. John Dewey accepted only value relative to a situation.

  <!-- nature-val-056 -->

- **Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness**

  Rachel Carson's Silent Spring: the book that turned the US against DDT, published in 1962, is often seen as the start of the movement. The Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss gave it a name, coining 'deep ecology' in 1972 and first using the phrase in a 1973 article. Deep ecology holds that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match. Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish. Næss set it against 'shallow ecology', which he criticized as utilitarian, human-centered and consumer-oriented. Deep ecology rejects nature as a resource to exploit. The materialist outlook, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced. Critics push back. Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores excessive consumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic. Others call it Eurocentric or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge. Its ideas also feed arguments for valuing ecosystems outside markets.

  <!-- nature-val-062 -->

- **Ecocentrism: valuing nature as a whole**

  Where anthropocentrism puts humans at the center, ecocentrism puts nature there. It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only, or the greater, bearers of intrinsic value. It values the biotic community, all the living things of a place, as a whole. It aims to keep ecosystems' composition and processes intact. It covers living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone. Aldo Leopold, forester of the land ethic conceived the ethic, and his The land ethic: citizens, not conquerors is central to it. Supporters argue that a human-centered ethic always makes protecting nature depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives protection a firmer basis. Critics reply that it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

  <!-- nature-val-063 -->

- **Biocentrism: equal worth for every living thing**

  The US Endangered Species Act has been described as unusually biocentric, because it puts non-human species first. Biocentrism is the environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things. It sits among close neighbors. Anthropocentrism is centered on humans. Sentientism values only beings that can feel pleasure or pain. Ecocentrism extends value to the whole of nature. Biocentrism rests on four pillars. Humans and other species share Earth's community, and all species depend on one another. Each organism pursues its own good, and humans are not inherently superior. The family includes Albert Schweitzer's 'reverence for life', Peter Singer's animal liberation and Paul W. Taylor's biocentric egalitarianism. Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, rights for animals and environmental protection. Critics call it anti-human, and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.

  <!-- nature-val-060 -->

- **Three ways societies value nature**

  Timber, clean water and air, carbon storage, pollination: these are the familiar ways nature serves people. They are only one of three kinds of value that societies see in the non-human world. The first kind is extrinsic, or instrumental, value: nature's usefulness to people, often called ecosystem services. Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value. That lets them enter impact assessments, Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses studies and national accounts. The second kind is intrinsic value. It holds that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans. The third kind covers meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural ties between people and nature. These are Relational values: ties between people and nature. IPBES: the scientists' voice for biodiversity, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

  <!-- nature-val-066 -->

- **Technocentrism: trusting science to fix nature**

  Not everyone who worries about the environment wants to shrink industry. Technocentrism is a set of values centered on technology. It holds that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science. Technocentrics accept that environmental problems exist, but they do not see cutting industry as the solution. Ecocentrics, by contrast, see themselves as subject to nature. They prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.

  <!-- nature-val-064 -->

- **Social ecology: how people treat nature and each other**

  'The ecological crisis is a social crisis,' Murray Bookchin argued. His 1982 philosophy of social ecology links how humans treat nature to how they treat each other. Practices such as monocropping, growing a single crop over and over, and taking too many fish mirror social tendencies to dominate people. Bookchin defined nature itself as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom. Social ecology calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

  <!-- nature-val-067 -->

- **Rights of nature: writing nature's rights into law**

  In 2008 Ecuador became the first country to put rights of nature in its constitution. Its Article 71 gives nature the right to respect for its existence and for the regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions and evolution. Rights of nature are the legal recognition that nature has rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law. The idea rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did. Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia have adopted such laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.

  <!-- nature-val-061 -->

- **Non-market goods: valuable but never sold**

  Clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests share an awkward trait for economists. They are non-market goods, things that are not bought and sold in markets. Most environmental goods fall into this group. Without prices, putting a value on them is inherently uncertain. That difficulty is one reason the environment is usually left out of measures of wealth. In 1947 S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed a way around it: surveys asking people what such a good is worth to them, the approach later called Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey.

  <!-- nature-val-073 -->

- **Non-use value: caring about what you never use**

  People can value a resource they have never used and never will. Economists call this non-use value. It is often attached to resources from nature, and it stands apart from use value, which comes from using a good directly. Non-use value has several strands. It can include Option value: paying to keep choices open, Bequest value: saving nature for future generations, Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it. All these categories grew from the first of them, introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964. Measuring them is hard. Market prices and other methods that read value from what people buy generally cannot capture it, because nobody is buying anything. Economists instead ask people directly in surveys, such as Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey. Attempts to value ecosystems sort the value of their services into use and non-use categories.

  <!-- nature-val-069 -->

- **Total economic value: adding up nature's worth**

  Most people will never see a tiger in the wild, yet knowing tigers live there is worth something to many of them. Total economic value tries to count that, along with everything else. It is the full value people get from a resource drawn from nature, a heritage site or piece of infrastructure, compared with not having it. In environmental economics it adds up the values an ecosystem provides. It is built in layers. Use value comes first, split into direct and indirect. Direct use covers removable products such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use covers non-removable things such as a sunset or a waterfall. Non-use value comes next. It covers simply knowing that a resource exists, as with those tigers. Two more strands look ahead. One, Option value: paying to keep choices open, is placed on keeping the possibility of using a resource in future, even when that use is unlikely. Another, Bequest value: saving nature for future generations, comes from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Adding the layers gives a single figure. Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses uses a similar approach.

  <!-- nature-val-052 -->

- **Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there**

  A wilderness can be worth money even if nobody ever walks into it. That was the argument of John Krutilla and the value of wilderness, in the essay that introduced the idea of existence value. It is the benefit people get simply from knowing that something exists, whether Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species. Because no direct use is needed, it is a leading example of non-use value. It is usually measured with Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey surveys. The idea has legal force. Since the case Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law. After the The Exxon Valdez spill: putting a price on damage, damages included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.

  <!-- nature-val-054 -->

- **Option value: paying to keep choices open**

  Why fund a rail service or a wildlife refuge that most taxpayers will rarely use? Option value is one answer. It is what people are willing to pay to keep a public facility or service available, even if they are unlikely ever to use it. Policy assessments use it to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services. In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened resources from nature so they might be used in future. Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964. He rested it on three conditions: future need is uncertain, loss would be irreversible or costly, and the thing itself cannot be stored. Later economists proposed refinements such as 'option price' and 'quasi option value', which stresses irreversibility. Option value in finance is a different idea, though both can be read as ways of valuing risk.

  <!-- nature-val-055 -->

- **Bequest value: saving nature for future generations**

  Part of what people value in nature is what they can hand on. Bequest value is the satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Together with existence value, it makes up non-use value. It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service. Attempts to value ecosystems count it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations. In some optimization models, mathematical models that search for the best plan, it goes by another name: the 'salvage value' of the system.

  <!-- nature-val-053 -->

- **Direct and indirect use: taking versus enjoying**

  Catching a fish and watching a waterfall both use nature, but only one takes something away. Direct use value comes from removable products such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use value comes from things like a sunset, where nothing is removed. When ecosystems are valued, indirect use value arrives through the positive externalities ecosystems provide, benefits that reach people without a price. For livestock breeds, direct use is milk or meat. Indirect use includes regulating services such as nutrient cycling, seed dispersal and fire control. Both can often be inferred from behavior, such as trip costs.

  <!-- nature-val-071 -->

- **Relational values: ties between people and nature**

  Some ties to nature are neither about usefulness nor about worth in itself. Relational values arise from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. In one framing of nature's values they sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means. Ignoring them has costs. Western Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild, not just sustain has been criticized for overlooking the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice: a wrong done to people in their capacity as knowers.

  <!-- nature-val-072 -->

### Valuation methods

Nobody sells a forest or a beach, so putting a number on one takes ingenuity. Economists have two broad routes. One reads value from the choices people actually make, such as the time and money they spend reaching a national park, or the price of a house broken down into its features. The other asks people directly in surveys, an approach important enough that a US panel chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow was convened to judge whether it could be trusted. Between them sit cheaper shortcuts, such as borrowing results from earlier studies or pricing what it would cost to replace something.

- **Revealed preference: judging people by their choices**

  Economists have long faced a measurement problem. Utility, the satisfaction behind people's choices, cannot be measured directly. In 1938 Paul Samuelson proposed a way around it: watch what people choose and work backward. This is revealed preference. It assumes that people's preferences show in their purchasing habits. The logic is simple. If someone chooses bundle a when bundle b was also affordable, a is said to be revealed preferred to b. A bundle is just a set of goods, and affordable means within the person's The budget constraint: what your money can buy. Rather than measure utility, economists defined it from observed behavior. The approach contrasts with Stated preference: asking people what they value, which ask people directly, and economists usually trust revealed preferences more. It matters for nature because ecosystem services rarely carry prices. Methods such as Hedonic regression: reading value from house prices and Travel cost analysis: valuing a park by the trip link a service to a market good to estimate Willingness to pay: the most you would hand over. Critics raise two objections. A purchase cannot show which alternatives were given up, and the theory wrongly assumes preferences stay constant over time. Several economists, including Amartya Sen and Stanley Wong, go further. They call the theory tautological, true by definition, or a failed research program.

  <!-- nature-val-094 -->

- **Ecosystem valuation: putting numbers on nature's services**

  In 1997 Robert Costanza and the $33 trillion valuation and colleagues made the first estimate of what the world's ecosystem services are worth: $33 trillion a year. Ecosystem valuation is the process behind numbers like that. It assigns a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides. The aim is practical. Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's flood control and carbon storage helps policy-makers compare policies through Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses. The tools come in two families. Survey methods, such as Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey, ask people what they would pay. Revealed preference methods, such as Hedonic regression: reading value from house prices and Travel cost analysis: valuing a park by the trip, infer it from behavior. The results vary enormously. TEEB found values from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs. Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded. Many are also non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use leaves no less for others, and no one can be kept out. Some programs go on to pay landowners; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests. Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and that the money value of services depends on how income is distributed. Behind this lies a philosophical and ethical dispute over whether nature should be priced at all.

  <!-- nature-val-087 -->

- **Hedonic regression: reading value from house prices**

  How much is a park worth to the people who live beside it? Part of the answer hides in their house prices. Hedonic regression treats a house as a bundle of features, such as bedrooms, lot size and distance from the city center, each with its own price. It breaks the sale price into contributions from each feature, usually with Regression analysis: the workhorse of empirical economics. In environmental work it measures how much a nearby amenity such as a park raises home prices, holding the other features fixed. Hedonic modeling was first published in the 1920s to value farm land, with roots also traced to Court's 1939 study of car prices. Today it is also used in real estate, marketing research and Consumer Price Index calculations. That last use is debated. Some critics argue it can understate US inflation, while studies abroad show that ignoring quality change can misstate inflation too.

  <!-- nature-val-092 -->

- **Willingness to accept: the price of putting up with harm**

  Willingness to accept is the least money a person would take to sell a good, or to put up with a harm such as pollution. It is the counterpart of Willingness to pay: the most you would hand over, the most a buyer would give up to get something or avoid something unwanted. Both are reservation prices, the limits past which a person walks away. A trade's price falls between the buyer's willingness to pay and the seller's willingness to accept, and the gap between them is the Economic surplus: the gains from trading. Formally, it is the payment that leaves a person's utility after an unwanted change equal to their utility before it. Which measure applies depends on property rights. If lakeside residents have a right to a clean lake, what counts is the compensation they would accept for its pollution. It can be estimated with choice experiments or asked directly in Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey surveys.

  <!-- nature-val-089 -->

- **Travel cost analysis: valuing a park by the trip**

  A park may charge no market price, but reaching it costs visitors time and money. Harold Hotelling and the price of running out suggested using that fact in a 1947 letter to the US park service. Travel cost analysis values a place without a market price, such as a park or beach, from what visitors spend to get there. People living farther away spend more to visit and come less often; those nearby visit more and spend less. Analysts group visitors into distance zones and use regression to relate each zone's visit rate to its travel cost. The result builds a The demand curve: buying at every price for the site. The area under that curve gives visitors' willingness to pay, which serves as the site's value in Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses. Trice and Wood refined the method in 1958, and Clawson in 1959.

  <!-- nature-val-088 -->

- **The weak axiom: a rule for consistent choice**

  Revealed preference needs a rule for what counts as consistent choice. The weak axiom of revealed preference supplies the basic one. If a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable. Stronger rules build on it. The strong axiom, SARP, adds that choices cannot be indirectly revealed preferred to each other. That preserves transitivity. Anyone who prefers a to b and b to c then prefers c least. The generalized axiom, GARP, extends SARP to cases where several bundles give equal utility, and rules out preference cycles.

  <!-- nature-val-095 -->

- **Afriat's theorem: from choices to a utility function**

  In 1967 Sydney Afriat proved a useful result for anyone studying choices. A finite set of observed choices that satisfies GARP, the generalized consistency rule, can be explained by a utility function, a rule that scores each option. His inequalities go further and let that function be built directly from the data. SARP, by contrast, only proves such a function exists for infinite datasets. The theorem is widely used in econometrics to test rationality and to build preferences from real data.

  <!-- nature-val-096 -->

- **Benefit transfer: borrowing values from earlier studies**

  When time and money rule out original research, benefit transfer offers a cheap way to value a project. It borrows the data, models and results of earlier studies of similar projects or sites. It comes in two forms. Value transfer moves a single unit value from an earlier site. Function transfer uses valuation functions drawn from many studies, and can be more accurate; Meta-analysis: combining many studies into one answer can help build one. Two errors lurk. Measurement error comes from biased study selection and assumptions. Transfer error arises when the original and new sites do not correspond.

  <!-- nature-val-103 -->

- **Replacement cost: what it takes to start over**

  An insurer valuing a television can pay the price of a similar new one today. That is replacement cost: the amount needed, at today's prices, to replace something with an undamaged equivalent. It can differ from market value, and from 'actual cash value', which subtracts Depreciation: the value an asset loses as it ages. The idea matters beyond insurance. In urban planning, the replacement cost of public infrastructure such as roads can push local governments toward bankruptcy.

  <!-- nature-val-093 -->

- **Stated preference: asking people what they value**

  Sometimes the only way to learn what people value is to ask. Stated preference methods measure value through surveys rather than by watching what people buy. Ecosystem valuation divides its methods into this family and the revealed preference family. The best known is Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey, which asks people their willingness to pay for an ecosystem or one of its services. Survey-based choice experiments are also used, and David Hensher and Jordan Louviere are credited with the first stated preference choice models. Non-use values are usually measured this way, because people's market behavior reveals nothing about them. Many economists remain unconvinced. They question whether survey answers can be trusted, and prefer the evidence of binding market purchases. One middle path combines revealed and stated data to get the advantages of both.

  <!-- nature-val-102 -->

- **Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey**

  In 1963 Robert K. Davis used a survey to value a wilderness area for hunters and tourists. It was the first application of contingent valuation, an idea S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup had proposed in theory in 1947. Contingent valuation puts a money value on things not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution. A survey usually asks how much people would pay to keep an environmental feature such as biodiversity. Or it asks how much they would need to be paid to accept its loss. That makes it a stated preference method, unlike methods that rely on prices people actually pay. It rose to prominence in the United States in the 1980s. Governments then gained authority to sue for damage to environmental resources held in trust for the public, including non-use values. The The Exxon Valdez spill: putting a price on damage was the first case where its surveys put numbers on damages. US government departments have since used it widely, for example to value river recreation below Glen Canyon dam. Critics warn of strategic answers, protest answers, response bias and respondents ignoring their income limits. Clive Spash found that many answers behaved like charitable donations rather than trade prices. Many economists therefore doubt that the answers reflect real values. Defenders reply that newer survey designs have fixed the early biases.

  <!-- nature-val-085 -->

- **The NOAA panel: can surveys be trusted?**

  Could surveys of willingness to pay be trusted? The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration convened a panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, to judge. It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993. Its verdict was a cautious yes. Well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values. Good design meant personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats. Preferring cautious estimates, the panel advised asking willingness to pay to protect a good, not willingness to accept its loss.

  <!-- nature-val-086 -->

- **The embedding effect: when part and whole do not add up**

  Willingness to pay for a project is larger when people are asked about it first than when it comes second. That is one face of the embedding effect. In contingent valuation, people struggle to value one public good that is part of a larger set of similar goods. Part-whole bias is related: what people would pay for two policies valued separately does not add up to what they would pay for both together. The effect suggests contingent valuation is not an unbiased measure of policy effects. One fix asks about the whole set first, then the named item's share.

  <!-- nature-val-101 -->

- **The WTA–WTP gap: selling dear, buying cheap**

  Ziv Carmon and Dan Ariely found that willingness to accept for basketball tickets was more than 10 times willingness to pay. Standard theory predicts the two amounts should match. Yet people ask far more to give something up than they would pay to get it. One explanation is income limits on what people can pay. Another is the The endowment effect: why owning something raises its value, where owning something triggers loss aversion. Plott and Zeiler argued the gap partly reflects participants misunderstanding the experimental task. Researchers still disagree. The answer matters for contingent valuation, where endowment effects are widespread.

  <!-- nature-val-090 -->

- **Compensating differentials: the extra pay for a bad job**

  Risky jobs have to pay extra to attract workers. A compensating differential is that extra pay, offered so someone takes an unpleasant or risky job instead of other work. For an especially pleasant job it runs the other way: workers accept lower pay. The idea, credited to Adam Smith, has been used to study injury risk, the money value workers put on their own lives, and regional wage gaps. A hedonic wage function plots how wages rise with a job's undesirable features, such as the chance of injury. Economists expect lower wages in pleasant places, so wage gaps can reveal what an area's attractiveness is worth.

  <!-- nature-val-097 -->

- **Choice modeling: learning value from trade-offs**

  Before the Bay Area Rapid Transit was built, Daniel McFadden used past transport choices to predict how many would ride it. The work earned him the 2000 Nobel economics prize. Choice modeling is the family of methods behind such forecasts. It models how a person or group decides, using real choices or choices stated in a set context. Usually it infers where items sit on a hidden scale, typically utility, from repeated choices of one option over another. Its roots lie in Thurstone's 1920s research on food preferences and in random utility theory, which McFadden developed in economics. A survey describes a good by attributes and levels. Combinations explode: a phone with 2 brands, 3 shapes, 3 sizes and 4 memory options has 72, so only a subset is shown. Respondents must weigh trade-offs, which lets analysts estimate an implicit price for each attribute. It is regarded as the best method for valuing quality improvements that vary in several dimensions at once.

  <!-- nature-val-091 -->

- **Discrete choice: modeling either-or decisions**

  Which mode of transport to take is a choice between separate options, not a question of how much to buy. Discrete choice models describe and predict such decisions. A model gives the probability that a person picks each alternative, based on features of the alternatives and of the person. The models can be derived from utility theory, and only differences in utility between alternatives affect the probabilities. The first applications were in transportation planning; in market research the approach is commonly called Conjoint analysis: pricing a product's parts. Common forms include binary logit and The probit model: predicting yes or no, multinomial, conditional and nested logit, and Mixed logit: letting tastes vary. They are usually estimated by Maximum likelihood: the settings that best explain the data. Standard logit assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives, a substitution pattern that is not always realistic. The last model on the list relaxes it by letting tastes vary between people.

  <!-- nature-val-100 -->

- **Conjoint analysis: pricing a product's parts**

  Products are bundles of attributes, and conjoint analysis asks which ones people really value. It is a survey-based statistical technique, mainly from market research. Respondents see a controlled set of products broken down by attribute. Their choices reveal the implicit value, or part-worth, of each attribute. Marketing professor Paul E. Green developed it, and Jordan Louviere pioneered the choice-based version that underlies discrete choice analysis. Because attribute combinations grow exponentially, fractional factorial designs cut the profiles respondents must judge. It is also called discrete choice modeling or stated preference research.

  <!-- nature-val-098 -->

### Valuation econometrics

Survey answers and observed choices are messy data, and turning them into values takes statistics. This chapter gathers the tools. Some treat choices as partly random; others sort people into hidden groups, or combine findings from many studies. The chapter also meets the traps: values that do not grow with the size of a problem, and distorted answers about goods nobody actually has to pay for. A 1989 disaster in Prince William Sound, Alaska, shows how much can ride on the numbers.

- **Random utility: why rational choices look random**

  Two people facing exactly the same options often choose differently. Classic economics assumes a rational person picks the alternative with the highest utility, which can be inferred from choices. A random utility model explains the variety. Each person's choices depend on a random, unobserved state. The model gives each person a distribution over utility functions rather than a single one, and assumes rational behavior given the hidden state. To an observer, the choices then look random. Choice experiments rest on this logic: how often item A is chosen over item B measures how much it is preferred. A popular version was developed by Luce and Plackett.

  <!-- nature-val-082 -->

- **Multinomial logit: choosing among many options**

  Multinomial logistic regression predicts the probabilities of more than two unordered outcomes from a set of explanatory variables. It extends Logistic regression: predicting yes or no, and goes by many names, including multinomial logit, and softmax regression. In discrete choice theory, each outcome's score is read as the utility a person gets from choosing it. A random part stands for unmodeled factors. Used for choices, it assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives: the odds between two options do not depend on what other options are present. Many psychology studies show that people often violate this assumption. Even so, it is often the first stage of analysis in Best–worst scaling: picking extremes studies, giving average utilities for items.

  <!-- nature-val-080 -->

- **The Exxon Valdez spill: putting a price on damage**

  On March 24, 1989, the supertanker Exxon Valdez struck Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska. Over the next few days it spilled more than 10 million US gallons of crude oil. It was the first case where contingent valuation surveys were used in a quantitative assessment of damages, and use of the technique spread from there. Existence values were part of the legal damage assessment. An Anchorage jury awarded $287 million in actual damages and $5 billion in punitive damages, which an appeals court ordered reduced.

  <!-- nature-val-076 -->

- **The probit model: predicting yes or no**

  Some outcomes take only two values, such as yes or no. A probit model is a regression model for such an outcome, built on the normal distribution, the bell curve. It estimates the probability that an observation with given characteristics falls into one of the two categories, the same problem Logistic regression: predicting yes or no handles. It can be motivated as a latent variable model: the outcome shows whether an unobserved variable is positive. It is usually estimated by maximum likelihood. Chester Bliss coined the term in 1934, though the basic model goes back to Fechner in 1860.

  <!-- nature-val-081 -->

- **Mixed logit: letting tastes vary**

  Mixed logit lets tastes vary randomly between people, which makes it a fully general model for analyzing discrete choices. It overcomes three limits of standard logit. It allows random taste variation, unrestricted substitution patterns, and correlation in unobserved factors over time. It also drops the restrictive assumption of independence of irrelevant alternatives. With suitable specification it can approximate any random utility model of discrete choice to any accuracy. The price is computation. Its choice probability has no closed form, so it is estimated by simulation, drawing repeatedly from the taste distribution.

  <!-- nature-val-079 -->

- **Best–worst scaling: picking extremes**

  Ask people to rate a list and every item risks being rated 'quite important'. Best–worst scaling avoids that. Respondents pick the best and the worst item from a subset of a longer list. The task repeats with subsets varied by a statistical design. Because people choose rather than rate, it avoids scale-use bias. Jordan Louviere invented it in 1987 at the University of Alberta, as a form of discrete choice experiment. Choices are usually analyzed with a random utility model. One difficulty remains: it is hard to combine best and worst answers when people use different decision rules for each.

  <!-- nature-val-099 -->

- **Scope neglect: when bigger harms do not count more**

  In one study people would pay $80 to save 2,000 migrating birds from drowning in oil ponds. For 20,000 birds they offered $78, and for 200,000, $88. The harm grew enormously; the price barely moved. This is scope neglect, a cognitive bias in which the value people place on a problem does not grow in proportion to its size. Other willingness-to-pay studies have found a logarithmic relationship, where value rises ever more slowly, or no relationship at all. Daniel Kahneman explains it as judgment by prototype. People price a mental image, such as one oil-soaked bird, rather than the number affected. It is a specific form of extension neglect, closely linked to the 'mass numbing' studied by Paul Slovic. For contingent valuation, the lesson is uncomfortable.

  <!-- nature-val-083 -->

- **Cheap talk: words that cost nothing**

  In Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game, cheap talk is costless communication between players whose messages do not directly change the payoffs. It is non-binding and cannot be verified by a third party. A speaker could lie freely, but may choose not to. That sets it apart from signaling, where sending some messages can be costly. Whether talk helps depends on the game. In a coordination game, a round of cheap talk can help players reach better outcomes. In the Prisoner's Dilemma it is ignored.

  <!-- nature-val-075 -->

- **Hypothetical bias: saying is not paying**

  Saying you would pay is not the same as paying. Hypothetical bias is the distortion in values people state in surveys about goods they do not actually have to pay for or give up. A public health study found it is greater when people have less information about a good and information is costly. When hypothetical bias is high, stated willingness to pay is lower, widening the WTA–WTP gap. John A. List studied whether explicit warnings remove it.

  <!-- nature-val-084 -->

- **Latent class models: finding hidden groups**

  Answers to a political questionnaire could reveal hidden groups that match political camps. A latent class model is a statistical tool for finding such groups. It sorts multivariate discrete data, many category answers per person, into hidden classes. It assumes the data come from a mixture of distributions, with the variables independent within each class. It is called latent because each data point's class is not observed.

  <!-- nature-val-077 -->

- **Meta-regression: why studies disagree**

  When many studies disagree, meta-regression tries to sort out why. It is a kind of Meta-analysis: combining many studies into one answer that uses regression to combine and compare findings while adjusting for study characteristics. It aims to reconcile conflicting studies or confirm consistent ones. Fixed-effect versions assume the studies do not really differ. Mixed-effect versions allow for variation between them, and are often the most flexible choice. It has been applied to the The value of a statistical life, energy and water policy, and price elasticities for water and energy. It is increasingly used to weigh evidence across many cost-benefit studies of a policy.

  <!-- nature-val-078 -->

### Cost–benefit analysis

Should a new regulation go ahead, or a project be built? The standard way to answer is to estimate the benefits and the costs, convert those at different times into present values with a discount rate, and compare them. The method reaches into hard places: it needs a money value for avoiding one death on average, and money values for things no market trades. Health economists use measures that count years in perfect health, or years of healthy life lost. Critics object that the method ignores who gains and who loses, discounts the future too heavily and leaves out what cannot be priced.

- **Net present value: future money in today's terms**

  A lender might pay 99 cents today for $1.00 due in a month, but much less for a dollar due in 20 years. Money now is worth more than the same money later, because money in hand can be invested at once and start earning. Net present value turns that principle into a test for investments. Each period's net cash flow is discounted back to the present at a rate equal to what a similarly risky investment could earn. The results are added up. A positive total means expected earnings exceed costs in today's money, and the Net Present Value Rule says only such investments should be made. The method dates at least to the 19th century, and it has weak spots. The answer depends heavily on the The discount rate: how fast the future shrinks and on knowing future cash flows, so sensitivity analysis is used to test it. When large costs fall late, such as mine clean-up and restoration, a high discount rate makes a project look too good. And it is purely financial, ignoring everything that is not money.

  <!-- nature-val-014 -->

- **Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses**

  Is this project worth doing? Cost–benefit analysis answers by estimating the benefits and costs of a project, policy or investment and comparing them. It also ranks options by their total expected costs and benefits. The method follows a sequence. Analysts list the alternatives and stakeholders, measure costs and benefits, and convert them to one currency. They discount future amounts for the time value of money, so flows at different dates can be summed as a net present value. A sensitivity analysis then checks how firm the answer is. Benefits are valued by listing everyone affected and adding up the money value each places on the change in their welfare, in effect their Willingness to pay: the most you would hand over. Costs are usually measured more fully than benefits, because market data on costs are relatively plentiful. In the 21st century, environmental effects are typically valued through the ecosystem services they provide to people, such as air and water quality. The tool is only as good as its estimates. Comparative studies find those estimates are often flawed, and interest groups may try to include or leave out large costs to sway the result.

  <!-- nature-val-001 -->

- **Shadow prices: money values where markets are silent**

  Clean air has no price tag, yet a cost–benefit analysis needs one. A shadow price fills the gap. It is a money value given to something not traded in a market, or a market price corrected for distortions and social effects. Shadow prices are needed for two reasons. Externalities, costs and benefits that fall on people outside a deal, go unpriced. And taxes, subsidies, quotas and tariffs distort market prices. Tools for estimating them include contingent valuation, benefit transfer, hedonic pricing and the travel cost method. Lacking reliable data, analysts often build them from assumptions, so they are subjective and somewhat inaccurate. They are still widely used to value intangible costs and benefits, especially for public goods rarely bought and sold. Measures of a nation's total wealth use them as weights on produced, human and natural capital. That use is controversial, because little is known about how life-supporting ecosystems produce their benefits.

  <!-- nature-val-017 -->

- **The value of a statistical life**

  Suppose 100,000 people would each pay $100 to cut their yearly risk of death by 1 in 100,000. Together they would pay $10 million for one statistical life saved. That figure is the value of a statistical life, a money value for avoiding one death on average. It values changes in the chance of death, not escape from certain death, so it differs greatly from the value of an actual life. Economists estimate it from extra pay for risky jobs, the Compensating differentials: the extra pay for a bad job, from surveys of willingness to pay, or from discounted lifetime earnings. Each method can overstate or understate it. Values vary widely. Sweden's estimates range from 9 to 98 million SEK, and the UK put preventing a fatal casualty at £1.7m in 2013 prices. Philosophers such as Elizabeth Anderson argue that the wage data are unreliable, and that life and environmental goods cannot share one money scale. Both the methods and the idea of pricing lives remain disputed. Health economics more often uses the QALYs: counting years by their quality, which scores quality of life from 0 to 1.

  <!-- nature-val-019 -->

- **Cost-effectiveness analysis: comparing without pricing**

  Pricing health strikes many as inappropriate, and cost-effectiveness analysis avoids it. It compares the costs and outcomes of different courses of action without putting a money value on the outcomes. That makes it common in health care. Results are usually a ratio of cost to a health gain such as years of life, and the most common outcome measure is the QALYs: counting years by their quality. A 1995 review of over 500 life-saving interventions found a median of $42,000 per life-year saved. For environmental goals with one physical outcome, such as cutting energy use, it can replace cost–benefit analysis with less labor. Climate economics prefers it when the benefits of climate mitigation and adaptation are hard to express in money. A variant, distributional cost-effectiveness analysis, also weighs how outcomes are spread, trading equity against efficiency.

  <!-- nature-val-008 -->

- **QALYs: counting years by their quality**

  A year lived at a health utility of 0.5 counts as 0.5 quality-adjusted life years. The QALY combines how long and how well people live. Scores run from 1 for perfect health to 0 for death. QALYs gained from a treatment equal the change in health utility times how long the effect lasts. Weights come from methods such as the time trade-off or questionnaires like the EQ-5D. Combined with costs, QALYs give a cost per QALY, used in cost-utility analysis to compare treatments. The UK's NICE has used pounds per QALY since 1999. In 2018 HM Treasury set a 1.5% discount rate for QALYs, lower than for other costs and benefits, because a QALY measures utility directly. The measure is openly contested. Critics say it undervalues people with disabilities and the elderly and ignores how health is distributed. Oregon's 1989 Medicaid plan using it was found discriminatory. Supporters reply that with limited health budgets it allocates resources in a roughly optimal way.

  <!-- nature-val-026 -->

- **Discounting: how much the future counts**

  How much should harm to future generations count today? Discounting is how cost–benefit analysis answers. It puts costs and benefits at different times on a common footing by converting them to present values with a discount rate. Net present value adds up each year's benefits minus costs, each divided by one plus the discount rate raised to the number of years ahead. The choice of rate is subjective, and for long-term projects it makes a large difference. A small rate treats current and future generations almost equally. A large rate, such as a market return, mirrors people's preference for money sooner rather than later. If long-run share-market returns are higher than risk alone explains, the equity premium puzzle, market rates would undervalue the distant future. Private firms often take their rate from models such as the capital asset pricing model. Critics argue that discounting biases the analysis against future generations and understates the harm from climate change. Scholars still disagree over whether, and how strongly, such effects should be discounted.

  <!-- nature-val-003 -->

- **The case against cost–benefit analysis**

  Cost–benefit analysis adds up gains and losses without asking whose they are. That is the root of most objections to it. It rests on the Kaldor–Hicks efficiency: could the winners pay off the losers criterion: a positive net benefit counts as decisive, whoever wins and whoever loses. As a result it can overlook equity and favor policies that help some groups while burdening others. Money itself is unevenly weighted. An extra dollar matters less to the rich, so unweighted willingness to pay gives wealthier people's preferences more weight. Time raises a second objection. Discounting may undervalue distant harms such as climate change and ignore the preferences of future generations. A third concerns what gets counted. Limiting benefits to economic values leaves out minority wishes, inclusiveness and respect for others' rights. Some writers judge the method unsuitable for analyzing climate mitigation as a whole. Supporters and critics still disagree on whether it can fairly judge policies with uneven or long-term effects.

  <!-- nature-val-006 -->

- **Multiple-criteria decision analysis: juggling conflicting goals**

  Whether and where to build a nuclear power plant is a decision with very high stakes. Multiple-criteria decision analysis exists for choices like that. It is a field of decision science that weighs several conflicting criteria explicitly when choosing among options. Cost is usually one criterion and some measure of quality another, and the two often pull in opposite directions. When stakes are high, structuring the problem and its criteria explicitly leads to better decisions. There is usually no single best answer, so the decision-maker's preferences are needed to tell solutions apart. Ecological economists favor it as an alternative to standard cost–benefit reasoning. It has been applied to sustainability assessment, desertification risk and wind farm siting.

  <!-- nature-val-011 -->

- **Regulatory impact analysis: testing a rule before it takes effect**

  A regulatory impact analysis is a document prepared before a new regulation is introduced, systematically appraising its likely impacts. Its central economic purpose is to make sure the regulation improves society's welfare, meaning its benefits exceed its costs. It usually compares different ways of reaching the same objective. The first ones are usually traced to the inflation impact assessments the Carter Administration required from 1978. Under Reagan, benefit–cost analysis became the required method. By 2000, 20 of 28 OECD countries required them, and virtually all OECD countries now use them; the World Bank has spread them to developing countries. The European Commission's impact assessments, introduced in 2002, weigh economic, environmental and social effects. In climate policy these analyses commonly use the The social cost of carbon: pricing one more ton.

  <!-- nature-val-016 -->

- **DALYs: measuring the burden of disease**

  A pneumococcal vaccine in Gambia cost $670 for each disability-adjusted life year saved. One DALY equals one year of healthy life lost to illness, disability or early death. The measure adds years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability into one number. Each condition gets a disability weight from 0, no disability, to 1; Alzheimer's and other dementias score 0.666. DALYs are not a money measure, but costs per DALY can guide health spending. Like the QALY, the DALY is a health-adjusted life year. Harvard developed it in 1990 for the World Bank's Global Burden of Disease Study, and the World Health Organization adopted it in 1996. Before 2010 the WHO used age weighting and 3 percent time discounting, criticized for valuing young adults above children and the old. Critics also say DALYs measure productive capacity. Defenders reply that disability weights reflect effects on life in general, not ability to work.

  <!-- nature-val-021 -->

- **Cost–benefit review comes to US regulation**

  Reagan's 1981 Executive Order 12291 made federal agencies produce regulatory impact analyses for rules with annual impacts above $100 million. OIRA reviewed them. Critics in the 1980s said the method could serve political goals, was biased against regulation and caused long delays. Clinton's Executive Order 12866 softened the test: benefits had to justify costs rather than exceed them. The practice continued under Obama. Analysts still disagree over whether cost–benefit analysis should be used in setting regulations at all.

  <!-- nature-val-005 -->

- **Distributional weights: making a poor person's dollar count**

  A dollar to a poor person can count for more than a dollar to a rich one, if analysts apply distributional weights. These weights reflect Diminishing marginal utility: why the twentieth candy disappoints. Without them, unweighted willingness to pay overstates gains and losses to the wealthy and understates them for the poor. Not weighting is itself a choice, one that in practice gives richer people a bigger weight. Weights are often derived from a Bergson–Samuelson social welfare function, a formula ranking outcomes for society as a whole. Another option measures willingness to pay as a share of income or wealth.

  <!-- nature-val-007 -->

- **From Dupuit's bridges to government policy**

  In 1848 Jules Dupuit measured the social benefit of a road or bridge by adding up what each user would be willing to pay for it. Alfred Marshall later formalized the idea. In the United States, the Federal Navigation Act of 1936 required it for federal waterway projects, and the Flood Control Act of 1939 made it federal policy. Otto Eckstein gave it a welfare-economics foundation in 1958. In the 1960s it was applied to water quality, recreation and land conservation.

  <!-- nature-val-002 -->

- **Handling risk in cost–benefit analysis**

  No forecast of costs and benefits is certain. Cost–benefit analysis handles that chiefly with probability, sensitivity analysis and simulation. Risk can be built into the discount rate, but it is usually treated separately, often allowing for people's Risk aversion: why a sure thing often wins. A sensitivity analysis shows how the result changes when the inputs change. A more formal risk analysis can use the Monte Carlo method, rerunning the calculation with randomly drawn inputs.

  <!-- nature-val-004 -->

- **Payback period: how long to break even**

  A $1000 investment that returns $500 at the end of each of its first two years has a two-year payback period. That is the time an investment takes to earn back its cost, or to reach the break-even point. It is often quoted for energy efficiency upgrades, such as a compact fluorescent bulb, where the return is lower operating costs. Economists are wary. It ignores the time value of money, risk and cash flows after payback, so they prefer net present value or internal rate of return.

  <!-- nature-val-024 -->

- **Shadow prices in optimization**

  A production line is already at its 40-hour limit. The most a manager would pay for one more hour is that limit's shadow price. In optimization, the shadow price is the change in the best achievable value of an objective when a constraint is relaxed by one small unit. Formally it equals the constraint's Lagrange multipliers: pricing the constraints at the optimal solution. Every constraint has one, also called a dual variable. In optimal control theory the idea reappears as costate variables. Under Hotelling's rule: why oil in the ground should gain value, the rent from a resource equals its shadow value.

  <!-- nature-val-018 -->

- **Pricing the energy that is never used**

  Energy saved is never consumed, and such savings are sometimes called negawatts. Cost-effectiveness analysis: comparing without pricing can price them in dollars per kilowatt-hour saved by an efficiency investment. The approach has a quiet advantage. It avoids guessing future energy prices, removing the main source of uncertainty in appraising efficiency investments.

  <!-- nature-val-010 -->

- **Evaluation versus design problems**

  Multi-criteria problems split in two, depending on whether the options are listed in advance. Evaluation problems have a finite list of known options, each scored on several criteria. The task can be picking the best option, sorting options into ordered classes, or classifying them into unordered groups. Design problems do not list the options explicitly. They are solved by multiple-objective mathematical programming.

  <!-- nature-val-013 -->

- **Nondominated solutions: when no option beats all others**

  When criteria conflict, there is often no single optimal solution. Multi-criteria analysis replaces it with the set of nondominated solutions: options that cannot be improved on one criterion without being made worse on another. From any option outside this efficient set, both objectives can be improved. On the set, improving one means sacrificing the other. The idea parallels Pareto efficiency: when no one can gain without someone losing. Maximizing a weighted sum of the criteria finds some of these solutions, those at corner points.

  <!-- nature-val-012 -->
