It works like a Pigouvian taxes: charging for harm done to others inside the firm, making fossil fuel use more expensive. Tools include internal emissions trading, proxy prices, carbon fees, implicit prices and hybrids of these. Proxy pricing, used by about two-thirds of reporting companies, writes a set carbon price into investment decisions without any actual payment. Companies often base their price on the The social cost of carbon: pricing one more ton or on the cost of the last cut needed to reach a target. An analysis of 500 firms reporting from 2011 to 2018 linked adoption to a significant fall in emissions per unit of revenue and per employee. Some researchers worry it can serve as Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action, deterring governments from stricter carbon rules.

  <!-- nature-pol-243 -->

- **Kyoto's flexible mechanisms: cutting emissions where it costs least**

  Cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, but it benefits the atmosphere equally wherever it happens. That idea underlies the three flexible mechanisms of the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries: emissions trading, the The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market and Joint Implementation: emission projects between rich countries. Each lets countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries. The protocol required Annex I countries, the developed nations with targets, to cut emissions on average 5.2% below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012. International emissions trading let parties buy Kyoto units from other countries to help meet their targets. The main argument for flexibility is cost-effectiveness, which keeps fairness separate from the efficiency of cutting emissions cheaply. Negotiators disagreed over whether that was wise. Critics feared rich countries would avoid domestic cuts and take up all the cheap reductions in developing countries. Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the The Paris Agreement: every country pledges are their successor.

  <!-- nature-pol-275 -->

- **The Acid Rain Program: America's first cap and trade**

  A US power plant that emitted a ton of sulfur dioxide beyond its allowances paid a fine of $2,000. That rule enforced the Acid Rain Program, the first cap-and-trade emissions program in the United States. Run by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), it cut sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides, the gases that cause Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky. Title IV of the 1990 amendments to the The US Clean Air Act set a falling cap on SO2, aiming to bring emissions to 50% of 1980 levels. In 2007 total SO2 emissions were 8.9 million tons, reaching the long-term goal ahead of the 2010 deadline. Its expected yearly cost by 2010, $1 billion to $2 billion, was only one fourth of the first prediction. A 2021 study found lasting air quality gains, cutting mortality risk by 5% over 10 years. The EPA, industry and economists call it a success, and it became a model for later greenhouse gas schemes. Skeptical environmentalists argue the cuts came from broader trends and other regulation. They note it cut SO2 by 40%, while conventional regulation in the European Union achieved more than 70%.

  <!-- nature-pol-262 -->

- **Europe's carbon charge at the border**

  Since 2026, firms bringing steel or cement into the European Union have had to pay for the carbon released in making it. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, is a Carbon tariffs: pricing the carbon in imports on carbon-intensive imports. Its main aim is to stop Carbon leakage: cuts at home, emissions abroad by charging imports the same carbon price that EU producers pay under the EU ETS. Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods. It covers aluminum, cement, electricity, fertilizers, hydrogen and iron and steel, with reporting from October 2023. Free ETS allowances in these sectors will be phased out by 2034. It may push other countries to price carbon: Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it. Some see it as the start of a Climate clubs: fixing free-riding by excluding outsiders of the kind proposed by William Nordhaus and the economics of climate. Critics are less impressed. An Asian Development Bank report says it will cut emissions only a little while harming imports to the EU. Questions also remain over its fit with The World Trade Organization: referee of world trade rules and its effect on least developed countries.

  <!-- nature-pol-261 -->

- **Joint Implementation: emission projects between rich countries**

  Joint Implementation is a mechanism of the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Under it, one developed (Annex I) country invests in an emission-cutting project in another and counts the cuts towards its own target. Projects earn credits (Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation), each equal to one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. These come out of the host country's own pool of units, so the total among Annex I parties does not change. Because hosts also have emission commitments, it raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market. Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, expected to total around 300 million units by 2012.

  <!-- nature-pol-277 -->

- **Baseline and credit: rewards for beating your own past**

  Not every trading scheme starts with a cap. In a baseline-and-credit scheme, polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their own historical emissions. Polluters that face a regulatory limit can then buy those credits. Programs usually require Additionality: would it have happened anyway?: the cuts must go beyond what existing rules already demand. That test is hard to define and monitor. Some companies deliberately raised their emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

  <!-- nature-pol-258 -->

- **From computer models to carbon markets**

  Emissions trading began as a computer result. Simulation studies of air pollution costs between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional ways of cutting pollution. The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant. The first cap-and-trade system was the US The Acid Rain Program: America's first cap and trade under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems. From US clean air policy, the approach then spread to the European Union and to global climate policy.

  <!-- nature-pol-255 -->

- **Linking carbon markets across borders**

  California and Québec linked their cap-and-trade systems in 2014, and the EU's scheme has linked with Switzerland's. Linking means each system recognizes the other's allowances for compliance. The result is a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity, the ease of finding a buyer or seller, and stabilize prices. Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy, built from existing national and regional schemes.

  <!-- nature-pol-259 -->

- **Measure, report, verify: keeping a carbon market honest**

  A permit market is only as good as its numbers. Monitoring, reporting and verification are the checks that make it credible: emissions are measured or calculated, reported, then verified by government or third-party auditors. Some emissions are measured by sensors in chimneys, but many activities rely on calculations instead. Acid Rain Program plants had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily. Polluters exceeding their allowances face fines and sanctions. The worries are the cost of checking and the risk of facilities lying. For voluntary credits, robust independent third-party validation and verification is one of the Core Carbon Principles: ten tests for a credit.

  <!-- nature-pol-281 -->

- **The safety valve: a cap with a price limit**

  A safety valve is a hybrid of a cap and a tax. Emitters can buy permits on the market, or from the government at a set trigger price, which holds the permit price below a maximum. Some designs instead hold it above a minimum. A trigger price set high enough, or a permit supply small enough, lets the system mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument (Prices or quantities: fix the cost or fix the amount?). Each limit has a cost. A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit. A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

  <!-- nature-pol-257 -->

- **Auctioning permits: making polluters pay up front**

  Businesses tend to oppose auctioning emission permits. Economists almost uniformly recommend it. Under auctioning, firms buy their permits at auction and the government receives their value. That revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes, the kind that discourage useful work and investment. Auctioning can also be more efficient and fairer than free allocation. And it removes the perverse incentive created by Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters.

  <!-- nature-pol-247 -->

- **Carbon trading and the neighbors of polluters**

  Carbon trading can move money from richer, higher-emitting countries to poorer, lower-emitting ones for climate action. That is its promise as a tool of Climate justice: those who suffer most did least. The problem starts at the factory gate. Schemes cap only greenhouse gases, so a factory can buy permits instead of cutting its local air pollution. Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap. The sources record both sides: trading can advance that cause, yet it has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.

  <!-- nature-pol-250 -->

- **Toward a single global carbon market**

  In 2023 carbon markets worldwide were worth $948.75 billion, a figure expected to reach 2.68 trillion dollars by 2028. A truly worldwide market in emission allowances is still a proposal, though the The Paris Agreement: every country pledges provides a legal basis for one. At COP 30, the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets formed with a plan for a global cap near current emissions, falling to net zero by 2050. Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries, while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programs.

  <!-- nature-pol-251 -->

- **Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters**

  Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create perverse incentives. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth, the pursuit of favors from government, and pressure on officials (Lobbying: influencing the people who make the rules).

  <!-- nature-pol-246 -->

- **Too many permits: how a carbon price collapses**

  A permit market lives or dies by the number of permits. Issue too many and the price sinks so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions. Issue too few and the risk flips to an excessively high price. Europe's trading scheme showed the first danger. Its price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession. Under the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse. Buying them would not have reduced emissions.

  <!-- nature-pol-248 -->

- **Certified emission reductions: credits from developing countries**

  Between 2001 and 7 September 2012, the The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market issued 1 billion certified emission reductions, or CERs. Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases (CO2e), measured against a baseline. Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their Kyoto targets. By 2013, 57% came from destroying just two gases, HFC-23 or N2O. Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012, amid recession and over-allocation in Europe's trading scheme.

  <!-- nature-pol-269 -->

- **Carbon revenue: what to do with the money**

  A carbon tax or a permit auction raises money, and governments must decide how to spend it. One standard proposal returns it to the public per person. Richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, so poorer people can come out ahead. Per-person refunds would not, however, cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses. Other proposals fund renewable energy support, research, public transport and car sharing. Revenue could also pay for negative emissions, which remove carbon dioxide and cost about $150–165 per ton depending on the technology.

  <!-- nature-pol-241 -->

- **Why renewable energy support adds nothing under a binding cap**

  Under a carbon tax, public support for renewable energy adds to the emission cuts. Under a binding cap, it does not. While the cap applies, renewable support brings no further emission cuts, because the cap has already fixed the total amount emitted. So the choice between a tax and a cap (Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon) also decides what other climate policies can achieve.

  <!-- nature-pol-242 -->

- **Assigned amount units: Kyoto's national allowances**

  Under the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries, each Annex 1 country received assigned amount units up to its emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period. Each unit allowed it to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. Under Article 17, countries below their targets could sell spare units to countries above theirs. Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action: a top-up to cuts at home, not a replacement.

  <!-- nature-pol-266 -->

- **Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation**

  A landfill releases methane, a gas with a 100-year Global warming potential: comparing gases with carbon dioxide of 25 compared with carbon dioxide. Capture and burn one tonne of it, and it yields nearly 3 tonnes of CO2, a saving of 22 emission reduction units. Each unit is a Kyoto credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project. The market for them later collapsed. ERU prices declined 89 percent in 2012, falling to 15 euro cents in December.

  <!-- nature-pol-271 -->

- **EU ETS2: a carbon market for buildings and road transport**

  EU ETS2 is a second European trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original scheme. It covers emissions upstream: fuel suppliers, not end consumers, must report and pay for them. Its cap aims for a 42% cut by 2030 compared with 2005. Part of the revenue funds a Social Climate Fund for vulnerable groups. Together the two systems will cover 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025, under pressure from member states worried about inflation and energy affordability, its start was delayed to 2028.

  <!-- nature-pol-274 -->

- **The Market Stability Reserve: soaking up surplus permits**

  The Market Stability Reserve changes how many EU permits are auctioned each year, according to how many surplus permits are in circulation. It runs on predefined rules, with no discretion for the Commission or member states. It did not work at first. Back-loading and the reserve law failed to cut the surplus or lift prices in 2014–2017, when prices stayed below €10/tCO2. Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated. About 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

  <!-- nature-pol-273 -->

- **Water trading: markets for the right to use water**

  Chile's 1981 Water Code made the right to use water (Water rights: who may take water from a river) freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial. Water trading is the buying and selling of water access entitlements between willing sellers and buyers. A seller holds rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more. Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more productive uses: urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers. The older first-in-time system of prior appropriation led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology. Water is a Common-pool resources: hard to fence, easy to deplete, but once rights make its use rival and excludable, it behaves like a private good. It is still no standard commodity. Supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin. Trades can also harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller. Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.

  <!-- nature-pol-264 -->

- **CORSIA: offsetting the growth of international flights**

  In October 2016 the International Civil Aviation Organization adopted CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation. It makes airlines buy credits (Carbon credits: buying a tonne of avoided emissions) to offset growth in emissions from international flights, aiming for carbon-neutral growth from 2020. It is voluntary from 2021 until 2027, when it becomes compulsory, though least developed and small island states are not required to join. Domestic flights are not included, and it will regulate 25% of aviation's international emissions. Supporters call it a compromise step forward. Critics say it won't reduce jet fuel demand, and one hundred organizations rejected it as letting warming pass 1.5 °C.

  <!-- nature-pol-267 -->

- **Personal carbon trading: an allowance for every adult**

  Personal carbon trading would give each adult an equal share of emission credits within a national limit on emissions. People would surrender credits when buying fuel or electricity. Those who emit more than their allowance would buy credits from those who use less, who would profit. Research finds it would be progressive, moving money from rich to poor, unlike a carbon tax before its revenue is redistributed. Norfolk Island trialed the world's first program starting in 2011. Proponents call it fair and effective. Critics point to complexity, high costs and possible political unacceptability, and a 2008 UK study found it ahead of its time.

  <!-- nature-pol-279 -->

- **Market design: engineering the rules of exchange**

  Some markets are built on purpose. Market design is the branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange: who gets what, and by what procedure. Its aim is to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes. It is closely related to Mechanism design: game theory run in reverse and auction theory. Alvin Roth pioneered applications in labor-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice. He and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design. Auction theory supplies results such as the Revenue equivalence: when the auction format does not matter: with independent private values, sealed first-price and second-price auctions bring the same expected revenue.

  <!-- nature-pol-278 -->

- **Voluntary emission reductions: offsets bought by choice**

  Not every carbon offset is bought to meet a legal target. A Voluntary Emission Reduction, also called a Verified Emission Reduction or VER, is traded in the voluntary market. Companies and individuals buy them to compensate voluntarily for their emissions. They are usually certified outside the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. One VER equals 1 tonne of CO2 emissions. Standards set how reductions are measured, and every VER should at least be verified by an independent third party.

  <!-- nature-pol-283 -->

- **Windfall gains: income that drops from the sky**

  A windfall gain is a sudden, usually unexpected addition to Income: what you gain over a period well above the norm. It comes from luck or circumstance rather than planning. A windfall profit is the business version, caused for example by unexpected demand or by government regulation. Europe's carbon market supplied a case: fossil fuel generators priced freely allocated permits into electricity and reaped a massive windfall gain. Some legislators favor a windfall profits tax, since taxing unforeseen profits should not hurt the company.

  <!-- nature-pol-285 -->

- **Cap and dividend: sell the permits, pay the citizens**

  Who owns the sky? Peter Barnes asked in the title of his 2001 book, Who Owns the Sky?, where he first proposed the idea as 'Skytrust'. Cap and dividend is a cap-and-trade system in which all permits are sold and the money is paid back to citizens to offset higher energy prices. The cap often falls on upstream sources such as fossil fuel suppliers, which must buy permits for their emissions. Unlike ordinary cap and trade, no permits are given away free. The pollution rents, the value of the scarce permits, are captured publicly rather than becoming private assets. Households that emit least receive a bigger dividend than they pay in higher prices, which rewards those who conserve. A 2009 US bill would have auctioned 100 percent of permits and returned all proceeds as a monthly dividend, but it did not pass. The policy was vigorously debated: one critic called it 'fatally incomplete', while Time magazine hailed it.

  <!-- nature-pol-263 -->

- **Green certificates: trading proof of renewable power**

  A green certificate proves that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, came from renewable sources. It represents the environmental value of that power and can be traded separately from the electricity itself. Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use such certificates as a more market-like alternative to Feed-in tariffs: guaranteed prices for clean power. There is a catch. Buying a certificate only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much renewable energy is generated.

  <!-- nature-pol-276 -->

- **Pollution hot spots: when location matters**

  Carbon dioxide has a similar effect wherever it is released, so for trading its location does not matter. Regional pollutants such as SO2, NOx and mercury are different. The same amount does far more harm in some places than in others, so under a cap it can pile up in hot spots. Carbon trading has a related blind spot. Because it limits only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits without cutting local air pollution, leaving nearby low-income communities exposed. One answer is markets in location-based pollution licenses, which cap the rise in pollution at each monitoring point (Ambient permits: trading the right to raise local pollution).

  <!-- nature-pol-286 -->

- **Ambient permits: trading the right to raise local pollution**

  An ordinary permit grants the right to emit a set amount. An ambient permit grants the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount. Pollution at each monitoring point is modeled as a weighted sum of all emissions, written q=H⋅e, where the diffusion matrix H records how each source's output spreads. A polluter that affects several points must hold a portfolio of licenses covering all of them. Montgomery showed that both kinds of market allocate licenses efficiently, but pollution-license markets apply more widely.

  <!-- nature-pol-260 -->

- **Water quality trading: cleaner rivers at the lowest cost**

  Different polluters in one watershed, the land draining to a river or lake, face very different costs to control the same pollutant. Water quality trading puts that gap to work. Sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly. Most programs trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen (Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing). The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programs must meet the The Clean Water Act: permits for every pipe. Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

  <!-- nature-pol-287 -->

- **White certificates: trading proof of saved energy**

  In some countries, suppliers of electricity, gas and oil must deliver efficiency measures equal to a set percentage of their annual sales, or pay a penalty. White certificates are tradable proof that a certain amount of energy saving has been achieved. They are cousins of green certificates. As with emissions trading, tradability in theory meets the overall saving target at least cost. Great Britain started a scheme in 2002, Italy in 2005, and France and Denmark a year later.

  <!-- nature-pol-284 -->

- **Carbon retirement: taking permits off the market for good**

  A record 164 million credits (Carbon credits: buying a tonne of avoided emissions) were retired in voluntary markets in 2023. Retirement means permanently removing emission allowances or credits from circulation, so they can never be sold or used again. Under a cap, retiring allowances shrinks supply, which raises their scarcity and price. The EU's Market Stability Reserve invalidated about 2.5 billion allowances on 1 January 2023, and more than 3 billion by 2026. In voluntary markets, companies retire credits to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate. Citizen groups have even bought and retired sulfur dioxide allowances in US EPA auctions, to cut the supply available to polluters.

  <!-- nature-pol-268 -->

- **Transferable development rights: paying land to stay open**

  Land carries a bundle of Property rights: the rules of who owns what, including the right to develop it. Transferable development rights let that one right be sold on its own. Developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area: farmland, wilderness or historic sites at risk of development. They use those rights to build more densely in a receiving area, an urban place suited to higher density. Landowners get paid for conserving environmental, heritage or farming values, and sprawl is curbed by concentrating development. Such programs operate in over 200 U.S. communities.

  <!-- nature-pol-280 -->

### Subsidies, information and voluntary approaches

Governments do not only tax polluters and cap their emissions; they also pay, inform and persuade. A {{ref:nature-pol-205}} passes taxpayers' money to people or firms to support them or encourage some activity, and support for coal, oil and gas is among the largest. Other tools work through information: an {{ref:nature-pol-186}} tells shoppers about a product's environmental impact, and voluntary standards let producers show good practice. Nudges change how choices are presented, steering behavior without forcing it. Behind many of these tools sits a question of caution: how to act on possible harm when scientific knowledge is still incomplete.

- **Subsidies: paying people to do more of something**

  Many governments spend several percentage points of their GDP on subsidies, year after year. A subsidy is government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses, to support them or to encourage some activity. The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations. Subsidies come in many shapes. Some are direct spending, such as the payments governments may hand out in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity. Others are Tax incentives: encouraging activity through the tax code, cheap loans, price support, or goods and services the government provides. Some do clear environmental good. Governments that subsidize rail and bus transport cut congestion and pollution compared with cars. But the tool cuts both ways. Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences, a theme that runs through this chapter.

  <!-- nature-pol-205 -->

- **The precautionary principle: caution before proof**

  When a new technology might cause harm and the science is still incomplete, who has to prove what? The precautionary principle answers by favoring caution and review first. Policy makers often use it when a decision might cause harm and conclusive evidence is not yet available. The English term is generally thought to come from the German Vorsorgeprinzip, adopted in the 1970s in response to forest decline and sea pollution. The principle has two core ideas. First, it shifts the burden of proof: whoever proposes an activity must show it will not, or is very unlikely to, cause significant harm. Second, the response should be proportionate to the risk and to the cost and feasibility of acting. It is not one fixed rule. One study found 14 different formulations in treaties and declarations. The EU's policies on the environment must be based on it, along with prevention, fixing damage at source and the The polluter pays principle. It is typically applied to climate change, new organisms such as GMOs, public health threats and the long-term effects of new technologies. Supporters see it as needed caution under uncertainty. Critics call it vague, self-cancelling, unscientific and an obstacle to progress.

  <!-- nature-pol-201 -->

- **Ecolabels: the environment on the package**

  Germany's Blue Angel, launched in 1978, was the world's first ecolabel. Today the Ecolabel Index counts 456 of them in 199 countries across 25 industry sectors. An ecolabel tells shoppers about a product's environmental impact. Ecolabels are voluntary, whereas green stickers are required by law. Some measure pollution or energy use with scores or units; others certify that a set of minimum practices was followed. Through certification, a farm, forest, fishing operation or mine can show it meets a standard and sell its products as certified. Labels put market pressure on industries to cut their impact, by linking products to the wishes of informed consumers. Trust is the weak spot. Some manufacturers have set up 'rubber stamp' labels to make products look greener than they are (Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action), so shoppers cannot take every label at face value.

  <!-- nature-pol-186 -->

- **Sustainability standards: voluntary rules for good practice**

  About 40% of global coffee production is certified, and about 15–20% of cocoa and tea production meets major sustainability standards. These standards are voluntary guidelines that producers, traders and retailers follow to show good environmental, social, ethical and food-safety practices. More than 400 exist around the world. A standard is usually written by stakeholders and experts in a sector and lists practices, such as how a crop should be grown sustainably. Certification checks that a business meets it. Traceability then follows certified goods along the supply chain, often ending in a label for shoppers. The standards grew up where national and global laws were weak but consumers and campaign groups demanded action. Some set a high bar and work with top performers; others aim to remove the worst practices across most of an industry. They also differ in whether a first, second or third party does the checking, and whether certified and uncertified material may be mixed. Researchers still debate how effective these schemes are and how they are governed.

  <!-- nature-pol-184 -->

- **Fair trade: a better deal for producers in poorer countries**

  Coffee is the most established fair trade commodity, but the movement also covers handicrafts, cocoa, wine, sugar, fruit, flowers and gold. Fair trade is a trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards. The current movement took shape in Europe in the 1960s. Sales only took off once Fairtrade certification labels arrived. Fairtrade labeling uses independent audits of producers and traders, and its most distinctive feature is a guaranteed minimum price. In 2011 more than 1.2 million farmers and workers in over 60 countries took part in Fairtrade International's system. Some propose direct trade, which skips the overhead of certification, as an alternative.

  <!-- nature-pol-221 -->

- **Energy subsidies: who pays for cheap power**

  In 2020 the International Renewable Energy Agency tracked some $634 billion in energy subsidies, around 70% of them for fossil fuels. About 20% went to renewable power, 6% to biofuels and just over 3% to nuclear. An energy subsidy is a government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs. It can be a direct cash payment or indirect support: tax exemptions, price controls, trade restrictions and limits on market access. Other forms include public research, cheap government services, demand guarantees, and failing to charge for external costs such as pollution. Which source gets the most support can affect the environment. Early support for solar power by the United States and Germany helped bring renewable energy to market and cut emissions worldwide. Because energy policies are interconnected across countries, regulating subsidies at the The World Trade Organization: referee of world trade is often seen as necessary.

  <!-- nature-pol-192 -->

- **Fossil fuel subsidies: public money for coal, oil and gas**

  Under a narrow definition, fossil fuel subsidies totaled around $725 billion in 2024, 0.6% of global GDP, or up to $900 billion. Under a broader one they reached $6.7 trillion, 5.8% of GDP. They are any government action that lowers the cost of producing coal, oil or gas energy, raises producers' prices or lowers consumers' prices. Most of the money supports oil and natural gas. Most are consumption subsidies, such as lower sales tax on home-heating gas, or production subsidies, such as tax breaks for oil exploration. Broad definitions also count letting fuel users pollute the air and warm the climate without paying, an unpriced Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else. In effect these subsidies act as a negative carbon price. They use government money that could be spent on other things. And they are poorly aimed: economists agree the rich get most of the absolute benefit, since the poorest people usually do not own cars. The human cost is large. Subsidies are estimated to cause hundreds of thousands of deaths from air pollution each year. Removing them would cut those health risks and greatly reduce global carbon emissions.

  <!-- nature-pol-197 -->

- **Sustainable procurement: buying for the whole life cycle**

  Public spending averages 12% of GDP in OECD countries and up to 30% in developing countries, which gives governments enormous purchasing power. Firms have similar clout: purchases can exceed 50% of a company's expenses, and over 80% in retail, electronics and cars. Sustainable procurement puts that power to work. It means buying goods, services and works that give value for money over the whole life cycle (Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave). The purchases should also be benefit society and stay within the environment's limits. Procurement has traditionally weighed only price and quality; the sustainable kind adds the third-party effects of buying decisions. It favors renewable or recycled materials and less waste, and checks suppliers for pollution or harm to habitats. It need not cost more. Sustainable options often cost about the same, and even pricier ones can save money through lower energy, water and waste costs over their life.

  <!-- nature-pol-234 -->

- **Extended producer responsibility: makers pay for the waste**

  In a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry, Thomas Lindhqvist first formally put forward a simple idea: make manufacturers pay for what becomes of their products. Extended producer responsibility, or EPR, holds producers responsible for environmental costs across a product's whole life cycle, mainly the cost of dealing with it as waste. The logic is that brand owners control product design, so they are best placed to cut toxicity and waste. Producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products. EPR can take the form of programs for reuse, buyback or Recycling: giving waste a second life, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products. Unlike Product stewardship: everyone shares the responsibility, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of reprocessing into the product price and relieves local governments. The deposit-refund system is described as based on its principles. In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%. A drawback is the administrative burden of rules that differ between countries and waste streams.

  <!-- nature-pol-194 -->

- **Nudges: steering choices without forcing them**

  More consumers chose renewable electricity when it was offered as the default option. That is a nudge at work. Nudge theory, from behavioral science, holds that changing how choices are presented, the Choice architecture: designing how options are presented, can steer behavior without forcing anyone. A nudge alters the setting so that fast, automatic thinking favors the desired choice. That sets it apart from education, legislation or enforcement. Nudges are small, cheap changes; techniques include defaults, social proof and making an option more noticeable. The 2008 book Nudge by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein made the idea popular. In tourism, nudges led people to reuse towels, choose more sustainable hotels and offset their carbon voluntarily. Governments use 'nudge units', such as the British Behavioural Insights Team set up in 2010. Whether nudges really work is disputed. A 2021 meta-analysis found nudging effective, with moderate Publication bias: the missing studies that skew the record. A later correction for that bias found no evidence of an effect.

  <!-- nature-pol-200 -->

- **The Common Agricultural Policy: Europe's farm support**

  Butter mountains and wine lakes: those were the nicknames for the huge surpluses the EU bought and stored under guaranteed prices. They came from the Common Agricultural Policy, the EU's farm policy, introduced in 1962. It runs a system of agricultural subsidies, risk management tools and other programs. Reforms have cut its share of the budget, from 73% in 1985 to 37% in 2017, and added rural development. The 'Agenda 2000' reforms split it into two pillars: production support and rural development. Many interests have criticized it since its start, and even the European Commission acknowledges its defects. Critics say it creates artificially high food prices, helped by import tariffs estimated at 18–28%. Because it has rewarded higher output, larger farms have gained far more from subsidies than smaller ones. A 2024 study reported that 80% of its subsidies in 2013 supported emissions-intensive animal products.

  <!-- nature-pol-213 -->

- **What a subsidy does to a market**

  A subsidy shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy (Supply and demand: the model behind prices). Which curve moves matters. A demand subsidy tends to raise prices, while a supply subsidy can lower them. In a competitive market, a subsidy pushes supply beyond the equilibrium quantity, the point where supply meets demand. The result is Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets: the amount by which the subsidy's cost exceeds its gains, which grows with the subsidy's size. The effects cross borders. Subsidized goods sold abroad lower world prices, hurting producers in poorer countries and causing trade tensions. In 2019 the OECD urged countries to use more environmental taxation and to phase out agricultural subsidies and environmentally harmful tax breaks.

  <!-- nature-pol-207 -->

- **Perverse subsidies: support that harms twice over**

  In 2005 US farmers received $14 billion in agricultural subsidies, and EU farmers $47 billion. Farm subsidies like these often fuel environmental damage, deforestation and Overfishing: taking fish faster than they breed. Perverse subsidies are those whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment. A subsidy rarely starts out perverse. It can become so if it is not withdrawn after reaching its goal. Perverse subsidies drain budgets away from priorities such as conservation, education and health. They cause resource overuse and pollution, and tend to benefit the rich at the expense of the poor. And they are hard to remove, because they become 'locked' into society through bureaucratic roadblocks and institutional inertia.

  <!-- nature-pol-208 -->

- **Tax incentives: encouraging activity through the tax code**

  The hybrid vehicle tax credit is a typical tax incentive: a part of tax policy that encourages a particular economic activity by lowering the tax owed. For individuals, incentives include deductions, exemptions and credits. Conservation projects have traditionally drawn on public money that includes tax incentives. The record is mixed, though. Incentives aimed at single companies are generally seen as inefficient, costly, distorting and regressive, favoring the better-off. A 2020 study found some job gains from US state and local business incentives but no evidence of wider economic growth. Badly designed incentives can harm a government's finances.

  <!-- nature-pol-237 -->

- **Feed-in tariffs: guaranteed prices for clean power**

  As of 2019, more than 50 countries had feed-in tariff policies. A feed-in tariff speeds up investment in renewable energy by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply. It usually guarantees access to the grid and pays prices based on generating costs. Contracts typically run 15–25 years, and the price often falls over time to follow and encourage technology cost cuts. Different technologies get different prices; wind and solar PV, for example, get more per kWh than tidal power. A 2008 European Commission analysis found well-designed feed-in tariffs the most efficient and effective support for renewable electricity. They have a cost. Funded by a surcharge on bills, they added 6.88 cents/kWh for German households in 2017. Yet renewables can also lower spot market prices through the The merit order effect: how wind and sun cut prices, as happened in Spain, Denmark and Germany.

  <!-- nature-pol-224 -->

- **Pollution registers: the public's right to know**

  After the 1984 Bhopal disaster and the 1992 Rio conference, which affirmed people's right to know about toxic chemicals, several countries set up pollutant release and transfer registers. These systems collect and publish information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities. The aim is to give nearby residents the same information as companies, since a level playing field matters for acceptance of permit decisions. A protocol to the The Aarhus Convention: rights to know, speak and sue requires its parties to set up such registers. That 2003 Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on them. The registers have a limit. Their data come mainly from facility questionnaires and remain the facilities' own estimates, even after official checks.

  <!-- nature-pol-232 -->

- **Environmental certification: choosing to be checked**

  Environmental certification is a voluntary form of environmental regulation. A company chooses to meet processes or goals set by a certification service. Most such services have a logo, commonly called an ecolabel, that certified products can carry. It is seen as a form of Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit, letting firms reduce environmental harm by following external, measured objectives. Companies take it up to sell ethical products, improve their image, get on better with stakeholders and earn more profit. Independent checks of their green claims can also shield them from accusations of Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action. The whole system rests on demand. It only works if there are consumers willing to buy the resulting green products, and consumers may be willing to pay extra for ethically produced goods.

  <!-- nature-pol-218 -->

- **ISO 14000: international standards for environmental management**

  As of 2017, there were more than 300,000 ISO 14001 certifications in 171 countries. The ISO 14000 family is a set of international standards for The environmental management system: a firm's green rulebook, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in March 1996. The standards help organizations cut their harm to air, water and land, comply with laws and keep improving. Like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made rather than the product itself. ISO 14001 is the core standard. It sets out a framework for such a system but no required level of environmental performance. The series is voluntary, and certification is done by third parties rather than by ISO itself. Firms that adopt it can cut waste, resource use and operating costs, and may gain a competitive advantage. Its predecessor was BS 7750, published in 1992 as the world's first standard of its kind.

  <!-- nature-pol-229 -->

- **Forest certification: a label for responsibly managed wood**

  About 10% of the world's forest is under at least one certification program. Forest certification is a voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard. An independent body writes the standard, and independent auditors certify forest operations that meet it. Credible programs protect biodiversity and water quality, keep harvests sustainable and require prompt replanting. The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), a collaboration of environmental groups, forest companies and social interests, pioneered third-party certification in the early 1990s. With no single international standard, more than 50 scheme owners now offer certification. The two largest are the FSC and the PEFC, which covers about two-thirds of certified forest area. Critics such as Greenpeace and Jared Diamond question the rigor of rival standards, which some say logging companies set up to confuse consumers. The schemes defend their standards. Demand comes from publishers' paper commitments, green buying by governments, green building standards and laws against Illegal logging: timber taken outside the law.

  <!-- nature-pol-211 -->

- **Fishing subsidies: paying for too many boats**

  In 2002 the WWF estimated that about 75% of the world's major fisheries were overexploited. Fishing subsidies help explain why. They are government support for fishing: direct aid to fishers, loans, tax breaks, infrastructure and price support. These subsidies expand fleets and catches, favoring large-scale operations over small-scale fishers. Together they keep marine fisheries overfished and overcapitalized, holding more boats and gear than the fish can sustain.

  <!-- nature-pol-209 -->

- **Direct or indirect, production or consumption: sorting subsidies**

  Subsidies are sorted in three ways: direct or indirect, production or consumption, and broad or narrow. Direct subsidies are cash outlays to a specific person or household, such as cash grants. Indirect ones include tax breaks and low-interest loans. Production subsidies help suppliers expand output by offsetting costs, while consumption subsidies lower the price consumers pay. Consumption subsidies are most common in developing countries, for basics such as food, water, electricity and education. Broad subsidies are hard to identify and include non-monetary support. Environmental externalities, harms no one pays for, are the most common type.

  <!-- nature-pol-206 -->

- **EMAS: the EU's scheme for environmental management**

  The European Commission developed the Eco-Management and Audit Scheme, or EMAS, in March 1993. It is the EU's voluntary environmental management instrument, open to any type of organization worldwide. It helps organizations assess, manage and keep improving their environmental performance. Registering involves an environmental review, policy, program, management system, internal audit and a public environmental statement. Only accredited independent verifiers supervised by government bodies may validate those statements. Since 2010, registered organizations must report indicators on energy, materials, water, waste, biodiversity and emissions.

  <!-- nature-pol-220 -->

- **Green industrial policy: governments growing clean industries**

  German green industrial policy helped build a renewable energy industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004. Green industrial policy is government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting Market failure: when free markets waste value and moving toward a The low-carbon economy. The case rests on hard beginnings. Green industries such as renewable energy face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable. New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones, because of Path dependence: why history matters, so governments nurture technological niches. Without government intervention, the market is unlikely to make that shift on its own. Subsidies for a targeted sector are the most common form. Other tools include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in tariffs, mandates and green buying by governments.

  <!-- nature-pol-226 -->

- **The Inflation Reduction Act: America's biggest climate law**

  The Inflation Reduction Act, a 2022 United States law, is the largest federal legislation ever to address climate change, mainly through tax credits and grants for clean energy. According to the CBO and JCT, it invests $783 billion in Energy security: when supply becomes a matter of state and climate provisions. Consumers get 10 years of tax credits for heat pumps, rooftop solar and efficient electric heating and cooling. It also created a $27 billion Green banks: public money that draws in private investors, the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, to finance smaller regional ones. After the act, Rhodium Group raised its forecast of 2030 US emission cuts from 17–30% to 29–42% below 2005 levels.

  <!-- nature-pol-231 -->

- **The Toxics Release Inventory: America's pollution register**

  The 1984 Bhopal disaster prompted Congress to create the Toxics Release Inventory in 1986, under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. It is a public US database of toxic chemical releases and waste management activities reported by industrial and federal facilities. For most listed chemicals, a facility must report if it makes 25,000 pounds, or processes or uses 10,000 pounds, a year. Reports cover releases to air, water and land, and amounts of waste sent off-site.

  <!-- nature-pol-233 -->

- **Counting fossil fuel subsidies: why the totals differ**

  In 2021 the UK government said it did not subsidize fossil fuels under the IEA definition, while others said it did under the OECD definition. Estimates add up payments, compare prices with world prices, and may count health and climate damage. Counting unpriced damage makes IMF estimates far larger than those using OECD and International Energy Agency definitions. One IMF paper found underpricing of local air pollution was the largest part of global subsidies, at 42%, followed by global warming costs at 29%. The fiscal cost of government support for fossil fuels was 1.1 trillion USD in 2023, 90% of it tied to consumption.

  <!-- nature-pol-198 -->

- **Rio Principle 15: the precautionary approach**

  Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration says that where serious or irreversible damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures. This precautionary approach is a softer form of the The precautionary principle: caution before proof, one that takes local capabilities and costs into account. Even the label is contested. The United States has opposed the word 'principle' in negotiations, because a principle of law is a source of law. The line between the two terms is described as diffuse and sometimes controversial. The The Cartagena Protocol: rules for moving modified organisms builds on the approach of Principle 15.

  <!-- nature-pol-203 -->

- **Strong and weak precaution**

  Buying a smoke detector or wearing a seatbelt is weak precaution, and people practice it daily. Weak versions of the precautionary principle only permit action without full proof. They allow benefits to be weighed against costs, and economic factors may justify delay. Strong precaution requires regulation whenever harm is possible, even if the evidence is speculative and the economic costs are high. This 'no-regrets' stance ignores cost. The 1982 UN The World Charter for Nature, 1982 gave the strong version its first international recognition.

  <!-- nature-pol-202 -->

- **The precautionary dilemma: trivial or incoherent?**

  A common objection says the precautionary principle is caught in a trap: its weak versions are trivial and its strong versions incoherent. Cass Sunstein argued that the weak version only states a truism. Strong precaution, meanwhile, can itself cause harm, by blocking innovation and keeping current harmful technologies in use. Banning nuclear plants over low-probability risks, for example, means continued reliance on fossil-fuel plants and their air-pollution deaths. Critics conclude that no version is both useful and coherent. Its defenders reject that view.

  <!-- nature-pol-204 -->

- **Plan, Do, Check, Act: the cycle behind ISO 14001**

  ISO 14001 environmental management rests on a four-step cycle: Plan, Do, Check and Act. Planning starts with a review of how the organization's operations interact with the environment, its 'environmental aspects'. In the Check stage, performance is measured against targets and internal audits are held. A management review then resets the targets. Each turn of the cycle feeds a process of continual improvement.

  <!-- nature-pol-230 -->

- **Who writes the rules: consensus standards and private ones**

  Sustainability standards fall into two groups. Voluntary consensus standards come out of an agreed process, as at the International Organization for Standardization. Private standards are written by individual companies for themselves, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices and Nespresso AAA. Some standards were launched by coalitions of firms, NGOs and development agencies to harmonize the rules. The Marine Stewardship Council standard is one.

  <!-- nature-pol-185 -->

- **The ecolabeling cycle: how labels spur green innovation**

  Ecolabeling is a repeating process, not a one-off stamp. Consumers, firms, governments and institutions interact through ecolabels, and the result is eco-innovation. Labeling encourages new green products and improves firms' environmental management strategy. Each turn of the cycle serves every party: consumers' expectations are met, firms gain value, and governments foster cleaner production and consumption.

  <!-- nature-pol-190 -->

- **Ecolabels as regulation without the state**

  At the 1992 Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties, countries agreed to bring environmental issues into manufacturing and to steer consumption toward Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later. Ecolabeling fits that aim. It is a self-regulating, market-based tool that partly takes over from government Command and control: regulating by rule and penalty. The standards are voluntary, but they put market pressure on large companies to adopt greener production. In this way ecolabeling has become a form of non-state authority, at national and international levels.

  <!-- nature-pol-189 -->

- **Can ecolabels become trade barriers?**

  Labels meant to help the planet can also hinder trade. To qualify for a foreign ecolabel, exporters must adjust to each market's production standards, which can cost money, information and expertise. Labeling programs often reflect the importing country's priorities and technologies, and may not fit the exporting country's environment. Hence the concern that ecolabels create obstacles to trade other than tariffs, the taxes on imports. Since 1995 the agreements of the The World Trade Organization: referee of world trade have covered the possible effects of voluntary product standards and labels.

  <!-- nature-pol-188 -->

- **Energy labels: efficiency at a glance**

  The yellow US EnergyGuide label estimates an appliance's energy use, compares it with similar products and lists rough yearly running costs. It is an energy label: a label on a consumer appliance showing whether it uses energy efficiently compared with similar products. Canadian law requires the EnerGuide label on every new electrical appliance made in or imported into Canada. These labels show the energy used in operation. Energy input labeling, by contrast, shows the energy used to make the product.

  <!-- nature-pol-191 -->

- **Energy Star: a small budget, a big claimed payoff**

  Supporters of Energy Star cited estimated yearly energy cost savings of more than $40 billion, against about $32 million in yearly EPA funding. The US Environmental Protection Agency set up this voluntary labeling program in 1992, first for computers and displays. It now covers more than 75 product categories, plus homes, commercial buildings and industrial plants. Before 2011, products qualified on manufacturers' own data, which auditors found open to fraud. Since then independent labs and certifiers must test them. The label shows a product beats minimum guidelines, but it is not always the most efficient option available.

  <!-- nature-pol-217 -->

- **Three types of environmental label**

  The International Organization for Standardization sorts environmental labels into three types, by what they cover and how strictly they are checked. Type I (ISO 14024) is a voluntary label based on many criteria, checked by an independent third party that looks at a product's life cycle impacts. Type II (ISO 14021) is a claim a manufacturer or retailer makes about itself, without third-party auditing. Type III (ISO/TR 14025) declares measured life cycle data. It does not rate the product but helps buyers compare. 'Type I-like' labels cover a single issue, such as a pass/fail energy limit for appliances.

  <!-- nature-pol-187 -->

- **Does fair trade help the farmers?**

  One estimate found US exporters received only 2% of a US$5 per pound retail premium on coffee. Studies disagree on whether fair trade raises producers' incomes and working conditions or mostly benefits intermediaries. A 2015 study found producer benefits close to zero, because of an oversupply of certification. Economists add a market argument. Coffee demand is highly inelastic, barely responding to price (Price elasticity of demand: how buyers react to price), so more fair trade output can push down prices for the many non-certified farmers. Yet a study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found fair trade meets many of its goals, though on a modest scale.

  <!-- nature-pol-223 -->

- **The fair trade premium: money for the community**

  In 2011 Fairtrade International's system paid €65 million in premiums to producers for community development. This social premium is extra money that buyers of fair trade goods pay to producer groups, which decide democratically how to spend it. Under Fairtrade it goes to the cooperative rather than directly to individual producers. Groups often spend it on public goods that government fails to provide, such as environmental projects, schools and water projects.

  <!-- nature-pol-222 -->

- **Energy subsidies: the case for and against**

  Should governments support energy prices or producers? Supporters say subsidies secure domestic supply, cut air pollution, help meet climate pledges, widen access to energy for the poor and protect jobs. Critics say fossil fuel subsidies raise consumption and waste, burden public finances and hold back cleaner technologies. They also miss the poor: in developing countries, most of the benefit goes to the richest 20% of households. The World Bank found subsidies to large energy companies unjustified, but saw a case for helping the poorest households get modern energy. Reform is hard, since many see it as governments taking something away.

  <!-- nature-pol-193 -->

- **Green public procurement: governments buying green**

  Rules can steer public bodies to buy efficient computers, recycled paper, electric vehicles and renewable energy. That is green public procurement, the part of sustainable public procurement that uses government buying power to reach environmental goals. It aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions, improve Resource efficiency: the same output from less and grow the market for greener products, which can drive green innovation. It relies heavily on Life cycle costing: the full price of owning something, which counts transport, installation, training, insurance and running costs as well as the purchase price.

  <!-- nature-pol-235 -->

- **Making electronics makers pay for e-waste**

  E-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash, contains lead, mercury, brominated flame-retardants and cadmium. All are dangerous to health and the environment. Producer responsibility rules tackle it by making producers pay for its Recycling: giving waste a second life. That may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics, so EPR is cited as a tool against Planned obsolescence: built to fail, products built to wear out early. Critics worry it could raise prices, slow innovation, or let manufacturers shred second-hand goods instead of reusing them. Whether it really speeds greener design is disputed.

  <!-- nature-pol-196 -->

- **Take-back programs: returning products to their makers**

  The earliest take-back schemes began in Europe, driven by scarce landfill space and hazardous parts. These waste policies require manufacturers to take back their products at the end of their useful life, or to help pay for collection and reprocessing. They were adopted where collection of hazardous products was lacking or too costly for local governments. The aims are to encourage designs that can be reused or remade, to put waste costs into product prices and to promote innovation in reprocessing.

  <!-- nature-pol-195 -->

- **The CAP's second pillar: money for the countryside**

  Since 2000 the EU farm policy has had a second pillar, which funds the economic, social and environmental development of the countryside. It works through seven-year rural development programs, of which there are 118 in the EU. One of its three axes supports land management that improves the environment and helps fight climate change. Projects can include protecting water quality, sustainable land management and planting trees against erosion and floods.

  <!-- nature-pol-216 -->

- **Paying farmers for conditions, not crops**

  On 26 June 2003 the EU reformed its farm support. It cut the link between subsidies and particular crops, and tied payments to environmental and other conditions. Under cross compliance, farmers who fail the strict environmental requirements face cuts in their subsidies. The aim was to free more money for environmental quality and animal welfare programs. In England, the Single Payment Scheme paid a flat rate of around £230 per hectare for keeping land fit for cultivation.

  <!-- nature-pol-214 -->

- **Hedgerows and birds: the farm policy's environmental record**

  Between 1980 and 2009 the farmland bird population fell from 600 million to 300 million, a loss of 50%. Critics blame EU farm subsidies, which drove a large expansion of production using fertilizers and pesticides. Removing hedgerows and plowing meadows made farming more efficient but cut farmland bird habitat. Reforms since 2004 claim to put the environment at the center of farm policy. In 2010 the EU said 31% of €5 billion for new agricultural challenges would go to protecting biodiversity in the countryside. Yet in 2024 the European Court of Auditors warned the policy was not aligned with the EU's Green Deal climate goals.

  <!-- nature-pol-215 -->

- **Voluntary agreements: environmental action by deal, not decree**

  Since the 1980s many governments have turned from regulation toward 'new' instruments, notably market instruments and voluntary agreements. In a voluntary environmental agreement, firms or other actors agree, without being forced, to take environmental action, often in a deal with government. This differs from command-and-control rules, where authorities dictate the performance or technology required (Command and control: regulating by rule and penalty). In industrial countries, such agreements let companies gain recognition for going beyond minimum regulatory standards. In developing countries such as in Latin America, they are more often used to fix widespread non-compliance with mandatory rules. Some do not last. The EU first tackled car CO2 emissions through a voluntary agreement, and later replaced it with mandatory limits for new cars.

  <!-- nature-pol-238 -->

- **Grid parity: when clean power matches the grid price**

  Grid parity is the point at which electricity from an alternative technology costs the same as the average grid electricity price in an area. It is a moving target: parity can vary over the day, over years and from place to place. In some areas wind, landfill gas and biomass power are already cheaper than grid electricity. Parity has been reached in areas that use feed-in tariffs.

  <!-- nature-pol-225 -->

- **Carbon labels: the emissions behind a product**

  In 2006 the Carbon Trust introduced the first carbon label in the UK, the Carbon Reduction Label. A carbon emission label states the carbon dioxide emitted in making, transporting or disposing of a consumer product, its Carbon footprint: one number for climate impact. Such labels focus on greenhouse gas emissions rather than direct energy use. The Carbon Trust label came with a condition: companies had to commit to cutting the product's embodied carbon or lose the label. The Swiss climatop label works differently. It marks products at least 20% better than others in their category.

  <!-- nature-pol-210 -->

- **Sustainable seafood guides and labels**

  Seafood advisory lists and certification schemes aim to make seafood supply chains transparent and to help shoppers choose seafood from well-managed fish populations. The Marine Stewardship Council, for instance, runs a certification program for consumer seafood products. The economic impact of these schemes is unclear, but they bring non-monetary gains such as better reputation and reorganized supply chains. Their spread has a cost. Many conservationists feel the growing number of seafood labels is confusing consumers.

  <!-- nature-pol-236 -->

- **Chain of custody: tracking certified wood to the shop**

  Between January 2009 and May 2010, PEFC and FSC chain-of-custody certificates rose 88% to 23,717 worldwide. Chain-of-custody certification tracks certified material through every stage of processing and distribution, from the forest to the consumer. It keeps certified material identified or separate from non-certified material during manufacture. That provides evidence that certified material in a product really comes from certified forests.

  <!-- nature-pol-212 -->

- **What environmental certification cannot do**

  Usually only the best-performing operators get certified, so firms with no interest in environmental management stay outside. That is the first limit of voluntary certification. The second is cost. Suppliers usually bear it, and the extra profit often does not cover it. Many certification costs are fixed, so large producers gain an advantage over small ones through economies of scale. The third is reach. Tropical deforestation usually comes from converting forest to other uses, which lies outside Running a forest: the business side of forestry certification.

  <!-- nature-pol-219 -->

- **Local content rules: buy local to qualify**

  Ontario's 2009 Green Energy and Green Economy Act made wind and solar farms use Ontario-made parts to qualify for subsidies. That is a local content requirement: a rule requiring producers to source a minimum share of goods, labor or services locally. The Ontario law created many jobs, cut emissions and greatly expanded the province's renewable energy industry.

  <!-- nature-pol-228 -->

- **Picking winners: the risks of green industrial policy**

  Can governments pick the right firms and industries? Proponents and skeptics of green industrial policy agree there are risks, but disagree on whether governments can choose well enough to justify it. Subsidies are especially prone to Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth, because special interests press to keep them even when they are no longer needed. Support also invites Regulatory capture: when the watchdog serves the watched, and policy may end up driven by political rather than economic concerns. Some failures are inevitable. Governments can reduce the risk by testing policies in parts of the country first.

  <!-- nature-pol-227 -->

### Choosing among instruments

Environmental policy is a government's commitment to deal with environmental problems, but commitment is only the start: it must pick its tools. They come in families: regulation, economic instruments that use prices and markets, and persuasion. Analysts still debate which works best, and whether a pollution tax, fixing the cost of cuts, beats a permit system, fixing the total. Rising costs can even spur firms to invent ways of using less of a costly input. Public choice adds a warning, studying politicians, officials and voters as self-interested actors, some of whom sensibly stay uninformed.

- **Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems**

  In 1863, after harmful chemical releases caused health problems, the UK adopted the Alkali Act and created the Alkali Inspectorate. It was an early example of environmental policy: a commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems. Such policy typically covers air and water pollution, waste, the management of ecosystems, biodiversity, resources from nature and endangered species. Its aim is to steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people. Why should government get involved at all? The usual answer is Market failure: when free markets waste value, such as the free rider problem and the tragedy of the commons. Some problems spur action faster than others. Pollution of air and water tends to move governments more than global warming does, because it causes immediate health problems. Success is judged by how far a policy reduces or solves environmental problems, and whether policies have done so remains debated.

  <!-- nature-pol-018 -->

- **Market-based instruments: using prices to cut pollution**

  David Lloyd George's fuel tax of 1909-1910 may have been Britain's first market-based environmental instrument. Such instruments are policy tools that use markets, prices and other economic signals to give polluters a reason to cut harmful side effects such as pollution. They are also called economic instruments, price-based instruments or new policy instruments for the environment. They tackle the market failure of an Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else in two ways. They charge for external costs through taxes, or they create property rights and a market for using environmental services. Examples include environmental taxes, charges and subsidies, emissions trading, deposit-refund systems, eco-labeling laws and property rights; the EU's emissions trading scheme is one. They differ from voluntary agreements and from command-and-control rules that dictate performance or technology, though they usually still need some regulation. Environmental advocates first opposed them. After successful credit trading in the US lead phasedown, they came to support trading, starting with the acid rain allowance market.

  <!-- nature-pol-027 -->

- **Public choice: politics without romance**

  James Buchanan described public choice as 'politics without romance'. It uses economic tools such as rational choice and Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game to study how politicians, officials and voters behave and interact. It stresses that political agents are self-interested, and that collective decisions combine many individual choices. It doubts that government simply maximizes social welfare. Instead it models officials who may also act for their own benefit, as in the budget-maximizing model of bureaucracy. Duncan Black, sometimes called its founding father, laid the groundwork for median voter theory in papers from 1948 to 1958. Its Nobel laureates include Kenneth Arrow, James Buchanan, George Stigler, Gary Becker, Amartya Sen, Vernon Smith and Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons. It has critics. Steven Pressman argues it fails to explain key political behavior, such as why politicians vote against their constituents' interests, or indeed why people vote.

  <!-- nature-pol-030 -->

- **Rules, prices and persuasion: the three families of policy tools**

  Governments carry out environmental policy with three main families of tools: regulation, economic instruments and persuasion. Regulation sets rules, often backed by law, that ban, require or limit behavior. Pollution limits and bans on hazardous substances are examples. Critics call it a top-down 'command and control' approach, because it leaves little choice in how goals are met. Economic instruments work through incentives instead: taxes, fees, subsidies, and markets for trading rights in pollutants or resources such as SO2, CO2, water and fishing quotas. They assume people act mainly from rational self-interest, a premise that studies of decision-making cast doubt on. The third family, normative or 'hortatory' instruments, relies on persuasion and information. Awareness campaigns and voluntary agreements with businesses belong here.

  <!-- nature-pol-019 -->

- **Which tool works best? The instrument debate**

  Market instruments are often promoted as a more efficient, cost-effective alternative to regulation. Not everyone is convinced. Many analysts argue that regulation, incentives, market instruments, taxes and subsidies can achieve the same results. Kemp and Pontoglio found no evidence that market-based approaches are better for eco-innovation, and some evidence that regulation spurs more radical innovation. Hahn called the performance of economic instruments 'not very impressive', and Tietenberg concluded they are 'no panacea'. Efficiency is not the only test. Instruments differ in how costs and benefits are shared, so distributional, ethical and political aspects matter too. That helps explain some choices. Tradeable permits handed to resource users are generally preferred by affected industries, which helps explain their popularity since the rise of neoliberalism. Analysts still disagree whether market instruments are truly more efficient and innovation-friendly, or simply spread costs differently.

  <!-- nature-pol-020 -->

- **Taxes or tradable permits: price certainty versus quantity certainty**

  A pollution tax fixes the cost of cutting pollution; a tradable permit system fixes the total amount allowed. Each choice has consequences. A permit system sets a cap and is likely to reach it more cheaply than other means, possibly undershooting it as technology improves. A tax has no cap. The pollution cut depends on the rate chosen, which can be adjusted until the incentive works best. Taxes have lower compliance costs than permits but are less reliable at hitting a target quantity. Tax revenue can be used to cut other distorting taxes, a possible 'double dividend', though less pollution also means less revenue. Permits can be auctioned or handed out free by grandfathering. Critics say formal emission rights amount to a license to pollute.

  <!-- nature-pol-028 -->

- **Induced innovation: expensive inputs spur new inventions**

  John Hicks proposed an idea in The Theory of Wages in 1932. When one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it. This is induced innovation. The classic illustration is higher wages encouraging labor-saving inventions. The idea has been applied to rising energy costs speeding up energy efficiency. Global GDP and CO2 emissions grew together until the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises cut consumption. After the oil shock, investment in alternative energy, efficient cars and heating meant CO2 grew more slowly than GDP, even after petrol prices fell in the 1980s. Farming shows the same pattern: when scarce inputs such as land rise in price, farmers seek technologies that use more abundant inputs instead. Not every model captures it. The DICE climate model treats innovation as external, so it leaves out induced technological change.

  <!-- nature-pol-026 -->

- **Environmental policy analysis: three ways to study policy**

  Environmental policy analysis is the academic study of how environmental policies are made, how well they work and how they could be improved. It has three main approaches. The analycentric or rational approach uses mainly quantitative methods to find the most cost-effective solution, favoring tools such as cost-benefit analysis, taxes and tradable permits. The policy process approach stresses politics and power, tracing steps from agenda setting through implementation to evaluation. The meta-policy approach studies how institutions, culture, economic systems and discourses shape policymaking.

  <!-- nature-pol-022 -->

- **Environmental policy integration: the environment in every policy**

  Transport, farming and trade policies all affect the environment. Environmental policy integration holds that policies in every area should take account of their effects on the environment and on other areas. The idea has been discussed since the 1980s, under names such as policy mainstreaming, policy coordination and holistic governance.

  <!-- nature-pol-023 -->

- **Implicit carbon prices: charging for carbon without saying so**

  Almost every country taxes gasoline, but only 39 have explicit carbon pricing. A fuel tax is an implicit carbon price.
