An efficient baseline assumes all resources are used efficiently, so the cost per unit cut can be high while the total cost stays low.

  <!-- nature-clim-238 -->

- **Forest reference levels: the benchmark for REDD+ results**

  A country claiming REDD+ results must first say what its forests would have emitted anyway. Its forest reference emission level is that benchmark, measured in tonnes of CO2e per year. Emissions and removals in the results period are compared with the reference period to measure performance. Reference levels usually combine historical data on changes in forest area with emission estimates. Each one submitted for results-based payments gets a UN technical assessment, and countries may improve them step by step. Choices of reference period, data, activities and carbon pools change how many results are counted. A simple projection of past forest loss has a perverse edge: it could tempt countries to clear more during the reference period to earn more credits later. Nesting links project baselines with these national levels to avoid counting the same cut twice.

  <!-- nature-mkt-113 -->

- **Forward crediting: selling cuts that have not happened yet**

  Forward crediting issues carbon credits for emission cuts or removals that are only projected, so buyers can claim them before the work is done. The practice is generally seen as risky and as producing lower-quality credits.

  <!-- nature-mkt-085 -->

- **The Gold Standard: credits with development benefits**

  In 2003 WWF and partners created the Gold Standard to make sure carbon credits are real, verifiable and help development that lasts. It is a certification label for emission-reduction projects in the Clean Development Mechanism and the voluntary carbon market. Projects must prove additionality, avoid double certification and contribute to at least three of the UN's The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals for 2030. Eligible types are renewable energy, energy efficiency, planting and replanting forests, and agriculture. The The Integrity Council and the quality of carbon credits lists it as eligible for its quality label.

  <!-- nature-mkt-091 -->

- **Markets or funds: the early fight over paying for REDD+**

  Should forests be saved by selling credits or by public money? Early in REDD+, countries and observers split over offset-based versus fund-based designs. Critics of the market route argued that floods of forest credits could depress carbon prices and weaken incentives to cut emissions at home. The UN settled on a compromise. Since the COP 17 climate conference, its decisions allow REDD+ to be financed by both market and non-market sources.

  <!-- nature-mkt-100 -->

- **The five activities REDD+ counts**

  REDD+ counts five kinds of action: reducing deforestation, reducing forest degradation, conserving forest carbon, managing forests sustainably, and enhancing the carbon forests hold. Together they cover avoiding forest loss, avoiding decline in forest condition, keeping the carbon already stored, and managing forests to sustain them. Enhancement means raising the carbon stored in forests over time, through replanting or natural regrowth. Logging done with less damage to the remaining forest can count as sustainable management.

  <!-- nature-mkt-093 -->

- **REDD+ in phases: getting ready before getting paid**

  REDD+ moves in stages: readiness, then national policies and measures, then fully measured actions paid by results. Readiness covers national strategies, monitoring capacity, reference levels, safeguards and the participation of stakeholders. It has been funded by bodies such as the UN-REDD Programme, set up by UNDP, UNEP and FAO, and the World Bank's The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility: the World Bank's REDD+ fund. Sources date UN-REDD to 2007 or 2008. Norway's International Climate and Forest Initiative, announced in 2007, has funded forest programs including Brazil's Amazon Fund.

  <!-- nature-mkt-094 -->

- **Forest inventories: counting the trees**

  In late 18th-century Europe, fear that wood, the main fuel, would run out drove people to start counting trees systematically. A forest inventory collects data about a forest, such as its trees, timber and wildlife, for assessment or analysis. Measurements include species, trunk diameter at breast height, height, site quality, age and defects. From these come trees per acre, basal area, timber volume and value. Today ground inventories are combined with satellite images in national forest monitoring for REDD+.

  <!-- nature-mkt-111 -->

- **National forest monitoring: watching forests from space and ground**

  Between 2005 and 2020, the number of countries with good satellite monitoring of their forests rose from 55 to 99. Those with good national forest inventories rose from 48 to 102. A national forest monitoring system is a country's institutions and techniques for tracking its forests and producing information for decisions and reporting. REDD+ countries are encouraged to build transparent systems that combine Remote sensing: watching Earth from above with ground inventories. The outputs include time series of forest area and change, maps, and estimates of biomass or stored carbon with their uncertainty. Having such a system, along with an assessed reference level, is a condition for results-based payments. Steady funding, coordination across agencies and consistent methods over time remain challenges.

  <!-- nature-mkt-114 -->

- **HFC-23: the offset that paid to make pollution**

  HFC-23, a by-product of making refrigerants, warms the climate 11,000 times more than CO2. Under the Clean Development Mechanism, destroying one tonne earned 11,000 credits. Destruction cost only 0.2–0.5 €/tCO2, while buyers paid around 20 €/tCO2. By June 2013, 23 such projects had received 38% of all credits issued. The EU banned HFC-23 credits from its trading system from 1 May 2013, citing perverse incentives and a lack of additionality. Critics condemned the windfall profits. The Carbon Trust argued that criticizing the scheme for finding cheap reductions was itself perverse.

  <!-- nature-mkt-107 -->

- **The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility: the World Bank's REDD+ fund**

  The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility is a World Bank fund that helps developing countries prepare for and carry out REDD+. Approved in 2007 and working from 2008, it reached roughly US$650 million after new pledges in January 2013. A Readiness Fund pays for preparation. A Carbon Fund pilots payments for verified cuts in forest emissions, made only after independent validation and verification. Early reviews found readiness grants slow and private investment in the Carbon Fund lower than hoped.

  <!-- nature-mkt-101 -->

- **Timber cruises: sampling a forest's wood**

  Nobody measures every tree in a stand. A timber cruise is a sample survey that estimates how much standing timber a forest stand holds. Measurements are taken in sample plots, usually laid out at random along survey lines. The most common design first groups the stand by age, soil or slope, then samples within each group. The number and size of plots set how certain the estimate for the whole stand is.

  <!-- nature-mkt-112 -->

- **Safeguards information systems: proving the rules are kept**

  A promise to respect safeguards means little without evidence. A safeguards information system is how a country reports that the Cancún safeguards are addressed and respected while REDD+ is carried out. It should give transparent, consistent and regularly updated information, run nationally and build on existing systems. Countries send periodic summaries on all the safeguards, which they need when seeking results-based payments. Indonesia's reporting separates safeguards being addressed, with policies in place, from being respected, with evidence that they work.

  <!-- nature-mkt-109 -->

- **The investigations into Verra's rainforest credits**

  On January 18, 2023, an investigation reported that about 94% of Verra rainforest credits did not represent a real tonne of CO2e. It found deforestation threats overstated by 400% on average. Earlier, a 2021 study had found that 11 of 12 projects examined showed no difference in emissions from control areas. The 2023 investigation drew on one peer-reviewed study and one not yet published or peer-reviewed, so how far its findings reach across the whole standard is disputed. Verra's chief executive resigned in May 2023 after months of criticism.

  <!-- nature-mkt-103 -->

- **The New York Declaration on Forests**

  In 2014, 37 governments, 53 multinational companies, 16 Indigenous groups and 63 NGOs signed the New York Declaration on Forests. The voluntary, non-binding pledge aimed to halve deforestation by 2020 and end it by 2030. It also pledged to restore hundreds of millions of acres of degraded land. A 2019 five-year assessment described large commitments but limited progress.

  <!-- nature-mkt-115 -->

- **The time value of carbon: why sooner cuts count more**

  Two paths can reach zero emissions on the same date yet put very different totals into the air: early deep cuts emit least, delayed cuts most. The time value of carbon holds that cutting a tonne now is worth more than cutting it later. Emissions are discounted over time, like money in Discounting: paying to put off a payment. This rate applies to the physical carbon itself, not to the money discount rate used to appraise projects. A high carbon discount rate rewards early cuts; a low one weakens the push to act now. If the time value is positive, even temporary storage in trees or soil has real value, because it delays warming.

  <!-- nature-mkt-116 -->

- **Corresponding adjustments: stopping two countries claiming one cut**

  When one country sells an emission cut to another, both might be tempted to count it. An accounting step under the The Paris Agreement: every country pledges prevents that double claiming. It subtracts the transferred cut from the seller's tally so that only the buyer counts it toward its national target. Each transfer is recorded as a gain for one party and a reduction for the other. Rules adopted at the COP26 conference set out how this works in practice. If a host government authorizes voluntary-market credits for use under Article 6, this adjustment may be required.

  <!-- nature-mkt-118 -->

- **Over-crediting: more credits than cuts**

  Over-crediting means issuing more carbon credits than the real cuts or removals a project achieved, sometimes producing so-called phantom credits. One estimate held that about 90% of rainforest credits under the Verified Carbon Standard were likely phantom. Perverse incentives can reward it when buyers focus on headline tonnes rather than real impact. Critics note it persisted even where programs already applied rules on additionality, cautious measurement and permanence, often through inflated baselines. The risk is a central worry for trading under Article 6 of the Paris climate treaty, though commentators dispute how much it undermines those markets.

  <!-- nature-mkt-117 -->

### Finance for conservation

Protecting land, water and wildlife costs money, and conservation finance is the business of raising and managing it. This chapter starts with the basic tools of finance: bonds, which are loans in tradable form, shares of company stock, and return on investment, the profit an investment earns against its cost. It then follows how those tools, along with foreign aid, are bent toward nature. Debt-for-nature swaps cancel part of a poor country's foreign debt in return for local conservation. Blended finance uses public and charitable money to draw private investors in, and every investor is told to spread money across many assets so that no single loss does too much harm.

- **Bonds: lending money in a form that can be sold**

  Governments, banks, companies and international institutions all borrow by selling bonds. A bond is a loan in the form of a tradable security. The issuer borrows money and promises to pay the holder Interest: the price of waiting for your money and repay the principal, the sum borrowed. Interest is usually paid at fixed intervals, often every six months or every year. The interest rate the issuer pays is the coupon, which can be fixed or float with a reference rate. Bonds fund borrowers' long-term investments or, for governments, current spending. Unlike shares, bonds usually have a fixed term, or maturity, and most last less than 30 years. Bondholders are lenders, while stockholders are owners, so bondholders are repaid first if a company goes bankrupt. Most bonds are bought by institutions such as pension funds and insurers.

  <!-- nature-mkt-065 -->

- **Return on investment: what you get back for what you put in**

  Return on investment, or ROI, is the ratio of the profit an investment earns to what it cost. A simple form takes the gain from the investment, subtracts its cost, and divides by the cost. Suppose $10,000 is invested plus $200 in fees, and after a year it is worth $12,500 with $300 in dividends: those figures give the year's return. A high ROI means the gains compare well with the cost. It is used to judge one investment or to compare several, and the highest is usually chosen first. It has two blind spots. It is not adjusted for time, so long-term investments need a discounted version based on Net present value: future money in today's terms. Traditional ROI also ignores the value and risks of natural and social capital, because it leaves out environmental, social and governance performance.

  <!-- nature-mkt-069 -->

- **Stock: owning a slice of a company**

  Buy one share and you own a fraction of a company. Stock is all the shares into which a company's ownership is divided. A share usually entitles its holder to part of the company's earnings, a vote, and part of what is left after debts if the company is wound up. Common stock usually carries votes; preferred stock usually does not, but gets dividends first. A company selling shares to the public on a stock exchange for the first time makes an initial public offering, or IPO. Raising money this way is equity financing. Issuing bonds is debt financing, which avoids giving up ownership. A share's price at any moment is set by supply and demand. Shareholders stand behind creditors in any claim on the company's assets.

  <!-- nature-mkt-076 -->

- **Environmental finance: making investment less harmful to nature**

  In 1992 Richard Sandor proposed a course on emission markets at the University of Chicago, later called Environmental Finance. The field it named is a branch of finance that uses market-based environmental policy tools, such as pricing and trading schemes, to make investment less harmful to nature. It seeks to move business resources toward sustainable investments while keeping profits. Inspired by the idea of social cost, Sandor focused on cap-and-trade along with taxes and subsidies. Under cap-and-trade, a total emissions cap is set, and firms receive permits they can buy or sell, rewarding cuts and penalizing excess. Investors gained new yardsticks too: the Dow Jones Sustainability Index, launched in 1999, rates the ecological and social impact of stocks. Money for climate is one part of the field. It splits into finance for cutting emissions, which takes over 90% of climate spending, and finance for adapting to change.

  <!-- nature-mkt-055 -->

- **Official development assistance: the measure of foreign aid**

  In 2019 rich countries gave US$168 billion in official development assistance, or ODA, of which US$152 billion came from donors in the OECD's Development Assistance Committee. ODA is the OECD's measure of foreign aid: money that rich countries' governments give to promote poorer countries' development and welfare. The committee adopted the concept in 1969. Most of it is grants, but loans on easy terms count if at least 25% of their value is effectively a gift. In 2019, 28% was pooled through bodies such as the EU, the World Bank's IDA and UN agencies. It is also a channel for public conservation money, through grants, cheap loans and technical help. Critics call it an untidy, somewhat arbitrary category that counts spending mainly benefiting donors, such as refugee costs at home. In 2025 aid from committee donors fell 23% after inflation, the biggest yearly drop on record.

  <!-- nature-mkt-056 -->

- **The economics of biodiversity: how life props up the economy**

  The WWF's 2018 Living Planet Report argued that the whole global economy, worth US$125 trillion, ultimately relies on nature. The economics of biodiversity studies that dependence, and the harm economic activity does in return. Biodiversity underpins ecosystem services and affects how productive ecosystems are. It supplies food, medicines and industrial materials such as wood, cotton, wool and silk, and it supports recreation and tourism. It inspires design too. Biomimetics copies natural models, as when the ridges on humpback whale fins inspired wind turbine blades. Yet most species have never been assessed for their present or future economic importance. Economists still debate whether biodiversity should be valued mainly for its benefits to people, and what its value in itself might be.

  <!-- nature-hist-027 -->

- **Conservation finance: raising money to protect nature**

  Conservation has traditionally been paid for by donations, foundation grants and government money, from tax incentives and ballot measures to bonds and agency budgets. Supporters of conservation finance argue that this falls far short. One widely cited estimate put yearly needs in the hundreds of billions of dollars, far above actual flows. Conservation finance is the raising and managing of money to protect land, water and other resources nature provides. It draws on public, private and nonprofit money at local to national scales, using tools from loans and grants to tax breaks and market-based mechanisms. It is sometimes set apart from fundraising. Fundraising gathers money that is never paid back, while conservation finance uses a wider set of tools to put capital to work for conservation results. To close the gap it tries to tap financial markets, through debt, tax benefits, private equity and project finance. Deals are usually built around a clear source of cash flow or budget that can pay for conservation over time. The early tools were Debt-for-nature swaps: trading debt for conservation in the 1980s, followed by approaches such as payments for ecosystem services. By the mid-2000s it was described as a distinct field. Recent analyses stress drawing in private capital through labeled bonds and Blended finance: using public money to draw in private investors.

  <!-- nature-mkt-012 -->

- **Debt-for-nature swaps: trading debt for conservation**

  In 1987 Conservation International bought US$650,000 of Bolivian debt for just US$100,000, in return for conservation commitments. It was the first debt-for-nature swap. Such a swap forgives part of a developing country's foreign debt, and in exchange the country invests locally in conservation. Thomas Lovejoy of WWF proposed the idea that same year, after the Latin American debt crisis had cut indebted countries' ability to fund conservation. Swaps work where the risk of default is high, so funders can buy debt well below its face value. The government then pays for conservation in its own currency. Most swaps happen in tropical, species-rich countries with rapid deforestation and fairly stable politics. Since 1987 they have generated over US$1 billion for conservation. They have grown rarer, falling from about five a year around 1990 to about two a year after 2000, partly because commercial debt became pricier. Their experience shaped later tools such as Conservation trust funds: money that lasts.

  <!-- nature-mkt-037 -->

- **Blended finance: using public money to draw in private investors**

  A $2 million layer of public or charitable money that draws in $10 million of private money multiplies it 5x. That is blended finance: using development and charitable funds strategically to attract private investment into developing countries. Public and private funds are mixed in one deal, each party using its expertise. The concessional money takes the first losses, which reassures private investors that their principal is protected. Each concessional dollar often attracts 3x to 10x as much private money. The target is the UN's The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals for 2030, which in 2017 estimates needed an extra $2.5 trillion a year. The OECD's aid committee adopted blended finance principles in 2018. It found 180 funds and facilities with $60.2 billion invested across 111 developing countries. In conservation, the approach helps overcome risk, small deal sizes and transaction costs that deter private investors. Critics, including scholars and NGOs, say it shifts profits to private, mostly Northern, investors while leaving risks with Southern governments. They add that its complexity weakens transparency.

  <!-- nature-mkt-049 -->

- **Diversification: not putting all your eggs in one basket**

  'Don't put all your eggs in one basket' sums up diversification: more risk of losing one egg, less of losing them all. It means spreading money across different investments so that no single asset or risk can do too much harm. A single stock can fall 50% in a year. If prices do not move in perfect step, a diversified portfolio varies less than the average of its parts. It narrows the range of outcomes: returns never beat the best single asset nor fall below the worst. A little goes a long way. A 1977 study found that 30 stocks gave almost the same risk reduction as 1,000, and even four gave most of it. The protection has a weak spot. Prices tend to move together in crises, just when investors need diversification most.

  <!-- nature-mkt-073 -->

- **Trophy hunting: can killing animals save them?**

  After South Africa legalized white rhino hunting, landowners reintroduced the species, and numbers rose from under one hundred to more than 11,000. Trophy hunting is hunting for sport in which parts of the animal, such as the head, horns or hide, are kept and displayed. Supporters say it gives economic reasons to conserve wildlife areas: 'if it pays it stays'. Poorly managed, it can upset age and sex structures, disrupt social groups and cause declines. Opponents call it immoral and say little money reaches local people.

  <!-- nature-mkt-064 -->

- **Fiduciaries: managing money in someone else's interest**

  Trustees, financial advisers and the managers of pension funds and endowments are all fiduciaries. A fiduciary is a person trusted to look after money or other assets for someone else and to act only in that person's interest. A fiduciary must not let personal interest conflict with duty, nor profit from the position without informed consent. Under Delaware law, which governs most large US firms, company directors owe duties of care, loyalty and good faith.

  <!-- nature-mkt-071 -->

- **Why the economy keeps eating into biodiversity**

  Failing to halt the loss of biodiversity on land between 2000 and 2010 was estimated to cost the global economy $500 billion. Economic activities often harm biodiversity, and because they make profits, they are usually favored over conservation and restoration. The main causes are habitat loss, changes in land use, pollution and overexploitation, meaning taking too much. BCG estimates that over 90% of human drivers of the loss come from agriculture, infrastructure, fashion and energy. The IUCN estimates that 79% of threatened species are affected by agriculture, infrastructure, energy and mining. Continued loss raises long-term risks such as pandemics, floods and droughts.

  <!-- nature-mkt-029 -->

- **Bond credit quality: will the borrower pay?**

  A bond is only as good as the borrower behind it. Credit quality is how likely the borrower is to pay the promised amounts on time rather than default. Credit rating agencies grade bonds, and high-yield bonds are rated below investment grade. Because they are riskier, investors expect a higher yield from them.

  <!-- nature-mkt-067 -->

- **Bond yield: the return a bond pays**

  When market interest rates rise, bond prices fall. Yield explains why. A bond's yield is the rate of return an investor earns from it. Current yield is the yearly interest divided by the bond's market price. Yield to maturity estimates the total return from buying at today's price and holding to the end, counting the present value of all payments. Because the payments are fixed, yield and price move in opposite directions.

  <!-- nature-mkt-066 -->

- **Types of bonds**

  Bonds are grouped by who issues them, their currency, their term and the conditions attached. Government or treasury bonds are issued by national governments; the safest, risk-free bonds pay the lowest interest. Bonds under five years are often called short, 5 to 15 years medium, and over 15 years long. Fixed-rate bonds pay a constant coupon, while floating rate notes pay a coupon linked to a reference rate. Convertible bonds can be swapped for the issuer's shares, mixing debt and ownership.

  <!-- nature-mkt-068 -->

- **Additionality, leakage and permanence: three tests of paid conservation**

  Paying for conservation raises three awkward questions. Would the result have happened anyway? Did the harm simply move? Will the gain last? The first is additionality: whether a financed action achieves conservation that would not have happened without the payment. The second is leakage, or spillover, when protecting one place pushes damaging activity to another and cuts the net benefit. The third is permanence. Worries arise wherever results depend on people keeping agreements over long periods. Durability then depends on contract length, enforcement, pressure on the land, and whether behavior persists after payments stop. All three rest on baselines and counterfactuals, which are hard to set in practice, and that weakens claims of impact.

  <!-- nature-mkt-015 -->

- **Return on integration: counting nature in the bottom line**

  Return on integration widens return on investment to count an investment's long-term environmental and social returns alongside its financial ones. The The social cost of carbon: pricing one more ton can be built in to capture the damage an investment's emissions do to society. The method supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, which combine financial, environmental and social results in one balance sheet. A related method, social return on investment, measures environmental and social value that ordinary accounts do not show.

  <!-- nature-mkt-070 -->

- **Tax breaks for giving up development rights**

  In the United States, a landowner who donates a qualifying Conservation easements: protection that runs with the land can earn federal income tax deductions and other tax breaks. The donation's value is the drop in the property's market value that the easement causes, set by a qualified appraiser. To qualify, the easement must be perpetual, held by a qualified public or nonprofit body, and serve a real conservation purpose. Easements can also cut estate taxes, since heirs pay on farmland value rather than development value. Some states give tax credits, and Colorado and Virginia let landowners sell them to others.

  <!-- nature-mkt-035 -->

- **Buying conservation easements outright**

  Not every easement is a gift. Governments, nonprofits and donors often buy conservation easements outright, paying landowners directly. The US Farm Bill is a key funder; in 2014 it created the Agricultural Conservation Easement Program for farmland and wetlands. States commonly pay for conservation through real estate transfer taxes, bonds and lottery proceeds. Many states and counties also run programs to buy farm easements that keep farmland from development.

  <!-- nature-mkt-036 -->

- **The 0.7% aid target that few countries meet**

  The best-known aid target says rich countries should give 0.7% of their national income as official development assistance. The UN General Assembly formalized it on 24 October 1970. Sweden and the Netherlands first met it in 1974, and few others have since. Donors in the OECD aid committee have given around 0.3-0.35% of their income as a group since the 1970s. In 2019 six countries met the target, and the UK cut its aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of income in 2021.

  <!-- nature-mkt-057 -->

- **Tied aid: help that must be spent at home**

  Tied aid is aid given on condition that the money is spent on goods from the donor country or a small group of countries. Its legitimacy has long been disputed within the OECD's aid committee, which has set targets to reduce it. The official figures may understate it. A review found that in 2009, 51% of contract value was spent in donor countries, though donors reported only 14% of aid as tied.

  <!-- nature-mkt-058 -->

- **The case against debt-for-nature swaps**

  Supporters describe debt-for-nature swaps as deals in which every party wins. Critics disagree. The debt relieved is under 1% of total foreign debt, even in countries that use swaps often. Early on, nearly three-quarters of swap money went to Costa Rica, while Brazil, despite rapid deforestation, took little part. Early swaps also often overlooked the people living on the land set aside, and some were labeled eco-colonialism.

  <!-- nature-mkt-039 -->

- **Three kinds of debt-for-nature swap**

  Debt-for-nature swaps come in three kinds. In a commercial three-party swap, an NGO buys debt from commercial banks on the secondary market and hands it to the debtor in return for conservation commitments. In a bilateral swap, a creditor country forgives part of another government's debt in exchange for environmental commitments. Multilateral swaps involve several parties. From 1987-2010, recorded three-party swaps raised nearly US$140 million for conservation, and bilateral and multilateral swaps nearly US$900 million.

  <!-- nature-mkt-038 -->

- **Farm biodiversity: the root of every crop**

  Every crop and farm animal began in biodiversity. Agricultural biodiversity is all the parts of biodiversity that matter for food and farming. It earns income through food and raw materials, and through services farms need, such as pollination, pest control, nutrient cycling and climate regulation. Around 25% of the world's people are estimated to work in agriculture, and by 2006 over 3 billion people depended on marine and coastal biodiversity for their livelihoods. Putting a money value on biodiversity in farming and wild food is both hard and controversial.

  <!-- nature-mkt-024 -->

- **Medicines from nature**

  Over 40% of pharmaceutical products come from nature, and 70% of all cancer drugs are natural products or inspired by them. Biodiversity is a source of medicines and of ecosystem services that protect health. Two drugs against malaria show the link: quinine comes from Cinchona bark and artemisinin from sweet wormwood. For many people the connection is direct. Over 60% of the world's population still relies on herbal medicine as its main health care.

  <!-- nature-mkt-026 -->

- **Nature tourism: wildlife as a money earner**

  The global ecotourism market was estimated at US$216.49 billion in 2023. Biodiversity earns money through recreation and tourism, such as hiking, fishing and wildlife watching, a cultural ecosystem service. Tourism as a whole accounts for 10% of the global job market. It also harms biodiversity, through habitat destruction and pollution, which led to the rise of sustainable tourism.

  <!-- nature-mkt-027 -->

- **Natural pest control and the cane toad warning**

  Biological pest control uses natural enemies to keep pests down, an ecosystem function that depends on biodiversity. Control species can cut crop losses without the harms of chemical pesticides, which brings economic benefits. Done carelessly, it backfires. Cane toads brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles became an invasive species.

  <!-- nature-mkt-025 -->

- **How blended finance lowers investors' risk**

  Development funders support private investors in blended deals in three main ways. Technical assistance uses grants to build investees' skills and lower transaction costs. Guarantees, insurance and concessional tranches, slices of a deal on generous terms, reduce risks such as currency swings, political instability and default. Market incentives make up the third. Because concessional money is meant to spark investment rather than keep flowing, it can be recycled into new projects once investors gain confidence.

  <!-- nature-mkt-050 -->

- **The illegal wildlife trade: a $23 billion business**

  The Zoological Society of London estimates the illegal wildlife trade is worth $23 billion a year. The trade profits by selling products from wild animals and plants, including endangered species. Demand comes partly from culture, such as bushmeat and traditional medicine, while criminal and terrorist groups use trafficking to raise money. It drives population declines, extinctions, loss of genetic diversity, and the spread of disease and alien species.

  <!-- nature-mkt-028 -->

- **Risks you can spread away, and risks you cannot**

  Some risk can be spread away and some cannot. Diversifiable risk comes from a single company. Systematic, or market, risk affects all assets. Holding one stock carries both company-specific risk and market risk. Buying all S&P 500 stocks leaves only the risk of the index moving. The company-specific part shrinks as more stocks are held, which is why it is called diversifiable.

  <!-- nature-mkt-074 -->

- **The math of diversification**

  Mixing assets can bring a portfolio's variance, a measure of risk, below that of even its least risky asset. Markowitz's 1952 mean-variance framework showed that portfolio risk depends on how returns move together, not just on each asset's own variance. Take a fraction q in asset X and 1-q in an unrelated asset Y. The portfolio's variance is q²σx² + (1-q)²σy². It is lowest at q = σy²/(σx²+σy²), giving σx²σy²/(σx²+σy²), which is below either asset held alone.

  <!-- nature-mkt-075 -->

- **Land trusts: holding land for a purpose**

  Land trusts date back at least to Roman times, but their clearest history begins in Henry VIII's England. They are nonprofit or fiduciary arrangements that own and manage land, and sometimes water. The three common types are real estate investment trusts, community land trusts for affordable housing, and trusts that protect nature. In Australia, Aboriginal land trusts hold freehold title to land on behalf of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

  <!-- nature-mkt-051 -->

- **Conservation land trusts: private groups that protect land**

  The Trustees of Reservations in Massachusetts, founded in 1891, was the first conservation land trust; by 2021 the US had over 1,300. Such a trust is a nonprofit that buys and looks after land, or holds conservation easements on it, to protect nature, farmland or recreation. Trusts rely on donations, grants and public programs, and landowners often donate easements or land. Many run on volunteers: in 2005, 54% of US land trusts were all-volunteer. Local and regional US trusts protected almost 9.4 million acres by 2003, double the 1998 figure.

  <!-- nature-mkt-054 -->

- **Natural Asset Companies: selling shares in nature**

  A Natural Asset Company is a corporation set up to hold and manage natural assets so that private investors can fund conservation and land use that restores nature. Each holds rights to land or sea areas, such as forests, ranches, grasslands or marine areas, and is run to maximize their ecological value. The New York Stock Exchange proposed listing them in 2021 but withdrew in January 2024 amid political backlash. Critics on the right fear locked-up public land and speculation; critics on the left doubt markets can be trusted to look after nature.

  <!-- nature-mkt-033 -->

- **Conservation trust funds: money that lasts**

  Short-term grants struggle to pay the running costs of a nature reserve year after year. A conservation trust fund is built for that job. It is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work. Many are endowments that live off their returns; others are spent down over time. Such funds help pay for managing land set aside for nature. Experience with debt-for-nature swaps helped shape them.

  <!-- nature-mkt-014 -->

- **Measuring what conservation money achieves**

  Conservation finance deals often require reporting both how money was spent and what ecological results it achieved. Reports may separate outputs, such as area under management, from outcomes, such as changes in ecological condition. The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures recommends reporting how a business depends on and affects nature, though gaps in data limit consistency. Payment schemes also raise questions of fairness: who can be paid, how schemes affect who holds land and how people live, and whether wealthier landholders benefit most.

  <!-- nature-mkt-017 -->

- **Where conservation money comes from**

  Money for nature comes from three broad sources: domestic public spending, international public finance including aid, and private spending and investment. Market-rate capital can come from private investors, and from public or charitable investors working through development finance institutions and multilateral development banks. Conservation NGOs and foundations often act as go-betweens that run projects. That creates a counting problem. Because NGOs get much of their income from governments and foundations, adding up total conservation finance risks counting the same money twice. Public and charitable money is sometimes called catalytic: it covers early costs or shares risk so that private investment follows.

  <!-- nature-mkt-013 -->

- **Transaction costs: the hidden price of conservation deals**

  Finding, assembling, checking, contracting and monitoring a conservation project all cost money. These Transaction costs: the price of making a deal are often cited as a barrier to scaling up conservation finance. They bite hardest where projects are small, varied, or need intensive monitoring and verification. They can make projects less attractive to investors and raise the cost of capital. A debt-for-nature swap, for example, needs coordination among debtor governments, creditors and NGOs.

  <!-- nature-mkt-016 -->

- **Catastrophe bonds: investors who bet against disaster**

  Hurricane Andrew and the Northridge earthquake prompted the first catastrophe bonds in the mid-1990s. Such a bond moves a defined disaster risk from a sponsor, usually an insurer, to investors. If the named disaster happens, the principal goes to the sponsor to fund recovery; otherwise investors get it back at maturity, plus interest. Rising climate-related disaster risk has led governments and insurers to use them when reinsurance, insurance for insurers, is unavailable or too costly. Swiss Re estimated the market at $43.1 billion at the end of 2023, with a record $15.4 billion issued that year.

  <!-- nature-mkt-052 -->

- **What sets off a catastrophe bond**

  A catastrophe bond pays out when its trigger is met. Triggers can be the insurer's actual losses, modeled losses, industry-wide losses, or measured features of the event itself. Triggers closer to the insurer's own losses protect it better; index and measured-event triggers spare investors from the insurer's claims handling. A trigger can apply to a single event or to the sum of losses over a period, usually a year. With a $90 billion threshold, for example, three $20 billion hurricanes and a $40 billion earthquake total $100 billion and trigger payout.

  <!-- nature-mkt-053 -->

- **Parametric insurance: paying out when the wind passes a line**

  Mexico's Quintana Roo insures a coral reef with a policy triggered by wind speed, paying up to $3.8 million a year. In 2020 Hurricane Delta set off an $850,000 payout. This is parametric, or index-based, insurance: it pays a pre-set amount when a measured trigger, such as a wind speed or rainfall level, is reached. Ordinary insurance pays the assessed loss after an event. Parametric cover only checks, through weather services, sensors or satellites, that the trigger was passed. The payoff is speed and lower transaction costs. The drawback is that payouts follow the measurements, so they may not cover the full damage.

  <!-- nature-mkt-059 -->

- **Sustainable finance: seeking returns while weighing the planet**

  Green and other sustainability-labeled bonds together reached $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025. They are among the products of sustainable finance: the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns. The term is often used as a synonym for ESG investing. The wider field also includes Impact investing: profit with a measurable purpose, Social finance: private money for public needs and ethical investing. Its reach is global. The The Paris Agreement: every country pledges asks countries to make finance flows consistent with low greenhouse gas emissions and development that can withstand climate change. Sustainable finance is also described as a cornerstone for reaching the UN's The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals for 2030, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals and 169 targets. Public money stays important. Much of the money for climate goals, though, is expected to come from the private sector. Over two decades, sustainable finance grew from a niche topic into a recognized field of research and university teaching.

  <!-- nature-mkt-018 -->

- **ESG: judging companies by more than their profits**

  By 2023, investments managed under the ESG label topped US$30 trillion. ESG, short for environmental, social and governance, is an investing approach that weighs a company's record on those three fronts alongside its finances. The term came to prominence in a 2004 UN-backed report, 'Who Cares Wins'. The environmental pillar covers issues such as emissions, biodiversity and waste, which often reflect externalities that markets do not handle. The social pillar covers effects on workers and communities. The governance pillar covers how firms are directed and controlled, including ethics, corruption and tax. A 2005 legal report for UNEP's finance initiative concluded that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably part of an investor's duty to clients. The backlash has been real. ESG funds saw outflows for the first time in 2023, and many US funds have dropped ESG terms from their names amid claims of misleading green marketing. Critics point to poor data and standards, and argue that big asset managers impose rules without democratic oversight. Its data, standards and political legitimacy all remain disputed.

  <!-- nature-mkt-040 -->

- **Green bonds: borrowing only for green projects**

  The World Bank issued the first labeled green bond in 2008, a year after the European Investment Bank's Climate Awareness Bond. A green bond is a bond whose money is used only for projects with environmental benefits. Like ordinary bonds, they can be issued by governments, development banks or companies, which repay the bond plus interest. Eligible projects include renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution control, sustainable land use, biodiversity, clean transport and adapting to climate change. Green bonds raised over $93 billion in 2016, still only around 1% of global bond issuance, and by 2024 total issuance had reached about $700 billion. Legally they barely differ from ordinary bonds: green promises are often not binding in the contract. Critics question some bonds' green credentials, as when the Climate Bonds Initiative refused to list a Repsol bond in 2017. The EU's Green Bonds Regulation, in force from 21 December 2024, created the 'European Green Bond'.

  <!-- nature-mkt-046 -->

- **Impact investing: profit with a measurable purpose**

  Many impact investors accept expected returns 2-4 percentage points lower in exchange for measurable social impact. Impact investing puts money into companies, organizations and funds meant to produce a measurable social or environmental benefit as well as a financial return. It lines up an investor's values with where the money goes, in fields such as renewable energy, education and microfinance. It spans private equity, venture capital and debt, and targets returns from below-market to above-market. The term was coined in 2005, and modern impact funds grew prominent soon after the Great Recession. In 2024 about 3,907 organizations managed an estimated $1.571 trillion in impact assets, far smaller than the $78 trillion global stock market. The UN development goals need an estimated $5-7 trillion of investment a year, mostly expected from private capital, and impact investors linked their funds to them.

  <!-- nature-mkt-030 -->

- **Climate, green and sustainable finance: three nested terms**

  Money for climate, green finance and sustainable finance are often treated as the same thing. The UN Environment Programme separates them as three nested circles. Climate finance: following the money, the smallest, mainly funds adaptation, resilience, cutting emissions, and a fair shift away from fossil fuels. Green finance covers that plus other environmental issues, such as protecting biodiversity. Sustainable finance adds social and governance concerns, making it the broadest term for finance that supports development able to last. The field has a short history. One review traces three periods: forerunners from the 1970s to 2010, an early phase from 2010 to 2021, and a mature phase since 2021.

  <!-- nature-mkt-019 -->

- **Green taxonomies: official lists of what counts as green**

  Which investments deserve the green label? A sustainable finance taxonomy answers with an official classification of the economic activities that count as green or sustainable. Its aim is to stop misleading green claims and help investors make greener choices. The European Commission set up a technical expert group in 2018 to define one, and the EU taxonomy came into force in July 2020. Investments are judged against six objectives: cutting emissions, adapting to climate change, reusing materials, pollution, water and biodiversity. The hardest calls were political. Classing fossil gas and nuclear energy as sustainable proved controversial, and some expert advisers threatened to resign over gas. Whether either belongs in the taxonomy is still disputed. The EU was not alone: Mongolia adopted a national green finance taxonomy in 2018, among the first countries to do so.

  <!-- nature-mkt-020 -->

- **Does ESG pay? The evidence on returns**

  Milton Friedman argued that social responsibility harms a firm's financial performance. Economists still disagree about whether attention to environmental, social and governance issues raises or lowers a company's value and investors' returns. Some evidence points the other way from Friedman. A 2011 study found the '100 Best Companies to Work For' beat their peers' stock returns by 2-3% a year. Other studies link ESG indicators to higher company value. Still others warn that overinvesting in ESG can hurt it. Some research suggests an inverted U: value rises with ESG spending up to an optimal level, then falls. The results so far are mixed, from positive to negative to that middle ground, and no single answer has won out.

  <!-- nature-mkt-042 -->

- **Five ways investors put their values to work**

  The best-known early case of responsible investing was the disinvestment from South Africa in the 1970s and 1980s, in protest against apartheid. Today responsible investors steer money using five main methods. Positive selection picks companies that meet ESG criteria, or the best performers in each sector. Exclusion removes sectors or firms from consideration on ESG grounds. Integration adds ESG risks and opportunities to ordinary financial analysis. Engagement and activism use dialogue with companies and shareholder voting to push them to change. Each method has trade-offs. Screening, for example, brings its own risks, such as concentrating money in a few sectors.

  <!-- nature-mkt-041 -->

- **Eco-investing: betting on clean technology**

  One tracker estimated that over $1.248 trillion has been invested in solar, wind, geothermal, ocean and other green sectors since 2007. Eco-investing, or green investing, is investing by values focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices. Unlike the broader field, it narrows to environmental issues, especially renewable energy and clean technology. New green technologies carry high up-front costs, which are harder to justify to investors.

  <!-- nature-mkt-077 -->

- **Aggregate confusion: why ESG scores disagree**

  Credit ratings from the largest agencies agree 99% of the time. One paper found that ESG ratings agree only 60% of the time. This spread is called the ESG ratings gap, or 'aggregate confusion'. Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting sustainability, so companies and funds are hard to compare. Many bodies write standards independently, including the GRI, the IFRS Foundation and the Carbon Disclosure Project, which has confused companies and investors. Because standards vary and change, some funds labeled ESG still hold oil and coal shares.

  <!-- nature-mkt-023 -->

- **Green central banking: should central banks fight climate change?**

  In 2018 eight central banks created the Network for Greening the Financial System, which has grown to nearly 116 central banks and supervisors. Green central banking is the idea that central banks should use their powers to help cut emissions and steer money to green investment. Their tools include Monetary policy: steering the economy through interest rates and rules on how much capital banks hold. Banks have proposed lighter capital rules for green loans, while central bankers and nonprofits prefer heavier charges on fossil-fuel assets. Many researchers argue that such goals strain the legitimacy of independent central banks, whose mandates rarely include climate aims, and the question remains disputed.

  <!-- nature-mkt-022 -->

- **Disclosure rules: making companies report climate risk**

  In 2015 the Financial Stability Board launched a climate disclosure taskforce. Its job was to push firms to report the risks climate change poses them and how they govern those risks. Sustainability disclosure rules ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them. Voluntary rules have limited effect, research shows. An EU reporting directive adopted in October 2022 makes reporting compulsory for more firms, widening coverage from about 11,700 companies to about 50,000.

  <!-- nature-mkt-021 -->

- **Sustainability bonds: green and social at once**

  Green, social and sustainability bonds differ in which projects their money may fund. A sustainability bond must fund a mix of both green and social projects. The ICMA principles, from the International Capital Market Association, are the most widely accepted framework for issuing all three kinds. Critics still warn of misleading claims, because no single definition says what makes a bond sustainable.

  <!-- nature-mkt-062 -->

- **ESG rating agencies: the scorekeepers of responsible investing**

  Sustainalytics counted over 600 ESG-rating companies in 2018, though takeovers are concentrating the market. These agencies score companies on their environmental, social and governance performance and are the main source of information for ESG investing. Each uses its own metrics, and no industry-wide standard exists. Scores can mislead the unwary. Risk raters measure how exposed a firm is to ESG risks, so a high score need not mean a strong positive effect on the world.

  <!-- nature-mkt-043 -->

- **The Equator Principles: banks' rules for risky projects**

  By October 2019, 97 institutions in 37 countries had adopted the Equator Principles, covering most international project finance debt. Launched in 2003 and based on International Finance Corporation policies, the principles are a framework banks use to assess and manage environmental and social risk in project finance. Adopting banks commit not to lend to projects whose borrowers cannot meet their social and environmental policies.

  <!-- nature-mkt-044 -->

- **The Principles for Responsible Investment**

  Set up in 2005, the Principles for Responsible Investment are a UN-backed framework for investors. They help investors analyze environmental, social and governance issues and act as responsible owners of the companies they hold. As of April 2019 the framework had over 2,350 signatories.

  <!-- nature-mkt-045 -->

- **The greenium: paying extra to be green**

  Investors want green bonds badly enough to accept less for them. The greenium is the lower yield, or pricing premium, that green bonds often carry because of that demand. Studies find high demand gives green bonds lower yields than ordinary equivalents. Estimates vary widely: from -85 to +213 basis points when bonds are first sold, and -1 to -9 basis points on average when they are traded later. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. Voluntary labels with weak oversight leave room for false green claims, which may lead investors to accept lower returns than on ordinary, or brown, investments.

  <!-- nature-mkt-048 -->

- **Fiduciary duty and ESG: may investors weigh the planet?**

  A 2015 report, 'Fiduciary Duty in the 21st Century', concluded that ignoring long-term value drivers, ESG among them, is itself a failure of fiduciary duty. A 2005 legal report for UNEP had found that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably required. In the United States, some question whether pension funds that weigh such factors break their duty to maximize returns. One state pension board blocked selling off its fossil fuel holdings on those grounds, though a 2019 analysis found the divested fund would have earned more. Investors and lawyers still dispute whether this legal duty bars ESG.

  <!-- nature-mkt-072 -->

- **Environmental investing: impact investing for the planet**

  By 2024 green bonds had reached about $700 billion of total issuance, and all sustainability-related bonds nearly $8 trillion. Environmental investing is the branch of impact investing aimed at a measurable positive effect on the environment alongside financial returns. It funds projects such as clean energy, public transport and sustainable water management. It arose from the recognition that tackling climate change needs huge private sums.

  <!-- nature-mkt-032 -->

- **Mission investing: foundations putting endowments to work**

  A foundation's endowment can do more than fund grants. Mission investments are investments by foundations, from part or all of their endowment, that further their charitable goals while earning a return. Program-related investments are made mainly for charitable aims at below-market terms, such as recoverable grants and cheap loans. For US private foundations they count toward the required 5 percent annual payout. Mission-related investments seek market-rate returns from mission-driven organizations while helping the endowment grow.

  <!-- nature-mkt-031 -->

- **Social finance: private money for public needs**

  Social finance grew quickly after the 2008 financial crisis, as investors sought ethical alternatives. It is financial services that use private capital to tackle social and environmental needs while giving investors a return. Unlike philanthropy, it sustains itself by being profitable rather than relying on donors. It has no agreed definition, but includes impact investing, investing by values and lending to social enterprises. It struggles with low returns, high start-up and regulatory costs, neglect by mainstream banks and poor access to ordinary savers. Critics argue it pulls money from productive uses, while backers say it adds investment where charity is declining.

  <!-- nature-mkt-060 -->

- **Social impact bonds: investors paid only for success**

  The first social impact bond, launched in the UK in 2010, funded the rehabilitation of prisoners at Peterborough Prison. In such a contract, private investors fund a public program, and the government repays them only if agreed goals are met. Unlike ordinary bonds, they have no fixed return. By 2022 there were 276 projects with $745m raised, used in 23 countries as of May 2023. Backers say taxpayers pay only for success; critics say the bonds displace other funding and are an expensive way to run programs.

  <!-- nature-mkt-061 -->

- **Sustainability-linked bonds: interest tied to targets**

  In September 2019 the Italian utility Enel issued the first sustainability-linked bond, promising a 25 basis point penalty on its interest if it missed its target. The terms of such a bond, such as its interest rate, change depending on whether the issuer meets set sustainability targets, tracked with key performance indicators. Unlike green, social or sustainability bonds, the money raised can be used for any purpose. Issuance was around $5 billion in 2019 and $10.6 billion in 2020. Over 85% were tied to environmental measures, most often cutting emissions.

  <!-- nature-mkt-063 -->

- **Blue bonds: green bonds for the ocean**

  A blue bond is the ocean version of a green bond. It raises money specifically for ocean conservation and sustainable activity at sea. Like green bonds, blue bonds earmark money for eligible projects and usually follow voluntary guidance on use of proceeds, project selection, management and reporting. Bonds tied to sustainable fisheries, such as the Seychelles government's blue bond, are discussed as a way to bring private capital to nature.

  <!-- nature-mkt-080 -->

- **The Green Bond Principles**

  The Green Bond Principles are voluntary guidance from the International Capital Market Association on how green bonds should be run. They recommend a defined use of the money raised, a process for choosing projects, careful management of the funds and regular reporting, sometimes with outside review. These practices aim to narrow the information gap between issuers and investors and to support accountability.

  <!-- nature-mkt-047 -->

### Economics of conservation

Conservation is also a set of economic choices about trade, land and limited budgets. CITES, a treaty, tries to protect endangered plants and animals from the threats of international trade, and the long fight over the ivory trade shows how hard that is. Closer to the ground, people and wild animals clash over crops, livestock and space, and projects try to make protecting nature pay for local people. Planners must decide where reserves go and how big they are, sometimes with software that finds networks of sites at low cost. Some protected areas exist only on paper, and conservationists must face the hard idea that not every species can be saved.

- **CITES: a treaty to police the wildlife trade**

  On 3 March 1973, 80 countries agreed in Washington, D.C. on the text of a treaty to protect wildlife from international trade. The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, or CITES, entered into force on 1 July 1975. It controls trade in listed species as they cross borders, including products made from them, such as traditional medicines. Over 40,900 species, subspecies and populations are protected. It is legally binding, but each member must pass its own laws to apply it. It works as a negative list: trade in any species is unregulated unless it is listed, so many species are traded with no review. Critics say it ignores habitat loss and poverty and does not tackle market demand, and that listings can even feed speculation in valuable species. As of 2002, 50% of members lacked one or more of its four main implementation requirements.

  <!-- nature-mkt-001 -->

- **Integrated conservation and development: making protection pay locally**

  In the mid-1980s WWF set out to fix the problems of 'fines and fences', a style of conservation that gave local people no say. Its answer was the integrated conservation and development project: a biodiversity project that also invests in rural development, so local people gain from protecting nature. Such projects are usually tied to a park or reserve and funded from outside by conservation and development agencies. They assume that more varied livelihoods will ease human pressure on biodiversity. Critics say many were designed with little local input and rarely shared costs and benefits with women and minority groups. They can also overlook outside pressures such as market demand and unlawful tree felling, and may collapse when outside funding ends. WWF says its projects work with local organizations, so the record remains disputed.

  <!-- nature-mkt-010 -->

- **The ivory trade and the fight over elephants**

  Between 1979 and 1989, African elephants fell from about 1.3 million to 600,000. Around 75,000 were killed each year for ivory worth about 1 billion dollars. The ivory trade, the commercial and often illegal trade in tusks of elephants and animals such as hippos, walruses and narwhals, is ancient. At its colonial-era peak, 800 to 1,000 tonnes a year went to Europe alone. The crash showed that the international ivory trade, more than habitat loss, was the main threat, and a ban followed in 1990. Southern African states opposed it. They said their herds were well managed and ivory revenue funded conservation, and Zimbabwe argued that wildlife needs economic value to survive. In 1997 CITES: a treaty to police the wildlife trade let Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe sell 49 tonnes of stockpiled ivory to Japan as an 'experiment'. Whether a total ban or regulated sales best protect elephants is still disputed. Demand can shift: the piano industry dropped ivory keys for plastic in the 1980s.

  <!-- nature-mkt-005 -->

- **Reserve design: where to put a park and how big**

  Bolivia expanded Amboró park into land people depended on for their living, and later had to shrink it again. Reserve design is the planning of a reserve's size, shape, location and links so that it actually protects biodiversity. Planners must weigh habitat needs, migration, climate change and public support. Size matters: reserves that are too small bring carnivores into contact with people, raising their death rate. Networks linked by wildlife corridors protect species that migrate and can raise movement between patches by up to 50%. For value for money, reserves should sit in species-rich places such as biodiversity hotspots. They must also allow for future ranges, since 80% of observed range shifts have moved toward the poles or uphill, at an average of 6.1 km per decade.

  <!-- nature-mkt-008 -->

- **Human–wildlife conflict: when people and animals collide**

  In Sri Lanka, up to 80 people and over 230 elephants die each year in clashes between the two. Elephants raid crops, and farmers kill them in revenge. Human–wildlife conflict covers such harmful encounters, which hurt both people and their property and wildlife and its habitat. It comes from competition for land, water and food and has grown with population and changing land use. The damage includes destroyed crops, livestock killed by predators, injury and death, damaged infrastructure and the spread of disease. There are hidden costs too, in health, opportunity costs and transaction costs. Fear itself matters: fear of predators can worsen conflict more than the damage they actually do.

  <!-- nature-mkt-003 -->

- **The three CITES lists**

  CITES sorts protected species into three lists, or appendices, by how much international trade threatens them. Appendix I species face extinction: commercial trade in wild specimens is banned, and other trade needs both import and export permits. Appendix II holds most listed species; they are not necessarily threatened but need controlled trade and an export permit. Appendix III species are protected in at least one country that has asked other members to help control trade. Captive-bred specimens of Appendix I species may be traded as if they were Appendix II.

  <!-- nature-mkt-002 -->

- **Fences, dogs and compensation: easing conflict with wildlife**

  Livestock-guarding dogs cut animal losses to, on average, 60 times lower than the norm. They are one of many methods for reducing harmful encounters between people and wildlife, from fences to paying people for their losses. The most successful solutions involve local communities in planning, running and maintaining them. Some governments pay compensation to discourage revenge killing, with mixed results because payments come late or fall short. Moving problem animals elsewhere is largely ineffective and can harm the species.

  <!-- nature-mkt-004 -->

- **Conservation triage: choosing which species to save**

  Extinction threats are estimated at 15 to 37 percent of all species by 2050. Faced with that, some conservationists argue for triage: since not every species can be saved, limited effort must go to chosen ones. Supporters see this as realistic priority-setting. Critics who defend the rights of nature say 'endangered species triage' decides which species to let go, instead of re-examining the economics driving the decline.

  <!-- nature-mkt-011 -->

- **Marxan: software that designs reserves**

  Marxan is the most widely used conservation planning software, behind systems covering about 5% of Earth's surface, including the Great Barrier Reef reserve network. It finds networks of sites that meet biodiversity targets at low cost. It uses simulated annealing, a trial-and-error search, to minimize a reserve system's total cost while covering a set share of each feature. In computing terms it solves a conservation version of the 0-1 knapsack problem: picking items of the most value within a budget. Exact tools such as prioritizr guarantee the best solution and can find cheaper ones faster.

  <!-- nature-mkt-006 -->

- **Paper parks: protected in name only**

  A 2020 study of 3,449 protected sea areas in Europe found that 70% faced at least one significant threat, and damaging fishing gear hit 86% of the network. That is the mark of a paper park: a reserve that exists on paper but have little real management or protection on the ground. They result from weak governance, weak regulations or lack of enforcement.

  <!-- nature-mkt-007 -->

## Natural resource economics

Every economy runs on things taken from nature, from sunlight and water to minerals, plants and wildlife. Some of these renew themselves within a human lifetime; others, once used, are gone for good. Natural resource economics studies how such resources are supplied, demanded and shared out, and why owning them can enrich a country or, surprisingly often, hold it back. This part follows that thread from minerals and fish to the payments that flow to whoever owns scarce land and ore.

### Renewable and non-renewable resources

Some resources come back and some do not. Forests, fish and other living things can replace what is taken within a human lifetime, while minerals, once used, are gone. This chapter follows that dividing line and what happens when people draw down a resource faster than it can recover. Along the way it meets the old fear that population will outrun food, the bell-shaped curve that tracks a resource's rise and fall, and the puzzle of why mineral wealth so often fails the countries that hold it.

- **Natural resources: where every product begins**

  Trace any man-made product back far enough and it ends in nature. A natural resource is something drawn from nature and used with few changes: sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife. Economists count these among the basic inputs to production, the Factors of production: land, labor and capital. Some resources are restored by natural processes. Many extractive industries, though, rely on materials that can be dug or pumped out only once. That difference shapes much of what follows. Who gets these resources sits at the center of many economic and political confrontations, and the fights sharpen as scarcity increases. Extraction is also a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage. In 1982 the United Nations' The World Charter for Nature, 1982 recognized the need to protect nature from further depletion by human activity. A whole field now asks how managing land, water, soil, plants and animals affects quality of life, for people alive today and for generations to come.

  <!-- nature-res-248 -->

- **Resource depletion: using nature faster than it returns**

  The problem is centuries old, but it became a major concern only in the 1970s. Resource depletion is the using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced. It takes many shapes: degraded wetlands and other ecosystems, eroded soil, drained underground water stores, and fish caught faster than they can breed. Its roots lie in colonialism and industrialization. With the Industrial Revolution, new technology and economic growth raised demand, and extraction of every kind of resource rose sharply. Markets register some of this. A resource's value depends on how much of it exists in nature and how costly it is to extract, and under Supply and demand: the model behind prices scarcer resources become more valuable. The burden is unevenly shared. Wealthy nations have been described as outsourcing depletion to poorer nations, which suffer the greatest ecosystem losses. Economists often explain why depletion happens with the The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused, where users of a shared resource each have reason to take more before others do.

  <!-- nature-res-204 -->

- **Non-renewable resources: the stock that does not come back**

  Coal, oil and gas took thousands of years to form, and people use them far faster than that. A non-renewable resource, also called a finite resource, is a natural resource that nature cannot replace quickly enough to keep up with use. Minerals and metal ores, fossil fuels, and the water in some underground stores all qualify. Ore deposits form only where geological processes concentrate metals, which takes tens of thousands to millions of years. On human time-frames, deposits near the surface will not come back. Fossil fuels remain the main energy source humans use today. Some argue carbon fuel is practically inexhaustible if methane hydrates on the sea floor are counted. No one knows whether they can be extracted at a viable cost. Economists put the idea simply: using more today means less is available tomorrow. David Ricardo argued that a mineral's price should rise over time. In his view the costliest mine in use sets the price, and cheaper mines earn a differential rent. Without regulation, people and firms tend to keep using these resources, because the easier, cheaper option is often not the environmentally friendly one.

  <!-- nature-res-209 -->

- **Renewable resources: the stock that regrows, if allowed**

  A forest can regrow and a fish population can breed back, but only if people let them. A renewable resource, also called a flow resource, replaces what is used through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale. Some sources, such as sun, wind, moving water and geothermal heat, are practically infinite and cannot be depleted. Resources whose recovery will probably never outlast a human time scale get a name of their own, Perpetual resources: too plentiful to run out. Water, forests, plants and animals stay renewable only as long as they are monitored, protected and conserved. Water shows the catch. It is renewable only when its use is carefully controlled, and underground water pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable. Overuse is not new: deforestation, overgrazing and fishing too hard were already large problems in early modern times. Unregulated industrial growth endangers these resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them. Fisheries show how far it can go, since an unregulated industry can wipe a renewable resource out completely. Even clean energy has a hidden draw: building renewable energy devices uses mined metals and land.

  <!-- nature-res-212 -->

- **Natural resource economics: running an economy within nature's limits**

  Fish, trees and ore: for decades, those three made up the core of the subject. Natural resource economics is the branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources. It began when researchers mainly wanted to know how to exploit stocks of resources commercially in the best way. Its traditional curriculum centered on models of fisheries, forests and mineral extraction. Its classic topics include welfare theory, how land is used, pollution control, resource extraction, valuing what markets do not price, exhaustibility and sustainability. Environmental economics was once a separate subject. More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond commercial exploitation alone. The field's main aim now is to understand nature's role in the economy, so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available to future generations. Put simply, it asks how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's resources. Not everyone is satisfied. Ecological economics: the economy inside the ecosystem criticizes the field for focusing mainly on efficient allocation, and less on fair distribution and on the scale of the economy.

  <!-- nature-res-213 -->

- **Exploiting natural resources to fuel growth**

  In the 19th century, mining, steam power and machinery pushed extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels. The exploitation of natural resources means using them, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development. Two forces speed it up: better technology, which makes extraction faster, and rising consumption and consumerism, which raise demand. The costs often land on others. Exploitation tends to bring environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict. Foreign industries often take raw materials from developing countries, and local communities see little of the profit. Soil shows the scale. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) finds that about 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and that more than 90% could be by 2050. The rule for sustainable use is simple to state: consume a resource no faster than it is supplied. Not everyone accepts that resources are finite at all. The economist Julian Simon argued that substitution, Recycling: giving waste a second life and new technology make scarcity ever more doubtful, a view others strongly dispute.

  <!-- nature-res-220 -->

- **Malthusianism: when population outruns food**

  In 1798 Thomas Robert Malthus published Malthus and the race between people and food, and its gloomy logic still carries his name. Malthusianism holds that population can grow exponentially while food and other resources grow only steadily. Living standards therefore fall until population declines. Better technology could raise resources, he argued, but the extra abundance would fuel more births until each person's share fell back. The predicted end is a Malthusian catastrophe, or trap: famine or war once population outpaces farm output. The pre-industrial record fits. From 1 to 1500 AD better technology raised population density but not living standards. A laborer's daily wage bought about 15 pounds of wheat in ancient Babylonia and 13 in England in 1800. After World War II, mechanized farming and the Green Revolution greatly raised crop yields, and most developed countries' populations grew more slowly than productivity. Critics from Ricardo onward disputed the theory, and the 20th century's growth did not bring the predicted catastrophe. Still, many models of resource depletion are Malthusian in shape, predicting that consumption will outrun new supply.

  <!-- nature-res-234 -->

- **Economic rent: income that rewards no effort**

  Some income rewards no effort at all. Economic rent is any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use. Unlike economic profit, rent counts as unearned income, and competition cannot wipe it out. In farming and extraction, rent arises because land, oil and minerals are scarce and unevenly spread. Scarcity rent is paid for identical land when supply falls short of demand. Differential rent is the surplus that better land earns over the poorest land in use. Governments can collect part of it as royalties on minerals, oil and gas. Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity, and proposed it as the main source of public revenue. Later, public choice theorists used the word for wealth transferred through rights the state grants, the origin of the term rent seeking.

  <!-- nature-res-218 -->

- **The resource curse: riches that hold countries back**

  In 1711 The Spectator observed that the most plentiful countries often had the poorest living. Much later, Richard Auty gave the pattern a name. In 1993 he used the term resource curse for mineral-rich countries that grew more slowly than countries without plentiful resources. The idea is that countries rich in oil and minerals often see slower economic growth, weaker democracy or worse development than countries with fewer resources. A 1995 study by Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found a strong link between resource abundance and poor growth. The stakes are wide. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) counts 51 countries as resource-rich, meaning nonrenewable resources supply at least 20% of exports or 20% of government revenue. Of these, 29 are low or lower-middle income. Several mechanisms are proposed. Oil and mineral prices swing widely, so revenues jump and crash, disrupting planning and debt payments. Extraction tends to form an enclave with few links to the rest of the economy. Its high profits draw the best workers and investment away from other industries. Economies dominated by extraction also tend to be less democratic and more corrupt, and petroleum is the resource most consistently tied to weaker institutions. Yet there is no academic consensus. Studies with empirical support reach contradictory findings, and most experts think the curse is not universal, striking certain kinds of countries under certain conditions.

  <!-- nature-res-200 -->

- **Ecological yield: the harvest an ecosystem can spare**

  A forest can give up some wood each year and still stand. Ecological yield is the amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover. It is most often measured in forests, where sustainable harvesting takes no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch. Take more than is renewed and the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time.
