In it, the cost of hauling goods to market eats into the Economic rent: income that rewards no effort land can earn, so centrality and transport decide what is grown where. It is considered the first example of marginal analysis, and an early abstract model to which mathematics could be applied. Its publication is said to mark the real start of location theory, and von Thünen has been called the father of location theorists. Critics say it oversimplified by assuming an isolated state or a single city.

  <!-- nature-res-176 -->

- **The human right to water and sanitation**

  On 28 July 2010, the UN General Assembly recognized clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right. The principle is that every life depends on them. Its clearest definition came in General Comment 15 of the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, drafted in 2002. Recognition is not the same as enforcement, though. Only a few countries have written the right into enforceable law.

  <!-- nature-res-167 -->

- **Water resource policy: blue, green and grey water**

  Water policy sorts water by color. Blue water is surface water and groundwater, green water is rain held in soil for plants, and grey water is water dirtied by use. Virtual water, the water hidden in traded goods, is a fourth category. Water resource policy is the policy-making and law that govern how water is collected, treated, used, disposed of and protected. It varies by region with water availability, the state of rivers and lakes, and local needs. Droughts are growing more frequent and intense with climate change, but water policy tends to react rather than plan ahead.

  <!-- nature-res-165 -->

- **Transboundary water agreements: sharing rivers across borders**

  About 60% of the world's fresh water flows across political boundaries, because basins do not follow national borders. Transboundary water agreements are the treaties and other deals by which countries share and manage that water. An estimated 3600 water treaties have existed, more than 150 of them new since 1950. Geography matters. Rivers that form a border and can be shared equally tend to cause less conflict than upstream–downstream arrangements. Growing scarcity, climate change and poorer water quality have increased international conflict over water.

  <!-- nature-res-166 -->

- **The water-energy nexus: two resources tied together**

  Gulf states spend 10–25% of their electricity on desalinating water. That is the water-energy nexus at work. Making energy takes water, and extracting, treating, moving, heating and disposing of water takes energy. Every form of energy needs some water, and every stage of water supply needs energy. Thermoelectric power plants, which use water for cooling, are by far the largest users. Some low-carbon options, such as biofuels, concentrating solar power, carbon capture and nuclear power, are quite water-intensive.

  <!-- nature-res-172 -->

### Managing the commons

Air, water and a habitable Earth belong to everyone, which raises an old question: who should look after them? Natural resource management is the work of caring for land, water, soil, plants and animals with an eye on people now and in the future. This chapter sorts resources by who holds the rights over them, the state, a private owner, a group or no one at all. It follows the commons from English common land, fenced off by enclosure, to community forests and the high seas beyond any nation's reach. Along the way it meets Elinor Ostrom, who found the rules that let shared resources thrive.

- **Natural resource management: caring for land, water and life**

  Strict preservation was supposed to save nature. In the 20th century people saw that it had not stopped resources declining, and a broader approach took in the social, economic and political sides. Natural resource management is the managing of land, water, soil, plants and animals with attention to how it affects life for people now and in the future. It deals with how people and natural landscapes interact, starting from the fact that livelihoods depend on healthy, productive land. It draws together heritage protection, land-use planning, water management, biodiversity conservation and the future of farming, mining, tourism, fishing and forestry. Its problems are complex and contested. Natural cycles are linked, so a change in one can have long-lasting, even irreversible, effects. Managers must also weigh many stakeholders, policies, politics, borders and economic effects. Mapping tools help. Geographic information systems, or GIS, overlay data sets such as rainfall, cleared land and erosion to plan where native bush should regrow.

  <!-- nature-res-177 -->

- **Who owns nature: four property regimes**

  A lake fishery that anyone may use tends to be the most exploited of all. That observation sits at the center of a simple classification. Resource management approaches can be grouped by who holds rights over a resource: the state, a private owner, a group, no one, or a mix. Under state property, the state owns and controls the resource, and others use it only with permission, as in US national forests and parks. Under private property, a defined person or company owns the resource and bears both its benefits and its duties. Common property is in effect the private property of a group, such as a community forest. Open-access resources have no owner at all, and anyone may use them. Many real cases are hybrids. Native vegetation in New South Wales, for example, is protected in the public interest, but most of it grows on private land. These categories build on the wider study of Types of property regimes: four ways to hold a resource.

  <!-- nature-res-178 -->

- **The commons: resources that belong to everyone**

  Before 1968, academic titles mentioning 'the commons' were very rare. Then an article by Garrett Hardin and the tragedy of the commons, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', turned an old English legal term for common land into a general word for shared resources. The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth. The word can also mean resources a group of users governs for itself, through rules it creates, rather than through the state or the market. How a commons is run makes a large difference. In Mongolia, where herders moved together between pastures, grassland degradation was about 9%. Under state or household pastures it was about 75% in Russia and 33% in China. Nepal handed forest control to communities from the late 1980s, giving locals a financial stake in preventing overuse. Globalization brings new pressures. Fish and timber are sold on world markets, which makes their impacts harder for local communities to monitor.

  <!-- nature-res-183 -->

- **Enclosure: fencing off England's common land**

  From the 1530s to the 1640s, enclosure riots were the leading form of social protest in England. Enclosure was the practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, stripping commoners of their traditional rights to use it. It merged scattered strips into large fields bounded by hedgerows, walls or fences, for the sole use of owners or their tenants. Parliament passed the first enclosure act in 1604. Its stated aim was more efficient farming, but enclosed land also became much more valuable. In Tudor England, high wool profits led lords to turn common fields into sheep pasture, evicting villagers. The movement probably peaked from 1760 to 1832, and surplus rural workers moved to towns to become industrial workers. The Hammonds said it ruined small farmers, cottagers and squatters. Chambers and Mingay argued it brought more food, more cultivated land and more rural jobs. Many Marxists see it as 'primitive accumulation' that laid the ground for capitalism.

  <!-- nature-res-191 -->

- **Community-based natural resource management**

  People protect what is tied to their quality of life. That is one of the assumptions behind community-based natural resource management, which combines conservation goals with economic benefits for rural communities. It also assumes that locals are best placed to conserve resources, and that people conserve only when the benefits exceed the costs. It rests on subsidiarity, the principle of handling decisions at the most local level that can manage them. Social capital, the trust and networks within a community, and gender shape how it works in practice. It has critics. Tania Murray found that in upland Southeast Asia it could force communities to meet discriminatory conditions before gaining legal rights to resources.

  <!-- nature-res-180 -->

- **Community forestry: forests run by the people who live there**

  In parts of Nepal, forest cover has risen by 37% under Forest User Groups run democratically by local people. That is community forestry, a participatory approach, prominent since the 1970s, in which local communities help manage forests and decide how land is used. The FAO defines it as any situation that closely involves local people in forestry. Communities manage forests for income from timber and Non-timber forest products: nuts, mushrooms and medicine, and for services such as watershed protection and carbon storage. It is seen as one of the most promising ways to combine forest conservation with rural development and poverty reduction. Success depends on secure land tenure, which decides whether communities can invest in sustainable practices. Unclear boundaries, capture by local elites and weak enforcement threaten projects. Certification and carbon credits open global markets, but high certification costs remain a barrier for smallholders. There is no single blueprint, because regional conditions differ.

  <!-- nature-res-193 -->

- **The global commons: oceans, air and space**

  Carbon dioxide that enters the atmosphere keeps driving climate change for at least a millennium. The atmosphere is part of the global commons, shared resource areas beyond the political reach of any single nation, along with the high seas, outer space and Antarctica. They hold Common-pool resources: hard to fence, easy to depletes: goods that are costly but not impossible to keep users out of, and that are used up by use. So they suffer congestion, overuse and degradation, and their governance must avoid a worldwide The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused. That is harder than locally. Global users are more varied, resources are less stable and harder to understand, and many are non-renewable on human time scales. Treaties between countries on the environment multiplied after the 1972 Stockholm conference. They are often slow, settle for the lowest common denominator and lack enforcement. There are successes. The The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked, in force from 1 January 1989, is widely seen as a highly successful model. The 1961 Antarctic Treaty sets Antarctica aside as a scientific preserve with no military activity.

  <!-- nature-res-187 -->

- **Ostrom's design principles for a lasting commons**

  Farmers in the Swiss Alps have run shared grazing land successfully for hundreds of years. Early work on the The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused suggested every commons was doomed, but later economists found many that worked. Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons won the Nobel Prize for analyzing them. From them she drew a set of design principles found in well-governed commons. They are clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognized rights to organize and nested enterprises. Graduated sanctions mean penalties that grow with repeated offenses. The principles work best when more than nine are used together. A related idea, the 'comedy of the commons', coined by Carol M. Rose in 1986, describes users policing themselves to keep or improve a commons.

  <!-- nature-res-184 -->

- **Common ownership: assets held as one**

  Forms of common ownership exist in every economic system. Common ownership means holding an organization's or community's assets as one undivided whole, not in the names of individual members. Advocates separate collective ownership, shared by agreement among members such as a producer cooperative, from common property open to all, such as a public park. In capitalist economies it is practiced by voluntary associations, non-profits and, implicitly, all public bodies. Common ownership of the means of production is a central goal of socialist movements.

  <!-- nature-res-188 -->

- **Customary land: held by custom, not by title**

  In Africa 90% of land is customary, and in Papua New Guinea 97%. Customary land is land held and used under unwritten local custom rather than written law. It is usually tied to indigenous communities, unlike statutory tenure, which was mostly brought in during colonial times. The gap between land the law recognizes and land managed by custom is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental damage. The World Bank and others promote formal land titles as a fix. Opinion is divided on whether this always helps the poor. Where several groups claim the same land, as often in Sub-Saharan Africa, formal titling can favor some and create tension.

  <!-- nature-res-190 -->

- **Integrated natural resource management**

  Conflicts over resources are cheaper to prevent than to settle. Integrated natural resource management brings all stakeholders in from the planning stage to reduce later conflict. It manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic sides to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals. Sustainability is its focus. It grew out of research on sustainable land use, participatory planning, integrated watershed management and Adaptive management: learning while you decide.

  <!-- nature-res-181 -->

- **Stakeholder analysis: who has a stake in a forest**

  Who has a stake in a river? The question sounds simple but is hard to answer, which is the main difficulty of stakeholder analysis. Borrowed from business management, it identifies the interest groups affected by how natural resources are used and conserved. Its stages include identifying decision-makers and stakeholders, investigating their interests, and mapping conflicts, trade-offs and synergies. One proposal would represent nature itself as a stakeholder. Many scholars have rejected it as hard to put into practice.

  <!-- nature-res-179 -->

- **Joint Forest Management in India**

  In 1988 the Indian state of Odisha began an experiment in sharing its forests. Joint Forest Management is India's term for partnerships in which state forest departments and local communities share forest protection and development. It is set out in the National Forest Policy of 1988 and guidelines of 1990. Along with Nepal's Forest User Groups, it was an early response to failing centralized forest policy.

  <!-- nature-res-199 -->

- **Commoning: the commons as something people do**

  A commons is not just a thing; it is also an activity. Commoning treats the commons as an ongoing practice, the process of people coming together to manage shared resources. Some authors separate three elements: the shared resources, the community that governs them, and commoning, the act of managing them together. In farming, commoning means looking after shared land jointly, and it matters to food systems in many communities worldwide.

  <!-- nature-res-185 -->

- **Urban commons: city spaces run by citizens**

  A public square is not automatically a commons. The geographer David Harvey argued that public spaces become commons only when citizens take political action there. Urban commons are city resources managed by citizens themselves, valued by their use and upkeep costs rather than their market price. They work alongside the state and the market rather than replacing them.

  <!-- nature-res-186 -->

- **The open-field system before enclosure**

  Before Enclosure: fencing off England's common land, English common land lay under the lord of the manor. A manor was made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own farm, the demesne. Tenants held rights such as pasture, pannage, the right to let pigs forage, and estovers, the right to gather wood. Landless peasants often farmed narrow 'waste' strips nobody officially used. The system ended with new methods such as the Norfolk four-course rotation, which raised crop and livestock yields by improving soil fertility and cutting fallow periods.

  <!-- nature-res-192 -->

- **Ostrom's IAD framework for studying the commons**

  Forests and pastures share a tricky pair of traits. They are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces what others get, and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical. To study how people manage such resources, Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons built the Institutional Analysis and Development framework, or IAD. Built on Rational choice: people as careful calculators assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, the positions of the people involved, called actors, and their formal and informal rules. It breaks complex problems of collective action into smaller 'action arenas'. Institutions are studied through seven types of rule: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

  <!-- nature-res-194 -->

- **Joint ownership and who controls an asset**

  No contract can foresee everything. In the incomplete-contracts approach of Oliver Hart and colleagues, ownership matters for exactly that reason. The owner holds residual control rights, the say over an asset in any situation a contract does not cover. Owners have stronger incentives than non-owners to invest in a relationship, so ownership can ease the hold-up problem, where one party fears the other will exploit its investment. A central result is that joint ownership, where each party can veto use of the asset, is suboptimal. Later work shows it can be optimal when parties are unequally informed, in long-term relationships, or able to share know-how.

  <!-- nature-res-189 -->

- **The International Association for the Study of the Commons**

  Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons was a founding member and the first president of the International Association for the Study of the Commons. The non-profit was founded in 1989 to advance understanding of institutions for managing resources held or used in common. It publishes the open-access International Journal of the Commons and holds global conferences every two years.

  <!-- nature-res-195 -->

- **Governing the Commons: Ostrom's answer to Hardin**

  Irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, mountain villages in Switzerland and Japan, fisheries in Nova Scotia and Indonesia: Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons studied them all. The result was Governing the Commons (1990), her best-known book. It shows that communities worldwide have managed shared resources successfully through local rules. In it Ostrom set out eight design principles found in long-lasting institutions for managing shared resources. The book argues that self-interest need not cause degradation, contrary to the The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused. It can instead lead people to care for property they hold in common.

  <!-- nature-res-197 -->

## Nature-based solutions

Some of the most useful infrastructure on Earth was never poured from concrete. Nature-based solutions are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle problems people face, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. This part follows that idea from rain falling on a city street to the work of controlling floods and storing carbon. It meets the engineers who design with ecology, the hybrids that pair living systems with concrete, and the people who use ecosystems to adapt to climate change and reduce disasters. It also meets the critics, who warn that nature-based solutions can become greenwashing and a distraction from cutting emissions.

### What nature-based solutions are

Can a restored ecosystem do a job usually given to engineers? Nature-based solutions say yes: they protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges while helping both people and biodiversity. Around that idea sit several close cousins, from ecological engineering to ecosystem-based adaptation, reducing disaster risk and natural climate solutions. This chapter sorts them out and shows why living and built defenses work best together. It also weighs the critics, who see greenwashing and an uneven evidence base.

- **Nature-based solutions: hiring ecosystems to do the work**

  A strip of mangrove forest along a tropical coast does four jobs at once. It breaks the force of waves and wind, stores carbon, nurtures fish and holds the shoreline against erosion. That bundle of benefits is the idea behind nature-based solutions, or NBS. They are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. The challenges are big ones: slowing climate change and adapting to it, securing water and food, and reducing disaster risk. Cities have their own versions. Roofs covered in plants or built to hold rain, and walls draped in greenery, can cool overheated city centers, capture rainwater, cut pollution and store carbon. The term came from practitioners in the late 2000s. The IUCN and the World Bank took it up to describe working with ecosystems rather than relying purely on engineering. The IUCN now treats NBS as an umbrella over Ecological restoration: repairing ecosystems already damaged, Ecological engineering: a small push that steers big natural forces, Ecosystem-based adaptation: living defenses against a changing climate and Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction: buffers that also feed people. The European Commission stresses that NBS are cost-effective and deliver environmental, social and economic benefits at once. The flood evidence is encouraging. A review of 386 cases found NBS as effective as conventional ways of handling floods, or more so, and 66% reported positive ecological outcomes. Politics has followed. Around 130 national climate pledges, known as Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge documents, commit to NBS: 65% of signatories. Yet those pledges rarely become measurable action.

  <!-- nature-nbs-220 -->

- **Ecosystem-based adaptation: living defenses against a changing climate**

  When a storm surge rolls toward a coast, a healthy reef, mangrove stand or marsh can take much of the blow. Using such living defenses on purpose is called ecosystem-based adaptation, or EbA. It uses biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change. In practice, EbA conserves, sustainably manages and restores forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs. The goal is less harm from storms, shifting rainfall and temperature extremes. The examples are concrete. Restored reefs, mangroves and marshes soften storm surges. Trees grown among crops, a practice called Agroforestry: trees and crops on the same ground, help farms ride out drought. Well-managed forests hold slopes in place and prevent flash floods. EbA can work alone or alongside engineered works such as dykes, hybrid measures such as artificial reefs, and systems that warn people early. Supporters claim a long list of side benefits: better health, food and water security, fewer disasters, stored carbon and conserved biodiversity. The IUCN coined the term in 2008, and the The Convention on Biological Diversity defined it officially in 2009. It sits inside the wider family of nature-based solutions. Many countries cite EbA in their climate pledges under the The Paris Agreement: every country pledges. It is increasingly seen as a way to tackle hardship and the climate crisis together in developing countries, where people depend on natural resources.

  <!-- nature-nbs-218 -->

- **Ecological engineering: a small push that steers big natural forces**

  In 1962 Howard Odum gave a name to a powerful trick: using a small input of human energy to steer large natural processes. He called it ecological engineering. The field combines ecology and engineering to design, build or restore, and manage ecosystems that serve both society and nature. Civil engineering focuses on built infrastructure; this field works with natural infrastructure and the bond between people and planet. Projects range from restored wetlands to greenhouses that turn wastewater into fertilizer, flowers and drinking water. They work at three scales: mesocosms of about 0.1 to hundreds of meters, ecosystems of about one to tens of km, and whole regions. Mitsch and Jorgensen set out five basic concepts. The field relies on ecosystems designing themselves, tests ecological theory, thinks in whole systems, saves non-renewable energy and supports Conservation biology: a science with a deadline. Choosing between designs should draw on Ecological economics: the economy inside the ecosystem, guided by values that favor conservation.

  <!-- nature-nbs-216 -->

- **The case against nature-based solutions**

  Not everyone cheers. The Indigenous Environmental Network calls nature-based solutions a tool for Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action. Turning non-forest land into plantations, it warns, can take land from smallholders and herders. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) adds that NBS cannot replace deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, or excuse delaying them. The dispute is plain: critics ask whether NBS are sold as a substitute for emission cuts, and whether they trample people's rights to land. Most case studies also come from the Global North. Of 257,266 papers on Natural climate solutions: land managed for carbon, fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.

  <!-- nature-nbs-223 -->

- **Green plus grey: why hybrids beat either alone**

  Should a city trust concrete or nature? Research suggests the best answer is often both. This hybrid approach combines nature-based solutions with conventional built infrastructure. Studies find NBS improve flood resilience but cannot act alone; they must be coordinated with grey works. Used together, the benefits reach beyond flood control to better social conditions, more stored carbon and stronger resilience planning. Researchers urge looking for such synergies rather than treating NBS as a rival to engineering.

  <!-- nature-nbs-222 -->

- **Three types of nature-based solution, from hands-off to built**

  Nature-based solutions come in three broad types, sorted by how much people engineer the ecosystem. Type 1 barely intervenes: protecting mangroves against storms, or creating marine reserves that export fish to nearby fishing grounds. Type 2 manages landscapes to be sustainable and do several jobs, as in growing trees among crops (Agroforestry: trees and crops on the same ground) or mixing tree species so forests resist shocks. Type 3 manages ecosystems intensively or creates new ones, such as planted roofs and walls or wetlands built from scratch. The typology carries a trade-off. The more services and stakeholder groups a solution targets, the less it can maximize any single one.

  <!-- nature-nbs-221 -->

- **Why ecosystem-based adaptation is slow to spread**

  Case studies show ecosystem-based adaptation can work and can save money. So why is it not everywhere? First, nobody knows beyond what limits ecosystems can keep providing protection as the climate changes. Second, methods vary and nobody measures success the same way, so the economic case is hard to argue. Third, governance is awkward, because EbA spans the sectors that manage ecosystems and the different sectors that benefit from them. Finally, low incomes, pressing development needs, limited finance and cultural preferences about landscapes all slow its uptake.

  <!-- nature-nbs-219 -->

- **Five ways to put an ecosystem to work**

  Mitsch and Jorgensen sorted ecological engineering designs into five classes by how the ecosystem is used. An ecosystem can solve a pollution problem, as wetlands that treat wastewater and planted beds that filter runoff do. It can be imitated to fix a resource problem, as with replacement wetlands and small planted hollows that soak up rain. It can be recovered after disturbance, as when old mine land or a lake is restored. It can be modified in an ecologically sound way. Or it can be used for benefit without upsetting its balance, as in growing trees among crops or raising several species together in fish farms.

  <!-- nature-nbs-217 -->

- **Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction: buffers that also feed people**

  Some of the best disaster defenses also put food on the table. This approach, a form of Disaster risk reduction: acting before the disaster known as Eco-DRR, uses ecosystems to prevent and reduce disasters. It keeps ecosystems working as buffers against dangerous natural events while they go on supplying communities with food and water. Its measures are often closely linked to those of ecosystem-based adaptation, or much the same. Because rivers and coasts cross borders, the The Sendai Framework: seven targets for safer societies calls for countries to cooperate on ecosystem-based approaches in shared river basins and coastlines. Research so far has focused on cities in the Global North. Coastal, dryland and watershed areas of the Global South need much more.

  <!-- nature-nbs-224 -->

- **Natural climate solutions: land managed for carbon**

  Canada has set up a CAD$2B Natural Climate Solutions Fund, including CAD$885M for climate solutions in agriculture over 2021–31. Natural climate solutions are conservation, restoration and better land-management actions that increase carbon storage or avoid greenhouse gas emissions. In effect, they protect and enlarge nature's carbon sinks. The research on them is vast but lopsided. A global evidence map found 257,266 relevant papers across 22 pathways. Yet fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.

  <!-- nature-nbs-225 -->

### Water and flood solutions

When rain falls on a city, it has to go somewhere. Stormwater, the water from rain and melted hail and snow, can overwhelm storm sewers and flood a built-up area. This chapter follows the ways people reduce that harm, from classic flood control to green infrastructure, a network of nature-like features that builds with nature. It meets planted channels, shallow hollows that let rain soak in, porous paving and artificial wetlands that clean dirty water. It also meets the many names for one big idea, SuDS, WSUD and LID among them, which all make city drainage work with natural water processes.

- **Stormwater: where city rain goes**

  In a forest, a heavy shower mostly disappears, because soil and plants absorb much of it. Stormwater is the water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow. It has four possible fates. It can soak into the soil to become groundwater, pond on the surface, evaporate, or run off over the land as Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in. Cities tilt the odds toward running off. Hard surfaces let less rain soak in, and drains rush the rest into waterways. The results are erosion and floods, with little water left to recharge groundwater. Unmanaged stormwater causes two main urban problems: flooding and water pollution. It is a major cause of flooding in cities. Most runoff reaches streams, rivers and other water bodies without any treatment. Phosphorus is one culprit it carries. Washed into lakes, it feeds blooms of algae and toxic cyanobacteria. Much of this chapter is about ways to make city rain behave more like forest rain.

  <!-- nature-nbs-209 -->

- **Flood management: living with water that rises**

  The US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) estimates that every $1.00 spent on flood mitigation saves $4.00. Flood management, also called flood control, covers the methods used to reduce or prevent the harm floodwaters do. Floods come from a mix of causes. Some are natural, such as extreme weather upstream. Others are human, such as changes to water bodies and to how rain runs off the land. More hard surfaces make flooding worse, and so do wildfires that strip away vegetation. The methods fall into two families. Structural methods physically hold water back; non-structural methods do not. Wetlands are one of nature's own tools. They hold excess water and, especially on coasts, shield inland communities from storm surges. Protection is not cheap, and its cost rises with the number of people and the amount of property it covers. Yet floods are not simply enemies. Natural seasonal floods renew soil fertility, restore wetlands and support biodiversity.

  <!-- nature-nbs-176 -->

- **Green infrastructure: building with nature**

  When people harness nature and use it as an infrastructure system, they have built green infrastructure. It is a network of natural or nature-like features, also called blue-green infrastructure, used to solve urban and climate problems by building with nature. Nature can shield communities from flooding and extreme heat. It can also improve the quality of air, soil and water. The list of jobs is long: managing stormwater, adapting to climate change, easing heat stress, supporting biodiversity, growing food, cleaning air and water, and offering recreation and shade. Examples range from city woodlands and planted roofs to artificial wetlands, rain-soaking gardens, basins that catch runoff and planted drainage channels, all met later in this course. The idea has deep roots. Its stormwater thinking began in mid-1980s proposals to reduce runoff volume and erosion and recharge aquifers. The term itself first appeared in the early 1990s, in a 1994 report on the Florida Greenways Project. There is still no widely agreed definition. People often stretch it to 'multifunctional' green infrastructure, meaning several functions share the same land.

  <!-- nature-nbs-161 -->

- **Urban flooding: when the drains give up**

  Floods are not only for riverside towns. Urban flooding is the flooding of land or property in a built-up area when rain or coastal storm surges overwhelm drainage such as storm sewers. It can strike whether or not a community sits on a floodplain or near water. Anything that enlarges sealed, impermeable surfaces raises the risk. Climate change is expected to make storm surges, heavy rain and river overflows more frequent and severe. The toll is heavy. In 2020, floods caused an estimated 6,000 deaths and US$51.3B in damages worldwide. Where homes have basements, urban flooding is the main cause of basement and sewer backups, and chronically wet houses are linked to respiratory illness. Responses include grey and green infrastructure, better drainage, and shifting land use toward more vegetated open space.

  <!-- nature-nbs-211 -->

- **Constructed wetlands: marshes built to clean water**

  A marsh can be built to clean dirty water. A constructed wetland is an artificial wetland made to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater. It is engineered, but it relies on the natural work of plants, soil and microorganisms to give wastewater a secondary treatment. Roots, stems and leaves give microbes a surface to grow on while they break down organic matter. Physical, chemical and biological processes together strip out nitrogen, phosphorus and dissolved metals. Stormwater versions copy natural wetlands to capture runoff, cut nutrient loads and create varied wildlife habitat. Because they largely run themselves, their lifetime costs are far lower than conventional treatment plants, and building them is often cheaper too. The catch is space, so they lose out where land is expensive. Cattails and common reed are the main plants, though both can turn invasive outside their native range. Stormwater wetlands can also become 'ecological traps' for amphibians, whose larvae suffer from the pollutants collected there.

  <!-- nature-nbs-158 -->

- **Bioswales: planted ditches that clean the street**

  In 1996, Portland installed 2330 lineal feet of bioswale at Willamette River Park. Small barriers called check dams cut the suspended solids entering the river by 50%. A bioswale is a channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution. Its sides slope gently, at less than 6%. The trick is patience. A bioswale keeps water as long as safely possible, because longer stays remove more pollutants. Plants catch the pollutants, which then enter the soil, where bacteria break them down. Bioswales suit streets and parking lots, where the first rain washes off car pollution. They also recharge groundwater, reduce flooding and erosion, and give pollinators habitat. There are four types: low grass, vegetated, low water use and wet. Neglect leads to costly repairs, so inspection at least once a year is advised.

  <!-- nature-nbs-174 -->

- **Sustainable drainage: making pipes behave like soil**

  In urban areas covered mostly by hard surfaces, more than half of the rain becomes runoff. A sustainable drainage system, or SuDS, is a set of practices that make modern drainage work with natural water processes, as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy. SuDS aim to reduce the harm development does to the water cycle, especially runoff and water pollution. They often bypass traditional drains and return rainwater to natural water bodies as soon as possible. Typical parts include bioswales, porous paving, artificial wetlands, ponds that hold rain, planted roofs, rain-soaking gardens and downspouts cut off from the sewer. Plants and soil remove pollutants by adsorption, where they stick to surfaces, and by filtration and plant uptake. Cost favors them: planting a garden to handle drainage usually costs less than digging tunnels and laying pipes.

  <!-- nature-nbs-171 -->

- **Water-sensitive urban design: rain as a resource**

  Conventional drainage treated city rain as a nuisance and sent it quickly to streams. Water-sensitive urban design, or WSUD, treats it as a resource. This planning and engineering approach builds the whole urban water cycle into city design: stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply. Its aims are to limit environmental harm and make cities more pleasant. The framework came out of Australia in the 1990s, and the term is used there and in the Middle East. It resembles Low-impact development: handling rain where it falls in the United States and sustainable drainage systems in the United Kingdom. Its principles include protecting urban creeks and wetlands, sending cleaner water out of cities and reusing as much stormwater, recycled water and greywater as possible. Common tools include planted filter beds, gravel trenches, porous paving, settling basins, constructed wetlands, swales and rainwater tanks. In Victoria, new housing developments must leave at least 20 percent of each site free of impervious surfaces. Regulatory barriers and institutions split across state and local government are its main obstacles.

  <!-- nature-nbs-184 -->

- **Bioretention: how a planted bed scrubs out metals**

  In laboratory tests, planted soil beds removed 94% of zinc, 88% of copper, 95% of lead and more than 95% of cadmium at typical stormwater levels. Such a bed is a bioretention cell. Bioretention is the removal of pollutants and sediment from stormwater runoff by a planted soil area. A cell has two goals: lowering peak runoff and removing pollutants. A typical one has a sand bed, layers of filter media and plants on top. Stored water seeps into the soil below over several days. The name refers to the plants and bacteria in the media, which hold, absorb, break down and cycle contaminants. Four processes do the cleaning: filtration, adsorption, chemical change and biological breakdown. Nutrients matter downstream. Untreated nitrogen and phosphorus in runoff cause eutrophication, an overgrowth fed by excess nutrients, and well-designed media can sharply reduce both. The cells have limits. Their capacity for heavy metals runs out, so where metal loads are high the media must eventually be replaced. Soils with more than 25 percent clay, slopes over 20 percent or unstable ground may rule bioretention out.

  <!-- nature-nbs-173 -->

- **Rain gardens: small hollows that swallow storms**

  In 1990, Prince George's County in Maryland replaced a conventional stormwater pond with something humbler: residential rain gardens. They proved highly cost-effective. A rain garden is a shallow planted hollow, also called a bioretention facility, that helps runoff soak back into the soil. It cuts the speed, amount and pollution of runoff from roofs, driveways, parking lots and compacted lawns. Plants and soil hold the water and filter its pollutants. Central urban areas can be 90 to 100 percent hard surfaces, against 5 to 10 percent in suburbs. A typical soil mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil. Native plants are usually chosen because they tolerate local conditions, root deeply and add habitat. A study rain garden in Xi'an held most of 28 large storms over four years; only 5 made it overflow. Water ponding for more than 48 hours may signal clogging, one of the most common problems.

  <!-- nature-nbs-183 -->

- **Low-impact development: handling rain where it falls**

  Conventional detention ponds in Prince George's County, Maryland, were not cost-effective and missed their water quality goals. So in 1990 the county tried low-impact development, or LID. This North American approach to land planning and engineering manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure. It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime, infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source. Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize the impact on water flows, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution. Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and collecting rainwater. Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of the water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks. Developers gain too, since dropping ponds on expensive land lets them build more homes on the same plot. In some municipalities LID is a cost-effective way to reduce combined sewer overflows, when pipes carrying both rain and sewage spill into rivers.

  <!-- nature-nbs-197 -->

- **Permeable paving: a parking lot that drinks**

  Permeable paving is made of porous material, or of solid blocks with gaps, that lets stormwater pass through into the ground below. Materials include pervious concrete, porous asphalt, paving stones and interlocking pavers. The surface reduces runoff and traps suspended solids, filtering pollutants out of the water. Downstream, that means less flooding and bank erosion and steadier base flows in rivers. Where the soil cannot absorb water, the pavement stores it and releases it slowly between storms. Some estimates put it at about one third more expensive than conventional paving, though it can reduce the need for other stormwater facilities. It needs care. Without regular cleaning its pores clog and it behaves like ordinary impervious paving. It should not be used at pollution 'hot spots' such as fueling stations, where it could contaminate groundwater.

  <!-- nature-nbs-203 -->

- **Stormwater management: from street sweeping to sewer fees**

  Sweeping a street is a form of water management. Stormwater management means controlling both the quantity and quality of stormwater, using engineered controls and everyday practices known as best management practices. These range from structures such as retention ponds to procedures such as street sweeping. Technical measures include controlling hazardous materials at the source, basins and filters, protecting natural waterways, and nature-based solutions working alongside pipes. Institutional measures include stormwater fees or utilities, asset management, updated regulations and community education. Conventional facilities let particles larger than 40 micron settle out and hold water back to reduce flooding downstream. But stormwater infrastructure is a costly long-term investment, and it performs worse as climate, cities and rules change. In the US, the Environmental Protection Agency regulates stormwater under the Clean Water Act. Farm runoff, though, counts as nonpoint source pollution and needs no permit.

  <!-- nature-nbs-210 -->

- **Structural flood control: walls, banks and reservoirs**

  Some flood defenses are ancient: planting vegetation to hold water, terracing hillsides and digging floodways to divert it. Structural flood control reduces flood effects with physical works such as reservoirs, levees, dredging and diversion channels. Levees and bunds, which are raised banks, along with reservoirs and weirs, keep rivers from bursting their banks. Many dams keep reservoir levels low before the rainy or melt season, leaving room for floodwater. On coasts, sea walls, added beach sand and barrier islands hold back the water. Floodwater can even become a resource. Diverted onto land that absorbs it, the excess recharges groundwater and eases later droughts.

  <!-- nature-nbs-177 -->

- **Non-structural flood management: maps, rules and stilts**

  Not every flood defense holds back water. Non-structural flood management reduces flood risk through zoning, mapping, modeling and planning. Zoning rules can limit how much is built on floodplains and other flood-prone land. Engaging stakeholders helps the public and officials agree on flood policy, including emergency and land-use planning. Property owners matter more and more. They can flood-proof homes by blocking doors and vents, waterproofing and sandbagging. Buildings can be designed for resilience, for example by raising homes on stilts, so a city recovers quickly after a flood. Unlike Structural flood control: walls, banks and reservoirs, these methods work on land, people and buildings rather than on the water itself.

  <!-- nature-nbs-178 -->

- **Green versus grey: what the ledgers show**

  Philadelphia faced a choice: a green plan costing $1.2 billion over 25 years, or a grey plan costing $6 billion. Comparing the two is the economics of green infrastructure versus the conventional kind described in Grey infrastructure: fighting water with concrete, weighing the costs and benefits of green infrastructure against concrete pipes and tunnels. Philadelphia's plan was also expected to raise property values by $390 million over 45 years, increasing the city's property tax income. New York City's green plan was expected to cost $1.5 billion less than a comparable grey one. Green does not always win. A 2012 study of 479 US projects found 44% reduced costs while 31% increased them. The biggest savings came from less stormwater runoff and lower heating and cooling bills. Quality matters: a 2016 UK study found residents willing to pay more for green infrastructure that was visibly greener, accessible and multifunctional. In fragile states, upfront building costs ran up to 8% higher than for other projects.

  <!-- nature-nbs-167 -->

- **Green gentrification: when a new park prices people out**

  A new park can be bad news for the people who live beside it. Green gentrification is the displacement of lower-income residents when new green spaces raise property values and attract wealthier people. Green amenities include parks, gardens, planted roofs and green, energy-efficient building materials. They make neighborhoods more liveable, and that is the problem. Rising housing costs can push low-income households out. Long-time residents can also be displaced culturally and politically. Greening can push out homeless people and others with poor access to housing, undoing some of its own benefits. The pattern shows up in real cities. Greening projects in Chicago have raised social justice concerns such as gentrification. A study of Los Angeles housing prices linked green infrastructure to 'green climate gentrification'. The benefits are often unevenly shared, usually serving wealthier, whiter neighborhoods. Sieg and colleagues coined the term in 2004, blending older ideas of gentrification and Environmental justice: who lives next to the dump?. The exact definition of this kind of gentrification is still debated. Planners are urged to combine environmental goals with social equity and to work with community residents.

  <!-- nature-nbs-168 -->

- **Sponge cities: China's bet on soaking up floods**

  In 2012 a flood in Beijing killed 79 people. In 2014 China made the sponge city national policy. Proposed by landscape architect Kongjian Yu, a sponge city uses green infrastructure, not just drains, to manage urban water and floods. The name says it: green landscapes store, slow and soak up water like a sponge. Its philosophy reverses the pipes, reservoirs and walls of conventional engineering. Retain water at the source, slow its flow, clean it naturally and adapt where it collects. Hard urban surfaces can raise surface flow from 10% to 60% and cut infiltration to nearly zero. Pilots began in 16 districts in 2015 and grew to 87 cities by 2017. Guidelines aim for cities to collect and use 70 percent of rainwater, on 20 percent of urban area by 2020 and 80 percent by 2030. Studies show less runoff and cleaner water. But monitoring data are scarce, and 19 of 30 pilot cities have flooded since.

  <!-- nature-nbs-198 -->

- **Beaver dams: flood control built by rodents**

  The largest known beaver dam is 775 metres long. Most run from a few metres to about 100 metres. A beaver dam creates a pond that protects its builders from predators and stores food for winter. By reshaping their surroundings, beavers act as a Keystone species: small numbers, outsized effects and as an Ecosystem engineers: species that build and reshape habitats. In their native range, the dams reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks. A dam stores floodwater and releases it gradually, lowering the flood wave and keeping streams flowing in dry spells. Bacteria in the debris behind it turn nitrates into nitrogen gas and break down some pesticides. In Alberta, beaver ponds held 5.7 times more young wood frogs than nearby free-flowing streams. Dams can also flood farmland, roads and railways. In Tierra del Fuego, introduced beavers are considered a plague. When dams are abandoned, their wetlands become meadows and then forest, slowly building up the valley floor.

  <!-- nature-nbs-195 -->

- **Flood peak attenuation: flattening the spike**

  Flood water tends to rise and fall very abruptly. Flood peak attenuation means slowing runoff so that a flood's short, steep peak is spread out over time and lowered. Many natural features do this. Marshes, river meanders, vegetation and porous materials each slow part of the flow. So does a river spreading out over its floodplain. Together they blunt the spike, so less water arrives at any one moment.

  <!-- nature-nbs-179 -->

- **Flood risk mapping: knowing where the water will go**

  In Bangladesh, nearly 80% of people live on low floodplains. Hazard maps there pick out the areas prone to repeated or severe floods. Flood risk mapping means drawing maps of where floods may reach, so policy makers can make informed decisions. It is described as the most effective way to reduce risk to people and property, and most countries have such maps. Flood modeling adds detail. It simulates flood hazards, how their drivers interact, and their effects on people and the environment.

  <!-- nature-nbs-182 -->

- **Managed retreat from floodplains: giving land back to the river**

  Sometimes the best flood defense is to leave. Planned withdrawal from floodplains, a case of what Managed retreat: moving out of harm's way describes, means removing buildings from flood-prone areas and turning the land into parks or wilderness. Nothing is left to damage, and the floodplain is free to flood. Programs in which governments buy out floodplain homeowners (Buyout programs: when government buys the house) have run in New Jersey, in Charlotte in North Carolina, and in Missouri.

  <!-- nature-nbs-180 -->

- **Storm surge barriers: gates against the sea**

  The North Sea flood of 1953 led to a new kind of defense. A storm surge barrier is a floodgate built to stop a storm surge or spring tide from flooding the area behind it. London's Thames Barrier has operated since 1982 to guard against surges like that of 1953. A barrier is almost always part of a larger system of floodwalls, levees and natural features. Storm surge warnings help decide when to close the gates.

  <!-- nature-nbs-181 -->

- **Barriers to green infrastructure: the funding gap**

  Above all, green infrastructure is held back by a lack of funding. There is a silver lining. Because green projects produce many benefits, they can compete for many different funding sources at once. Some government tax incentive programs can also attract finance. Fragile states face harder limits. Weak governance and limited institutional capacity can stop them benefiting from green infrastructure investment.

  <!-- nature-nbs-169 -->

- **Blue infrastructure: the water in the city**

  Rivers, ponds, lakes and harbours are infrastructure too. Blue infrastructure is the part of a city's infrastructure that involves water. Combined with green infrastructure, it becomes blue-green infrastructure. It can support aquatic insects, amphibians and water birds in the middle of a city. When people can reach it, blue infrastructure is called blue space, and access to it may benefit their health and wellbeing.

  <!-- nature-nbs-162 -->

- **Floating wetlands: gardens that clean the water beneath**

  A wetland can float. A constructed floating wetland is a planted structure that rides on a lake, river, estuary or coastal water and supports wetland vegetation. Its plants dangle roots into the water and can remove heavy metals and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen. They may store carbon too. The rafts give habitat to insects and wildlife and soften the look of hardened urban shorelines.

  <!-- nature-nbs-164 -->

- **Downspout disconnection: unplugging the roof from the sewer**

  In heavy rain, a building's downspouts can pour 12 gallons of water a minute into the sewer. That raises the risk of basement backups and sewer overflows. Downspout disconnection cuts a roof's downspout off from the sewer and sends the roof water onto ground that can soak it up. It is especially useful in cities with combined sewer systems, where rainwater and sewage share the same pipes.

  <!-- nature-nbs-165 -->

- **Green and blue roofs: putting the roof to work**

  Since 1991, Zurich has required that flat roofs not used as terraces be greened. Roofs can be covered with plants and soil, as in a Green roofs: gardens on top of buildings, or built to collect and hold rainfall, as in a Blue roofs: storing the storm on top. A planted roof can hold back forty to eighty percent of the rain that falls on it and release the rest slowly. It also improves air and water quality and lowers energy costs. A water-holding roof stores rainfall and drains it to sewers and waterways at a controlled rate.

  <!-- nature-nbs-163 -->

- **Green infrastructure planning: mapping nature's work first**

  Green infrastructure planning starts by mapping what the natural environment does for a place. It then protects the key natural areas through regulation or planning policy. Where natural life-support functions are missing, plans may add them through landscaping or engineering. In the UK the approach now appears in national, regional and local planning documents. In the US, programs run by the EPA aim to improve water quality by managing stormwater runoff more widely and easing the load on sewers.

  <!-- nature-nbs-170 -->

- **Stormwater basins: hollows that catch the rain**

  A stormwater basin is a planted hollow in the ground that collects rainwater. It cuts runoff to sewers, reduces erosion, filters water and prevents flooding. Older basins were mowed grass. Newer designs use sturdier plants and are often called bioretention basins. They are good at removing pollutants and trapping sediment. Stormwater basins are an important part of the sponge city idea for managing floods.

  <!-- nature-nbs-166 -->

- **Floodplain restoration: reconnecting rivers to their land**

  At Nijmegen, engineers moved a dike 350 metres inland and dug a side channel. Peak water levels fell by about 35 cm. That is floodplain restoration: returning all or part of a river's floodplain to its state before levees were built and wetlands drained. It is a nature-based solution that lowers flood risk by helping the ecosystem slow and hold water. Methods reconnect rivers to floodplains by setting back levees, removing dams or weirs, and restoring drained wetlands. The goals include fewer floods, habitat for aquatic species, cleaner water and more groundwater recharge. Vegetation helps: it can cut wave energy during floods by about 70% in salt marshes and 65% in mangroves. Restoration works best for frequent, low to moderate floods and helps little against extreme floods on its own. Coastal wetlands are accepted as large carbon sinks, but whether restoration raises their storage rates is debated. Projects can stall when immediate flood defense and current land uses are valued above ecological benefits.

  <!-- nature-nbs-187 -->

- **Stream restoration: healing rivers for fish, floods and people**

  A US database built in the 2000s held over 35,000 stream restoration projects. Stream restoration is work to improve a river or stream's environmental health, for biodiversity, recreation, flood control or landscape. It differs from river engineering, which alters water bodies for navigation, flood control or water supply without an ecological aim. Activities range from fixing a culvert or removing a weir that blocks fish, to stabilizing banks, restoring riparian zones or adding constructed wetlands. Projects usually begin by assessing climate, geology, hydrology, sediment movement, channel shape and flood records. Approaches split in two. Form-based restoration physically reshapes the stream; process-based restoration revives its natural water and sediment processes. How well any of it works remains poorly measured, because data are thin, monitoring is scarce and yardsticks differ. Even so, it is entering law, as in the European water framework's commitment to restore surface waters.

  <!-- nature-nbs-188 -->

- **Dam removal: letting rivers run free again**

  About 900 US dams were removed between 1990 and 2015, and by 2015 the pace was 50 to 60 a year. Dam removal means demolishing a dam to return natural flow to a river. The decision weighs a dam's benefits, such as hydropower, flood control, irrigation and navigation, against its harms. Dams can reduce a river's biological productivity, its biodiversity and its native species. As they age, they weaken, fill with sediment and cost more to maintain. Many removals aim to restore river habitat and native fish, as in the Elwha Ecosystem Restoration. Released sediment can rebuild habitat downstream, but toxic sediment can do harm, as when PCBs escaped after a Hudson River dam came down. Removal is always costly, and owners and government usually share the bill. Europe counts at least 150 000 barriers in its rivers that no longer serve a purpose. The EU Biodiversity Strategy aims to restore free flow to 25,000 kilometres of river by 2030.

  <!-- nature-nbs-199 -->

- **What urban floods cost**

  FEMA says almost 40% of small businesses never reopen after a flooding disaster. Urban floods impose financial costs on property owners, businesses and cities. US experts estimate that wet basements can lower property values by 10%-25%. Urban flooding is estimated to cost £270 million a year in England and Wales. Warming would raise the bill. Under 2–4°C of warming, expected annual surface water damages in the UK may rise by £60–200 million.

  <!-- nature-nbs-214 -->

- **Grey infrastructure: fighting water with concrete**

  Grey infrastructure is conventional infrastructure such as dams, sea walls, pipes and channels, built of concrete or other impervious materials to control water. Its logic is to centralize water in big reservoirs, speed it through pipes and fight it with higher walls. That is the opposite of sponge city design. It can prevent flood damage and be economically valuable. But models suggest it may grow less effective as climate change intensifies floods. Overused, it can cause water shortages, pollution and the loss of water ecosystem services.

  <!-- nature-nbs-213 -->

- **Integrated urban water management: one city, one water**

  Integrated urban water management handles a city's freshwater, wastewater and stormwater together, as parts of one plan for the river basin. It is seen as a way to achieve the goals of water-sensitive urban design. Treating the urban water cycle as a whole aims to use resources more efficiently, with economic, social and environmental gains. Integrated stormwater management, for example, can improve runoff quality, cut flood risk and add to the drinking water supply.

  <!-- nature-nbs-215 -->

- **Three kinds of urban flood**

  Planners distinguish three kinds of urban flood. Pluvial floods come from heavy rain. Fluvial floods come from a river overflowing. Coastal floods often come from storm surges. Each type has different impacts and needs different defenses. Erratic rainfall is expected to make both pluvial and fluvial flooding more frequent and severe. Coastal cities may be hit hardest, facing rising seas and heavier rain at once.

  <!-- nature-nbs-212 -->

- **Subsurface flow wetlands: cleaning water out of sight**

  In a subsurface flow constructed wetland, wastewater flows among plant roots below a gravel surface, so no water shows on top. Keeping the water hidden makes the system more efficient and less smelly. It also attracts fewer mosquitoes and suffers less in winter. It needs less land than a surface flow wetland. Its cost depends mainly on the sand used to fill the bed. It is a secondary treatment, so solids must first be removed in a primary treatment step.

  <!-- nature-nbs-159 -->

- **Surface flow wetlands: open water that kills germs**

  A surface flow constructed wetland, also called a free water surface wetland, has open water flowing horizontally across plant roots. It is used to polish the effluent from wastewater treatment plants and to treat stormwater drainage. In the open water, sunlight, predators, settling and natural decay destroy pathogens. The drawbacks are real. It needs more land than a subsurface system, may smell more and works less well in winter. Open water can also breed mosquitoes, which makes it harder to fit into city neighborhoods.

  <!-- nature-nbs-160 -->

- **Infiltration trenches: gravel that lets rain sink in**

  An infiltration trench is a shallow trench filled with gravel or rock. It holds stormwater underground and lets it seep slowly into the soil and groundwater. Its main job is not cleaning water, but it can hold back some pollutants and sediment. Sand filters work on the same principle. They suit runoff from car parks and dense built-up areas.

  <!-- nature-nbs-185 -->

- **Sedimentation basins: the first stop for dirty runoff**

  A sedimentation basin holds stormwater briefly and slows it, so that coarse and medium sediments settle to the bottom. It is often the first element in a treatment train, a series of steps that clean water in turn. By catching sediment early, it keeps later elements from being smothered. Constructed wetlands often use a sedimentation basin as their inlet zone.

  <!-- nature-nbs-186 -->

- **Retention basins: ponds that never dry**

  A retention basin, also called a wet pond, is an artificial pond with plants around its edge and a permanent pool of water. It manages stormwater by controlling runoff, guarding against floods and erosion, and improving the quality of nearby water. It differs from a detention basin, or 'dry pond', which holds water only after a storm and then drains at a controlled rate. It also differs from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

  <!-- nature-nbs-172 -->

- **Four families of permeable pavement**

  Permeable pavement comes in several families, each suited to different uses. Pervious concrete is widely available and carries frequent traffic. Porous asphalt is laid like normal asphalt but leaves out the fine aggregate, so open voids let water through. Plastic grids filled with gravel or turf make a fully porous surface popular with homeowners. Permeable interlocking concrete pavers have open spaces between units and carry both light and heavy traffic.

  <!-- nature-nbs-204 -->

- **Room for the River: the Dutch stop raising dikes**

  In 1993 and 1995, floods forced the evacuation of over 200,000 people near the Rhine delta. The Dutch response was Room for the River, a government plan run from 2006 to 2015. It protects against floods by giving rivers more space while improving landscape and environment. Measures included moving dykes back, lowering floodplains and the low cross-walls that trap sand, deepening side channels, removing obstacles and building a flood bypass. A basic package of forty projects had a budget of €2.2 billion. Its Nijmegen project marked a policy shift from ever-higher dikes toward working with the river's natural dynamics.

  <!-- nature-nbs-207 -->

- **The flood pulse concept: why floods feed rivers**

  Older theories saw floods as catastrophes. The flood pulse concept, developed by W. J. Junk in 1989, sees the annual flood as the most biologically productive feature of a river ecosystem. The regular cycle of flooding and drying controls the exchange of water, nutrients and organisms between channel and floodplain. The pulse maintains species and genetic diversity and brings in oxygen. Dams, channelization and levees disrupt it and can devastate riverside ecosystems. It is one of three main models of large rivers. Many theorists criticize its assumptions and prefer the river continuum concept, while its authors argue that rival does not fit large rivers.

  <!-- nature-nbs-202 -->

- **Beaver dam analogs: building dams for beavers**

  People can build a beaver's dam for it. A beaver dam analog is a human-made structure that imitates a beaver dam, either to gain its benefits or to coax beavers into settling. Builders may drive wooden posts into the stream bed to hold branches that would otherwise wash away. Even if beavers never move in, analogs provide many of the benefits of natural dams, such as holding water and creating wetland ponds.

  <!-- nature-nbs-196 -->

- **Taming a dam without tearing it down**

  Fewer than 1% of US dams are being considered for removal, so most rivers need other fixes. Better equipment, environmental flows and fish ladders can reduce a dam's harm while it stays. Varying the water released by season mimics a river's natural flow changes. How well fish ladders help fish reach spawning grounds is debated, though some fish passing beats none. Plans for decommissioning and river restoration should be drawn up well before a dam reaches the end of its design life.

  <!-- nature-nbs-201 -->

- **Four ways to take down a dam**

  Removing a dam is mostly a question of what to do with the sediment behind it. There are four common methods. Notch and release drains the reservoir slowly through cut notches, so the ecosystem can adjust; it can take over a year. Rapid release is quickest and cheapest but can cause severe flooding and erosion downstream. Dig and dewater, usually the most expensive, removes dried sediment for safe disposal, which is needed when it contains toxins. Retained sediment leaves the sediment in place and reroutes the river around the site.

  <!-- nature-nbs-200 -->

- **Replanting riverbanks: plant them or let them return**

  Riverside plants can come back in two ways. Active revegetation plants them. Passive revegetation removes the disturbance and lets them return on their own. Active planting may be fastest but can cost too much. Passive methods can work well: fencing out cattle can let riparian plants recover quickly and shift toward natural communities. The risk is that exotic species colonize first and undermine the recovery.

  <!-- nature-nbs-206 -->

- **Engineered log jams: putting wood back in rivers**

  Straightened channels and the loss of beavers stripped many streams of their natural log jams. An engineered log jam places large wood back in a stream to recreate them. The logs change how water moves. They add riffles, pools and temperature variation to the flow, giving the stream more varied places for life.

  <!-- nature-nbs-193 -->

- **Form-based restoration: reshaping the channel**

  Form-based stream restoration changes a channel's physical shape to improve its condition. Its tools include deflectors, cross-vanes, weirs and step-pools, engineered log jams, bank stabilization and redesigning the channel. The change is immediate. But it can fail when the damage comes from a wider area than the reach being fixed. Scientists criticize the approach on two counts. They say it works at too small a scale, and that it aims for what people think a stream should look like rather than what its setting supports.

  <!-- nature-nbs-189 -->

- **Natural Channel Design: a cookbook for streams**

  Natural Channel Design is a US method from the 1990s. It classifies a stream by its shape, slope and bed, then redesigns the channel to a target form. The design phase alone has 8 phases and 40 steps. Fluvial geomorphologists, who study how rivers shape land, are critical. They call it a 'cookbook' approach that untrained practitioners misuse, leading to failed projects. Its focus on channel stability can also limit a stream's ability to adapt.

  <!-- nature-nbs-191 -->

- **Process-based restoration: let the river do the work**

  Process-based stream restoration rebuilds the water and sediment processes that shape a stream, rather than its form. It has grown in popularity since the mid-1990s as a more ecosystem-centred approach. It restores connections between stream and floodplain and along the stream itself, often by removing levees, dams or grade controls. The aim is a system that is as resilient as possible and needs little maintenance. The catch is patience, because benefits can take time to appear.

  <!-- nature-nbs-190 -->

- **Freedom space: a corridor for a wandering river**

  Rivers move, and some planners now let them. A stream corridor, or freedom space, is a band of land set by a stream's hydrology and landforms within which it may move with minimal interference. The idea has many names. It is the river corridor in the US, room for the river in the Netherlands, and making space for water in the UK. A cost-benefit analysis found it could pay off over the long term through lower maintenance costs, less erosion and flood damage, and ecological services.

  <!-- nature-nbs-192 -->

- **Streambank bioengineering: roots instead of rock**

  Stream banks can be held in place by living plants. Streambank bioengineering stabilizes banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap, loose rock armor, and gabions, wire cages of stone. Live branches sprout roots that anchor the soil and prevent erosion. That makes these structures more natural and adaptable than concrete and rock. Some bank erosion is welcome anyway, since it is generally seen as good for the diversity of aquatic and riverside habitats.

  <!-- nature-nbs-194 -->

- **The first flush: a storm's dirtiest minutes**

  The first runoff of a rainstorm is the dirtiest. This first flush washes off pollution that has built up on hard surfaces, and in towns and suburbs it is described as highly toxic. Bioswales are built to handle it, which is why they suit roads, parking lots and roofs. Rainwater tanks may use a first-flush diverter to keep contaminants out of the stored water.

  <!-- nature-nbs-175 -->

- **Source water protection: guarding drinking water at the start**

  In Walkerton, Ontario, drinking water was contaminated with E. coli. Canada responded by adopting source water protection as part of a multi-barrier approach. Source water protection is planning by water utilities and governments to protect drinking water sources from overuse and contamination. It applies to lakes, rivers and groundwater. The work involves identifying sources, assessing contamination threats, informing the public and acting to remove contamination. Researchers have begun bringing ecosystem service assessments into source water protection.

  <!-- nature-nbs-208 -->

### Coastal solutions

Where land meets sea, waves, currents, tides and storms carry sediment and rock away, and the shoreline retreats. People have long answered with hard defenses such as seawalls, but there are other choices: retreating, rebuilding beaches with sand, or stabilizing dunes. This chapter weighs them all, from managed retreat to deliberately breaching old sea defenses so salt marsh can return. It also meets the living defenders, oyster reefs and coastal plants, and the people who rebuild them. And it follows blue carbon, the carbon that coastal ecosystems take up and store in ways people can manage.

- **Blue carbon: the climate value of coastal mud**

  Coastal mud can hold carbon for millennia. Blue carbon is carbon taken up and stored by living marine systems, especially coastal ones, in ways people can manage. Most often it means the carbon captured by tidal marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows. These vegetated coastal ecosystems bury carbon fast, piling it up in their soils and sediments. Those sediments lack oxygen, so the carbon can be preserved for decades to millennia, far longer than most carbon stocks on land. The term was coined in 2009 to stress that these ecosystems store far more than their share of the world's carbon. Seagrass, salt marshes and mangroves are sometimes called 'blue forests', in contrast to green forests on land. The flip side is stark. When these ecosystems are damaged or lost, they release their carbon back to the air. Managing them counts as an ocean-based, biological form of Carbon dioxide removal: taking CO2 back out of the air, and it can serve both climate mitigation and ecosystem-based adaptation. How effective blue carbon is over the long term, though, is still debated.

  <!-- nature-nbs-034 -->

- **Coastal erosion: the sea takes back the land**

  In 1917 the village of Hallsands in Devon was washed into the sea. Shingle had been dredged from its bay, leaving it unprotected. Coastal erosion is the loss of land, or long-term removal of sediment and rock, along a coastline. Waves, currents, tides, wind-driven water, ice and storms all do the work. They act through the hydraulic force of water, abrasion by hurled stones, attrition as stones grind each other down, and seawater chemically dissolving rock. Softer rock erodes faster than harder rock, carving tunnels, arches and pillars, until over time the coast evens out. Storms can erode coasts hundreds of times faster than normal weather. Rising seas let waves reach further inland, speeding the retreat. The losses compound. Erosion destroys the dunes, wetlands, beaches and barrier islands that buffer storms, and it reduces biodiversity. It damages infrastructure and property, raises protection costs, and harms tourism and fisheries.

  <!-- nature-nbs-064 -->

- **Coastal management: defending where people crowd**

  Coastal zones cover less than 15% of Earth's land, yet host more than 40% of the world's people. Nearly 1.2 billion people live within 100 km of a coastline and 100 m of sea level. Coastal management is the work of defending coasts against flooding and erosion, including techniques that stop erosion to claim land. Its importance is growing as climate change speeds up the rise of the seas this century. Before the 1950s, the norm was hard structures such as Seawalls: holding the line in concrete, sloping stone revetments and sand-trapping walls. From the late 1940s, cost and ugliness pushed engineers toward artificial beaches and stabilized dunes that copy natural protection. One lesson came hard. Measures often worked locally but made problems worse elsewhere, sometimes tens of kilometres away.

  <!-- nature-nbs-053 -->

- **Managed retreat: moving out of harm's way**

  Kiribati, a low-lying country facing flooding, is planning to relocate its people. Managed retreat is the planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk. It can answer floods, wildfire, drought and other hazards, and its form depends on the place, the hazard and local policy. Retreating from high-risk areas such as floodplains reduces exposure. Rising seas are now drawing the attention of politicians, insurers and residents of low-lying coasts. Retreat is controversial. Programs have met lawsuits and resistance from residents worried about home values and insurance costs. Yet more communities consider it as the costs of adaptation rise. One New Zealand coastal hazards expert argues retreat is mainly a social and political issue, not a technical one. Whether migration counts as adaptation is itself debated; the IPCC says it may or may not.

  <!-- nature-nbs-040 -->

- **Seawalls: holding the line in concrete**

  At least 43 percent of Japan's coastline is lined with seawalls or similar structures. Yet in 2011 the tsunami overwhelmed seawalls in most areas. A seawall is a hard coastal defense built where the sea acts directly on the land, to protect people, property and activities from tides, waves or tsunamis. It works by reflecting wave energy back out to sea. That reflected energy has costs. It can scour and lower the beach in front, and the wall can speed erosion of neighboring unprotected coasts. Being fixed, a seawall clashes with a moving coast and blocks the exchange of sediment between land and sea. Rising seas raise both normal water levels and storm waves, which existing walls may not withstand. High costs and side effects have led to more use of soft options such as beach replenishment. A cost-benefit approach helps decide whether a wall is worth it.

  <!-- nature-nbs-071 -->

- **Oyster reefs: living breakwaters that filter the sea**

  Over two centuries, 85% of the world's oyster reefs have been removed. An oyster reef is a dense colony of oysters that builds up into a large reef, also called an oyster bed, bank or bar. New reefs start on stone or hard debris, because oyster larvae must settle on hard surfaces. Young oysters then settle on older shells, and the reef grows. Overharvesting, lime production and coastal degradation drove the decline. What was lost was valuable. Oysters filter phytoplankton and organic matter from the water, buffering estuaries against eutrophication.
