A common objection is that focusing on these technologies could undermine efforts to cut emissions. Effective governance and international oversight are widely seen as essential.

  <!-- nature-clim-199 -->

- **Solar radiation modification: dimming the sun**

  Solar radiation modification is the only known way to lower global temperatures within months. Also called solar geoengineering, it limits warming by reflecting more sunlight from Earth back to space. It is meant to complement, not replace, emission cuts. Models consistently show it could reduce warming and many climate effects, though effects would vary by region and season. Direct costs could be billions to tens of billions of US dollars per degree Celsius of cooling, low compared with climate damages. But it does not lower CO2, so it does nothing about ocean acidification. Some fear a 'moral hazard', weakening the will to cut emissions, though experts dispute its size. Because it is cheap and feasible, one country could deploy it alone, and no comprehensive global framework regulates it. Scientists, NGOs and governments disagree on whether it should be researched or deployed at all.

  <!-- nature-clim-211 -->

- **Can net-zero pledges be trusted?**

  As of 2023, only 5% of companies with a net zero commitment had a credible plan. Credible targets covered only 7% of emissions. Most such pledges are voluntary and lack enforcement, so their trustworthiness is hotly debated. Heavy reliance on carbon credits is a main reason many claims lack credibility. The UN has condemned the net zero pledges of fossil fuel companies, made while they expand production, as greenwashing. Some climate scientists go further. They argue that net zero lets actors put off cuts today by relying on unproven future technologies. Standards bodies, meanwhile, are trying to make pledges robust, so the debate is about how to fix the idea as much as whether to keep it.

  <!-- nature-clim-166 -->

- **What carbon removal costs**

  Removing a tonne of CO2 costs less than $50 through nature-based solutions such as reforestation. Biochar costs $200 to $584, and direct air capture $94 to $600. Costs vary with how mature each method is and with the markets for removals and by-products. Price also reflects durability. Biochar sells for more than nature-based removals because it stores carbon for hundreds or thousands of years, while forests are a more volatile store. Land differs too. A direct air capture plant taking 1 MtCO2 a year uses 0.4–1.5 km2, while roughly 46 million trees would need about 3,098–4,647 km2. As of early 2023, financing fell short of what high-tech removal would need. Most new money came from voluntary private initiatives, a concern because voluntary markets have historically been far smaller than those created by government policy.

  <!-- nature-clim-140 -->

- **Enhanced weathering: grinding rock to capture carbon**

  Over geological time, rainwater and CO2 form carbonic acid that slowly dissolves minerals, which helps stabilize Earth's climate. Enhanced weathering speeds this up by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so it reacts with water and air. The CO2 ends up in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity, which also slows ocean acidification. It could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year. A 2020 analysis put the cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne, comparable to BECCS and large-scale direct air capture. Uncertain dissolution rates make its cost and speed uncertain. Mine tailings and steel slag can be used first, though more basalt mining might eventually be needed.

  <!-- nature-clim-196 -->

- **Biochar carbon removal: the leader in delivered removals**

  In 2022/2023, biochar carbon removal accounted for 87–92% of all carbon removals actually delivered. The method turns leftover biomass into biochar by pyrolysis and stores it in soil or durable materials. It is also called pyrogenic carbon capture and storage. Plants take CO2 from the air as they grow. Heating them to 350–900 °C with little oxygen locks that carbon into a stable form that can last centuries to millennia, with bio-oil and pyrogas as by-products. Its potential is put at 0.3 to 4.9 billion tonnes of CO2 per year. It is quick to deploy and capital-efficient, suiting farmers and rural diversification in developing countries. How fast biochar decays is disputed. Some studies report fast decay or more soil emissions, while a 2025 re-analysis says common decay models overestimate decay.

  <!-- nature-clim-180 -->

- **Net zero for short-lived gases like methane**

  Methane does not have to reach zero to stop adding warming. Because it is short-lived, cutting its emissions lowers its warming effect at once. That is one reason net zero for CO2 alone can come sooner than for all gases, along with the difficulty of phasing out farm methane. Short-lived gases still push temperatures up in the short term and could breach 1.5 °C earlier. Robust net zero standards therefore cover all greenhouse gases, not only CO2.

  <!-- nature-clim-165 -->

- **Could carbon removal become an excuse?**

  Removal plans in countries' 2023 climate pledges would need 1.2 billion hectares, as much land as all the world's cropland. That points to a worry: promises of future removal could weaken efforts to cut emissions now. In 2018, relying on large-scale removal was seen as a major risk to the 1.5 °C goal, given uncertainty about how fast it can grow. A 2019 NASEM report said that delaying mitigation on the promise of a removal backstop misrepresents removal's real capacity. Critics insist it is no substitute for cuts, while others see it as a needed complement for hard-to-abate sectors.

  <!-- nature-clim-141 -->

- **Removing carbon through the ocean**

  The ocean's dissolved carbon stays in balance with the CO2 in the air, so drawing carbon down in the sea pulls it from the sky. Ocean alkalinity enhancement dissolves minerals such as olivine or limestone so that carbonate settles on the sea floor, at an estimated US$100 to $150 per tonne. Electrochemical methods strip carbonate from seawater and are much cheaper when combined with desalination. Ocean fertilization would store carbon for only 10–100 years.

  <!-- nature-clim-142 -->

- **How long does removed carbon stay put?**

  Removing carbon helps only while it stays stored. Forests, kelp beds and other plants store carbon as they grow, but these stores are volatile, because long-term storage cannot be guaranteed. Wildfires, disease, economic pressure and changing politics can release the carbon again. Injecting CO2 underground, or locking it into insoluble carbonate salts, stores it more securely.

  <!-- nature-clim-139 -->

- **Residual emissions and removals that match**

  Methane lasts around 12 years in the air, carbon dioxide between 300 and 1,000 years. That gap shapes net zero rules. Residual emissions are those not practical to cut for technical reasons. Robust rules say they must be balanced by removals that store carbon as long as the gas would last, so removals balancing CO2 must last far longer. Weaker carbon neutrality standards also allow avoided-emissions offsets, which cut emissions against a baseline but remove nothing from the air. Critics worry such offsets delay real cuts and aid greenwashing.

  <!-- nature-clim-163 -->

- **Glacial geoengineering: holding back the ice**

  Melting ice reflects less sunlight, a feedback that could trigger climate tipping points. Fear of that drives glacial geoengineering: proposed interventions to slow the loss of glaciers, ice sheets and sea ice. Methods include regional sunlight reflection, reflective surfaces, draining water from under glaciers and curtains on the seabed. The research is early, and effectiveness is highly uncertain.

  <!-- nature-clim-200 -->

- **Who governs geoengineering?**

  No single treaty governs geoengineering. The rules are mostly specific to each method. In 2010 the treaty described in The Convention on Biological Diversity set a non-binding framework requiring scientific justification, environmental assessment and oversight. A 2013 amendment to the London Protocol created a binding framework for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization. It has not entered into force.

  <!-- nature-clim-201 -->

- **Marine cloud brightening**

  Spraying tiny sea-water droplets into low ocean clouds could make them reflect more sunlight. The cooling from such marine cloud brightening would be felt quickly, and it could be reversed on fairly short time scales. But technical barriers remain, it could not offset all current warming, and its risks are unclear.

  <!-- nature-clim-213 -->

- **Stratospheric aerosols: copying a volcano**

  Volcanic eruptions release sulfates into the upper atmosphere, and the planet cools. Stratospheric aerosol injection would do this on purpose, putting small reflective particles high up to reflect sunlight. Sulfates are the usual proposal for that reason. It is the most-researched form of solar radiation modification, and the IPCC found high agreement that it could limit warming to below 1.5 °C. A key risk is delaying the recovery of the ozone layer.

  <!-- nature-clim-212 -->

- **Termination shock: the danger of stopping**

  Solar radiation modification masks warming rather than removing its cause. Stop it suddenly while greenhouse gas levels are high, and the hidden warming would arrive fast. This termination shock would bring rapid temperature rise, rising seas and weaker carbon sinks. Large-scale use would likely need a commitment of decades to a century. The IPCC notes that a gradual phase-out alongside mitigation would reduce the impact.

  <!-- nature-clim-214 -->

- **BiCRS: storing the carbon in plant waste**

  Direct air capture is costly and energy-hungry. Biomass carbon removal and storage, or BiCRS, lets photosynthesis do the capturing instead. It collects biomass such as farm waste, then uses engineering to store its carbon-rich residue permanently or semi-permanently. The family includes BECCS and biochar carbon removal. Challenges include measuring the carbon stored in buried biomass and extra demand for farmland, so think tanks urge limits on which biomass may be used.

  <!-- nature-clim-184 -->

- **Biochar carbon credits**

  In 2024, biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases. Their certified removals are sold as biochar carbon credits in carbon markets. Because abatement costs are high, these credits trade about an order of magnitude above credits from emission cuts or nature-based solutions. To be certified, suppliers must be carbon net-negative, storing more carbon than they use making and distributing the biochar.

  <!-- nature-clim-181 -->

- **The energy transition: leaving fossil fuels behind**

  Energy production and use cause most human greenhouse gas emissions, and fossil fuels still meet over three-quarters of energy needs. An energy transition is a major structural change in how energy is supplied and used. Today it means the shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy. The current transition aims to cut energy emissions mainly by phasing down fossil fuels and running as much as possible on low-carbon electricity. It is not the first. During the Industrial Revolution, societies moved from wood and biomass to coal, then to oil and gas. The term itself arose after the 1973 oil crisis, and Jimmy Carter popularized it in 1977. Since the late 2010s, falling solar and wind costs have driven the change. Yet progress is slow. Despite decades of climate policy, transitions have not sped up beyond historical trends, and they remain off track for agreed warming goals.

  <!-- nature-clim-167 -->

- **Sustainable energy: meeting needs without borrowing from the future**

  Fossil fuels provide 85% of world energy use, and the energy system causes 76% of greenhouse gas emissions. Sustainable energy is energy that meets present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs. It is judged by its effects on environment, economy and society. Those effects range from greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution to energy poverty and toxic waste. Around 790 million people still lack electricity, and 2.6 billion cook with polluting fuels such as wood or charcoal. Renewables such as wind, hydro, solar and geothermal can harm the environment, but they are generally far more sustainable than fossil fuels. Whether non-renewables belong is disputed. Nuclear avoids carbon and air pollution but brings waste, proliferation and accident risks. Efficiency matters as much as supply: the IEA says it could deliver 40% of the emission cuts the Paris goals need. The bill is large. The IPCC estimates US$2.4 trillion a year must be invested in energy from 2016 to 2035 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.

  <!-- nature-clim-215 -->

- **Just transition: leaving no one behind**

  In the 1980s, US trade unions sought protection for workers hit by environmental rules. Tony Mazzocchi of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union proposed a 'Superfund for Workers' to compensate and retrain them. He is believed to have coined the term just transition. The principle holds that the shift to a low-carbon economy should treat people fairly and leave no workers, places or countries behind. Unions won just transition and decent work language in the preamble of the 2015 Paris climate deal. The IPCC stresses low-emission industries, fair jobs, equitable energy access and economic diversification. As of 2022, 38% of 170 countries mentioned it in their short-term climate plans. The EU's Just Transition mechanism helps regions dependent on fossil fuels move to a greener economy.

  <!-- nature-clim-174 -->

- **Phasing out fossil fuels**

  Fossil fuels cause over 70% of greenhouse gas emissions, so phasing them out is the largest part of limiting warming. The proposal is a gradual reduction of their use and production to zero, to cut air pollution, limit climate change and gain energy independence. Policies include demand-side measures that cut consumption and supply-side measures that limit production. Alternatives include switching to electricity, green hydrogen and biofuel. Most premature deaths from air pollution are due to fossil fuels, and the health benefits of phase-out, valued in money, exceed the cost of the 2 °C goal. Governments still subsidized fossil fuels by about $500 billion a year as of 2019, and the IMF's wider definition gave $5.2 trillion in 2017. As of 2024, global fossil fuel use was still rising, as it has since 1965. Workers and politicians tied to fossil industries tend to oppose phase-out unless they have strong alternatives.

  <!-- nature-clim-197 -->

- **Electrification: running the world on clean power**

  The National Academy of Engineering called electrification the greatest engineering achievement of the 20th Century. Electrification means switching to electricity as the power source. In sustainable energy, it means moving end uses such as transport and heating onto clean electricity. The reason is simple. Clean energy such as renewables and nuclear is mostly produced as electricity, so end uses must be electrified for a sustainable system. Electric vehicles and heat pumps are two key areas. Electrification and economic growth are highly correlated, and 1900 to 1940 was a period of high productivity growth. Access is still uneven. About 840 million people, mostly in Africa, had no grid electricity in 2017, down from 1.2 billion in 2010. Electricity is a 'sticky', multi-source form of energy. It is resilient in the long term but unstable in the short term, because supply must match use instantly.

  <!-- nature-clim-193 -->

- **Energy justice: who gains and who pays**

  Cities often gain from energy systems while rural areas bear the burdens. Energy justice aims for communities to gain affordable, safe and sustainable energy and to take part in decisions about it. It seeks to share benefits and burdens fairly across social groups, regions and generations. Its three main tenets are distributive justice, recognition justice and fair process. Distributive justice concerns how revenues, infrastructure sites and costs are shared. Recognition justice asks who is ignored. Fair process, explored in Procedural justice: fair process, not just fair results, requires transparent decisions and meaningful consultation. Some scholars add restorative and cosmopolitan justice to capture international inequalities and harms from fossil fuels. The energy justice cycle follows the system from extraction through production, supply and consumption to decommissioning and waste. The stakes are real, because transitions may worsen energy insecurity for low-income households.

  <!-- nature-clim-172 -->

- **The collapsing cost of wind, solar and batteries**

  From 2010 to 2019, unit costs fell 85% for solar, 55% for wind and 85% for lithium-ion batteries. That steep drop has made them the cheapest new power in many regions. Onshore wind or solar with a few hours of storage already has a lower levelized cost than gas peaking plants. Investors noticed. In 2021, renewables made up more than 80% of new electricity generating capacity.

  <!-- nature-clim-169 -->

- **Renewable energy sources**

  Hydropower is the largest renewable source of electricity, supplying 17% of the world's power in 2020. Renewable energy sources are those naturally replenished: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, bioenergy and marine energy. They generally strengthen energy security and emit far fewer greenhouse gases than fossil fuels. Wind is catching up fast. It provided well over 10% of global electricity in 2024, and onshore wind is often cheaper than existing coal plants. Solar PV is expected to have the largest installed capacity of any electricity source by 2027. Renewables are not harmless, though. Projects can threaten biodiversity when high-value areas become bioenergy, wind or solar farms.

  <!-- nature-clim-216 -->

- **Coal phase-out**

  Coal is the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel. The IEA estimates it caused over 30% of warming above pre-industrial levels. Coal power emits about a tonne of CO2 per megawatt hour, twice as much as gas. Stopping coal burning in power plants and elsewhere is therefore central to the fossil fuel phase-out. Its health and environmental benefits exceed its costs, by over 1% of GDP a year according to one estimate. The IEA's 1.5°C pathway would require closing around 70% of existing coal capacity early. Germany uses reverse auctions to pay coal plants to close early, and some countries retire coal miners early. Economists have suggested a Coasean bargain, in which developed countries help pay for developing countries' phase-out. In 2021 the pact described in The Glasgow Climate Pact: phasing down coal agreed to a coal phase-down.

  <!-- nature-clim-190 -->

- **Climate policy and stranded fossil assets**

  For a 50 percent chance of 1.5°C, a 2021 study found, nearly 60 percent of oil and gas reserves must stay unused. So must 90 percent of coal reserves. Those reserves would lose their value. Climate-related asset stranding is this loss of value for fossil fuel reserves and carbon-intensive plants as policy, technology and markets shift. It hits oil, gas and coal companies, industries such as steel, aluminium and cement, and fossil-exporting countries and workers. Risk factors include environmental change, carbon pricing, falling clean-tech costs, changing social norms and litigation. A 2026 estimate found early closure of coal plants for a 1.5°C pathway would strand around $842 billion. Fossil fuel importers gain from switching, while exporters face the losses.

  <!-- nature-clim-176 -->

- **100% renewable energy**

  Could every bit of energy come from renewable resources? That is the goal of 100% renewable energy. It is motivated by emissions, pollution, and economic and energy security concerns. The research is fairly young, with few studies before 2009.

  <!-- nature-clim-173 -->

- **Critical minerals for the energy transition**

  The IEA lists 37 critical minerals for clean energy technologies, and expects demand for them to rise 235 per cent by 2050. For mineral-rich countries of Sub-Saharan Africa, that boom may drive the lasting progress described in Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later. It has a cost. Mining for these minerals can threaten conservation areas, and in 2023 it contributed strongly to deforestation.

  <!-- nature-clim-170 -->

- **Transition or addition?**

  Has humanity ever really switched energy sources? One school, described by Vaclav Smil, sees successive transitions in the shares of the energy mix: biomass, then coal, then oil, then a mix. Jean-Baptiste Fressoz's school disagrees. It notes that 19th-century coal did not replace wood, because more wood was burned too. On this view, new sources are simply added on top of old ones. As of 2024, use of every form of primary energy had increased, leading some to call 'transition' a slogan. Historians still disagree.

  <!-- nature-clim-168 -->

- **The geopolitics of the energy transition**

  Changing energy sources changes the fortunes of countries and companies. Owners of fossil or renewable resources face big losses or gains, depending on how the transition unfolds. The shift is expected to reduce reliance on long-distance fossil fuel trade and raise the role of regional markets. Security matters too: energy security became a stronger driver in Europe after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

  <!-- nature-clim-171 -->

- **Clean cooking**

  Cooking with biomass, together with fossil fuel pollution, causes an estimated 7 million deaths a year. Clean cooking replaces polluting fuels such as wood and dung with clean facilities. Polluting fuels release harmful smoke and can drive forest degradation. Universal clean cooking would greatly improve health with minimal effect on climate.

  <!-- nature-clim-219 -->

- **Paying for the energy transition**

  The energy transition needs investment of about 2.5% of world GDP, small compared with its economic and health benefits, most studies find. Raising that money is uneven. Underfunding is acute in least developed countries, which attract little private investment. Developed countries' Paris pledge of an extra $100 billion a year for poor countries has not been met. Money could also be freed. Ending fossil fuel subsidies could cut global carbon emissions by 28% and air pollution deaths by 46%.

  <!-- nature-clim-220 -->

- **Hydrogen: a fuel for the hardest jobs**

  Almost all hydrogen today comes from fossil fuels by steam methane reforming, emitting 6.6–9.3 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of hydrogen. Cleanly made hydrogen could instead serve as a fuel where cheaper low-carbon options are scarce, such as heavy industry and long-distance transport. Splitting water with clean electricity gives sustainable hydrogen, but it costs more and wastes much energy in conversion. It can supply the intense heat for steel, cement and glass, and replace coke in steelmaking.

  <!-- nature-clim-218 -->

- **Is bioenergy really green?**

  Biomass can be burned for heat and power or made into biofuels such as biodiesel and ethanol. Whether this cuts emissions depends on how the biomass is grown and sourced. Land-use change, cultivation and processing can make bioenergy emit more carbon overall than fossil fuels. Energy crops can displace ecosystems, degrade soils, use water and compete with food. Algae, waste and crops on land unfit for food are relatively sustainable sources. Its climate benefit is therefore contested, case by case.

  <!-- nature-clim-217 -->

- **What counts as 'unabated' fossil fuel?**

  Should the world phase out all fossil fuels, or only 'unabated' ones, burned without measures such as carbon capture that substantially cut emissions? Negotiators have argued over exactly this. The 2023 UN climate conference agreed to phase down unabated coal but left 'abated' undefined, which critics say invites abuse. The IPCC counts power plants as abated only if they capture 90% or more of emissions. Countries still disagree on the scope of phase-out targets.

  <!-- nature-clim-188 -->

- **Electrifying heat**

  Heat pumps provide only 5% of global space and water heating, the IEA estimates, but could provide over 90%. Heating electrification switches space, water and industrial heating from burning fuels to electricity, mainly heat pumps. Some industrial processes need very high temperatures, such as 900 °C for ethylene, and require new electric processes. The need is social too. Many households cannot afford enough heating or cooling, and existing heating is often polluting.

  <!-- nature-clim-195 -->

- **Electrifying transport**

  Producing electricity sustainably is easier than producing liquid fuels sustainably. That is the case for transport electrification: replacing fuel-burning vehicles with electric ones. Not every vehicle fits. Hydrogen may suit long-distance lorries, while shipping and aviation may rely more on sustainable liquid fuels.

  <!-- nature-clim-194 -->

- **Ending sales of petrol and diesel cars**

  Many countries have set dates to stop selling new petrol and diesel cars, requiring new cars to be electric or otherwise zero-emission. Many US states have zero-emission vehicle mandates requiring a rising share of electric car sales. Gas burning has no such deadline: no timetable exists for ending it.

  <!-- nature-clim-198 -->

- **Peak coal**

  Coal's share of global energy peaked in 2008 at 30%. Peak coal is the point of highest coal consumption, after which use is expected to decline. It was once expected to come from running out of reserves. Now falling demand drives it, as climate policy and cheaper gas and renewables spread. Use is falling in the US and Europe but rising in India, Indonesia and China.

  <!-- nature-clim-191 -->

### Adaptation and resilience

Cutting emissions limits how much the climate changes, but some change is already locked in. The oceans are rising, and faster than before, as warmer seawater expands and land ice melts. This chapter is about living with that: adjusting to climate change, coping with its floods and droughts, and bouncing back afterward. It asks what makes some people more open to harm than others, what adapting costs, who pays for it, and why private investors hold back. It ends where adaptation runs out, at the limits beyond which no adjustment can protect people or ecosystems.

- **Climate change adaptation: learning to live with a warmer world**

  A seawall, a new insurance scheme, a farmer sowing a few weeks earlier, a green roof on a city block. Each is a form of adaptation, the process of adjusting to the current and expected effects of Climate change: a warming world and why it matters. The goal is to reduce harm and to take advantage of any opportunities the change brings. Adaptation usually goes alongside mitigation, which limits warming by cutting greenhouse gas emissions. One deals with the causes, the other with the The effects of climate change, from reefs to economies. Adaptation can be reactive, responding to impacts after they arrive. It can also be proactive, preparing for change before it comes. It matters most in developing countries, which are the most vulnerable to climate change. The idea took a while to win respect. In the early 1990s many saw adaptation as a distraction from mitigation. It gained attention only in 2009–2010, after the Copenhagen Summit. Today more than 70% of countries have adaptation plans, but actual implementation is limited and uneven. Knowledge gaps, behavioural resistance and market failures all slow it down, which is why policy is needed. Politics adds a deeper problem. Politicians are rewarded for short-term change, so long-term adaptation is hard to carry through.

  <!-- nature-clim-002 -->

- **Sea level rise: the ocean that keeps climbing**

  Between 1901 and 2018 the world's average sea level rose 15–25 cm, faster than in at least 3,000 years. Sea level rise is this climb in average ocean level, and it has sped up sharply. By 2013–2022 the rate had reached 4.62 mm per year. Two causes dominate. From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers caused 44% of the rise, the process described in Melting ice sheets and the long rise of the seas. Thermal expansion, water swelling as it warms, caused another 42%. The sea responds slowly. It lags temperature by decades, so it will keep accelerating to 2050 from warming already caused. What happens after that depends on emissions. By 2100 the sea could stand 30 cm to 1.0 m above the early 2020s with very deep emission cuts, or up to 1.9 m with high emissions. The damage takes many forms: more storm-surge flooding, coastal erosion, lost mangroves, saltier irrigation water and damaged ports. Low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands face the greatest near-term impact, and many may become uninhabitable this century. Socially and economically vulnerable communities are often more exposed and have fewer resources to adapt.

  <!-- nature-clim-037 -->

- **Climate resilience: coping, recovering and learning**

  When a flood or drought strikes, some communities recover and others do not. Climate resilience is how well people or ecosystems can cope with, and bounce back from, such hazards. The IPCC defines it as the capacity of social, economic and ecosystems to cope with a hazardous event, trend or disturbance, including the ability to reorganise and learn. The definition is heavily debated, in concept and in practice, because the idea crosses many disciplines. One framework splits it into three capacities: adaptive, anticipatory and absorptive. Resilience differs from Climate change adaptation: learning to live with a warmer world, which is any adjustment to climate impacts; resilience is a more systematic way of absorbing change and reorganising. Most resilience work so far maintains existing systems, such as seawalls protecting a coastal town. That is an incremental approach, not a transformational one. Long-lived infrastructure needs risk-based engineering and economic analysis to be designed for resilience under uncertain projections.

  <!-- nature-clim-014 -->

- **Vulnerability: what makes some places easy to hurt**

  The same storm can wreck one town and spare another. Vulnerability is the state of being open to harm; for hazards, it means the features of a community, system or asset that make it susceptible to damage. In disasters, vulnerability ties people's relationship with their environment to social forces, institutions and cultural values. It is not just about the weather. Risk rises with it: the more vulnerable a community, the more risk it faces. Indicators of vulnerability cover external shocks and stresses as well as an internal inability to cope. Climate vulnerability is generally a bigger problem in low-income countries than in high-income ones.

  <!-- nature-clim-025 -->

- **Adaptive capacity: the stock of ways to adjust**

  Adaptive capacity is the ability of people, institutions, ecosystems and other organisms to adjust to potential harm, seize opportunities or cope with consequences. In climate risk it sits alongside hazard, exposure and Vulnerability: what makes some places easy to hurt as a key ingredient. It works like a stock of resources and assets, drawn on as future conditions require. In societies it rests on institutions that learn, flexible decision-making and power structures that respond to everyone with a stake. The ODI's local adaptive capacity framework names five features: assets, institutions and entitlements, knowledge, innovation, and flexible forward-looking governance. A stable, prosperous economy helps, and wealthier nations are generally better prepared. Barriers to adaptation can be overcome, whereas limits cannot. A common external barrier is a lack of land to relocate to. For species, adaptive capacity depends on phenotypic plasticity, the ability to change form or behavior, on dispersal ability and on genetic diversity.

  <!-- nature-clim-001 -->

- **The adaptation gap: a bill far bigger than the budget**

  Adapting to climate change is expensive, and the price rises sharply with each extra step of warming. Globally the cost likely runs to tens or hundreds of billions of dollars a year for decades. The IPCC puts it at $15 to 411 billion per year to 2030, with most estimates above $100 billion. The adaptation gap is the shortfall between that cost and the money available. UNEP's 2023 report put the gap in funding at $194 billion to $366 billion a year. Developing countries' needs, $215 to $387 billion a year, are 10–18 times current international public money for adaptation. The gap is widening because most tracked money for climate action goes to Climate change mitigation: cutting the cause instead. The spending would often pay off. In many specific settings, adaptation costs less than the damage it avoids, though global estimates are very uncertain.

  <!-- nature-clim-004 -->

- **Why private money avoids adaptation**

  A solar farm sells electricity. A flood barrier sells nothing. That contrast explains why private investors find adaptation harder to fund than Climate change mitigation: cutting the cause: adaptation usually lacks a clear income stream. It often serves non-market sectors or public goods that benefit many people at once, so few projects attract private money. Timing works against it too. The costs come now while the benefits come later, and investors prefer short-term returns. Uncertainty about future impacts and benefits leaves them short of information. Still, innovation is increasing the potential for private finance to help close the adaptation gap.

  <!-- nature-clim-009 -->

- **Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three parts of climate risk**

  A storm is only part of the story. Climate risk needs three ingredients together: the hazard, the exposure of people and assets, and their vulnerability. Exposure is the presence of people, livelihoods, ecosystems and assets in places that could be harmed. It falls when people retreat from floodplains. Better early warning and evacuation also reduce it. Vulnerability: what makes some places easy to hurt, in the IPCC's words a propensity to be adversely affected, includes sensitivity and a lack of capacity to cope. Insurance, more varied livelihoods, social protection and sturdier infrastructure all reduce it. So does nature. Protecting mangroves, which dampen storm energy, is ecosystem-based adaptation that cuts vulnerability.

  <!-- nature-clim-012 -->

- **Climate change vulnerability: who stands to be hurt most**

  About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people were estimated in 2021 to live in highly vulnerable contexts. Climate change vulnerability is how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change; formally, their propensity to be adversely affected. It includes their capacity to cope and adapt, and it is one component of climate risk. The definition has shifted. Earlier IPCC reports made vulnerability a function of exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity; the Fifth report moved exposure out as a separate element of risk. People with low incomes, Indigenous peoples: who they are, and who decides, women, children and the elderly tend to be more vulnerable. Developing countries were judged more vulnerable, partly because adaptation costs are high relative to their GDP, the total value of what an economy produces. Vulnerability can be reduced by adaptation, by tackling poverty, inequality and conflict, and by mitigation that makes impacts less severe.

  <!-- nature-clim-027 -->

- **Disaster risk reduction: acting before the disaster**

  After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, 77% of the deaths in North Aceh were female. Disasters do not strike everyone equally, and women and girls are disproportionately harmed. Disaster risk reduction, or DRR, tries to change the odds beforehand. It covers actions that make disasters less likely and less damaging, by preventing new risk, reducing existing risk and managing what remains. Disaster risk is the potential loss of life, injury or damaged assets, arising from hazard, vulnerability and exposure together, the Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three parts of climate risk. DRR aims to make communities stronger and better prepared: more resilient and less vulnerable. Its scope is much broader than conventional emergency management. Disaster risk management, a name sometimes used for the whole field, is its practical implementation. Since the mid-1970s the field has shifted from response and recovery toward understanding causes and reducing risk in advance. Experts often see climate change adaptation as one of many processes within it.

  <!-- nature-clim-226 -->

- **International adaptation finance: helping poorer countries adapt**

  In 2009 rich nations pledged $100 billion a year by 2020 for mitigation and adaptation in developing countries. By December 2020 that money had not been fully delivered. It is money from richer countries and international funds that helps developing countries adapt. Several UNFCCC funds serve this purpose: the Special Climate Change Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and The Adaptation Fund: paying for adaptation through carbon credits. The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels, created in 2010, is another channel. Adaptation still gets the smaller share. It received only 21% of public climate money provided in 2020. Multilateral development banks gave over €19 billion for adaptation in 2021. In 2022 nations agreed to set up a fund for harms beyond what adaptation can handle.

  <!-- nature-clim-005 -->

- **Limits to adaptation: where adjusting stops working**

  Adaptation cannot protect against everything. Its limits are the points beyond which it can no longer shield people or ecosystems from climate risks. The IPCC's 2022 report separates soft limits, where options exist but are not yet usable, from hard limits, where none remain. Some systems in Australia, small islands, the Americas, Africa and Europe have already hit soft limits. At 1.5 °C, glacier-dependent regions and small islands reach hard limits. At 2 °C many staple crops hit soft limits. As risks grow, small incremental adjustments stop being enough. Larger and costlier transformational adaptation becomes necessary.

  <!-- nature-clim-008 -->

- **Loss and damage: the harms nobody prevented**

  Some climate harms get through every defense. Loss and damage names those harms, the ones mitigation and adaptation fail to prevent, and the question of how to deal with them. Loss means irreversible harm, such as an extinct species or an island lost to the sea. Damage means harm that can be repaired or compensated. Economic losses affect traded goods and services. Non-economic losses, such as lost family members or cultures, involve things no market trades. The idea covers sudden disasters like cyclones and slow change like sea level rise. The IPCC found such residual risks will rise with further warming. How to respond is disputed. Small island and least developed countries have long sought liability and compensation, which developed countries resist. In 1991 small island states proposed an insurance pool funded by countries' shares of emissions and income; it was rejected. A 2026 study estimated that US CO2 emissions from 1990 to 2020 had caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020.

  <!-- nature-clim-018 -->

- **Maladaptation: when adapting makes things worse**

  An air conditioner cools a hot room, but if it runs on carbon-intensive electricity it adds to the emissions behind the heat. That is maladaptation: an adaptation action that ends up increasing vulnerability or reducing the ability to adapt sustainably later. The IPCC introduced the term in 2001. It describes actions that may raise climate-related risk through higher emissions, shifted vulnerability, more unequal outcomes or reduced welfare. The harm is usually unintended. Seawalls can waterlog fields and reduce soil fertility. Adapting to short-term climate swings can also clash with longer trends, as when irrigation was expanded into Egypt's Western Sinai desert despite projected drying. Community-driven, bottom-up approaches generally carry a lower risk of maladaptation than top-down technical fixes.

  <!-- nature-nbs-081 -->

- **Retreat, accommodate or protect: adapting to rising seas**

  Cutting emissions can slow Sea level rise: the ocean that keeps climbing after 2050 but cannot stop it, so adaptation is inevitable. Societies have three broad choices: retreat, accommodate coastal change, or protect coasts with defences. Hard adaptation relies on capital-intensive infrastructure such as seawalls. Soft adaptation strengthens natural defences like dunes, using local, modular means. The economics can be striking. Without adaptation, annual flood costs in 136 large coastal cities could reach $1 trillion by 2050. Adaptation costing $50 billion per year could cut that to a little over $60 billion. But protection is not shared evenly. Higher-value areas are more likely to be defended, leaving lower-value areas to retreat. Retreat often costs people their livelihoods, and displaced people can strain their new communities. Planning lags too: in a 2023 survey, 98% of planners knew the projections, but 26% had not yet put them into policy.

  <!-- nature-clim-038 -->

- **Climate risk insurance: fast money after the storm**

  Climate risk insurance is designed to cover the financial risks of climate change, especially Extreme weather: the far ends of the range. Its appeal is speed. It provides money quickly after a disaster for relief and rebuilding, and helps prepare to reduce future vulnerability. It is often seen as a way to make poor and developing communities more resilient, and as an important adaptation measure. Its scale is a challenge. Insurance works by pooling many separate risks, but weather disasters hit whole regions at once and trigger many claims together. Because climate risks are partly correlated in this way, pooling works less well, so cover must be sold at a large, diversified scale. High premiums in risky areas could discourage people from settling there. The InsuResilience Global Partnership, launched at COP23, supports such schemes. Opinion is split. Supporters see a safety net, while critics say it puts the cost on communities that emitted least, and start-up and data costs are high for low-income countries.

  <!-- nature-clim-225 -->

- **Early warning systems: buying time before a hazard hits**

  Interest in early warning surged after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004. An early warning system is a chain of sensors, detection and communication that spots hazards early and gives people time to prepare and limit harm. A complete system has four parts: risk analysis, monitoring and warning, spreading the message, and the capability to respond. Technology alone is not enough. To work, a system must involve at-risk communities, raise awareness, deliver alerts effectively and keep people prepared. The UN recommends early warning systems as key to climate adaptation. It runs the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems partnership for high-risk countries.

  <!-- nature-clim-034 -->

- **The Adaptation Fund: paying for adaptation through carbon credits**

  The Adaptation Fund pays for projects that help developing countries adapt, under The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. It was established in 2001 at COP7 in Marrakech and officially launched in 2007. Its original income was unusual: a 2% share of the credits issued for The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market projects. As carbon prices fell, donations from rich countries became more important. Its direct access mechanism lets accredited national and regional bodies in developing countries receive money directly. By 2024 it had committed over 1 billion US dollars since 2010 and reported over 43 million beneficiaries.

  <!-- nature-clim-031 -->

- **When adapting and cutting emissions help or hinder each other**

  Actions to adapt to climate change and actions to limit it can reinforce each other or work against each other. Public transport is a synergy. It produces lower emissions per kilometre and makes evacuation easier in disasters. Compact cities show the trade-off. They cut transport and building emissions, but packing buildings close together can worsen the urban heat island, the extra warmth that builds up in cities.

  <!-- nature-clim-010 -->

- **Additionality: new money or relabelled aid**

  Additionality is the principle that adaptation money should be extra to existing development aid, not redirected from it. Four main definitions exist. They range from finance additional to the Millennium Development Goals to climate money unconnected to aid budgets. The difference matters. Denmark raised adaptation aid from 0.09% to 0.12% of GDP between 2010 and 2020 by taking it from other aid. Critics also say the principle encourages business as usual, because it ignores future climate risks.

  <!-- nature-clim-006 -->

- **Climate services: climate information people can use**

  A forecast is only useful if someone can act on it. Climate services are systems that deliver usable climate information to people and organisations, to support decisions on adaptation, mitigation and risk. They help users foresee and manage the hazards of a changing climate. They are demand-driven. Instead of handing over research products, providers design them together with users, a process called co-design.

  <!-- nature-clim-013 -->

- **Four kinds of adaptation: built, institutional, behavioral and natural**

  Adaptation comes in four kinds. Infrastructural options use the built environment to protect against flooding, sea level rise and extreme heat. Institutional responses change the rules, through zoning, building codes, insurance schemes and coordination. Behavioural options change what people do, such as farmers shifting planting times or switching crops and livestock. Nature-based solutions work with ecosystems, aiming to benefit both people and biodiversity.

  <!-- nature-clim-003 -->

- **The economics of prevention: five to ten dollars saved per dollar**

  Every dollar spent on reducing disaster risk saves between $5 and $10 in disaster losses. The economics of Disaster risk reduction: acting before the disaster looks at what disasters cost and makes the case for spending on prevention rather than only on response and recovery. The costs are large. Climate-related disasters cost over US$330 billion a year on average over 2015–2021, likely an underestimate. Yet the money flows the other way. Around 90% of international DRR funding goes to response and recovery, and only about 0.5% of development aid goes to reducing risk before disasters. For many countries, less than 1% of the national budget is available for DRR. New instruments are emerging, including rules requiring firms to disclose risk, resilience bonds and green bonds.

  <!-- nature-clim-024 -->

- **Climate resilient development: three goals pursued together**

  Climate resilient development pursues adaptation, mitigation and Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later together, using their synergies and reducing trade-offs, as described in When adapting and cutting emissions help or hinder each other. It has become a new paradigm for development, especially in the water sector, though the paradigm itself is contested. Governments on every continent are adopting policies for climate-resilient economies, pushed by The Paris Agreement: every country pledges and The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals for 2030.

  <!-- nature-clim-015 -->

- **Measuring resilience with proxies**

  Money spent on resilience should go where it helps most. Resilience measurement provides tools and indicators for tracking the Climate resilience: coping, recovering and learning of households, communities or nations. It helps locate vulnerability hotspots and judge whether interventions work. The difficulty is that resilience has no single observable metric. It includes intangibles like social capital, the trust and networks people can draw on. So toolkits rely on long lists of proxy indicators, stand-ins that track it indirectly. Common objective measures include FAO's RIMA and the Livelihoods Change Over Time index.

  <!-- nature-clim-016 -->

- **Climate risk management: reducing harm and seizing gains**

  Climate risk management is a general approach to climate-sensitive decisions. It draws on adaptation, disaster management and development that can last to reduce vulnerability. Its tools include early response systems, diversification, flexible rules for allocating resources, insurance, infrastructure design and capacity building. It is not only defensive. It also seeks gains, such as farmers using a favourable seasonal forecast to raise their yields.

  <!-- nature-clim-032 -->

- **Ecological anthropology: how cultures fit their environments**

  Ecological anthropology is the branch of anthropology that studies how human cultures adapt to and shape their environments. It emerged in the 1960s from Julian Steward's cultural ecology. Roy Rappaport's work with the Maring of Papua New Guinea examined how ritual shaped the relationship between culture and nature. Critics said the field assumed static equilibrium and oversimplified systems, prompting a shift toward Political ecology: power and the environment. Its practical legacy endures. Long-term Traditional ecological knowledge can inform adaptation strategies and community monitoring.

  <!-- nature-clim-030 -->

- **The Sendai Framework: seven targets for safer societies**

  On March 18, 2015, countries adopted the Sendai Framework, an international plan setting seven targets for reducing disaster risk to 2030. Its targets aim to cut disaster deaths, the number of people affected, economic loss and damage to infrastructure. Others aim to widen access to warning systems, increase aid to developing countries and spread national DRR strategies. That last goal has made progress. Countries with national strategies rose from 55 to 123 by 2022.

  <!-- nature-clim-023 -->

- **The Loss and Damage Fund: a breakthrough after three decades**

  At COP27 in Egypt in 2022, countries agreed to create a fund for communities where adaptation is inadequate or comes too late. It came after three decades of negotiation on Loss and damage: the harms nobody prevented, and many saw it as a major breakthrough. It operates as a financial mechanism of The Paris Agreement: every country pledges. How to fill it remains open. Before the June 2023 Paris finance summit, over 100 economists proposed an extreme wealth tax to fund loss and damage; it was not adopted.

  <!-- nature-clim-093 -->

- **The Warsaw International Mechanism: talking about loss without liability**

  Created in 2013, the Warsaw International Mechanism is the UN body that addresses Loss and damage: the harms nobody prevented in highly vulnerable countries through research and dialogue. It recognises that such harm can go beyond what adaptation can reduce. But it makes no provision for liability or compensation. The Paris Agreement: every country pledges states that it gives no basis for either. Developed countries, particularly the United States, insisted on that no-liability clause.

  <!-- nature-clim-019 -->

- **Social vulnerability: harm shaped by society**

  Social vulnerability is the inability of people, organisations and societies to withstand harm from multiple stresses, such as social exclusion and natural hazards. It arises partly from social interactions, institutions and cultural values. At the individual level, marital status, employment and income all affect it. The lesson is that a catastrophe cannot be understood from the size of the shock alone. It also requires looking at people's assets and entitlements, what they own and what they can claim.

  <!-- nature-clim-026 -->

- **Biophysical and social vulnerability**

  Climate vulnerability splits into two main kinds. Biophysical vulnerability concerns the effects of physical hazards. Early studies focused on it, drawing on natural hazards research. Social vulnerability, described in Social vulnerability: harm shaped by society, is shaped by political, economic and social structures. It is a people-centred view of why some are harmed more, driven by poverty, poor governance and conflict. Where the two meet, in a particular place, vulnerability peaks where sea level rise and changes in ecosystem services such as food access strike.

  <!-- nature-clim-028 -->

- **Climate vulnerability assessment: scoring who is at risk**

  To act on Climate change vulnerability: who stands to be hurt most, decision-makers first need to measure it. Assessment tools range from global indices to local models and participatory methods. Global indices include the ND-GAIN Country Index, the INFORM Risk Index and the WorldRiskIndex. Such composite indices usually average a set of standardised indicators into one score. At a finer level, vulnerability curves link the size of a hazard, such as extreme heat or sea level rise, to the damage it causes.

  <!-- nature-clim-029 -->

- **Crop insurance: governments step in for farmers**

  Crop insurance is government-subsidised cover bought by farmers against crop losses from disasters such as hail, drought and floods, or against lost revenue. Governments stepped in because markets failed to give farmers tools to manage production risk. Hail is the exception. It is a narrow, local peril, so private firms insure it, while multi-peril cover is exposed to large-scale events. In the United States the federal government pays on average 62 percent of the premium, and about 90% of crop acreage is insured. India's National Agriculture Insurance Scheme insures whole areas instead of single farms, paying for yield shortfalls against the past five years.

  <!-- nature-clim-033 -->

- **Index-based insurance: paying out by rainfall, not by claim**

  Sending an assessor to every small farm after a drought costs more than the farms' policies are worth. For smallholders in developing countries, traditional indemnity insurance, which pays for each person's verified loss, is usually not viable. Index-based insurance offers a workaround. It pays out when an index closely tied to losses, such as rainfall or yield, crosses a set trigger. Paying by index avoids the cost of checking individual claims. It also sidesteps Moral hazard: taking risks someone else pays for, because no one can manipulate the weather that triggers payment. Weather disasters hit many people at once, unlike thefts, which makes them hard to insure conventionally. Many indices now use satellite imagery. The results so far are modest. In developing countries it has needed subsidies to be viable, and uptake among smallholders remains low.

  <!-- nature-clim-035 -->

- **Flood insurance: protection that can encourage risk**

  Flood insurance covers losses from flooding and is one of the most widely used forms of Climate risk insurance: fast money after the storm. Rising sea levels, floods and windstorms threaten its affordability in exposed areas. It can also shape behavior. Critics say the subsidised US programme encouraged building and rebuilding in floodplains and on coasts. Its rules make flood-prone homes more likely to be rented cheaply to low-income, older or infirm people. That is an example of adverse selection, where the riskiest cases end up concentrated among those covered.

  <!-- nature-clim-039 -->

- **The base flood: the one-in-a-hundred-year benchmark**

  The base flood is a flood with a one percent chance of being equalled or exceeded in any year. It is also called the 100-year flood, and it is used to define floodplains. Its likelihood is worked out by statistical analysis of streamflow records. Urban growth increases runoff, so flood maps based on older data may understate the hazard.

  <!-- nature-clim-040 -->

- **Basis risk: when the index and the farm disagree**

  Index-based insurance: paying out by rainfall, not by claim has a weak spot. Basis risk is the mismatch between what the index pays and the losses a particular farmer actually suffers. An index covers a whole area, and rainfall can differ from field to field. So some farmers lose their crops but get no payout, while others are paid without a loss. Because of this, farmers are reluctant to pay the same premiums as for standard insurance. Researchers aim to reduce basis risk with new data sources.

  <!-- nature-clim-036 -->

### Climate finance and agreements

No country can stop climate change alone, so the world has tried to do it by treaty. At the center sits a UN convention whose stated goal is to keep greenhouse gases below the level that would dangerously disturb the climate. Each year its member countries meet at a conference to negotiate, and from those meetings came two landmark treaties, one in Kyoto and one in Paris. Under the second, every country writes its own pledge for cutting emissions and adapting. Behind every pledge sits a question of money: who pays to cut emissions, adapt and build resilience, and whether investors should pull their money out of fossil fuels.

- **The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates**

  At the 1992 Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties in Rio de Janeiro, 154 states signed a treaty on Climate change: a warming world and why it matters. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or UNFCCC, entered into force in 1994. It is both a treaty and the UN process built on it, through which countries negotiate how to limit dangerous climate change. Its ultimate aim, in Article 2, is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system. It also set a principle of fairness, Common but differentiated responsibilities: a shared duty, unequally held. Every country shares the duty, but developed countries are expected to lead because of their larger historical emissions. By 2022 the convention had 198 parties. Its supreme body, the Conference of the Parties, meets every year. Its work now centres on carrying out The Paris Agreement: every country pledges, which entered into force in 2016. Decisions are taken by consensus, so any party can block them. That has a cost. The convention has been criticised as unsuccessful at cutting emissions.

  <!-- nature-clim-053 -->

- **Climate finance: following the money**

  Global climate finance was estimated at around $1.3 trillion per year in 2021/2022, up from more than US$600 billion in 2019 by one estimate. Climate finance is money used to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change or build resilience. It can take the form of loans, grants or government budget spending. It can come from private or public sources, and can pass through intermediaries such as multilateral development banks, lenders owned by many governments, and development agencies. Under the UN Climate Convention the term is narrower. It means transfers of public money from high-income to low- and middle-income countries, in line with their duty to provide new and additional resources. It has two main parts. Mitigation finance: the bulk of climate money aims to reduce emissions, and Adaptation finance: the public money that keeps people safe responds to the consequences of climate change. Most of the money stays home: 84% in 2021/2022 was raised and spent within the same country. It is far from enough. A 2024 report estimated that flows must rise at least sixfold, to $8.5 trillion per year by 2030. Public budgets are widely seen as too small, so private finance is expected to matter for closing the gap. The main challenges are tracking the flows, supporting developing countries fairly and giving private investors suitable incentives.

  <!-- nature-clim-042 -->

- **The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked**

  Often called the most successful environmental treaty between nations, the Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it. It was agreed on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989. With 198 parties, it was the first universally ratified treaty in UN history. It helped poorer members. Under Article 5 developing countries get extra time to comply, and a financial mechanism under Article 10 helps them pay. The results show. Concentrations of the main CFCs, ozone-destroying chemicals, have levelled off or fallen, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly recovering. The treaty also helped mitigation, because HCFCs, which it phases out, are very potent greenhouse gases. It is cited as a precedent that the UN consensus approach to global problems can work.

  <!-- nature-clim-094 -->

- **Fossil fuel divestment: pulling money out of oil and coal**

  It began on US university campuses in 2011. By 2015 fossil fuel divestment was reportedly the fastest-growing divestment movement in history. Divestment means pressuring institutions to sell their stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change. As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions with over $40.5 trillion in assets had begun or committed to some form of it. Divesters have three kinds of reason: to align investments with values, to fight the fossil fuel industry, or to protect portfolios from climate-related financial risk. One financial motive is stranded assets, the 'carbon bubble': reserves that cannot be burned safely and would have to be written off. The aim is to speed the shift to renewable energy by stigmatising fossil fuel companies. Those companies have partly blamed divestment pressure for the rising cost of raising money.

  <!-- nature-clim-086 -->

- **The COPs: the yearly climate summits**

  Every year the parties to The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates meet to assess and negotiate climate action. These meetings are the United Nations Climate Change Conferences, known as COPs. The first, COP 1, was held in Berlin in 1995. Since 2005 they also serve as the meeting of the parties to The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. From 2011 to 2015 they were used to negotiate The Paris Agreement: every country pledges. Any final text must be agreed by consensus. Hosting rotates among the five UN regional groups. Not everyone present is a negotiator. More than 5,350 fossil fuel industry lobbyists attended the four conferences from 2021 to 2024.

  <!-- nature-clim-100 -->

- **Annex I, Annex II and the rest: sorting countries by duty**

  The climate convention does not treat all countries alike. Since 1992 it has sorted them into groups with different duties. Annex I holds industrialised countries and economies in transition. There are 43 Annex I parties, including the EU. Fourteen of them are economies in transition, the former Soviet-bloc economies. Annex I countries should adopt national policies to limit their emissions and report on returning to their 1990 levels. Annex II is a smaller, richer group. Its 24 parties are OECD members, the club of wealthy market economies, and they must give financial and technical support to transition economies and developing countries. Everyone else, mostly developing countries, is non-Annex I. Among all parties, 49 are least-developed countries with special status. The lines can move. Developing countries may volunteer to join Annex I once sufficiently developed.

  <!-- nature-clim-055 -->

- **The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries**

  Adopted in Kyoto on 11 December 1997, the Kyoto Protocol extended The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates with commitments to reduce Greenhouse gas emissions: who emits, and how much. It entered into force on 16 February 2005. Its main feature was legally binding emission-cut commitments for Annex I, the industrialised parties described in Annex I, Annex II and the rest: sorting countries by duty. That followed the principle of Common but differentiated responsibilities: a shared duty, unequally held. It covered seven gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. The first commitment period ran from 2008 to 2012. The 36 fully participating countries pledged a 4% combined cut from 1990 levels. They achieved emissions 24.2% below 1990 in 2008–2012. That success came largely from the Soviet Union's collapse and the 2008 financial crisis. Meanwhile global emissions rose by 32% from 1990 to 2010, because the committed countries made up only 24% of global emissions in 2010. The United States never ratified the treaty, and Canada withdrew effective December 2012. It was followed in 2015 by The Paris Agreement: every country pledges, a separate instrument under the convention, not an amendment.

  <!-- nature-clim-056 -->

- **The Paris Agreement: every country pledges**

  In 2015, 196 parties met near Paris for the UN climate conference and negotiated a new treaty. The Paris Agreement covers mitigation, adaptation and finance, and entered into force on 4 November 2016. It aims to keep warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and preferably to 1.5 °C, with emissions reaching net zero by mid-century. Its design breaks with The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Each country sets its own contributions, and each new target should go beyond the last. Nothing forces a country to set a specific target. It also blurs the line between developed and developing countries, so developing countries must submit emission-cut plans too. The EU and 194 states, covering over 98% of greenhouse gas emissions, have ratified or joined it. The United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026. The agreement recognises loss and damage as a separate pillar, but states that it cannot be used as a basis for liability. Global emissions kept rising after it was signed, and most experts say it is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal.

  <!-- nature-clim-074 -->

- **Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge**

  At the heart of The Paris Agreement: every country pledges lies a simple idea: each country decides for itself what to contribute. A nationally determined contribution, or NDC, is a country's own pledge of how it will cut greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change. NDCs must be renewed every five years, and each should be more ambitious than the last, a rule called the principle of progression. The legal force is limited. The pledges themselves are not binding, but preparing, communicating and updating them is. There is no way to force a country to meet its target. Some pledges are unconditional. Others depend on outside finance, technical support or other countries' ambition. NDCs are the first UNFCCC emission targets that apply equally to developed and developing countries. They still fall short. Emission cuts must rise 80% beyond current NDCs to likely meet 2 °C. On current trends, the chance of staying below 2 °C is only 5%.

  <!-- nature-clim-071 -->

- **Article 6: how countries can cooperate on their pledges**

  Article 6 is the part of the 2015 Paris Agreement that sets out how countries may cooperate voluntarily to carry out their Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge. The aim is to allow higher ambition in mitigation and adaptation while promoting Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later. That depends on environmental integrity, transparency and robust accounting. There are three pathways: cooperative approaches that trade emission reductions between countries (6.2), a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4) and cooperation without trading, Non-market approaches: cooperation without trading. The core 'Article 6 rulebook' was adopted at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. It succeeds the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, with the transition expected to be completed by 2025. Its impact is debated. Some analysts say the transfers lower costs and mobilise finance. Others fear they undermine integrity through over-crediting, weak baselines and surplus allowances, Hot air: surplus allowances that cut nothing.

  <!-- nature-clim-066 -->

- **The convention's ultimate goal: avoiding dangerous interference**

  Article 2 of The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates sets its ultimate objective: stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate. It adds a speed limit. This should happen fast enough to let ecosystems adapt naturally, keep food production safe and let economic development continue sustainably. Stabilising concentrations requires global emissions to peak and then decline, and earlier for lower stabilisation levels. One word is hard. Science can describe climate risks, but deciding which risks count as dangerous needs value judgements. Article 3 acknowledges the precautionary principle, so uncertainty about climate effects is no reason for inaction.

  <!-- nature-clim-054 -->

- **Climate targets: goals set by politics and science**

  At least 164 countries have climate targets written into their national law. A climate target, also called a climate goal or pledge, is a measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy aimed at limiting climate change. Politicians set temperature targets based on research into the likely effects of different levels of warming. These targets underpin carbon budgets and emission targets. Under Kyoto, countries pledged an average 5.2 percent cut on 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012. An emissions target may differ from what science allows, because it can reflect what is politically palatable. Many targets lie above the scientifically allowable emissions. Many also rely on negative-emission technologies, ways of pulling carbon out of the air, that are not yet developed.

  <!-- nature-clim-083 -->

- **Common but differentiated responsibilities: a shared duty, unequally held**

  All countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage, but not to the same degree. That principle, common but differentiated responsibilities, was set in the 1992 UN climate convention. Developed countries industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change, so they agreed to take greater responsibility for mitigation. Article 3 says they should take the lead. The principle can be read as a form of polluter pays, measuring responsibility by historical contribution and ability to act. Its meaning changed over time. Under Kyoto it meant a rigid split in which only industrialised countries had strict limits. Under Paris each country sets its own contribution as its circumstances change. It remains disputed. Critics, including US negotiators, argued it gave developing countries an unfair economic advantage. Developing countries replied that their emissions are for survival, while rich countries' are 'luxury emissions'.

  <!-- nature-clim-084 -->

- **Adaptation finance: the public money that keeps people safe**

  Adaptation finance is the part of Climate finance: following the money that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change. It can come from governments, development finance institutions and Multilateral climate funds: pooled money from many governments, and from banks, investors, companies and households. In practice, around 98% of tracked adaptation finance has come from public sources. Adaptation projects rarely have a clear income stream or attractive return. Only around 4-8% of total climate finance has gone to adaptation. The benefits can be large: every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion. A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion per year up to 2030. Of adaptation-specific funding, 63% came as loans and 36% as grants, and only 66% of committed amounts were paid out.

  <!-- nature-clim-044 -->

- **Mitigation finance: the bulk of climate money**

  Mitigation finance is investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions. It dominates, accounting for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance. Around 70% of mitigation money has gone to renewable energy; energy efficiency and transport are the other key sectors. Of the estimated US$83.3 billion provided to developing countries in 2020, US$48.6 billion, or 58%, targeted mitigation. The needs are far larger. The 2018 Biennial Assessment put mitigation financing needs for 2020 to 2030 at US$1.7-2.4 trillion per year. The IEA estimates that keeping warming below 2 Celsius needs an average of $3.5 trillion a year of energy-sector investment until 2050.

  <!-- nature-clim-043 -->

- **The global stocktake: checking the world's progress**

  Every five years, the Paris Agreement asks a collective question: how far has the world as a whole got toward its goals? The global stocktake is that review. It links countries' Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge to the Paris goals, and its results are meant to feed into their next pledges and raise ambition. It looks at collective progress, so individual countries are not singled out. Its scope was debated. In the end it covers mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation and support, including finance. It runs in three phases. First comes collecting information, then technical assessment, and finally political messages for policy. The second stocktake begins in November 2026 at COP 31 and concludes two years later at COP 33.

  <!-- nature-clim-089 -->

- **The enhanced transparency framework: checking what countries do**

  Pledges mean little if no one can check them. The enhanced transparency framework, set by Article 13 of The Paris Agreement: every country pledges, is a common system for checking countries' climate action. It covers monitoring, reporting and verifying what they do and the support they give or receive. Parties are legally bound to have their progress toward their NDCs checked by technical expert review. Developed and developing countries alike report every two years and face technical and peer review. It has flexibility in scope, detail and frequency of reporting for countries with less capacity.

  <!-- nature-clim-076 -->

- **Climate debt: who owes whom for a warming planet**

  At the 2009 Copenhagen conference, developing countries led by Bolivia demanded repayment of a debt. Not a loan, but climate debt: what developed countries are said to owe developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions. The idea is part of the broader concept of Ecological debt: what the North owes the South and was first put forward by NGOs in the 1990s. It has two main parts. Adaptation debt: paying for harm others caused is the help owed for adapting to climate change. Emissions debt: overusing the atmosphere is owed for excessive past emissions. Views split along familiar lines. Support comes mainly from developing countries and environmental NGOs, and criticism mostly from developed nations. Critics argue that emissions made before their harm was understood, or by earlier generations, should not create guilt or debts. Others say that even if the idea is ethically sound, its adversarial framing may undermine climate negotiations.

  <!-- nature-clim-079 -->

- **Action for Climate Empowerment: education and participation**

  Since 2015, Action for Climate Empowerment has been the name for the climate convention's work on education, training, public awareness, participation, access to information and cooperation on these. It refers to Article 6 of the 1992 convention text. It calls on governments to run education and awareness programmes, train experts, open up information and encourage the public to take part.

  <!-- nature-clim-064 -->

- **Why critics say the UN climate process has failed**

  Critics argue that the UN climate convention and The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries have failed to cut greenhouse gas emissions as intended. With over 190 countries deciding by consensus, small groups of countries can often block progress. Competition gets in the way. In 2010 Japan refused a second Kyoto term because it would face limits that its competitors China, India and Indonesia did not. The convention also failed, mainly under Kyoto, to transfer environmentally sound technologies to developing countries. Historical responsibility for emissions remains contentious in the talks.

  <!-- nature-clim-063 -->

- **National communications: each country's climate report**

  Each country party to the UN climate convention submits a national communication, a report on its climate measures and vulnerabilities. Developed countries must submit one every four years; developing countries should. They are often several hundred pages long, much longer and more detailed than the pledges made under the Paris Agreement. Some least developed countries have not submitted one in 5–15 years, mostly for lack of capacity.

  <!-- nature-clim-065 -->

- **The Doha Amendment: Kyoto's shrinking second act**

  On 8 December 2012 in Doha, countries extended The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries with a second commitment period running to 2020. Thirty-seven countries held binding targets, and 2015 was set as the date for a successor agreement. Japan, New Zealand and Russia took on no new targets, and the second period covered only about 11% of global annual emissions. The ending was awkward. The amendment entered into force on 31 December 2020, after 144 states accepted it, on the very day the second period ended.

  <!-- nature-clim-060 -->

- **Hot air: surplus allowances that cut nothing**

  Under Kyoto, Russia, Ukraine and the new EU-12 states got emission targets set above their actual emissions. That left them with a large surplus of allowances, permits to emit, which became known as hot air. These transition economies saw the surplus as 'headroom' to grow their economies. Countries short of allowances could buy them from those with a surplus. But without further commitments that trade would not reduce emissions at all.

  <!-- nature-clim-058 -->

- **Kyoto's compliance mechanism: penalties with little bite**

  The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries had a system for checking whether parties met their commitments and penalising those that did not. A party that missed its emissions limit had to make up the difference in the second commitment period, plus an additional 30%. It was also suspended from making transfers under Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits. Some doubted the bite. Grubb judged the consequences for non-compliance weak compared with domestic law, and the compliance section was hotly contested in the Marrakesh Accords.

  <!-- nature-clim-059 -->

- **The 2 degree target: the line the world drew**

  Keep global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels. That is the 2 degree target, an international policy goal. It is a political decision, based on science about the likely consequences of warming, and dates from the 2009 Copenhagen conference. It is central to the Paris Agreement. It is often criticised as too high, since two degrees of warming would have serious effects on people and nature.
