The IPCC's 2018 special report warned that 2 °C rather than 1.5 °C would worsen extreme weather, sea-ice loss, sea-level rise, coral bleaching and ecosystem loss. The world is not on course to meet it. The UNFCCC predicts a likely 2.1 to 2.9 °C of warming by 2100. An 'overshoot pathway' would pass 2 °C and then bring warming back down late in the century, requiring management over many decades.

  <!-- nature-clim-077 -->

- **Is the Paris Agreement working**

  Most experts say The Paris Agreement: every country pledges is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal, though some argue it is too early to judge. UNEP said in 2020 that current commitments would likely lead to more than 3 °C of warming by 2100. Studies in Nature found that as of 2017 none of the major industrialised nations was implementing its pledged policies. The other side has numbers too. The stocktake report credits the agreement with a large effect: expected 2100 warming fell from 3.7–4.8 °C in 2010 to 2.4–2.6 °C at COP 27.

  <!-- nature-clim-075 -->

- **Intended nationally determined contributions: the first drafts**

  Before the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries made initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges called intended nationally determined contributions. These became their first Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge. Parties were asked to publish them at the November 2013 Warsaw climate conference. The term was a compromise between Kyoto's binding 'QELROs' for developed countries and 'NAMAs' for developing ones. Switzerland submitted the first on 27 February 2015. The timing was tight: 85% of surveyed countries said the short time frame was a challenge.

  <!-- nature-clim-072 -->

- **The ratchet mechanism: tightening pledges every five years**

  A ratchet turns only one way. The Paris Agreement's ratchet mechanism is a five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges designed to raise climate ambition over time. Countries publish progress reports every two years, which undergo technical review. These feed a global stocktake, on an offset five-year cycle, that judges whether all pledges together are enough. Its findings are meant to shape each country's next, more ambitious pledge.

  <!-- nature-clim-073 -->

- **Pledge and review: from rejected idea to central approach**

  Japan first proposed it in 1991. At the first COP in 1995 it was rejected in favour of binding targets, which led to The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Pledge and review is a way of organising climate action in which each country makes its own pledge, others review its progress, and stronger pledges follow. It is 'bottom-up', unlike legally binding targets imposed 'top-down' by a central body. Revived at Copenhagen in 2009, it drew pledges from countries producing about 80% of global emissions. Kyoto's first targets had covered 25%. By 2015 it was the central approach, though at Paris the pledges were renamed Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge. It won because binding targets proved hard to agree and impossible to enforce on powerful nations. Opinion remains divided. Critics called it 'hedge and retreat' or 'second best', while others called it an essential pillar of mitigation.

  <!-- nature-clim-098 -->

- **The Glasgow Climate Pact: phasing down coal**

  On 13 November 2021, the COP26 conference in Glasgow produced the first climate agreement explicitly planning to reduce unabated coal use. Late in the talks, a pledge to 'phase out' coal became 'phase down', at the urging of coal-reliant countries such as India and China. Countries agreed to revisit their emission plans in 2022 to keep the 1.5 °C target within reach, and committed to climate finance for developing countries. Around the summit, more than 140 countries pledged net-zero emissions and more than 100 pledged to reverse deforestation by 2030.

  <!-- nature-clim-087 -->

- **The adaptation finance gap: needs ten times the money**

  Between 2017 and 2021, international public finance to developing countries for adaptation stayed well below US$30 billion per year. The adaptation finance gap is the difference between the estimated cost of adapting and the money available for it. A 2023 study of 85 countries' plans put developing countries' needs at US$387 billion a year up to 2030. On 2017–2021 data, needs are around 10-18 times current public flows, and the gap has widened since earlier assessments. Several things could help close it: more public and private finance, remittances, the money migrants send home, and reform of how vulnerable countries' debts are managed.

  <!-- nature-clim-045 -->

- **The climate finance gap: hard to measure, easy to inflate**

  The climate finance gap is the shortfall between the climate investment needed and what is actually provided. Its size depends on who is counting. Estimates vary with the places, sectors, timescale, target and assumptions used. The reported side is shaky too. Research finds bilateral climate finance, money passed from one country to another, well below official figures. Part of the reason is that there is no agreed definition of international climate finance and no oversight. That has let non-climate projects be counted and raised doubts about official reporting.

  <!-- nature-clim-046 -->

- **Debt-for-climate swaps: turning repayments into projects**

  Seychelles redirected $27 million of debt to marine parks, ocean conservation and ecotourism. A debt-for-climate swap works this way. A country's debt is repaid on new, discounted terms, and the repayments, in local currency, go to domestic climate projects instead of foreign lenders. Projects can include carbon sequestration, renewable energy and protecting biodiversity and oceans. In one Argentine swap, $38,100,000 of debt was addressed and $3,100,000 went to biodiversity, forest and other climate work. The Seychelles deal was a similar debt-for-nature swap.

  <!-- nature-clim-049 -->

- **Multilateral climate funds: pooled money from many governments**

  Multilateral climate funds are governed by several national governments together and pay out money for climate action. As of 2022 the UN climate convention coordinated five. They were The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund, the Special Climate Change Fund and the Global Environment Facility. The World Bank coordinates the Climate Investment Funds, active since 2008, made up of the Clean Technology Fund and the Strategic Climate Fund. Some funds give only grants. Others also use cheap loans, equity and risk tools meant to draw in other finance. In 2016 the four main multilateral climate funds approved $2.78 billion of project support.

  <!-- nature-clim-047 -->

- **The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels**

  Based in Songdo, South Korea, the Green Climate Fund is considered the world's largest fund of its kind. It was set up under The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates to help developing countries with mitigation and adaptation. It is the largest of the five Multilateral climate funds: pooled money from many governments the convention coordinates. It was named in the 2009 The Copenhagen Accord: a deal the conference only noted, formally established at the 2010 Cancun conference, and its governing instrument was adopted in Durban in 2011. A 24-member board and a secretariat run it. As of November 2026 its portfolio was over $22.3 billion USD, or over $87.1 billion USD including co-financing from other investors. Its Private Sector Facility is among its most controversial features. Many rich countries want it to attract large institutional investors. Developing countries and NGOs want pro-poor finance for small firms. In March 2015 its board refused an explicit ban on fossil fuel projects, effectively allowing coal plants to be funded.

  <!-- nature-clim-051 -->

- **Private climate finance: why public money is not enough**

  Banks, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, companies and households all invest in climate projects. That is private climate finance. Public budgets are often too small for large infrastructure projects, especially in lower-income countries, so private money is seen as needed to fill the shortfall. But climate-friendly projects can cost more up front and carry more risk than fossil-fuel ones, so they must be bankable, able to attract lenders. Over 90% of private climate flows are estimated to stay within national borders. The IMF and OECD warn that private capital alone cannot close the gap. Many adaptation and innovation projects bring high social benefits but low private returns.

  <!-- nature-clim-048 -->

- **The Kigali Amendment: tackling the ozone fix that warms**

  HFCs replaced CFCs and do not harm the ozone layer. But they are greenhouse gases with a high global warming potential. In 2016, the Kigali Amendment to The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked committed countries to cut their use of these hydrofluorocarbons by more than 80% over 30 years. It came into force on 1 January 2019. The stakes are large. A 2009 study calculated that a fast HFC phasedown could avoid up to 8.8 Gt CO2-eq per year of emissions by 2050.

  <!-- nature-clim-095 -->

- **The Montreal Protocol's Multilateral Fund**

  The Multilateral Fund helps developing countries with low use of ozone-depleting substances comply with The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked. It serves countries using less than 0.3 kg of such substances per person a year; 147 of the 196 parties qualify. It embodies the principle that all share the duty to protect the global commons, but not equally. An executive committee with equal numbers of industrialised and developing countries runs it. It was the first treaty fund managed democratically in this way.

  <!-- nature-clim-096 -->

- **Climate clubs: fixing free-riding by excluding outsiders**

  Why cut emissions if other countries will not? Climate clubs answer the The free-rider problem: benefiting without paying. A climate club is a voluntary coalition of countries that agree on a common climate standard, such as a carbon price, and penalise non-members. Membership is voluntary and excludable, so not every country must agree. Countries join for the shared benefit of lower global emissions and to escape sanctions, such as tariffs, imposed on outsiders. The economist William Nordhaus and the economics of climate pioneered the idea in 2015: members price carbon and charge a fee on imports from countries without similar pricing. A 2025 Econometrica paper found such a club could achieve 33–68% of the globally optimal carbon reduction. The G7 Climate Club, launched in December 2022, favours partnerships over penalties and had 46 member states as of May 2025. Opinion is divided. Exporting countries fearing fees and researchers sceptical of Carbon pricing: charging for the harm of greenhouse gases have criticised it, while others argue supposed losers such as China and India would gain. The EU's CBAM has been called a possible first climate club.

  <!-- nature-clim-078 -->

- **Additionality of climate finance: is the money really new**

  Climate finance given to developing countries is supposed to be new money, additional to existing development aid. The Cancun agreements require this, including for money through The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels. New means pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years. But there is no strict definition of additionality. The same vagueness has already caused problems, and even fraud, in judging emission reductions under The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market.

  <!-- nature-clim-052 -->

- **Climate reparations: compensation as a moral debt**

  A 2023 study estimated that the top 21 fossil fuel companies will owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative reparations over 2025–2050. Climate reparations are requested loss-and-damage payments, framed as compensation owed for historical emissions, possibly including debt cancellation. Unlike plain Loss and damage: the harms nobody prevented, the term treats payment as an ethical and moral obligation. Proposed channels include an international compensation commission, lawsuits, the polluter pays principle, debt forgiveness and direct grants. The wealthiest nations have consistently opposed reparations at the UN climate talks, and some argue current generations are not responsible for past emissions. Before COP27, talks were steered to 'cooperation and facilitation' rather than liability.

  <!-- nature-clim-082 -->

- **Green banks: public money that draws in private investors**

  A green bank is a usually public or quasi-public lender that works with private investors to speed the spread of clean energy technologies. It targets technologies that are commercially viable but slow to spread. It uses public funds to lever in private investment, lowering investors' risk with tools such as cheap loans, guarantees, co-investment and bundling loans for resale. Its public capital can be reinvested again and again across many projects. The US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allotted $27 billion to green banks through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund.

  <!-- nature-clim-091 -->

- **The Bali Action Plan: a road map toward Copenhagen**

  In December 2007, COP 13 in Bali set a timeline and structure for negotiating a climate framework for after 2012. Developed countries agreed to comparable quantified emission targets. Developing countries agreed to nationally appropriate mitigation actions, supported by technology, finance and capacity building. A new body, the Ad Hoc Working Group on Long-term Cooperative Action, ran these talks through 2008 and 2009 toward Copenhagen. The conference also drew attention to the 20% of global emissions caused by deforestation.

  <!-- nature-clim-101 -->

- **ITMOs: emission cuts that cross borders**

  In January 2024 Thailand and Switzerland reported the first completed trade of its kind. Internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, or ITMOs, are measured emission reductions or removals that one country transfers to another under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. They count toward the buyer's Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge. Countries trade them through bilateral or multilateral deals, without the central crediting mechanism. They can be measured in tonnes of CO2-equivalent or other metrics, and can come from crediting projects or linked emissions trading systems. By 2024 over 80 bilateral agreements were in place. Commentators disagree on whether the transfers mainly cut costs or risk over-crediting and Hot air: surplus allowances that cut nothing.

  <!-- nature-clim-067 -->

- **Corresponding adjustments: counting each cut once**

  If one country sells an emission cut to another, both cannot claim it. A corresponding adjustment is the accounting step that makes sure a transferred reduction counts in only one country's pledge. It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit. Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this appears in their accounts. Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.

  <!-- nature-clim-070 -->

- **Non-market approaches: cooperation without trading**

  Not all cooperation under the Paris Agreement involves trading emission cuts. Under Article 6.8, countries can cooperate voluntarily with no international transfer of reductions at all. These non-market approaches can combine mitigation and adaptation and involve finance, technology transfer and capacity building. A work programme and the Glasgow Committee on Non-market Approaches were set up at COP26 in 2021, and the committee began work in 2022.

  <!-- nature-clim-069 -->

- **The Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism: UN-supervised credits**

  Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement set up a UN-supervised scheme that registers emission-cutting activities and issues credits for verified reductions or removals. Its credits are called A6.4ERs and are tracked in a registry with unique identifiers. Activities are validated, registered, monitored and independently verified before units are issued, overseen by the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body. Two features aim beyond simple offsetting. A share of proceeds goes to The Adaptation Fund: paying for adaptation through carbon credits. A portion of units is cancelled to deliver an overall cut in global emissions.

  <!-- nature-clim-068 -->

- **The global climate regime: the rules of the game**

  The global climate regime is the worldwide framework of rules for regulating how human activity affects the climate, in order to limit climate change. The UN climate convention set its framework, and its first legally binding result was The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Between 2013 and 2015 there was no legally binding global regime, and the voluntary pledges of The Copenhagen Accord: a deal the conference only noted served in practice. The 2015 Paris Agreement then became the regime. All countries signed on to balancing greenhouse gas sources and sinks in the second half of the century.

  <!-- nature-clim-088 -->

- **Soft loans: borrowing below the market rate**

  A soft loan carries an Interest rates: the cost of money now instead of later below the market rate. It may also offer other concessions, such as long repayment periods or interest holidays. Governments usually give soft loans to projects they consider worthwhile. The World Bank and other development institutions give them to developing countries. Some official development assistance is counted as the concessional value of soft loans, the gift hidden in their cheap terms.

  <!-- nature-clim-099 -->

- **Contraction and Convergence: equal shares per person**

  Contraction and Convergence is a proposed framework with two moves. Total greenhouse gas emissions shrink to a safe level, and every country's emissions per person converge on the same level. The Global Commons Institute conceived it in the early 1990s and expressed it as a simple mathematical formula. Entitlements start from current emissions and move toward equal shares per person at a negotiated rate. That rate is called a key equity lever. Earlier convergence gives more entitlements to low-emitting, typically poorer, countries. Critics say a per-person basis could reward countries whose populations grow, so the model lets negotiators fix a population base year.

  <!-- nature-clim-085 -->

- **The ICJ climate opinion: a court weighs in**

  Pacific island students drove it, and Vanuatu led the request. On 29 March 2023 the UN General Assembly asked the International Court of Justice what international law requires states to do to protect the climate. The Court answered on 26 July 2025. It unanimously held that the climate treaties create binding obligations, including submitting national pledges and acting on Common but differentiated responsibilities: a shared duty, unequally held. Breaching them is an internationally wrongful act that can require full reparation, given a clear causal link. Any state may invoke another's breach, because the climate is a global common good. The opinion is not binding but is expected to be used in courts.

  <!-- nature-clim-097 -->

- **The New Collective Quantified Goal: from $100 billion to $300 billion**

  In 2009, developed countries set a goal, agreed at Cancún in 2010, to mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries. They missed it in 2020 and reached it only in 2022. An OECD report gave $132.8 billion in 2023 and $136.7 billion in 2024. The New Collective Quantified Goal is its successor, negotiated at COP29 in 2024 to cover support after 2025. In Baku, delegations agreed that developed nations would pledge $300 billion a year by 2035, from public and private sources. Poorer nations called this insufficient, and many pushed for at least $500 billion. Some critics, including UN officials, called it a betrayal. The donor base was a key tension. The US and EU wanted countries such as China and the Gulf states to contribute, but the text only encouraged voluntary contributions. Talks at COP30 were expected to address scaling finance from $300 billion to $1.3 trillion.

  <!-- nature-clim-102 -->

- **A short history of climate policy**

  Formal global environmental politics began in June 1972, with the UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm. The first World Climate Conference, in 1979, framed climate change as a global political issue. The IPCC followed in 1988. Most efforts since have sought consensus at the UN under its climate convention, with the 1987 Montreal Protocol cited as proof this can work. Critics of that top-down approach propose bottom-up governance instead. Adaptation was long seen as a distraction from mitigation. It gained attention only around 2009 and 2010, after the Copenhagen summit made progress on emissions look harder. Climate policy also became increasingly polarised in the late 2000s. By 2020 the US partisan gap was the widest in history.

  <!-- nature-clim-092 -->

- **The first global stocktake: a verdict delivered in Dubai**

  On 13 December 2023, COP 28 in Dubai concluded the first The global stocktake: checking the world's progress, part of the UAE Consensus. Its verdict was blunt. A 43 percent emissions cut by 2030 was needed, but only a 5 percent cut was expected. It set 2030 targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double global energy efficiency. For the first time at a UN climate conference, it called on all countries to transition away from fossil fuels to reach climate neutrality by 2050. It also set up the loss and damage fund, with $700 million in start-up capital, to be run by the World Bank.

  <!-- nature-clim-090 -->

- **Adaptation debt: paying for harm others caused**

  Poorer nations suffer the worst consequences of a problem they did little to cause. Adaptation debt is the compensation developing countries claim they are owed for climate damage caused by the developed world's emissions. The burden compounds. Lacking infrastructure and capital, poor countries often borrow at higher interest to recover from disasters, worsening their prospects. The UN climate convention notes that the debt can be met through financial aid and help coping with natural disasters.

  <!-- nature-clim-081 -->

- **Emissions debt: overusing the atmosphere**

  Since around 1750 the United States alone has produced 25% of all carbon emissions, and developed countries together 70%. Emissions debt is the part of Climate debt: who owes whom for a warming planet owed for that imbalance. The atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions is called the total carbon space. The claim is that rich countries used more than their fair share of it. Repayment would mean helping poorer countries industrialise cleanly and sharing out the remaining carbon space by population.

  <!-- nature-clim-080 -->

- **Too weak or too strong: the case against Kyoto**

  Critics attacked The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries from opposite sides. Some environmentalists and scientists found its commitments too weak, while several economists thought them stronger than justified. Stavins called it 'too little, too fast'. Stern said its lack of a long-term goal kept it from sending a credible signal. Others objected that it set cuts only for rich countries and none for fast-growing economies such as China and India. Nordhaus argued that its limits on quantities were less efficient than setting a price, and that it might be better redesigned as a global carbon tax.

  <!-- nature-clim-057 -->

- **The Cancún agreements: pledges and a new fund**

  At the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún, 76 developed and developing countries made voluntary mitigation pledges. Together they produced 85% of global annual emissions in 2010. Parties agreed that future warming should stay below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. Developed countries committed to jointly mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries, and created The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels. That finance had to be 'new' and 'additional' to existing aid.

  <!-- nature-clim-062 -->

- **The Copenhagen Accord: a deal the conference only noted**

  The 2009 Copenhagen conference had been seen as the chance to agree a successor to The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Instead a group of countries produced the Copenhagen Accord, which the conference only 'took note of'. It said warming should be limited to below 2.0 °C, which the UN climate secretariat reads as relative to pre-industrial temperatures. In all, 114 countries agreed to it. Seventeen developed parties plus the EU-27, and 45 developing parties, submitted mitigation targets. It set the goal of sending $100 billion a year to developing countries by 2020 and proposed the Green Climate Fund.

  <!-- nature-clim-061 -->

## Ecological economics and sustainability

What if the economy is not the whole picture, but one part of a larger living system? Ecological economics starts from that question, studying how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together. It sits among the heterodox schools, the economic traditions outside the mainstream, and borrows from ecology and physics alike. The laws of energy and of entropy, the measure of how spread out energy is, set hard limits on what any economy can do. From there come sharp arguments: that growth can make life worse, that businesses shift their costs onto others, and that Earth is a spaceship with limited supplies.

### Ecological economics

This chapter builds a way of seeing the economy as a subsystem of nature. It starts with the field of ecological economics, its history since the 19th century, and its place among schools outside the mainstream. Then it turns to physics: energy cannot be created or destroyed, and entropy, the spreading out of energy, always tends to rise. Those laws rule out a perpetual motion economy. They also give ecological economists their sharpest claims, from the gap between growth and real development to the idea of Earth as a spaceship whose crew must share limited supplies.

- **Ecological economics: the economy inside the ecosystem**

  Mainstream economics usually draws the economy as the whole, with nature as one input among many. Ecological economics flips that drawing. It is a field drawing on many disciplines that studies how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together over time and space. Here the economy is a subsystem of Earth's larger ecosystem, which sets it apart from Environmental economics: weighing what markets leave out (see also Two schools: environmental and ecological economics). Two commitments follow. Ecological economists stress keeping Natural capital: nature as the stock behind the economy intact, and they favor strong Sustainability and the hard question of what to keep: human-made capital cannot stand in for nature. They also try to ground economic thinking in physical reality, especially the The laws of thermodynamics: why no machine runs forever, the physics of energy, and knowledge of living systems. Efficient allocation is not enough. The field adds two more problems: fair distribution, and the size of the economy relative to the ecosystems it relies on. Where mainstream economists tend to be technological optimists, ecological economists lean towards skepticism and precaution, since destroying key environmental resources may be irreversible. Economist Malte Faber sums the field up by its focus on nature, justice and time. Its topics range from weak versus Strong sustainability: some nature cannot be replaced to Energy accounting: following every joule, Cost shifting: when harm is the business model, modeling and monetary policy. It was founded as a modern discipline in the 1980s by European and American academics.

  <!-- nature-eecon-059 -->

- **Heterodox economics: the schools outside the mainstream**

  Somewhere between 5 and 10 percent of American economists were heterodox, Frederic S. Lee estimated in 2007. Heterodox economics is a broad term for schools of economic thought not generally seen as part of the mainstream. It has no fixed definition, because it is defined by contrast with whichever schools dominate at a given time and place. The usual list includes Austrian, ecological, Marxist-historical, post-Keynesian and modern monetary approaches. Four frames are central to them: history, natural systems, uncertainty and power. These schools often see Neoclassical economics: the mainstream's core as flawed. Defenders disagree: economist Marcos Lisboa argues that the assumptions critics attack are often not essential to it. Student movements such as Rethinking Economics campaign for more pluralism in economics degrees.

  <!-- nature-eecon-115 -->

- **Systems ecology: ecosystems as complex systems**

  An ecosystem, in systems ecology, is more than the sum of its species. This holistic branch of ecology studies ecosystems as complex systems with emergent properties, features that appear only in the whole. It applies general systems theory to ecology, and its central tool is energetics, the principles of energy applied to systems at every scale. Howard T. Odum: ecosystems as electric circuits was its most notable proponent. Ecological work deals almost entirely with open systems, which exchange with their surroundings across their boundaries. Because the field cares about how human interventions affect ecosystems, it brings economics into the study of ecological-economic systems. Combined with engineering design, it becomes ecological engineering.

  <!-- nature-eecon-130 -->

- **Cost shifting: when harm is the business model**

  Mainstream economics calls pollution an Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else, a side effect that falls on people outside a deal. Karl William Kapp and the true social costs thought the word was a misnomer. In his account, modern business makes profit by shifting costs onto others as normal practice, not by accident. Clive Spash makes the same point from the other side. Externality theory, he notes, wrongly treats environmental and social problems as small exceptions in an otherwise efficient system. Suppose the harm is structural. Then internalizing an odd externality, making one polluter pay for one harm, does nothing about the underlying problem. Joan Martinez Alier and the environmentalism of the poor adds a twist about who pays. Most affected consumers are future generations, who cannot influence today's prices. Paul Hawken frames it as a hidden subsidy: unsustainable goods are cheaper only because the environment, communities or future generations quietly cover part of the bill. This is a live dispute. Ecological economics: the economy inside the ecosystem rejects the mainstream view that such harms can be fixed by internalizing externalities one at a time. Mainstream economists continue to defend that view.

  <!-- nature-eecon-063 -->

- **The case against putting a price on nature**

  Bee pollination near a Costa Rican farm was valued at over US$60,000 a year. Then coffee prices fell, the fields were replanted with pineapple, which needs no bees, and the bees' value vanished. For Douglas McCauley and others, that story shows how putting money values on nature can harm conservation. The critique, aimed at Ecosystem valuation: putting numbers on nature's services, has several strands. Not every Ecosystem services: the work nature does for people pays: mangroves protect coasts, but wolves hunt cattle. Money values tie conservation to fluctuating markets. Human ingenuity can replace some services by artificial means, which lowers their value further. And conserving an ecosystem is not always more profitable than changing it, as the local fish trade after the Nile perch was introduced to Lake Victoria shows. McCauley concludes that campaigns should appeal to morality rather than money. The question remains contested. Monetary valuation of nature is widely accepted among ecologists and conservationists, while some critics argue it is inherently false.

  <!-- nature-eecon-064 -->

- **Growth versus development: more is not the same as better**

  An economy can get bigger without people's lives getting better. Ecological economics draws a line between growth, a quantitative rise in economic output, and development, a qualitative improvement in quality of life. Its practitioners argue that neoclassical economics confuses the two, treating Economic growth and the power of small percentages as progress in itself. Beyond modest levels, higher consumption per person may not raise well-being, and may harm the environment and society. Growth of that harmful kind is sometimes called Uneconomic growth: when getting bigger makes life worse. Well-being here also means something different from the welfare concept used in mainstream and environmental economics.

  <!-- nature-eecon-062 -->

- **From Malthus to a journal: how ecological economics began**

  The roots run back to the 19th century: the Romantics, Malthus's worries about population and Mill's hope for an economy that stops growing. In 1926 Frederick Soddy attacked the idea of the economy as a perpetual motion machine able to create infinite wealth. A 1971 book by Georgescu-Roegen gave the field a framework built on flows of materials and energy. Organized meetings began in Sweden in 1982, and after a series of conferences the field was formally founded in 1988. In 1989 the The International Society for Ecological Economics was born, along with the journal Ecological Economics, with Robert Costanza and the $33 trillion valuation as first president and editor. The main founders were Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing and Costanza from the US, AnnMari Jansson, bridge between ecology and economy from Sweden and Juan Martínez-Alier from Spain.

  <!-- nature-eecon-065 -->

- **The laws of thermodynamics: why no machine runs forever**

  No inventor has ever built a perpetual motion machine, and the laws of thermodynamics explain why none ever will. These basic physical laws govern energy, heat, work and temperature. There are traditionally three, plus a more basic "zeroth law" defining temperature, added later. The first says energy cannot be created or destroyed. The second says the total Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out of interacting systems never decreases. Together they rule out machines that make work from nothing and machines that turn heat spontaneously into work. Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson had established both by 1860. Ecological economics uses them to build models that respect physical limits. By these laws, a perpetual motion economy is impossible.

  <!-- nature-eecon-118 -->

- **Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out**

  Entropy is the only physical quantity that seems to give time a direction, sometimes called the arrow of time. It is often described as a measure of how spread out, or dispersed, energy is in a system; loosely, its degree of disorder. By the second of the The laws of thermodynamics: why no machine runs forever, the entropy of an isolated system tends not to decrease. Lower entropy marks more useful energy: heat supplied at a high temperature does more than the same amount at a low one. Rudolf Clausius named the concept in 1865, from the Greek word for "transformation". Georgescu-Roegen: entropy and the economic process brought it into economics, coining Entropy pessimism: can technology beat physics?, which Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing continued to promote. The practical sting: recovering materials scattered as pollution and waste takes energy and resources that rise steeply as the recycled share grows.

  <!-- nature-eecon-109 -->

- **Uneconomic growth: when getting bigger makes life worse**

  Growth is supposed to make people better off. Uneconomic growth is the kind that reflects or causes a fall in quality of life. Economist Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing says it happens when extra production costs more in resources and well-being than the goods made are worth. The costs come from the social and environmental sacrifices of an economy encroaching on its ecosystem. In the 1990s David Suzuki argued that ecosystems can sustain only about 1.5–3% new growth per year, so demanding more from farms or forests eats into Natural capital: nature as the stock behind the economy. In a "full-world economy", the ecological costs of growth may exceed its benefits. The idea is usually credited to Daly, though some credit Marilyn Waring, who developed it studying the UN System of National Accounts.

  <!-- nature-eecon-090 -->

- **Spaceship Earth: one ship, limited supplies, one crew**

  Earth, in this picture, is a spaceship: limited supplies, no resupply, and passengers who must act as one crew for the common good. The phrase first appears in Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879). Kenneth Boulding's 1966 essay gave it economic force. He contrasted the past "cowboy economy" of seemingly endless resources with a coming "spaceman economy". The spaceman economy has no unlimited reservoirs for extraction or pollution. Boulding argued that the economy must fit itself to an ecosystem with limited pools of resources. Buckminster Fuller popularized the phrase in his 1968 Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth. UN Secretary-General U Thant used it on Earth Day: a teach-in that became a global event 1971. Not everyone finds the image comforting: sociologist Steffen Roth argues a realized Spaceship Earth would be the most total institution in human history.

  <!-- nature-eecon-127 -->

- **The first law of thermodynamics: energy is never made or lost**

  Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. That is the first law of thermodynamics, the conservation of energy applied to heat and work. In an isolated system, the total of all forms of energy stays constant. Energy moves into or out of a system in two main ways: as heat and as work. The law has been precisely supported, and never violated, in many careful experiments. Kenneth Boulding drew an economic lesson from it. Because matter and energy are conserved, the flow of resources through the economy roughly measures GNP, the yearly value of a nation's output. GNP, he argued, should therefore be treated as a cost to minimize.

  <!-- nature-eecon-114 -->

- **Embodied energy: the energy hidden inside things**

  Every product carries an invisible energy bill. Embodied energy is the total energy needed to produce a good or service, counted as if it were stored inside the product. It aims to add up a product's whole life cycle, from extracting raw materials through transport, manufacture and installation to disposal, much as Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave does. Since energy use usually brings greenhouse gas emissions, it helps judge whether a product adds to or reduces global warming. A key use is comparing the energy a product produces or saves with the energy used to make it. Common units are MJ/kg and tonnes of CO2. Values vary widely, because there is no international agreement on data and methods, but products can still be ranked. The main methods grew out of Wassily Leontief's input-output model, adapted by Hannon to ecosystem energy flows.

  <!-- nature-eecon-095 -->

- **Exergy: the part of energy that can do work**

  Energy is never lost, yet it gets used up. Exergy resolves that puzzle. It is the maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system as it comes into balance with its surroundings, often called "available energy". It depends on both the system and its environment, arising from the difference between them. By the The first law of thermodynamics: energy is never made or lost, energy in and out always balance. But in real processes some exergy is always destroyed, as the The second law of thermodynamics: why heat never flows uphill requires. Solar radiation provides most of the exergy for processes on Earth, including those that sustain life. Zoran Rant proposed the concept in 1956, building on Gibbs and Helmholtz. It has spread from engineering into ecological economics and systems ecology, where some see it as nature's equivalent of money.

  <!-- nature-eecon-110 -->

- **Energy return on investment: it takes energy to get energy**

  In 1919, finding US fossil fuel returned about 1000 units of energy for every unit spent. By the 2010s the ratio was only 5:1. That ratio, usable energy delivered divided by the energy spent to obtain it, is the energy return on investment, or EROI. If it falls to one or less, a source becomes a net energy sink. A major source needs at least 3:1 to be viable. Only human-applied energy counts as invested: sunlight driving biofuel crops is left out. When EROI falls, energy gets harder to obtain and its relative price may rise. Charles A. S. Hall popularized the idea, and his 1984 paper on the cover of Science gave it its greatest exposure. Measurement is disputed. Researchers disagree on how far back into the supply chain to count, and an IEA-endorsed method gives more favorable values for solar panels.

  <!-- nature-eecon-102 -->

- **The stationary state: the classical end of growth**

  The classical economists expected growth to stop. Farmland was scarce, while population and Capital: goods made to make other goods kept growing. Once the rate of profit fell to a minimum or zero, capital accumulation would end. The economy would then settle into a stationary state, with constant population and capital. Adam Smith believed every national economy would sooner or later get there, and he and Ricardo saw it gloomily. John Stuart Mill did not. He welcomed the stationary state, making what has been called a quality-of-life argument for it.

  <!-- nature-eecon-073 -->

- **Buddhist economics: the most well-being from the least stuff**

  In 1955, advising Burma's government, E. F. Schumacher, who named natural capital coined the term "Buddhist economics". It is a spiritual and philosophical approach that aims for the most well-being with the least use of resources. Its starting point is that people are interdependent with one another and with nature. Where traditional economics seeks profit and individual gain, it seeks to reduce suffering and simplify desires. Drawing on "Right Livelihood", Schumacher held that work should develop a person's abilities, connect them with others and produce what a decent life needs. Using non-renewable resources, in this view, means living on capital rather than income. It also counts "primordial stakeholders", such as future generations and the natural world, who have no purchasing power. Since 1972 Bhutan has promoted gross national happiness, built on Buddhist values, instead of judging development by GDP.

  <!-- nature-eecon-093 -->

- **Thermoeconomics: an economy run on physics**

  Thermoeconomics, also called biophysical economics, is a Heterodox economics: the schools outside the mainstream school that applies the The laws of thermodynamics: why no machine runs forever to economic theory. It studies how societies get and use energy and resources to produce, distribute and consume goods, while generating waste and environmental impacts. Its practitioners model economies as thermodynamic systems involving matter, energy, Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out and information. The global economy is an open system, and economic activity a dissipative system, one that thrives by consuming free energy. The school develops economic versions of the first and second laws. A 2020 analysis drew a sobering conclusion: GDP in advanced economies is likely to fall. That happens once credit can no longer prop up consumption, and energy becomes lower in quality and more costly.

  <!-- nature-eecon-089 -->

- **Social metabolism: the material flows that keep a society alive**

  A body takes in food and air and gives off waste. Social metabolism extends that idea to society: the flows of materials and energy between nature and society, between societies, and within them. People take materials and energy from nature, transform, circulate and consume them, and finally return them as waste. These flows also build and maintain in-use stocks, such as buildings, vehicles and infrastructure, that provide shelter, transport and communication (see Stocks and flows: what you have versus what moves). Every society has such flows, but their size and variety depend on its culture, or "sociometabolic regime". Each process's impact depends on how it is done, how much, where, and nature's capacity to regenerate. John Bellamy Foster built on Marx's ideas here to develop Metabolic rift: the broken loop between city and soil.

  <!-- nature-eecon-086 -->

- **Costanza's $33 trillion price tag for nature**

  In 1997 a team led by Robert Costanza and the $33 trillion valuation published in Nature a total money value for the world's ecosystem services. It came to $33 trillion a year, within a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion. Global GDP that year was $27 trillion. Half the value came from nutrient cycling. Estuaries, swamps, floodplains, seagrass and algae beds had the highest values per hectare. The study averaged values from very specific local studies and transferred them without regard to setting. Even critics in Ecological Economics granted that valuing the global ecosystem had positive potential.

  <!-- nature-eecon-061 -->

- **Ecological-economic modeling: equations for economy and nature**

  Ecological-economic modeling uses mathematical models to analyze how economies and ecosystems interact. The toolbox is wide: evolutionary, input-output, entropy and thermodynamic, multi-criteria and agent-based models, the The environmental Kuznets curve: does growth clean up after itself?, and stock-flow consistent frameworks. For changing landscapes, system dynamics and GIS, digital mapping, are used to simulate change across space.

  <!-- nature-eecon-069 -->

- **Energy accounting: following every joule**

  Energy accounting tracks energy into and out of a system, the useful work done and the energy lost, to judge resource use and environmental impact. An energy balance uses the first and second laws of thermodynamics to show how much energy each point in a system needs, and in what form. A key idea is net energy gain. Every source needs an initial energy investment, so its return must exceed one to be useful. For coal, oil and gas, that gain has fallen over time, because the easiest sources were used first.

  <!-- nature-eecon-071 -->

- **The green economy: low-carbon, efficient and fair**

  A green economy is low-carbon, efficient in its use of resources and socially inclusive. The idea grew in policy circles, first as a response to financial crisis and then as a vehicle for growth and development. In 2011 UNEP developed its definition to stress a fair shift to such an economy. It looks to cleaner, resource-saving technologies. Green economics: the economy as part of the ecosystem is close to Ecological economics: the economy inside the ecosystem but more politically applied. Critics dispute whether market-based green policies can reach the real causes of environmental crisis.

  <!-- nature-eecon-140 -->

- **Money and ecological economics**

  Ecological economists also study money itself, aiming for monetary policy that serves sustainable scale, just distribution and efficient allocation. The work traces back to Frederick Soddy's writing on money. It asks what money is, whether interest-bearing debt forces an economy to grow, and whether alternatives such as alternative currencies and public banking would help.

  <!-- nature-eecon-070 -->

- **Buen Vivir and Ecological Swaraj: non-western roots**

  Some ecological economic thinking comes from outside the West. Buen Vivir, "Good Life", is a South American movement that rejects the western development model and does not value piling up material wealth. Ecological Swaraj, from India, respects physical limits and non-human species and pursues equity through direct democracy. Both stress Harmony with Nature. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful: economics as if people mattered brought such ideas, including Buddhist economics: the most well-being from the least stuff, into mainstream thought.

  <!-- nature-eecon-067 -->

- **Schools of ecological economics: from pragmatists to radicals**

  Ecological economics is not one camp. Clive Spash sorts environmental work into three groups: new resource economists, new environmental pragmatists and radical social ecological economists. At the radical end, Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose is a growing strand that tackles biophysical limits and global inequality. New resource economists who criticize it point instead to the momentum of Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later and the The green economy: low-carbon, efficient and fair.

  <!-- nature-eecon-066 -->

- **The second law of thermodynamics: why heat never flows uphill**

  A cup of hot coffee always cools in a cold room; a cold room never heats the coffee. That is the second law of thermodynamics in its simplest form, the Clausius statement: heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder body to a hotter one. More generally, the total Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out of interacting systems never decreases, so all natural processes are irreversible. Reversible processes are only a theoretical limit. Sadi Carnot first formulated the law in 1824, studying the motive power of fire. Georgescu-Roegen called it the "entropy law" and put it at the center of his economics.

  <!-- nature-eecon-119 -->

- **Conservation of mass: matter is only rearranged**

  Burn a log and its matter does not vanish; it is rearranged. In a system closed to matter flowing in or out, total mass stays constant. In a chemical reaction, the starting materials weigh the same as the products. Antoine Lavoisier confirmed this in the late 18th century, building on Jean Rey's 1630 demonstration. Tracking how mass moves through a system over time is the engineering method of mass balance. Hydrologists use it as a water balance to estimate how long water stays in a reservoir. The law holds only in the classical limit: Einstein's E=mc2 merged it with conservation of energy.

  <!-- nature-eecon-094 -->

- **Metabolic rift: the broken loop between city and soil**

  Between 1815 and 1880, England's soils grew so exhausted that Britain imported bone and guano for fertilizer. Karl Marx wrote during this "second" agricultural revolution. Drawing on Justus von Liebig's 1840 account of how soil nutrients feed plants, he saw a one-way "robbing of the soil". Nutrients went to cities as food and never returned to the land, linking urban pollution with Soil fertility: the power to give steady harvests loss. Sociologist John Bellamy Foster, not Marx, coined the term metabolic rift, starting with his book Marx's Ecology. It names capitalism's break in the Social metabolism: the material flows that keep a society alive between society and nature. Foster sees it as proof Marx held an ecological outlook. The idea now extends to marine ecology and a "carbon rift" from carbon dioxide emissions. Its reading is disputed: historical materialists such as Jason W. Moore see the rift's origins very differently.

  <!-- nature-eecon-120 -->

- **Entropy pessimism: can technology beat physics?**

  Every technology turns valuable resources into waste and so raises Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out. Entropy pessimism holds that technology therefore cannot escape the laws of physics. Neoclassical production functions treat technology as a factor of production with no mention of natural resource inputs. In ecological economics, technology is simply the way natural resources are transformed. Robert Solow replied in 1997 that "elementary physics" had not by itself prevented growth in industrialized countries. Economists still disagree on whether technology can overcome resource limits.

  <!-- nature-eecon-076 -->

- **Resource decoupling: growing on less**

  Can an economy grow while using less of nature? Resource decoupling means needing fewer natural resources per unit of output, measured by the ratio of resource consumption to GDP. Relative decoupling is a fall in resource use per unit, all else equal; absolute decoupling is a fall in total resource use while GDP keeps growing. The record is poor. A 2019 review found that attempts to grow without environmental destruction had not succeeded.

  <!-- nature-eecon-081 -->

- **Four books, six years: the founding works**

  Between 1966 and 1972, four works put natural resources at the heart of economics. Boulding's 1966 essay on Spaceship Earth: one ship, limited supplies, one crew argued the economy must fit a closed, cyclical system. Georgescu-Roegen's 1971 book argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used. In Environment, Power and Society, also from 1971, Howard T. Odum: ecosystems as electric circuits proposed the The maximum power principle: winning by using more energy. A 1972 report, The Limits to Growth: a computer model meets a finite planet, projected that output, food per person and population would peak and then decline.

  <!-- nature-eecon-077 -->

- **Escaping to space: a way out of limits to growth?**

  If Earth is full, why not build new worlds? Some proposed that settling outer space could ease Overpopulation in ecology and resource limits. In the 1970s Gerard K. O'Neill planned space settlements to solve the problems of too many people and finite resources without political repression. The idea answers worries about How many people can the Earth support? by moving the boundary rather than living within it.

  <!-- nature-eecon-083 -->

- **Sustainability science: a field built around problems**

  Most fields are defined by their methods. Sustainability science, says William C. Clark, is defined by the problems it tackles. This applied discipline, emerging in the 1980s, studies sustainability and Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later and links knowledge to action. It grew from publications such as the World Conservation Strategy (1980) and the Brundtland report of 1987, Our Common Future: defining sustainable development. It was launched as an international field at a 2001 world congress in Amsterdam. At its core is the recognition of humanity's epochal impact in the Anthropocene.

  <!-- nature-eecon-129 -->

- **Ecologically unequal exchange: trade that drains the South**

  Half of all materials consumed by high-income countries are extracted from poorer countries, Dorninger and colleagues found, while the rich countries still run trade surpluses. Ecologically unequal exchange is the idea that world trade hides an unfair flow of materials, energy and environmental damage, not just labor, from poorer to richer countries. It builds on world-systems theory, which splits the world economy into a rich core and a poorer periphery. Southern countries serve as sources of raw materials, sinks for waste and places written off as a Sacrifice zones. A study of EU consumption from 1995 to 2019 found much of its environmental impact outsourced abroad, while more than 80% of the economic benefits stayed home. The logical result is an Ecological debt: what the North owes the South owed by North to South. Jason Hickel proposes Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose in the North to end it. Most cited studies support the theory, but Peter Somerville calls it confused and internally inconsistent.

  <!-- nature-eecon-085 -->

- **Unequal exchange: the hidden transfer from poor to rich**

  From 1990 to 2015, Hickel and colleagues calculated, the drain from the Global South equaled 242 trillion in 2010 US dollars. Unequal exchange is the hidden transfer of labor and ecological value from poor countries to rich ones through structurally unequal trade. Because the terms of trade are biased, poor countries must export far more labor and resources than they import to keep trade balanced in money. The theory rejects the claim that free trade based on Comparative advantage: why the best at everything still trades benefits everyone. Arghiri Emmanuel and Samir Amin traced it mainly to wage gaps between core and periphery. Northern power rests partly on patents: 97% of all patents are held by corporations in high-income countries. Critics say wage gaps reflect higher productivity in the North. Supporters reply that productivity itself is measured by prices, so the dispute continues.

  <!-- nature-eecon-133 -->

- **Stock-flow consistent models: macroeconomics that adds up**

  Stock-flow consistent models are macroeconomic models built on strict accounting: one party's asset is another's liability, and no money appears from or vanishes into nowhere. Unlike mainstream DSGE models, they do not assume equilibrium, and they are popular with post-Keynesians. Wynne Godley used them to warn from 2000 that the US housing market would weaken and cause a recession. Ecological macroeconomics now adds resource, energy and ecosystem stocks and flows, drawing on Georgescu-Roegen's flow-fund models.

  <!-- nature-eecon-128 -->

- **Do people really maximize? The heterodox objection**

  Neoclassical economics pictures people as rational agents maximizing their own utility or profit, and for many economists that is simply what economic behavior means. Heterodox critics object. Social constraints, coercion or poor judgment may stop people from maximizing. Shiozawa argues that in a complex world agents cannot reach maximum utility and instead pick from a repertoire of ready-made rules. The two sides still disagree over whether rational maximization describes real behavior.

  <!-- nature-eecon-116 -->

- **Do markets really settle? The heterodox objection**

  In microeconomic theory, many cost-minimizing buyers and sellers produce prices that clear the market, and under certain assumptions the result is efficient. Mainstream microeconomics is built on this optimization and Equilibrium: when the market stops moving. Heterodox economics centers instead on institutions, history and social structure. Austrians, post-Keynesians and others dispute that equilibrium models capture real markets, while the mainstream still relies on them.

  <!-- nature-eecon-117 -->

- **Ecological energetics: following energy through food webs**

  Ecological energetics is the quantitative study of how energy flows through ecological systems. It looks for the principles that govern how energy passes through trophic levels, the feeding steps of ecological networks. In Systems ecology: ecosystems as complex systems, these "ecosystem laws" count as formally analogous to the principles of energetics.

  <!-- nature-eecon-132 -->

- **Counting embodied energy: three ways to fill the database**

  Databases estimate Embodied energy: the energy hidden inside things in three ways. Bottom-up process data from manufacturers is more reliable and specific, but usually leaves out much of a product's energy. Top-down environmentally-extended input-output (EEIO) data from national statistics fills the gaps but is much less reliable for any one product. Hybrid methods use process data and fill its gaps with EEIO data.

  <!-- nature-eecon-096 -->

- **Embodied energy in transport: more than the fuel**

  Driving uses more energy than the fuel tank shows. Embodied energy in transport covers making, maintaining and recycling vehicles and building transport networks. One French institute notes that people use more embodied energy in transport spending than direct energy. France's ADEME puts a car's embodied energy at 20 800 kWh and an electric vehicle's at 34 700 kWh, the gap coming from battery and electronics. With a fuel EROEI of 8, fuel use should be raised by 14.3% to cover the fuel's own embodied energy.

  <!-- nature-eecon-098 -->

- **Embodied energy in buildings: the energy in the walls**

  About 30% of all energy used over a building's lifetime can be embodied energy, depending on its age, climate and materials. That is the energy to extract, process, transport, assemble, maintain and finally dispose of its materials. Its share has risen as efforts focused on cutting operating energy such as heating and cooling. Rating schemes such as USA LEED now include it when judging a building's impact.

  <!-- nature-eecon-097 -->

- **Energy quality: not all joules are equal**

  A unit of electricity can do more than a unit of warm water. Energy quality measures how much of a form of energy can become useful work: the ratio of its Exergy: the part of energy that can do work to its energy. Electrical, kinetic and chemical energy are fully recoverable as work. Heat and radiation are not; for heat the upper limit is the Carnot efficiency, found by Sadi Carnot in 1824. High-quality carriers can do more kinds of work, so they can be held to have more economic value.

  <!-- nature-eecon-111 -->

- **Emergy: pricing everything in sunlight**

  How do you add a liter of fuel to an hour of human labor? Ecologist Howard T. Odum: ecosystems as electric circuits studied energy flow in ecosystems from the 1950s. He argued that different energy sources cannot be added until they share a common measure of quality. His answer was emergy: the total energy of one kind, usually sunlight, used directly and indirectly to make a product or service. Sunlight, fuel, electricity and human services are each expressed as the solar energy needed to produce them, in solar emjoules (seJ). Odum's first formal statement came in 1973; David Scienceman proposed the name in 1986. In practice, an analyst draws a system diagram, tables the flows of resources, labor and energy, converts each to emergy and sums them. The goal is an "ecocentric" valuation that adds to economic values rather than replacing them. Emergy remains controversial. Critics call it an energy theory of value, say the sunlight behind oil cannot be measured objectively, and fault it for ignoring market values.

  <!-- nature-eecon-099 -->

- **Exergy destruction: the work potential thrown away**

  Every real process wastes some of its potential to do work. That loss is exergy destruction, also called irreversibility, the lost part of Exergy: the part of energy that can do work. Highly efficient systems destroy little; inefficient ones destroy a lot. In a cycle, the total destroyed is the sum of what each process in it destroys.

  <!-- nature-eecon-113 -->

- **Exergy as a tool for environmental policy**

  Some propose using Exergy: the part of energy that can do work analysis to make environmental policy fairer and more effective. It has already exposed a gap: national greenhouse gas balances often leave out emissions from international transport, and so ignore the impacts of imports and exports. Early cases also suggest that exergy-based taxation could reduce the tax burden on citizens.

  <!-- nature-eecon-112 -->

- **EROI by source: from oil shale to hydropower**

  Hydropower plants run for about 100 years return about 110 units of energy for each unit invested. Nuclear plants range from 20 to 81, and refined fuel from conventional oil from around 18 to 43. Oil shale is typically around 1.4–1.5, barely above break-even. Wind turbines average around 16 unbuffered and 4 buffered in the literature, and operating turbines averaged 19.8 in 2018 data. A 2015 review found mean values between 8.7 and 34.2 for solar panels, with payback times of 1.0 to 4.1 years.

  <!-- nature-eecon-103 -->

- **Energy cannibalism: growth that eats its own power**

  Building a new power plant takes energy, and in a fast-growing energy industry that energy comes from the existing plants. This is energy cannibalism, and it limits how fast an energy technology can grow when climate neutrality is demanded. A solar breeder, a panel factory powered by its own panels, overcomes some of the problem.

  <!-- nature-eecon-108 -->

- **Energy stored on energy invested: is storage worth building?**

  For a storage device, the key ratio is electricity stored over its lifetime against the embodied electricity needed to build it. Reported values include 10 for a vanadium redox battery, 704 for pumped hydro and 792 for compressed-air storage. A Stanford team found that without pumped storage, pairing wind with today's batteries would not be worth the investment.

  <!-- nature-eecon-107 -->

- **Point of use, extended, societal: widening the EROI count**

  Basic Energy return on investment: it takes energy to get energy stops at the wellhead. Point-of-use EROI adds the cost of refining and transporting the fuel, which lowers the result. Extended EROI also adds the infrastructure needed to deliver the refined energy. Societal EROI sums the EROIs of all fuels a nation uses; it has never been fully calculated.

  <!-- nature-eecon-106 -->

- **Falling EROI and the collapse of civilizations**

  Thomas Homer-Dixon argues that falling energy returns were one reason the Western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century CE. Joseph Tainter goes further, suggesting a diminishing Energy return on investment: it takes energy to get energy is a chief cause of the collapse of complex societies. Some historians link humanity's growing use of outside energy to sources that were easy to exploit and gave high returns.

  <!-- nature-eecon-105 -->

- **The Jevons paradox: why efficiency can raise consumption**

  Make a resource cheaper to use and people may use more of it. The Jevons paradox holds that technology which makes resource use more efficient tends to increase total use. Efficiency lowers the effective cost; if demand responds strongly to price, use rises enough to outweigh the saving. Energy-saving bulbs lower bills but free money for spending elsewhere, an example of the The rebound effect: when efficiency eats its own savings. Faster computers lead to more computers being bought. Mainstream economists argue growth from knowledge may not be uneconomic. Economists still debate how often the paradox occurs.

  <!-- nature-eecon-163 -->

- **Net energy and payback time**

  Net energy is what a source yields after subtracting the energy invested; Energy return on investment: it takes energy to get energy expresses the same thing as a ratio. A process with an EROI of 5 yields a net gain of 4 units for each unit spent. Break-even is an EROI of 1, a net gain of 0. The time a source takes to reach it is its energy payback time.

  <!-- nature-eecon-104 -->

- **Throughput: the river of matter running through the economy**

  Textbooks often draw the economy as a closed loop of money passing between firms and households. That circular flow ignores a one-way river underneath it. Throughput is the flow of matter and energy that enters the economy from nature as resources and leaves again as waste and pollution. Economist Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing describes the journey in terms of Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out. Low-entropy resources are taken from nature and turned into goods. Eventually the whole throughput returns to the environment as high-entropy waste. Too large a flow depletes geological capital and damages nature's life-support services. This makes throughput the quantity that ecological economists want to control. Daly's The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth keeps stocks of capital and people constant with a minimal throughput. Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose mainly aims to cut the material throughput of affluent societies. Technology offers no clean escape: any use of it adds to the cumulative flow of matter and energy, which limits purely technological fixes.

  <!-- nature-eecon-136 -->

- **The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth**

  Can an economy be healthy without growing? The steady-state economy says yes. It keeps a constant stock of physical wealth, or capital, and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time. It can apply to a city, a region, a country or the whole world. The idea updates the classical The stationary state: the classical end of growth. Its main champion since the 1970s, Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing, added the ecological piece: both stocks are kept constant by a flow of natural resources, the Throughput: the river of matter running through the economy. Both stocks should be as durable as possible. Longer-lasting capital needs a smaller resource flow. A durable population means long lives with low birth and death rates. The reasoning starts from a view of the economy as an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem. A part cannot grow forever inside a whole that does not grow. That contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households, with no physical contact with nature. Daly admits the limits of his own idea. A steady state only postpones, and does not prevent, the eventual exhaustion of minerals. Even sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

  <!-- nature-eecon-072 -->

- **The declining-state economy: should the economy shrink?**

  Georgescu-Roegen: entropy and the economic process thought Daly's The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth did not go far enough. As finite minerals are extracted, he argued, Earth's carrying capacity will fall, so the world economy is heading for collapse. A shrinking economy, not a steady one, would stretch those minerals furthest. He proposed a "minimal bioeconomic program" with restrictions stricter than Daly's. Daly does not reject a declining path. He sees the steady state as the necessary first step: an economy must stop before it can reverse. Others, including Rifkin, Latouche and Kerschner, argue directly for declining-state strategies, and today's Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose thinkers share the view. The disagreement is real and unresolved. Steady-state advocates want the economy to stabilize; their more radical allies want it to shrink. Both accept that Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out and finite Non-renewable resources: the stock that does not come back stocks set the terms of the argument.

  <!-- nature-eecon-078 -->

- **Can capitalism stop growing?**

  Radical critics ask whether a steady or shrinking economy can be laid on top of capitalism at all. They point to growth drives built into it: the profit motive, jobs that depend on sales, credit creation by banks and labor-saving technology. Governments need tax revenue from economic activity, and globalization forces countries to compete. Daly disagrees with framing it this way. He holds that the debate between growth and a steady state cuts across the left-right divide. The question remains open.

  <!-- nature-eecon-080 -->

- **Daly's three institutions for a steady state**

  Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing proposed building a The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth by policy, through three state institutions. The first sets minimum and maximum incomes and a maximum on wealth. The second issues transferable reproduction licenses at the replacement fertility level. The third sells depletion quotas that cap the flow of resources. Unlike taxes, quotas directly minimize Throughput: the river of matter running through the economy. Daly calls the mainstream faith that prices and technology can overcome any scarcity "growthmania".

  <!-- nature-eecon-074 -->

- **Degrowth as the road to a steady state**

  Christian Kerschner argues that rich countries should shrink their economies as a route to a fair world The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth. Shrinking rich economies would leave ecological room for poorer countries to catch up. Kerschner admits a world steady state may stay out of reach, but says such goals can still guide action. Two comparative studies found no analytical difference between Daly's steady-state economics and European Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose.

  <!-- nature-eecon-079 -->

- **The Great Stagnation: a critique of degrowth**

  Wim Naudé argues that Western economies already look like Degrowth: shrinking production on purpose. They are in a "Great Stagnation" of falling innovation and entrepreneurship. In prolonged stagnation, he notes, the economy increasingly works like a zero-sum system, where one person's gain is another's loss. His critique disputes the benefits claimed for Degrowth as the road to a steady state and the steady state.

  <!-- nature-eecon-084 -->

- **Overdevelopment: when rich countries have too much**

  Development is usually something poor countries lack. Overdevelopment turns that around: the rich countries of the global north are too developed, which increases humanity's ecological impact and causes problems for rich and poor countries alike. The idea comes from Leopold Kohr's 1977 book The Overdeveloped Nations, which was mainly about Overconsumption: using up faster than nature refills.

  <!-- nature-eecon-082 -->

- **The solar-income budget: living on sunlight**

  Before industrialization, people lived within what Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing calls a solar-income budget. Daly sees two sources of wealth. One is a stock of minerals, which we can extract as fast as we choose. The other is a flow of solar energy that is beyond our control. Since the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, the mineral stock is the crucial scarcity. The Industrial Revolution broke the budget by extracting minerals at a rapidly increasing rate.

  <!-- nature-eecon-075 -->

- **Post-normal science: when facts are uncertain and stakes are high**

  Some decisions cannot wait for certainty. Post-normal science is a problem-solving approach for science used in policy when "facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent". Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz developed it in the 1990s. In such cases it sets aside the traditional ideal of truth and focuses on quality, checked by internal and extended peer communities. Its diagram plots system uncertainties against decision stakes, separating applied science, professional consultancy and post-normal science. It complements risk analysis and Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses rather than replacing them. It is meant for pandemics, ecosystem collapse, biodiversity loss and the shift to sustainability. In modeling it favors "models to map our ignorance about the future" over models to predict it. Critics say it adds nothing new, turns climate scientists into "stealth advocates" and undermines empiricism.

  <!-- nature-eecon-124 -->

- **Emergy ratios: judging how a process uses resources**

  Emergy: pricing everything in sunlight accounting produces ratios that judge how a process uses local, renewable and purchased resources. The emergy yield ratio (EYR) measures how far an investment lets a process exploit local resources. The environmental loading ratio (ELR) compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy, signaling stress on ecosystems. The emergy sustainability index (ESI) is EYR divided by ELR.

  <!-- nature-eecon-101 -->

- **Transformity: how much sunlight a joule costs**

  If 10,000 solar emjoules are needed to make a joule of wood, the wood's solar transformity is 10,000 seJ/J. Transformity is the Emergy: pricing everything in sunlight needed per unit of available energy produced, and so a measure of energy quality. Sunlight absorbed by the Earth has a solar transformity of 1.0 by definition. Odum's 1975 table of "energy quality factors" first stated the principle behind it: quality is measured by the energy used in transformations.

  <!-- nature-eecon-100 -->

- **Vienna and Barcelona: two ways to measure social metabolism**

  Two schools measure Social metabolism: the material flows that keep a society alive. Both build on material flow accounting, which tracks a state's or region's inputs and outputs of materials and energy, imports and exports included. The Vienna school's MEFA, founded by Marina Fischer-Kowalski, studies national economies over time and standardizes data for comparison. The Barcelona school's MuSIASEM: accounting across scales, built around Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi, studies subsectors of present economies with tailor-made accounts within a set "grammar".

  <!-- nature-eecon-088 -->

- **MuSIASEM: accounting across scales**

  MuSIASEM, Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism, is an accounting method for social-ecological systems that can simulate possible development paths. It keeps assessments consistent across scales and across economic, demographic and energy measures in different units. It tracks who uses which resources and why, the environmental pressures that result, and how far needs and pressures are shifted abroad through trade. Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi created it around 1997 at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. It suits the nexus of food, energy, water and land, and has been tested with the FAO.

  <!-- nature-eecon-123 -->

- **Hunters, farmers, industry: three sociometabolic regimes**

  Rolf Sieferle divided human history into three regimes by main energy source. Hunter-gatherers relied on "passive solar energy" from recent photosynthesis, giving nomadic societies with few people per area. The Neolithic Revolution brought an agrarian regime of "active solar energy use": forests cleared for farms, settled life and faster Population growth: from one billion to eight. The industrial regime runs on fossil fuels. Historians reconstruct this using indicators such as Total Primary Energy Supply and Human Appropriation of Net Primary Production (HANPP).

  <!-- nature-eecon-087 -->

- **Eco-urbanism: closing the city's loops**

  Eco-urbanism tries to heal the Metabolic rift: the broken loop between city and soil at city scale. It brings a city's energy, water, food and waste flows back within its own systems. The aim is greater self-reliance through "closed-loop systems" that reduce dependence on outside networks. Critics link it to "managerial environmentalism" and doubt that sustainable cities are possible within global capitalism.

  <!-- nature-eecon-122 -->

- **Jason Moore's rival reading of the metabolic rift**

  Jason W. Moore dates metabolic rifts to the birth of capitalism in the "long" 16th century, recurring in every phase of its development. He traces them to capitalist relations based on the law of value, not to industrial agriculture. Moore holds that splitting social from natural systems is empirically false and arbitrary. James O'Connor adds that capitalism's undervaluing of nature leads to economic crisis, a "second contradiction of capitalism". Moore's view diverges widely from Foster's on what causes ecological crisis.

  <!-- nature-eecon-121 -->

- **Declining terms of trade: coffee buys less every year**

  Working for the UN Economic Commission for Latin America, Raúl Prebisch saw that exports such as coffee and copper bought fewer manufactured goods over time.
