Much of the difficulty starts at the drawing board: products are often not designed to be recycled. In the USA only about 6 to 7 percent of plastic is recycled. Money drove the first big push. Large investment in recycling came in the 1970s, when rising energy costs made saving energy pay.

  <!-- nature-eecon-038 -->

- **Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste**

  Extracting and processing material resources accounts for over 55 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. The usual economy treats those materials as a one-way flow: extract them, use them, throw them away. Critics call this the linear 'take-make-waste' economy, and it puts heavy pressure on the environment. A circular economy is the alternative. It is an Economic systems: who owns, who decides that tries to keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible. The European Parliament describes it as sharing, leasing, reusing, repairing, refurbishing and recycling existing materials and products for as long as possible. There are four ways to make an economy more circular. Narrowing the loop means using fewer resources. Slowing it means reuse and repair. Closing it means Recycling: giving waste a second life. The fourth is substituting renewable or less harmful inputs. Done worldwide, circularity could cut emissions by 22.8 billion tons, equal to 39% of global emissions in 2019, a large lever for Sustainability and the hard question of what to keep. The idea is older than the name. In 1966 Kenneth Boulding wrote 'The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth'. It contrasted an open 'cowboy economy' with a closed one, and it is often cited as the idea's first expression. Pearce and Turner's 1990 book described a system where waste from extraction, production and consumption is turned back into inputs. The concept also draws on the study of industrial material flows, on design that copies nature, and on Cradle to cradle: materials as nutrients that circulate. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation spread it in Europe and the Americas.

  <!-- nature-eecon-001 -->

- **Plastic pollution: cheap to make, slow to vanish**

  More than 900 marine species are affected by plastic pollution, the build-up of plastic objects and particles in the environment. Bottles, bags and microbeads all harm people, wildlife and habitats. Plastics are cheap and durable, so manufacturers favor them, but most resist natural breakdown and degrade slowly. Debris is sorted by size into micro-, meso- and macro-debris; macrodebris is larger than 20 mm. Around 275 million tonnes of plastic waste is generated each year, and between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes of it is dumped into the sea. Packaging is the largest use, at 219 Mt as of 2024. Industry leaders knew in the early 1970s that most plastic would never be recycled, yet later ran a $50 million a year campaign saying it was. Governments most often target bags, by bans or fees, then cutlery and microbeads. Many academics and NGOs want a legally binding treaty to cap plastic production, a direct answer to this Pollutants: when a substance becomes a problem.

  <!-- nature-eecon-032 -->

- **Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems**

  A natural The ecosystem, from a rock's surface to the whole planet has no waste: what one organism discards, another uses. Industrial ecology takes that as a design model. It is the study of how materials and energy flow through industrial systems. It aims to move industry from open loops, where resources end as waste, to closed loops, where wastes become inputs for new processes. The field was popularized in a 1989 Scientific American article by Robert Frosch and Nicholas Gallopoulos. They asked a simple question: why could one industry's outputs not be another's inputs? Today the field combines engineering, economics, sociology, toxicology and the natural sciences. Its research covers industrial metabolism, life-cycle assessment, eco-design, extended producer responsibility and Eco-industrial parks: neighbors that share. Its principles now appear in circular economy policy, for example using waste heat from one process to run a cooler one.

  <!-- nature-eecon-008 -->

- **Resource recovery: treating waste as raw material**

  Lithium, cobalt and vanadium for electric vehicles and wind turbines can be pulled from industrial landfills and old mine wastes. That is resource recovery: using wastes as raw material to make valuable new products. It aims to cut waste and the need for landfill while getting the most value out of what is thrown away. It also delays the need to dig up fresh raw materials. Recovery is one piece of a Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste, which minimizes both resource extraction and waste. It goes beyond Recycling: giving waste a second life to include any way of winning value back from Municipal solid waste: what a city throws away and industrial waste. Its potential shrinks with time. Through manufacture, use and landfilling, materials are irreversibly mixed and diluted; physicists would say their entropy, their disorder, rises. The more scattered a material becomes, the harder it is to win back. Some recovery is a sign of failure. Capturing landfill gas for energy counts as recovery, but it is a last resort, because the whole point is to avoid landfill altogether.

  <!-- nature-eecon-044 -->

- **The waste hierarchy: a pyramid of better and worse**

  In 1979 a Dutch member of parliament, Ad Lansink, proposed ranking ways of dealing with waste. 'Lansink's Ladder' became the waste hierarchy. It orders the options from the most to the least environmentally preferable, usually drawn as a pyramid. Its aim is to get the most practical benefit from products while generating the least waste. The EU's 2008 Waste Framework Directive set five steps in order. Prevention comes first, then reuse, then recycling. Next is other recovery, including energy recovery. Safe disposal is the last resort. An early EU proposal had put recycling level with incineration; it was heavily criticized and replaced by the five-step version. Applied well, the hierarchy can cut greenhouse gas emissions and other Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill, save energy and resources, create jobs and spur green technology. It is a rule of thumb, not a law of nature. Looking at a product's whole life can justify breaking it. Replacing an old, inefficient washing machine is often better than keeping it, because most of its impact comes while it runs.

  <!-- nature-eecon-022 -->

- **Zero waste: designing waste out from the start**

  Only 9% of global plastic is currently recycled. Zero waste aims at a far bolder target: sending nothing to landfills, incinerators, oceans or anywhere else in the environment. It is a set of principles for preventing waste by redesigning how resources flow, so that all products are reused or repurposed. The approach rejects managing waste at the end of the pipe. It calls for a 'whole systems' change in how materials move through society. That means products that are easy to take apart for Recycling: giving waste a second life, durable and repairable, with minimal packaging. For households, Bea Johnson's '5 Rs' (refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, rot) extend the familiar three. Many organizations and cities adopt the slogan, though, without pressing for its key changes.

  <!-- nature-eecon-057 -->

- **Dematerialization: doing more with less stuff**

  Cars weigh 30% less than in the early 1960s, and aluminium soda cans are six times lighter. Both are examples of dematerialization: making more goods, or meeting the same economic needs, with less material. The shift can be absolute or relative. Absolute means a cut in total material use. Relative means less material per unit of economic output, such as Gross domestic product: an economy in one number, even if the total still rises. Products shed material in three ways. Optimizing means using less mass. Digitizing turns paper into an e-book. Servitizing means renting instead of selling. The United States offers a striking case. Between 1977 and 2001 the material needed to meet Americans' needs fell from 1.18 to 1.08 trillion pounds, while population grew by 55 million. Critics are not convinced the trend is real at a global scale. Extraction of six minerals and cement production grew faster than GDP from 1960 to 2019. Part of rich countries' dematerialization comes from moving material-hungry production to developing countries. Some critics say there is little evidence of global dematerialization at all, only regional shifts caused by that outsourcing. The question remains disputed, and it matters for whether Economic growth and the power of small percentages can coexist with smaller demands on Natural resources: where every product begins.

  <!-- nature-eecon-007 -->

- **Does recycling pay? The economics of recycling**

  Virgin plastic resin costs 40 percent less than recycled resin. For many cities it is also cheaper to landfill household waste than to recycle it. Numbers like these fuel the economics of recycling, a dispute over whether recycling's economic and environmental benefits outweigh its costs. Critics argue that collecting and trucking materials costs money and burns energy, enough to outweigh the savings in production. Supporters answer that comparing market prices alone leaves things out. Making new plastic causes extra pollution that nobody pays for, an Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else. Life cycle assessment can measure such hidden costs, and tools such as a carbon tax can build them into market prices. How a program is set up matters too. Communities save money when recycling replaces their usual waste system rather than adding to it. The two sides still disagree over whether recycling's Economic cost: counting what you pass up and energy use exceed its savings, and the answer may differ from place to place.

  <!-- nature-eecon-040 -->

- **The sharing economy: using what sits idle**

  The average car sits unused 95% of the time. The sharing economy puts such spare capacity to work. It is an economic system in which people share in making, distributing, trading and using goods and services, often through online platforms. It can be run by non-profits, like a lending library, or by companies for profit, such as Uber and Airbnb. By sharing, it can cut the number of goods that must be produced, and so reduce environmental harm. There is no consensus on its definition, and its effects are disputed. Critics say platforms avoid taxes, regulation and insurance costs, and can push wages into a The race to the bottom. Whether its workers are independent contractors or employees is still debated. So is whether its gains come from real efficiency or from dodging rules.

  <!-- nature-eecon-050 -->

- **Circular business models: profit from keeping things in use**

  A firm can make money by selling a product as a service, running a sharing platform or extending product life. These are circular business models: ways of earning a Profit: what is left after every cost while keeping resources in use. They aim to use resources better, cut waste and create value for firms and customers. The key idea is to build loops that recapture value that would otherwise be lost. Early talk centered on 're-X' steps such as recycling, Remanufacturing: rebuilt as good as new, reuse and recovery. Today four strategies are named. Narrowing loops uses fewer materials. Slowing loops relies on repair, reuse, resale and rental. Closing loops recycles into new production, and the fourth regenerates natural systems. Digital tools such as the internet of things, big data and AI are seen as key to scaling up. Hurdles remain in technology, consumer habits and profitability. Firms switching to secondhand raw materials do not necessarily cut short-term costs.

  <!-- nature-eecon-004 -->

- **Critiques of the circular economy: can loops really close?**

  Physics sets a ceiling on circularity. Under the second law of thermodynamics, scattered materials take energy to gather back up, and that energy rises steeply as the recycled share rises. Recovery can therefore never reach 100%. This is one of several critiques of the Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste: objections that it leaves growth unquestioned, ignores economics and thermodynamics, and neglects social justice. The economic objection came from Zink and Geyer. They argued that supporters treat the world as an engineering system. They also questioned whether closing loops really prevents new primary production, or simply adds recycled material on top of it. Growth is a third worry. Efficiency gains for each product can be swamped by growth in total consumption. Some scholars therefore call for a post-growth circular economy. The fourth critique concerns fairness. Most circular economy plans do not ask who controls the technologies or how the costs and benefits are shared. That gap has prompted calls for a 'circular society'. These questions are open. Scholars still dispute whether closing material loops actually displaces primary production, and whether circularity is compatible with growth at all.

  <!-- nature-eecon-003 -->

- **R-hierarchies: ranking refuse, reuse, recycle and the rest**

  In 2018 Reike and colleagues compared 69 different R hierarchies and found 38 distinct 're' words. R-hierarchies are ranked lists of 're-' actions, such as refuse, reduce, reuse, repair and recycle. They order circular strategies by how much value they keep or how much waste they avoid. They are probably inspired by the 1970s motto 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle', and they extend the logic of the The waste hierarchy: a pyramid of better and worse to the Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste. Reike's team unified the jumble into a 10R framework. At the top sit refusing and reducing raw material use, because the best waste is the one never created. Next come reuse, repair, refurbishing, rebuilding to factory standard, and finding new uses, which keep a product or its parts working. Recycling ranks near the bottom, since it breaks products down to their materials. Lowest of all is energy recovery by incineration, which keeps only the heat.

  <!-- nature-eecon-002 -->

- **Cradle to cradle: materials as nutrients that circulate**

  The usual life of a product runs 'cradle to grave', from making to disposal. Cradle-to-cradle design plays on that phrase. It is a nature-inspired way of designing products and systems in which materials are treated as nutrients that circulate safely and endlessly, as they do in an The ecosystem, from a rock's surface to the whole planet. The goal is systems that are not just efficient but essentially waste-free. It builds on John T. Lyle's regenerative design and can apply to cities, buildings, economies and social systems. At Ford's River Rouge plant, a planted roof formed part of an $18 million rainwater system that saved Ford $30 million in mechanical treatment facilities. Today's recycling works against the idea. Sites usually crush whole products rather than take them apart. That makes recovering rare-earth elements and sorting alloys uneconomical. The name 'Cradle to Cradle' is a trademark of the consultancy MBDC. After criticism, MBDC handed its certification to an independent non-profit institute in 2012.

  <!-- nature-eecon-013 -->

- **Waste valorization: turning residues into value**

  Red mud from alumina production, mine tailings and even spent nuclear fuel can be turned into something useful. Waste valorization gives economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials. It usually means using the leftovers of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another, the core idea of Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems. Industrial wastes suit it best. They are more consistent and predictable than household waste, so a factory can plan around them. Household rubbish varies from bin to bin. Interest grew in the 1990s and 2000s for two reasons. Regulators tightened the rules on residues, making them costlier to dump. At the same time, ideas of sustainable development and the circular economy spread. Valorization is a close cousin of Resource recovery: treating waste as raw material, with the stress on the value created.

  <!-- nature-eecon-055 -->

- **Remanufacturing: rebuilt as good as new**

  A remanufactured machine should meet the same customer expectations as a new one. That promise sets remanufacturing apart from other recovery processes, which stop short of it. Remanufacturing rebuilds a used product to the original maker's specifications, from a mix of reused, repaired and new parts. The process is thorough. A discarded product is taken fully apart. Usable parts are cleaned and refurbished. Then it is reassembled into a unit equal to new, and sometimes better. This goes further than simple Reuse: keeping things in service. The product may keep its identity or lose it. Photocopiers and toner cartridges are typical examples of the kinds of goods rebuilt this way. The practice is still small. In 2020 it made up 2% of all US manufacturing and 1.9% in the EU. As a way of slowing the loop, it is one of the stronger tools of a Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste.

  <!-- nature-eecon-043 -->

- **Upcycling: making trash worth more than before**

  Before the Industrial Revolution, upcycling to repair goods was common. Mass production and a linear habit of throwing things away pushed it aside. Upcycling turns waste or unwanted products into new materials or products seen as having greater quality or value, such as artistic or environmental value. It is a subset of Recycling: giving waste a second life that adds value. Its opposite, Downcycling: each round a little worse, turns waste into lower-quality products. Both words first appeared in print in a 1994 SalvoNEWS article. Upcycling is a circular economy strategy. By raising a product's value and stretching its life through repair and new uses, it cuts resource use. The same act can mean different things in different places. In poorer countries, upcycling often reflects a lack of access to new goods. In rich countries, it more often reflects concern for the environment.

  <!-- nature-eecon-053 -->

- **Material flow analysis: following matter through a system**

  Matter is never created or destroyed, so every tonne entering a system must leave it or pile up inside. Material flow analysis builds on that fact. It is a method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system, and a core method of Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems. It rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance, the conservation of matter. Every analysis has a boundary, processes, flows between them and stocks within them. Unlike economic accounting, it also tracks waste, emissions and natural resources that have no market. It can cover a single plant, a supply chain, a product's life or a whole national economy. The method was developed during the 1980s and 1990s.

  <!-- nature-eecon-019 -->

- **The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources**

  Crops, forests, fish, animals and micro-organisms supply the bioeconomy. It is the part of the economy that uses Renewable resources: the stock that regrows, if allowed from land and sea, plus biotechnology, to produce food, materials, products and energy. Its products include food, feed, bio-based products, bioenergy and services based on biological resources. Its aims are to secure food, use Natural resources: where every product begins more sustainably and reduce dependence on fossil resources and minerals. The term became popular from the mid-2000s, when the EU and OECD adopted it as a policy framework; the OECD (2006) and EU (2012) created bioeconomy strategies. Not everyone is persuaded. Critics fear its 'green growth' framing keeps an unsustainable model in place, and may turn living things into economic commodities. Whether it changes the economy or merely sustains it is disputed.

  <!-- nature-eecon-009 -->

- **Collecting recyclables: curbside, drop-off and buy-back**

  Recycling: giving waste a second life starts with collection, and there are three main ways to gather recyclables from the waste stream: drop-off centers, buy-back centers and curbside collection. Each trades public convenience against government ease and expense. Buy-back centers pay for cleaned, sorted recyclables, a clear incentive. Drop-off centers are easiest to set up but handle low, unpredictable amounts. Source separation, where each material is sorted before collection, gives the purest recycled material.

  <!-- nature-eecon-041 -->

- **Recycling policy: securing supply and creating demand**

  Recycling needs a steady supply of material and buyers for what it makes. Recycling supply and demand policies are laws that secure both. Supply comes from mandatory collection, container deposit laws and bans on throwing certain things away. Demand is raised by minimum recycled-content mandates, utilization rates, government purchasing policies and labels on recycled products. Together they help build a Markets: where buyers meet sellers for recycled goods.

  <!-- nature-eecon-042 -->

- **Types of recycling: mechanical, chemical, closed and open loop**

  Not all Recycling: giving waste a second life is the same. Sorted by process, mechanical recycling shreds, melts and reforms materials, while chemical recycling breaks them into their chemical components. Sorted by outcome, closed-loop recycling makes the same product without significant loss of quality. Open-loop recycling makes different, often lower-quality products. Closed-loop recycling is generally seen as more sustainable, because it loses fewer resources along the way.

  <!-- nature-eecon-039 -->

- **The circular bioeconomy: biology meets the closed loop**

  According to the European Commission's science service, the circular bioeconomy produces €1.5 trillion in value added, 11% of EU GDP. It is a The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources run on circular principles. It produces food, materials and energy from renewable biological resources while reducing dependence on other natural resources. One study found it may be necessary for a carbon-neutral future in line with the Paris Agreement.

  <!-- nature-eecon-010 -->

- **Circular economy standards: rules for going circular**

  In 2017 the British Standards Institution launched BS 8001:2017, the first circular economy standard. Such standards are formal guides that help organizations apply circular economy principles. The international body ISO followed, setting up technical committee TC 323 in 2018. In 2024 and 2025 it published four ISO 59000-series standards, including ISO 59020 on measuring circularity performance.

  <!-- nature-eecon-005 -->

- **The EU Circular Economy Action Plan**

  The European Union has a policy program for moving its economy toward circularity: the Circular Economy Action Plan. The first plan, 'Closing the loop', had 54 measures aimed at competitiveness, growth and jobs. The European Commission adopted a new plan in March 2020. It targets resource-hungry industries, waste reduction and decarbonization, the cutting of carbon emissions, and it makes sustainable products the standard.

  <!-- nature-eecon-006 -->

- **Pay as you throw: a bill for every bag**

  In Ferrara, Italy, waste fell by 30% overall and recycling rose by 40% once households paid by the bag. Pay as you throw charges households for rubbish collection according to how much waste they put out, instead of a flat fee. Under a flat rate or tax, everyone pays the same, so there is no Incentives: what moves people to act to throw away less. The scheme rests on the The polluter pays principle and on shared responsibility. Waste can be measured by weight, size, or counts of special bags, tags or containers. Recycling and composting are often collected free, which nudges people toward them. In North America, it cut residential waste by 9-38% and raised recycling by 6-40%. There is a catch: charging for waste can lead to illegal dumping, known as 'fly-tipping'.

  <!-- nature-eecon-031 -->

- **Product-service systems: selling light, not light bulbs**

  Philips sells some customers a promised level of light, not lamps. They pay per lux. A product-service system is a business model in which a firm sells a combined package of Goods and services: things and activities that together meet a customer's need. Customers want the function a product provides, not necessarily to own it, so firms may be paid per unit of service. Xerox's pay-per-copy model works the same way. Research names three classes. In product-oriented systems, ownership passes to the customer with added services. In use-oriented ones, the provider keeps ownership and sells use through sharing, pooling or leasing. In result-oriented ones, services replace products. The concept was first developed at the Politecnico di Milano between 1993 and 1996. Not every such system cuts material use, but some authors claim they can improve Eco-efficiency: more value, less damage by a factor of 4 or more.

  <!-- nature-eecon-036 -->

- **Biorefineries: an oil refinery for plants**

  The pulp and paper industry is considered the first industrialized biorefinery system. A biorefinery is a facility that converts biomass, material from living things, into energy and other useful products such as chemicals. The IEA defines biorefining as sustainable processing of biomass into food, feed, chemicals, materials and bioenergy, the full product range of the The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources. It works like an oil refinery. Biomass is split into intermediates such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Each refining step is called a cascading phase. Systems are classified by platform, product, feedstock and conversion process, which may be mechanical, biochemical, chemical or thermochemical. The goals are broad: supplying fuels and chemicals, creating rural jobs, getting value from waste and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Biobased does not automatically mean harmless. Growing the biomass can still cause land-use change, pesticide pollution and eutrophication, the overloading of water with nutrients. So life cycle assessment is used to compare biobased products with conventional ones.

  <!-- nature-eecon-026 -->

- **Repurposing: giving junk a new job**

  An old tyre can become a boat fender, and a drum can become a feeding trough or compost bin. Repurposing means using an item for a purpose other than the one it was made for, usually something considered junk. It is a form of Reuse: keeping things in service. Earthship houses take it furthest, using tyres as insulating walls and bottles as glass walls.

  <!-- nature-eecon-048 -->

- **Right to repair: who gets to fix your phone**

  Broken and used electronics became the fastest-growing waste stream as smartphones and computers spread. The right to repair is the legal right of owners to maintain, repair or modify their own devices and equipment, such as cars, electronics and farm machinery. The obstacles are deliberate. Manufacturer-only servicing, restricted parts and tools, and software locks create a 'repair monopoly', a form of Monopoly: the market with one seller. Such monopolies have been found to raise prices, cause delays and reduce consumer choice. The movement aims to favor repair over replacement and to make repairs cheaper, supporting a more sustainable economy with less electronic waste. The EU adopted its Right to Repair Directive on 30 May 2024. Canada became the first country with a national right-to-repair law on 7 November 2024.

  <!-- nature-eecon-049 -->

- **Microplastics: the plastic too small to see**

  By 2050 the weight of microplastics in the sea is estimated to exceed that of fish. Microplastics are tiny insoluble plastic particles, from 1 micrometre to 5 mm across, that pollute water, soil and air. Primary ones, such as microbeads, clothing microfibers and pellets, are already small when released. Secondary ones come from larger items breaking down. Because some plastics take hundreds to thousands of years to degrade, these particles are likely to be eaten and build up in living things.

  <!-- nature-eecon-033 -->

- **Composting and digestion: letting microbes recycle food**

  Food scraps and garden waste can become compost, fertilizer and energy. Composting and anaerobic digestion are biological processes that break down such organic waste; digestion works without oxygen. Methane from digestion can be captured to generate electricity and heat. Anaerobic digestion of the organic part of municipal waste has been found more environmentally effective than landfill, incineration or pyrolysis, the breaking down of waste by heat. It is a clear case of Resource recovery: treating waste as raw material.

  <!-- nature-eecon-046 -->

- **Mining sewage: recovering resources from wastewater**

  Sewers were first built only to carry waste away. Since the 1970s the focus moved to cleaning water, and since about 2003 to recovering resources. Resource recovery from wastewater wins back water, energy, nutrients and other materials from wastewater, sewage sludge and human excreta. Nutrients from these sources are widely reused in farming, often unsafely. WHO guidelines from 2006 set a framework for doing it safely.

  <!-- nature-eecon-045 -->

- **The Zero Waste Hierarchy: from best use to last resort**

  The Zero Waste Hierarchy ranks policies and strategies for a Zero waste: designing waste out from the start system, from the highest and best use of materials down to the lowest. It adds depth to the familiar 3Rs of reduce, reuse and recycle. It also steers policy and investment toward the top of the ranking. It is meant for everyone from policymakers to industry and individuals, and it helps them judge proposed solutions.

  <!-- nature-eecon-058 -->

- **Cradle to Cradle certification: grading products by their materials**

  The Cradle to Cradle Products Innovation Institute runs a certification that scores products against Cradle to cradle: materials as nutrients that circulate criteria. One criterion is material health, which identifies the chemicals in a product. Another is material reutilization, which covers recovery and recycling at end of life. Materials are ranked green for low risk, yellow for acceptable, red for those to be phased out, and grey where data are incomplete.

  <!-- nature-eecon-016 -->

- **Downcycling: each round a little worse**

  A plastic computer case might become a plastic cup, then a park bench, and finally plastic waste. That slide is downcycling: reusing materials to make products of lower quality or value than the original. It is the common fate of much Recycling: giving waste a second life. Cradle-to-cradle design aims to stop it, keeping technical materials cycling at full quality instead.

  <!-- nature-eecon-015 -->

- **Technical and biological nutrients: two loops, not one**

  Cradle-to-cradle design splits all materials into two kinds. Technical nutrients are non-toxic synthetic materials, such as plastics and metals, that cycle in industry and can be used again and again without losing quality. Biological nutrients are organic materials that decompose into soil and feed small life forms without harming the environment. In a hypothetical cradle-to-cradle shoe, the sole is a biological nutrient and the upper a technical one, separated when the shoe is returned.

  <!-- nature-eecon-014 -->

- **Life cycle thinking: from raw material to rubbish**

  A greener factory is no gain if it makes the product dirtier to use. Life cycle thinking guards against that. It looks at a product's environmental impacts at every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal, and tries to reduce them. A core aim is to avoid burden shifting, where an improvement at one stage causes harm at another, adding to Environmental degradation: 70% of the land, already altered. Companies use it to design greener products, consumers to choose products, and governments to write regulations. Its tools include life-cycle assessment, life cycle management, Life cycle costing: the full price of owning something, Design for the environment: cutting harm at the drawing board, product-service systems and Integrated product policy: acting where it counts. Life-cycle assessment follows impacts from raw material extraction through manufacture, distribution, use, repair, disposal and recycling. The EU Waste Framework Directive brought this thinking into waste policy.

  <!-- nature-eecon-028 -->

- **Eco-efficiency: more value, less damage**

  In 1992 the World Business Council for Sustainable Development coined the term eco-efficiency in its publication 'Changing Course', and the 1992 Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties endorsed it. It means providing Goods and services: things and activities that meet human needs while steadily cutting their environmental impact and resource use over their whole life cycle. Put simply: more goods and services with fewer resources and less waste and pollution. It is measured as a ratio, such as Gross domestic product: an economy in one number produced per unit of CO2 emitted. Alongside consistency and eco-sufficiency, it is one of the three basic sustainability strategies. It relies on technological innovation, business, markets and an acceptance of growth. That reliance draws criticism. Huesemann and Huesemann showed with historical evidence that efficiency gains have not reduced overall resource use and pollution. Critics argue efficiency alone is not enough, though the point remains debated.

  <!-- nature-eecon-027 -->

- **Product stewardship: everyone shares the responsibility**

  Australia's TV and computer scheme has recycled about 230,000 tonnes of e-waste under the country's Product Stewardship Act 2011. That act created voluntary, co-regulatory and mandatory schemes. Under product stewardship, everyone who makes, sells, buys, uses or disposes of a product shares responsibility for its impacts. Those are its environmental and health effects over its whole life, the focus of Life cycle thinking: from raw material to rubbish. For manufacturers, it includes planning, and if necessary paying, for recycling or disposal at end of life. Products can be redesigned to use fewer harmful substances and to be more durable, reusable and recyclable. It differs from extended producer responsibility, which puts the burden on manufacturers alone. This approach spreads it to retailers, consumers and recyclers too.

  <!-- nature-eecon-034 -->

- **Container deposits: a refund for every bottle**

  A container deposit scheme adds a refundable fee to a bottle or container, which the buyer gets back on returning it. The refund is an Incentives: what moves people to act to bring containers back. Anyone who finds and returns a bottle can claim it, so collecting them is a means of survival for some homeless people in US cities. Unclaimed fees can pay for landfill or litter control. The same idea applies to paint and tyres, where buyers pay up front for disposing of the toxic waste they become.

  <!-- nature-eecon-035 -->

- **Industrial symbiosis: one firm's waste, another's input**

  At Kalundborg in Denmark, a power station's gypsum by-product becomes raw material for a plasterboard maker. That is industrial symbiosis, a part of Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems in which separate firms exchange materials, energy, water and by-products. Such networks use material and energy better than any single process could alone. Collaboration and nearness are seen as the keys, though being close is neither necessary nor sufficient. Kalundborg's web of exchanges evolved spontaneously over a long time; designing one from above in a short time is hard. Information is a barrier too: by-products are usually treated as waste and listed on no exchange. Keeping resources in use longer eases demands on Earth's resources, a stepping-stone toward a Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste.

  <!-- nature-eecon-017 -->

- **Eco-industrial parks: neighbors that share**

  An eco-industrial park is a group of businesses on shared land that work together on environmental and resource issues. The goal is better environmental, economic and social performance for all of them. Firms in such parks physically exchange materials, energy, water and by-products, a form of Industrial symbiosis: one firm's waste, another's input. They may share waste treatment, pass by-products between plants, and reuse one plant's processed water in another.

  <!-- nature-eecon-018 -->

- **Food waste valorization: from scraps to feed**

  About 30% of the food livestock eat comes from food waste or from crops grown and processed in the supply chain. Food waste valorization turns food waste into food or feed products, or extracts food or feed ingredients from it. It is a branch of Waste valorization: turning residues into value. Landfilled food waste releases methane and other harmful compounds. Processed instead, it can yield biofertilizers, Bioplastics: plastic from living sources, biofuels, chemicals and nutraceuticals, and it can even be turned into insect protein.

  <!-- nature-eecon-056 -->

- **Bioplastics: plastic from living sources**

  Biodegradable plastic has been made from chicken feathers, which are 90% keratin and over 6 million tons of waste a year in the EU and US. Bioplastics are a family of plastics made from biological rather than fossil sources, with different properties and uses. Some are made from sugar by genetically modified microbes. They are one of the material products of the The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources.

  <!-- nature-eecon-012 -->

- **Cascading use of biomass: highest value first**

  Cascading use processes biomass in an ordered pattern so that it yields the highest-value products before lower-value ones. The order runs from fine chemicals and medicines, through chemicals, bioplastics and transport fuels, down to electricity and heat. Those last need the most biomass for the least value. Finding the best pattern for a given biomass is called biorefining, a core skill of the The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources.

  <!-- nature-eecon-011 -->

- **Source reduction: stopping waste before it starts**

  The surest way to deal with waste is to never make it. Source reduction cuts hazardous and other waste before it arises, by changing how things are produced, the top step of the The waste hierarchy: a pyramid of better and worse. It works through changes in manufacturing technology, raw materials and product recipes, and is sometimes called pollution prevention. A more controversial form, toxics use reduction, targets the use of toxic chemicals early in production. Chemical manufacturers have opposed it.

  <!-- nature-eecon-023 -->

- **Servitization: selling the service, not the thing**

  Servitization meets customer needs by selling a product's function or output, or a product-service package, rather than the product itself. It turns a one-time sale into a long-term service relationship, such as a maintenance-free service contract. It can also give access to people who cannot afford to buy outright, as with car-pooling, car-sharing or rent-to-own. Alongside optimizing and digitizing, servitizing is one of three main ways to dematerialize a product, and the heart of a Product-service systems: selling light, not light bulbs.

  <!-- nature-eecon-037 -->

- **Sustainable materials management: the whole life of stuff**

  During the 20th century, global raw material use rose about twice as fast as population. Each 1 percent rise in GDP has raised raw material use by 0.4 percent. Sustainable materials management responds with a systemic approach to using and reusing materials more productively across their whole life cycle. Unlike waste management, which deals only with end-of-life waste, it holds every industry and consumer along the way responsible. The OECD and the US EPA have adopted it; the OECD issued a policy brief on it in 2012.

  <!-- nature-eecon-051 -->

- **The linear economy: take, make, waste**

  The conventional economy runs in a straight line: resources are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away. This linear 'take-make-waste' economy uses up finite reserves of Natural resources: where every product begins to make short-lived products that end in landfills or incinerators. It puts great pressure on the environment through extraction, energy-hungry production and huge amounts of waste. The circular economy and Circular fashion: clothes that come back around are both defined against it.

  <!-- nature-eecon-052 -->

- **Integrated product policy: acting where it counts**

  Integrated product policy is a form of Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems that reduces product-related environmental damage by acting at whichever life-cycle stage works best. Rather than rely on one measure, it combines economic instruments, bans on substances, voluntary agreements, eco-labels and design guidelines. The European Commission issued a green paper, a discussion document, on it on 7 February 2001.

  <!-- nature-eecon-030 -->

- **Life cycle costing: the full price of owning something**

  Life cycle costing adds up all the costs a product or system incurs over its whole life, to find the cheapest way of providing it. The sticker price is only the start. Life cycle thinking: from raw material to rubbish shows that the environmental cost of owning a product depends on its running costs for energy and consumables. Product-service systems use life cycle costing by lowering the maintenance and storage costs a consumer would otherwise bear.

  <!-- nature-eecon-029 -->

- **Circular fashion: clothes that come back around**

  A 2017 Ellen MacArthur Foundation report, 'A New Textiles Economy', brought circular fashion into the mainstream. It applies the Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste to clothing, so that fashion products last longer and are reused, recycled or repurposed instead of discarded. It replaces the take-make-use-dispose model with reduce, reuse, recycle and regenerate. Practices include designing clothes for longevity, using sustainable materials, running recycling programs and supporting second-hand markets.

  <!-- nature-eecon-024 -->

- **Circular procurement: buying for the loop**

  Circular procurement means buying goods and services that follow circular economy principles, favoring reuse, durability and recycling to extend product lives and cut waste. It may mean buying durable or reusable goods, shared-use models, refurbished assets or products with recycled content. It is often seen as part of Sustainable procurement: buying for the whole life cycle and supports SDG 12's target on sustainable public procurement. Risks include greenwashing. Barriers include high infrastructure costs and a lack of standard definitions.

  <!-- nature-eecon-025 -->

- **Urban mining: digging gold out of old gadgets**

  A 2010 Japanese government study estimated that 6,800 tonnes of gold could be recovered from used electronics in Japan. Urban mining recovers rare metals from a society's stockpile of discarded electronic waste, its 'urban mine', by mechanical and chemical treatment. Its main aim is winning back materials, whereas landfill mining aims to fix problems at the disposal site. In developing countries e-waste is often recycled informally, even inside homes, without proper equipment. Shifting from primary production to urban mining needs detailed accounts of materials in use and in obsolete stocks.

  <!-- nature-eecon-054 -->

## Governance, equity and justice

Every rule about nature is really a rule about people. Governance is how societies decide what they may take from the environment, and who gets a say in those decisions: governments, businesses and ordinary citizens. Some of those decisions are written into treaties between countries, meant to bind them all. Others come from looser plans, like the action plan and the 27 principles that came out of the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. This part follows how those choices are made, and how fairly their costs and benefits are shared.

### Environmental governance

Nobody manages a river or a forest directly. What gets managed is people: how they fish, farm, build and dump. This chapter looks at the machinery for that, from national parks and local plans to treaties among countries and the institutions that help nations cooperate across borders. It also traces a shift in thinking, away from managing single resources and toward managing whole ecosystems, humans included, while learning from monitoring as decisions go.

- **Managing people, not nature**

  A forester cannot negotiate with a forest. What foresters, fishery officers and planners actually manage is people: how societies use, change and harm the environment around them. That is environmental resource management. Its goal is to keep ecosystems intact and protect the services nature provides for future generations, weighing ethical, economic and ecological concerns together. The reason is simple. The economy works inside nature and depends on the goods and services that natural ecosystems supply. The field links several older trades, including fisheries, forest and wildlife management. It also takes in the formal systems firms use to track their environmental impact. ISO 14001 is the most widely used standard of this kind. It lines up closely with the EU's Eco-Management and Audit Scheme. Underneath every strategy lies a view of how humans relate to nature. At one end sits anthropocentrism, which values nature only for what it does for people. At the other sits ecocentrism, which grants nature value in itself. Thinking has shifted too. Resilience thinking, which asks how systems absorb shocks, urges managers to stop chasing maximum sustainable yield, the largest harvest that can be taken year after year. It asks them to manage whole ecosystems instead.

  <!-- nature-gov-159 -->

- **Adaptive management: learning while you decide**

  Every management decision is also an experiment, whether anyone admits it or not. Adaptive management makes that explicit. It is a structured, repeated way of deciding under uncertainty, described in Uncertainty: deciding without knowing: act, monitor what happens, learn, and adjust. Each decision chases management goals while also gathering information that will improve the next one. The approach was developed by C. J. Walters and his colleague Holling at the University of British Columbia. They split it into two forms. Passive adaptive management values learning only because it leads to better outcomes. Active adaptive management writes learning into the objective itself. Its main features are decisions made in rounds, feedback between monitoring and those decisions, and treating uncertainty as a chance to understand more. In conservation it has three parts: testing assumptions, changing interventions in light of monitoring, and recording lessons. The hard part is balance. Managers must weigh learning for the future against getting the best result now from what they already know. Proving that the method works is also hard. Nobody can watch another approach play out in exactly the same situation.

  <!-- nature-nbs-146 -->

- **Environmental governance: who decides about nature**

  In a 2018 study of 461 waterbird species at more than 25,000 sites, one factor stood out. Strong environmental governance was among the most reliable predictors of whether conservation succeeded. Environmental governance is the way decisions get made about controlling and managing the environment and natural resources. Governments take part, but so do businesses and civil society. Its key principles include building the environment into every level of decision-making. Cities, economic life and politics are treated as part of the environment, not separate from it. It also pushes a shift from cradle-to-grave systems, where products end as waste, toward cradle-to-cradle systems that loop materials back, such as zero-waste strategies. The obstacles are large. Global agreements are weak, and the UN, governments, business and civil society coordinate poorly. Trade and finance bodies such as the WTO carry more weight than environmental ones. The gap between a human action and its environmental effect can last a generation. Since the 1970s many new international institutions have appeared, which brings overlap and fragmentation but also chances to cooperate. Locally, the emphasis has moved toward community participation and decentralization, a bottom-up break from earlier top-down, state-driven approaches.

  <!-- nature-gov-117 -->

- **Treaties for the planet: international environmental agreements**

  The first one, in 1857, dealt with water flowing from Lake Constance to Austria and Switzerland. By 2012, countries had concluded 747 more like it. An international environmental agreement is a treaty among countries, meant to be legally binding, whose main purpose is to prevent or manage human impacts on natural resources. A deal between two nations is bilateral. One among three or more is a multilateral environmental agreement, or MEA. Their numbers grew after the 1972 Stockholm Conference, whose declaration was the first universal document of importance on an environmental issue. They face a basic weakness. No country can be forced to join, so a nation facing costs may shirk while others comply and still enjoy the benefits. That is the classic free-rider problem, explained in The free-rider problem: benefiting without paying. Treaty makers have tools against it. Trade sanctions can target non-signatories. Shared funds can spread costs, like the Montreal Protocol's $240 million fund. Differential obligations, as in the Kyoto Protocol, set different targets based mainly on each country's level of development, which can widen participation. Even so, critics call these agreements slow. They say the deals drift toward the lowest common denominator and lack monitoring and enforcement.

  <!-- nature-gov-141 -->

- **National parks: protected land and its critics**

  In 1872 the United States set aside Yellowstone, widely held to be the world's first national park. A national park is government-owned, protected land kept for conservation because of its outstanding natural, historic or cultural value to the nation. The IUCN, a global conservation body, ranks such parks as Category II reserves. Its 1971 criteria included a minimum size of 1,000 hectares and a ban on exploiting natural resources. Many countries use the term loosely. In the UK a national park is a scenic, lightly developed area with planning limits, and it may hold sizeable towns. Parks Canada, set up in 1911, is the world's oldest park service, and Canada has 450,000 km2 of national park space. Parks also draw tourists: in Costa Rica, park tourism rose by 400% from 1985 to 1999. Not everyone celebrates them. Critics say parks in former colonies pushed native communities off their land, a kind of eco-land grabbing. They argue this spreads the idea that nature is protected only where people are absent.

  <!-- nature-gov-148 -->

- **The European Green Deal and its discontents**

  In 2017, more than 75% of the European Union's greenhouse gas emissions came from producing and using energy. The European Green Deal, a package of European Commission policies approved in 2020, aims to make the EU climate neutral by 2050, with net-zero emissions. It reviews every existing law for its climate effects. It adds new laws on the circular economy, building renovation, biodiversity, farming and innovation. Its parts include the Farm to Fork food strategy, a Zero Pollution Action Plan, the EU Biodiversity Strategy and a binding law on restoring nature. A Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism puts carbon tariffs on imports from countries that cut emissions more slowly. A Just Transition Mechanism sends more aid to countries with more coal and oil shale workers or higher emissions. The deal pleases few completely. Environmental groups say it falls short of ending fossil fuels. Some governments, industries and farmers blame it for higher energy prices, lost competitiveness and farmer protests.

  <!-- nature-gov-135 -->

- **The Rio Declaration: 27 principles for a fair future**

  The Rio Declaration fits on a few pages. Produced at the 1992 summit in Rio, described in Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties, it sets out 27 principles to guide countries toward sustainable development. Its first principle puts people at the center: they are entitled to healthy, productive lives in balance with nature. Principle 15 states the precautionary principle, to be applied by each state according to its capabilities. Principle 16 encourages the polluter pays principle where it serves the public interest and does not distort trade and investment. Principle 10 stresses citizens' right to take part and to see environmental information, ideas later spelled out in a treaty signed in Aarhus, Denmark. The declaration built on the declaration of the 1972 Stockholm Conference, aiming for principles states could write into their own laws. It raised environmental awareness. Yet evidence from 2007 suggested that little of its environmental goals had been achieved.

  <!-- nature-gov-152 -->

- **Agenda 21: a global plan with local roots**

  In June 1992, 178 governments at the summit in Rio de Janeiro voted to adopt Agenda 21. It is a United Nations action plan for sustainable development, and it binds no one. It has four sections. They cover social and economic issues, managing resources, the role of major groups in society, and the means of putting it into practice. It is meant to work at local, national and global levels. Every local government is expected to write its own local version. Because carrying it out is voluntary, results have varied from country to country. Its ideas lasted. The 2015 global development goals took up its goals and reaffirmed them, in 17 goals. In the United States, the plan also became a target of conspiracy theories that called it a UN plot against property rights and sovereignty.

  <!-- nature-gov-127 -->

- **Ecosystem management: keeping the whole system working**

  American fire suppression shows what goes wrong when one goal rules. Putting out every fire let fuel build up, and later fires burned hotter. Industrial societies often managed nature this way, maximizing the yield of a single resource. Ecosystem management takes the opposite view. It aims to keep an ecosystem's functions and services going over the long term while meeting people's social, economic, political and cultural needs. Indigenous communities practiced it implicitly for millennia. It became a formal concept in the 1990s, and US Forest Service chief F. Dale Robertson formalized the term in 1992. Unlike command-and-control management, which often weakens an ecosystem's resilience, its ability to recover from shocks, it is holistic and adaptive. It treats long-term production of goods and services as a precondition, not an afterthought. It works through adaptive and strategic management, conservation across whole landscapes and broad involvement of the public. The idea is still ambiguous and controversial. Some versions rest on contested claims about policy and science.

  <!-- nature-gov-134 -->

- **Global governance: rules without a world government**

  No world government exists, yet countries still make, monitor and enforce rules together. Global governance is the set of institutions that coordinates behavior across borders. It helps actors cooperate, settles disputes and eases collective action problems, where everyone gains from cooperation but each is tempted to hold back. Power in it is spread out. Intergovernmental bodies, NGOs, businesses and civil society all exercise influence alongside states. Its arrangements can be formal laws and institutions, or informal guidelines, practices and coalitions. The League of Nations, founded in 1920, was one of the first organizations to promote it. Treaty secretariats, like that of the UN climate convention, carry real influence but cannot enforce laws. For sustainability, the system is badly fragmented. A 2022 study counted 335 international organizations in the field, often weakly connected and competing for resources.

  <!-- nature-gov-137 -->

- **Ecosystem-based management: no park is an island**

  In 1979 the Craigheads found that Yellowstone's grizzly bears could not survive inside the park's boundaries alone. Their finding backed an older insight. Back in 1932, an Ecological Society of America committee had argued that US national parks must protect all the ecosystems they contain. Ecosystem-based management grew from such ideas. It weighs every interaction within an ecosystem, humans included, instead of tackling single issues, species or services one at a time. Its roots also run through Great Lakes policy of the late 1970s. The 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement rested on the claim that "no park is an island." Its goals must cover social, cultural and economic values as well as scientific ones, and communities take part throughout. At sea, it means weighing all the human activities that affect marine life together. Since linked human and natural systems cannot be fully predicted, adaptive management is recommended. Scientists now favor this approach for fisheries, though a debate continues over whether it has been fully put into practice.

  <!-- nature-gov-116 -->

- **The ecosystem approach of the biodiversity convention**

  Under the UN's biodiversity treaty, one idea became central in November 1995: the ecosystem approach. It is a framework for managing land, water and living resources together, promoting conservation and fair, sustainable use. It brings people, the economy and ecology into the solution of a given problem. At their fifth meeting, the parties asked their scientific advisory body to describe the approach, and that description came with 12 principles. It has two close relatives, ecosystem management and ecosystem-based management. All three aim to conserve ecosystems but differ in framework and methods. Applied to fishing, it becomes the ecosystem approach to fisheries, which builds a local strategy for each fishery's ecosystem.

  <!-- nature-gov-133 -->

- **Public participation: a say for those affected**

  People affected by a decision have a right to help make it. That is the core of public participation: involving the public, especially those affected or interested, in the decisions of an organization or project. It goes further than stakeholder engagement, because it implies that what the public says can change the outcome. It is a recognized environmental principle, enshrined in the Rio Declaration. Governments cannot solve environmental problems alone, and involving the public can improve transparency, accountability and compliance with environmental law. Taking part is not equally easy for everyone. Low-income citizens often struggle with childcare costs, time off work and limited access to education about public matters. And the hoped-for gain in public trust has yet to be confirmed.

  <!-- nature-gov-149 -->

- **The Basel Convention and the waste trade**

  A ship loaded with incinerator ash from Philadelphia dumped half its cargo on a beach in Haiti. The Khian Sea incident helped trigger the Basel Convention, a treaty limiting movement of hazardous waste between countries, especially from rich to poorer ones. The trade had grown because tighter laws in rich countries in the 1970s made disposal costly. Opened for signature on 21 March 1989, the convention entered into force on 5 May 1992 and had 191 parties as of June 2024. It requires notice, consent and tracking for every cross-border shipment. It also aims to deal with waste as close to its source as possible, which rewards producing less. In May 2019 it was amended to cover plastic waste, over the objection of the United States, a non-party. It calls illegal waste traffic criminal, yet contains no enforcement provisions.

  <!-- nature-gov-129 -->

- **Climate governance: steering the world on climate**

  A country that stays out of a climate agreement still gains when others cut their emissions. That free benefit haunts climate governance, the diplomacy and mechanisms meant to steer societies to prevent, slow or adapt to climate change. It rests on three pillars: mitigation, which cuts emissions; adaptation, which copes with change; and the means to carry them out. A milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which hoped to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, each country submits its own pledge, a nationally determined contribution that is not legally binding. A divide runs between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones. It underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Governance works at many scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts acting beside states. It leans increasingly on markets, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, alongside command-and-control rules.

  <!-- nature-gov-124 -->

- **Taking climate change to court**

  In 2021 a court in The Hague ordered Royal Dutch Shell to cut its global carbon emissions by 45% by 2030 from 2019 levels. The order even covered emissions from the products it sells. Climate change litigation uses lawsuits to set legal precedents that push governments and companies to act. It grew because climate politics was slow to deliver emission cuts. Cases usually rest on one of five kinds of claim: constitutional, administrative, private law, fraud or consumer protection, or human rights. They rose from 884 in 24 countries in 2017 to at least 1,550 in 38 countries by July 2020, most in the United States. In the Urgenda case, Dutch courts ordered the government to cut carbon dioxide emissions by 25% from 1990 levels by the end of 2020. In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights became the first international court to rule that state inaction on climate violates human rights. Results are mixed. Companies may hit back, as RWE did with a claim against the Netherlands under the Energy Charter Treaty.

  <!-- nature-gov-131 -->

- **The Aarhus Convention: rights to know, speak and sue**

  Signed in Aarhus, Denmark, on 25 June 1998, this UNECE treaty gives the public three environmental rights. People may get environmental information, take part in decisions, and go to court when environmental law is broken. It entered into force on 30 October 2001. By April 2023 it had 49 parties, 48 states plus the European Union, almost all in Europe and Central Asia. It binds public authorities but not private companies, whose disclosure stays voluntary. Its compliance system is unique in international environmental law: members of the public can complain straight to a committee of legal experts. Its Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on pollutant release and transfer registers, inventories of pollution from industry and other sources. Kofi Annan called it the most impressive elaboration of Principle 10 of the Rio Declaration. Critics disagree. They say its focus on procedure makes it vague, that ordinary citizens lack the means to take part, and that NGOs may not faithfully represent them.

  <!-- nature-gov-126 -->

- **Multi-level governance: power up, down and sideways**

  Cities may produce up to 75% of global carbon dioxide emissions. National climate targets therefore depend on what towns and regions do. Multi-level governance describes this spread of power. It runs vertically across levels of government and horizontally across many non-state and quasi-state bodies. Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks developed the idea in the early 1990s, studying the structures the EU built under the 1992 Maastricht Treaty. They saw authority shifting both up, from central states to bodies like the EU, and down, to regions and cities. The vertical side links higher and lower governments. The horizontal side covers cooperation between regions or municipalities. Critics say talk of "levels" implies a neat hierarchy, when real levels interact in tangled, non-hierarchical ways.

  <!-- nature-gov-147 -->

- **Spatial planning: deciding what goes where**

  Housing, industry and nature all want the same land. Spatial planning manages that contest. It makes and enforces plans that limit how land and space can be used and developed. National, regional or local governments usually do it, balancing demands from the state, the market and local communities. It spans several disciplines: land-use, urban, regional, transport and environmental planning, and maritime spatial planning at sea.

  <!-- nature-gov-153 -->

- **The law of the sea and the constitution of the oceans**

  About 64% of the world's oceans are international waters governed by the law of the sea. This body of international law sets out what states may and must do at sea, from shipping to coastal waters and seabed minerals. The modern rules began with a land grab offshore. In 1945 US President Truman claimed the natural resources of the American continental shelf. Chile, Peru and Ecuador soon claimed 200 nautical miles. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, UNCLOS, in force since 1994, is sometimes called the "constitution of the oceans." It gives each coastal state an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles, with sole rights to fish, minerals and seabed deposits. By June 2019, 168 states had ratified it. Non-parties such as the US still treat its rules as customary law. Bodies such as the International Seabed Authority and a tribunal in Hamburg enforce it.

  <!-- nature-gov-142 -->

- **Global environmental governance: a crowded, tangled system**

  As of 2020 the world had almost 1300 multilateral environmental agreements and over 2200 bilateral ones. Global environmental governance is the worldwide web of institutions and agreements that tackles problems crossing borders, such as climate change, biodiversity loss and land degradation. A 2020 publication called it one of the most dynamic areas of world politics over the previous thirty years. Growth has brought clutter. Policy made separately by theme, sector or territory has produced treaties that overlap or clash. UNEP, the UN body that coordinates environmental responses, is widely considered weak. And some countries of the Global South see the whole effort as a "luxury" priority of the Global North that conflicts with economic development.

  <!-- nature-gov-140 -->

- **The race to the bottom**

  If one country lets factories dump untreated chemical waste, firms may move there to avoid paying for treatment. Rival countries may then loosen their own rules to keep the business. That spiral is a race to the bottom. Governments, firms or individuals compete by steadily lowering standards to cut costs and attract economic activity. Ordinary competition tends to improve goods and services. This kind erodes labor laws, tax rates and environmental rules. The phrase traces to US Justice Louis Brandeis, describing states competing for corporations in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Globalization adds pressure: a producer who ignores biodiversity can undercut one who protects it. Whether the race really happens is debated. Daniel Drezner calls it a myth, and a 2022 study found no evidence of it in labor standards. Nita Rudra did find it in developing countries. Some US states even run a "race to the top," with bold environmental policies that others copy.

  <!-- nature-gov-150 -->

- **Stewardship: caring for what you hold**

  The word comes from the household steward, the keeper of the hall who looked after an owner's property. Stewardship is the ethical practice of planning and managing resources responsibly. Applied to nature, it means managing resources with an eye on quality of life for people now and in the future. Stewardship councils certify products made this way, such as the Forest Stewardship Council since 1993 and the Marine Stewardship Council since 1996.

  <!-- nature-gov-154 -->

- **The Vienna Convention: a framework to save the ozone layer**

  Research in the 1970s showed that CFCs, man-made chemicals used in refrigerators and other products, break down ozone high in the atmosphere. The 1985 Vienna Convention set the framework for cutting them worldwide. It entered into force in 1988. It set no binding cuts itself but led to the binding Montreal Protocol. Ratified by 198 states and the European Union, it is among the most universally accepted treaties ever. A Multilateral Fund has aided projects in nearly 150 countries, preventing the use of roughly 250,000 tons of ozone-destroying chemicals.

  <!-- nature-gov-158 -->

- **Local Agenda 21: sustainability at town hall**

  Chapter 28 of Agenda 21: a global plan with local roots asks towns and cities to carry out its plan locally. Many did. The Rio+10 report found over 6400 local governments in 113 countries engaged in Local Agenda 21, 5120 of them in Europe. Sweden reported that 100% of its municipalities had adopted it by 2002. ICLEI-Local Governments for Sustainability, formed in 1990, is widely seen as a model of how to do it.

  <!-- nature-gov-128 -->

- **The Bloomington school and the governed commons**

  One researcher at Indiana University, Ostrom, looked at pastures, fisheries and irrigation systems around the world and found something the theory said should not exist. Communities were managing shared resources well, without either the state or private owners in charge. Her 1990 book Governing the Commons challenged the tragedy of the commons, the idea that shared resources are always overused. She and Vincent Ostrom built a research tradition around such questions at the Bloomington campus. Its home, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, opened in 1973. The Bloomington school studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems, especially common-pool resources, decentralization and self-governance. Her work named eight design principles for lasting commons, including clear boundaries, collective decisions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and ways to resolve conflict. In 2009 she won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to receive it. Critics raise two doubts. Some economists question whether her findings scale up to national or global problems. Critical scholars say the school neglects power and inequality.

  <!-- nature-gov-121 -->

- **Fisheries co-management: sharing the helm**

  Fishers tend to ignore rules they do not understand, such as a sudden cut in the total allowable catch. Top-down fisheries management often failed for that reason. Fisheries co-management is the response: fishing communities and government share responsibility for managing aquatic resources. Five types are recognized, from government-led to user-led: instructive, consultative, cooperative, advisory and informative. Unlike pure community management, government takes part, and rules are made and enforced jointly. It blends scientific and traditional knowledge. Fishers who agree to rules are more likely to obey them and help enforce them. It is slow and costly, though. Some argue it entrenches the power of the already wealthy, while others see it as a way to empower communities.

  <!-- nature-gov-119 -->

- **A treaty against air pollution that crosses borders**

  Air pollution ignores borders, so smoke from one country can fall as acid rain on another. The Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, a UNECE treaty, commits its parties to limit, reduce and prevent such pollution. It opened for signature on 13 November 1979 and entered into force on 16 March 1983. It now has 51 parties. Eight protocols set specific cuts, such as the 1985 Helsinki Protocol on sulphur and the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol on acidification and ground-level ozone. It was an early effort to treat the atmosphere as a shared global resource.

  <!-- nature-gov-132 -->

- **The London Convention: no more dumping at sea**

  Ships, aircraft and platforms once dumped waste into the sea with few limits. A treaty signed on 29 December 1972 set out to control that pollution. It entered into force on 30 August 1975, using a "black list" of banned materials and a "grey list" needing special care. Its Protocol of 17 November 1996 flipped the logic to a "reverse list": any dumping not explicitly allowed is banned. The protocol also wrote in the precautionary approach and the polluter pays principle. In 2013 its parties adopted binding rules for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization. It does not cover pipes and outfalls on land.

  <!-- nature-gov-145 -->

- **The Forest Principles: a compromise on the world's forests**

  At the 1992 summit in Rio, forests split rich and poor nations. Developing countries in the Group of 77 wanted more aid to pay for forest reserves, and the final text was a compromise. The Forest Principles are non-binding recommendations for conserving and sustainably developing every kind of forest. They tied deforestation to third world debt and weak technology transfer. They said the extra cost of saving forests should be shared fairly. They led in 1994 to the Montréal Process, which set criteria and indicators for temperate and boreal forests.

  <!-- nature-gov-136 -->

- **Earth system governance: steering a planet in the Anthropocene**

  Humans now change the whole Earth system, so who steers that change? Earth system governance is the research field built around the question. In simple terms, it studies the rules and efforts of actors at every level, local to global, that aim to prevent, reduce and adapt to environmental change. Frank Biermann developed the idea in a lecture published in 2007, and the global Earth System Governance Project began in 2009. It draws on political science, sociology, economics, ecology, policy studies, geography, sustainability science and law. Its research centers on five linked problems: architecture, agency, adaptiveness, accountability and legitimacy, and allocation and access. Four themes cut across them: power, knowledge, norms and scale. Every level matters, not just the global one. Critics call the field too top-down. Mike Hulme argues it is hubristic to try to control the global climate through universal regimes. Defenders reply that this reading of the concept is too narrow.

  <!-- nature-gov-112 -->

- **Managing the coast as one system**

  Coastal margins cover 8% of the world's surface but provide 25% of global resources. About 70% of people live within a day's walk of a coast. Integrated coastal zone management tries to manage this crowded strip sustainably, across geographic and political boundaries, weighing nature, society and the economy together. It was developed at the 1992 summit in Rio and set out in Chapter 17 of Agenda 21. It runs in five steps: assess the situation, plan, embed the plan in institutions, implement, and keep evaluating. Its main obstacles are institutional, not technical. Because the coast is treated as common property, top-down control is hard.

  <!-- nature-gov-123 -->

- **The three Rio Conventions**

  The June 1992 summit in Rio de Janeiro, described in Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties, produced three conventions, on climate, biodiversity and desertification. The UNFCCC aims to hold greenhouse gas levels where they prevent dangerous human interference with the climate. The CBD has three goals: conserve biodiversity, use it sustainably, and share fairly the benefits drawn from the genes of living things. The UNCCD ties sustainable land management to land degradation and aims for no net loss of healthy land, with a focus on restoring drylands. The summit also produced Agenda 21, the Forest Principles and the Rio Declaration.

  <!-- nature-gov-151 -->

- **Polycentric governance: many centers, no single boss**

  Must every shared resource be run either by a central government or by private owners? Vincent Ostrom said no. Polycentric governance means rule by many overlapping, independent decision-making centers at different scales, instead of one central authority. Ostrom argued that such systems can improve efficiency, accountability and problem-solving. The idea suggested that self-organizing systems often beat top-down solutions. His fellow Bloomington scholar, Elinor, added that key management decisions should be made as close as possible to the events and people involved. The approach has limits. A resource that cannot be monitored as a whole, such as space debris, is less likely to be well managed in a polycentric network. Critics also question whether it works where institutions are weak or corruption is high.

  <!-- nature-res-198 -->

- **Governing through goals**

  Some global governance works without binding law. In global goal-setting, countries sign up to goals that are not legally binding, keep flexibility in how they meet them, and lack strong institutions to enforce them. The UN's goals for sustainable development from 2015 to 2030 are an example. They followed the Millennium Development Goals, which ran from 2000 to 2015.

  <!-- nature-gov-138 -->

- **Orchestration: steering the world indirectly**

  An international organization often lacks the power to order anyone around. Orchestration is its workaround. It is a soft, indirect form of global steering: the organization recruits willing intermediaries, who then influence a target group. It complements existing regimes and fills their gaps through three activities: agenda setting, coordination and support. The UN's five regional economic commissions, for example, act as orchestrators for the UN's goals for sustainable development.

  <!-- nature-gov-139 -->

- **Institutional fit: matching rules to the problem's size**

  A river basin may span three countries while each country manages only its own stretch. Institutional fit is the match, or mismatch, between the scale of an environmental problem and the level at which policy tackles it. Mismatches make interventions work less well. The political economist Ostrom and others argued that mismatch often causes unsustainable management, and no simple fixes have been found. Getting agencies and communities to cooperate across scales is one attempt to close the gap.

  <!-- nature-gov-118 -->

- **Marine spatial planning: zoning the sea**

  A single stretch of sea may host fishing boats, shipping lanes, wind farms and protected habitat at once. Marine spatial planning is a public process that maps and allocates where and when human activities happen at sea, to meet goals set through politics. It works like land-use planning for marine waters, using maps of how an area is used and what habitats it holds. Planners can weigh the combined effects of maritime industries and reduce conflicts among users. The aim is to use marine resources within clear environmental limits, so ecosystems stay healthy. The EU required its coastal member states to set up plans by 2021, covering fishing, aquaculture, conservation, shipping and renewable energy.
