Land rights describe how far society accepts that ownership in practice. UN research finds that rural landlessness strongly predicts poverty and hunger. Customs often bar women from inheriting or buying land, leaving them dependent on male relatives even when they farm it.

  <!-- nature-gov-218 -->

- **Putting a number on ecological debt**

  How much might rich countries owe? Most attempts compare each country's emissions with its fair share per person. In 2000, Neumayer calculated a "historical emissions debt": the gap between a country's actual past emissions and an equal per-person share. Matthews's 2015 method compares the warming each country has caused since 1960 with its share of world population. A "modified equal shares" approach weights shares by each country's basic needs. In principle, a money value could add up the outside costs of past extraction and the pollution poor countries bear from rich countries' consumption.

  <!-- nature-gov-200 -->

- **The Hoodia case: the San people get a share**

  The San people of southern Africa long used the Hoodia plant. In 1996, South Africa's CSIR research council isolated a weight-loss molecule from it, P57, and the patent rights were sold to Pfizer and Phytopharm. The San demanded restitution. A confidential benefit-sharing deal gave them royalties, knowledge exchange and jobs.

  <!-- nature-gov-192 -->

- **The neem tree fights back**

  Indian farmers have used extracts of the neem tree for around 2,000 years, against pests and fungi. In 1994, the company W.R. Grace patented a neem oil antifungal spray anyway. The challenge to such US and European patents became a landmark. The European Patent Office overturned the patent in 2000. The neem tree became a symbol of resistance to corporate control of Indigenous knowledge.

  <!-- nature-gov-191 -->

- **Conservation refugees**

  In Guinea, 663,000 people have been displaced from protected areas. Liberia claims over 120,000 conservation refugees, and Senegal has 65,000 displaced. A conservation refugee is a person, usually Indigenous, pushed from their homeland when a park or reserve is created. Many were already marginalized. They end up on the edges of towns with few opportunities and rarely have legal recourse. The idea behind it is old. John Muir's view that wilderness should be emptied of inhabitants became US policy with the 1964 Wilderness Act. The anthropologist Darrell Posey disagreed, arguing that landscapes that look natural may have been shaped by Indigenous peoples.

  <!-- nature-gov-197 -->

- **Locally unwanted land uses**

  Nobody wants a landfill, power plant or prison next door. Planners call such a project a locally unwanted land use: a facility a community opposes because of the harms it expects. Those harms include health hazards, ugliness, lower home values and sometimes higher utility bills. Such facilities tend to land in poor, minority or politically weak places that cannot fight them off. They then keep wealthier buyers away, trapping low-income residents in cheap housing near dumps and highways. Of more than 1,000 US Superfund toxic sites, 25% lie on or near Native American reservations.

  <!-- nature-gov-219 -->

- **Sacrifice zones**

  Louisiana's "Cancer Alley" runs 85 miles along the Mississippi, lined with over 200 petrochemical plants. Its population is disproportionately Black and low-income. It is a sacrifice zone: an area permanently damaged by heavy environmental change or economic neglect, often through land uses no one else would accept. A 2022 UN report found that millions of people live in pollution sacrifice zones, mostly around heavy industry and mining, with marginalized groups hit hardest. The phrase has roots in a 1973 US National Academy of Sciences report on strip-mined coal lands in the American West, which spoke of a "national sacrifice area." Sacrifice zones have a mirror image, "abundance zones." Damage in some places sustains privilege elsewhere. Naomi Klein argued in 2014 that an economy run on fuels that release poisons when extracted has always needed sacrifice zones.

  <!-- nature-gov-224 -->

- **Thinking seven generations ahead**

  Live and work for the good of the seventh generation to come. That principle is believed to come from the Great Law of the Haudenosaunee, which judges decisions by their effects seven generations ahead. The often-quoted line does not actually appear in written versions of the Haudenosaunee constitution. That text instead urges leaders to consider future generations. Some green economists advise judging a project's impacts from the viewpoint of the seventh generation.

  <!-- nature-gov-225 -->

- **Ethnoecology: how cultures read their environment**

  According to the WHO, almost 80% of the world's people rely on traditional plant-based remedies as a main source of treatment. Ethnoecology studies how different groups of people understand the ecosystems around them and their own place in them. Harold Conklin coined the term in his 1954 dissertation on how the Hanunoo culture relates to plants. To learn how cultures classify their surroundings, it borrows methods from linguistics and anthropology. It treats humans as part of ecosystems. People can act as a keystone species, shaping soil formation, seed dispersal and biodiversity.

  <!-- nature-gov-208 -->

- **Atmospheric colonization**

  Countries of the Global North hold 19% of the world's people but account for 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions. The Global South accounts for 8%. Atmospheric colonization is the idea that rich countries have taken over most of the sky's capacity to absorb greenhouse gases, leaving poorer countries to bear the results. Countries such as Ecuador emit relatively little carbon dioxide but have far fewer resources to cope with local climate impacts.

  <!-- nature-gov-194 -->

- **Climate apartheid: when only the rich escape**

  When Superstorm Sandy hit in 2012, most of New York lost power. Goldman Sachs's headquarters had its own generator and sandbags. UN Special Rapporteur Philip Alston cited that contrast in June 2019. He warned of climate apartheid, a world where only the rich can escape climate change. He said it could undermine human rights, democracy and the rule of law.

  <!-- nature-gov-195 -->

- **Ecological distribution conflicts**

  When a factory pollutes a river, the market usually puts no price on the harm, so the people downstream go uncompensated. In 1995, Joan Martínez-Alier and Martin O'Connor coined a term for such fights: ecological distribution conflicts. These are clashes over unfair access to natural resources and unequal pollution burdens. Mainstream economics treats such harms as externalities, costs to outsiders that could be priced. Ecological economists and political ecologists reject the idea that money can measure them. Movements may ask for money when weak, but argue from values money cannot measure when strong.

  <!-- nature-gov-203 -->

- **The environmentalism of the poor**

  Chipko villagers hugging trees in India, Indigenous groups resisting Brazilian agribusiness, Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement: all are examples of the environmentalism of the poor. These are movements that arise when poor people fight powerful state or private interests threatening their livelihood, health, sovereignty and culture. Mainstream environmentalism centers on conservation and efficiency. This kind puts social justice first. Martinez-Alier describes it as poor people's struggles in conflicts where an activity's harms fall unevenly and unjustly. Peruvian historian Alberto Flores Galindo suggested the term in 1988. In 1997 Martinez-Alier and Ramachandra Guha contrasted it with the "full-belly environmentalism" of the global North. Women often lead, because fetching water and growing crops bring them into direct contact with nature. The risks are mortal. Leaders such as Berta Cáceres and Chico Mendes were assassinated. International justice networks now help local defenders seek support against large corporations.

  <!-- nature-gov-206 -->

- **Who pays for green policy?**

  A carbon tax that keeps its revenue hits the poorest households hardest. That is because it is regressive: its burden falls, as a share of income, the richer people are. The distributional effects of an environmental policy describe how its costs and benefits fall on different groups, and whether it widens or narrows injustice. They are one of the standard tests for judging policy, alongside efficiency and cost-effectiveness. The pattern varies. One study found carbon pricing is on average progressive in countries with incomes below USD 15,000 a head, but tends to be regressive in richer ones. A 2019 study found energy efficiency standards more regressive than energy taxes. Because carbon pricing leans regressive, economists say poor people should be compensated. Not all agree on the premise: Gilbert Metcalf disputed that a US carbon tax would be regressive. Global estimates of climate damage usually leave these effects out.

  <!-- nature-gov-228 -->

- **The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples**

  In 2007 the United Nations adopted a declaration setting out the collective rights of Indigenous peoples. Those rights include self-determination and the protection of cultures, identities, languages, ceremonies and access to resources. The declaration does not define Indigenous peoples. It affirms instead their right to decide their own identity. It is the clearest statement of free, prior and informed consent in international development. It also offers benchmark standards on Indigenous land rights.

  <!-- nature-gov-183 -->

- **Environmental personhood: when a river becomes a person**

  In 2017, New Zealand declared the Whanganui River a legal person. It is represented by two guardians, one from the Māori iwi and one from the Crown. Environmental personhood is a legal idea that gives natural features, such as rivers or forests, the status of a legal person. That brings rights and liabilities. A river cannot go to court, so a guardian acts for it. And a legal person cannot be owned. Christopher D. Stone first proposed the idea in the 1970s, in an article titled "Should trees have standing?" An Indian state court gave the Ganges and Yamuna rivers similar status in March 2017. Skeptics noted that words alone would not stop the pollution. In 2022 Spain made the Mar Menor lagoon the first ecosystem in Europe with its own rights. Supporters say people can then sue for nature without showing harm to humans. Critics ask who is liable if a river is sued over a flood. Even some environmentalists reject it.

  <!-- nature-gov-205 -->

- **Rawls's three kinds of procedural justice**

  In A Theory of Justice, John Rawls split procedural justice into three forms. Perfect procedural justice has an independent standard of a fair result and a procedure that guarantees reaching it. Imperfect procedural justice has the standard but no procedure that guarantees the fair result. Pure procedural justice has no standard of a just result apart from the procedure itself.

  <!-- nature-gov-221 -->

- **Environmental reparations**

  Environmental reparations are payments or investments made to people judged to be harmed by industry. Recipients might be people living near industry, disaster victims or climate refugees. The forms vary widely: direct payouts, funds to clean waste sites, air monitors in low-income neighborhoods, or public transport.

  <!-- nature-gov-174 -->

- **Climate refugees and the gap in the law**

  Asian and African mega-deltas and small islands face high risks of floods and storms, and possibly displacement on a large scale. People forced to move by climate change fall into a legal gap, because international law does not yet cover such migration. The International Organization for Migration defines environmental migrants as people obliged or choosing to leave home because environmental change harms their lives. Climate migration is one of the most disputed effects of climate change. How many people will move, and who counts as a climate refugee, remain undefined in law.

  <!-- nature-gov-188 -->

- **Aboriginal title: land rights that outlive conquest**

  In 1971, Meriam people in Australia began a case that would overturn a legal fiction. In the Mabo case, the High Court recognized native ownership and rejected terra nullius, the doctrine that the land had belonged to no one. Aboriginal title is the common-law rule that Indigenous peoples' customary land rights survive after a settler state takes sovereignty. It is called native title in Australia, customary title in New Zealand and original Indian title in the US. American law went the other way first. In Johnson v. McIntosh (1823), the doctrine of discovery was used to rule that Native Americans had only rights of occupancy.

  <!-- nature-gov-216 -->

- **Three kinds of environmentalism**

  Joan Martinez-Alier divides environmentalism into three currents. The cult of the wilderness, tied to older conservation campaigns, tries to keep economic activity away from nature, mainly through reserves. It has at times expelled poor and Indigenous people to create them. The gospel of eco-efficiency accepts growth but wants growth that uses fewer resources and makes less waste. Critics say physical laws limit efficiency gains, and that rich economies cut material use only by outsourcing heavy production to poorer countries. The third current is environmental justice, the environmentalism of the poor.

  <!-- nature-gov-207 -->

- **Ancestral domain: more than a land title**

  Many Indigenous peoples would rather be called custodians of their lands than owners. Tradable private land was often a colonial import. Ancestral domain, a term used especially in the Asia-Pacific region, means the lands, territories and resources of Indigenous peoples. Unlike a land title, "domain" covers spiritual and cultural ties, not just ownership that can be sold. The Philippines' Indigenous People's Rights Act of 1997 defines it to include lands, inland waters, coasts and natural resources. International law shifted too. The ILO's 1957 Convention No. 107 assumed Indigenous peoples would be absorbed into wider society. Convention No. 169 replaced it in 1989.

  <!-- nature-gov-189 -->

- **Feminist political ecology**

  Environmental policies that seem gender-neutral can overlook what women know about managing resources. Feminist political ecology studies how gender shapes people's access to, control over and knowledge of natural resources. It treats three areas as gendered: knowledge, environmental rights and grassroots activism. It explains differences in experience through social ideas about gender, not biology. A key founding text is the 1996 book Feminist Political Ecology by Dianne Rocheleau and colleagues.

  <!-- nature-gov-211 -->

- **Writing the rights of nature into law**

  Ecuador's 2008 constitution gives nature, or Pachamama, the right to exist and to renew its vital cycles. Any person may demand those rights be respected. Rights of nature law writes this idea into constitutions, statutes, treaties, local laws and court rulings. It treats ecosystems and species as having inherent rights, much like human rights. As of 2022 such laws existed in 39 countries, and initiatives grew from 409 in June 2021 to 495 in May 2024. In 2019, Bangladesh's High Court declared the Turag River, and by extension all the country's rivers, living entities with legal rights.

  <!-- nature-gov-223 -->

- **Gender and the environment**

  Women do 80% of food production in sub-Saharan Africa, 60% in Asia and 50% in Latin America. Men generally own the land. The study of gender and environment examines how relations between women, men and nature shape resource use, divide responsibilities and affect well-being. Interest grew from Ester Boserup's 1960s book Woman's Role in Economic Development, and policymakers paid more attention from the 1980s. Improving women's access to farm resources could raise their yields by 20–30% and total farm output in poor countries by 2.5–4%. Some feminist economists argue that the focus on growth sustains gender and environmental injustice, and propose shorter, shared work.

  <!-- nature-gov-229 -->

- **ILO Convention 169**

  In 1989 the International Labour Organization adopted a treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples. ILO Convention 169 aims to end discrimination against them and give them a role in decisions, built on participation and consultation. The duty to consult falls on the state, not on companies. Its aim is agreement or consent to a proposed development.

  <!-- nature-gov-181 -->

- **Consent protocols written by Indigenous peoples**

  Since the early 2000s, Indigenous peoples have written their own rules for how consent processes must run. These are FPIC protocols. The first were tied to specific sectors. The second were bio-cultural protocols linked to the Biodiversity Convention's rules on access to genes. The third, mostly from Latin America, are autonomous protocols.

  <!-- nature-gov-182 -->

### Poverty, development and the environment

Most of the world's people live on less than $10 a day, and the poorest depend most directly on land, water and forests. When that land degrades, food and income fall, and families can sink into a cycle of poverty that later generations cannot escape. Whole countries can be stuck the same way, held back by degraded land, disease, war and poor infrastructure. This short chapter looks at how poverty and environmental damage reinforce each other, and at ways of thinking about livelihoods that last.

- **Poverty: lacking the basics**

  As of 2019, measured in dollars adjusted for local prices, 85% of people lived on less than $30 a day. Two-thirds lived on less than $10, and 10% on less than $1.90. Poverty is lacking the money and essentials needed for a basic standard of living. Absolute poverty compares income with what basic needs cost, such as food, clothing and shelter. Relative poverty compares living standards with others in the same time and place. The famous "dollar a day" line, introduced in 1990, became US$1.90 a day in 2015. It is measured at purchasing power parity, meaning what money buys locally, rather than at exchange rates. Poverty and nature are closely tied. Poor people are more exposed to the environmental effects of industry, climate change, disasters and extreme weather. Economic pressure on poor communities often plays a part in deforestation and biodiversity loss. Growth does not always help: the poorest citizens of middle-income countries often fail to gain enough of the new wealth to escape. Sustainable Development Goal 1, "No Poverty," adopted in 2015, sums up the international framework for ending it.

  <!-- nature-gov-005 -->

- **Does poverty damage nature, or protect it?**

  Developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change. Yet about 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to the Global North. That lopsided split of burdens and benefits gave rise to the global movements for environmental justice and climate justice. The link between poverty and environmental damage runs both ways. The poor tend to suffer most when natural resources are exploited and ecosystems degrade. A 2016 UN report claimed that by 2030 climate change could push an additional 122 million people into extreme poverty. Does poverty also cause degradation? Here the experts split. The Brundtland Report concluded that it does. The environmentalism-of-the-poor view holds the opposite: the global poor may be the most important force for sustainability. Conservation itself can burden the poor too. Fortress conservation has evicted Indigenous people, and green colonialism grabs land in the name of environmentalism.

  <!-- nature-gov-006 -->

- **Degraded land and deprivation: a vicious circle**

  In 2025, 47 million stunted children under five lived where stunting overlaps with large harvest losses from land degradation. Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are where degraded land and deep poverty coincide. Land degradation and deprivation reinforce each other. Damaged land brings lower yields, less food, more exposure to floods and droughts, lost homes and economic trouble. It can also lose its natural ability to store and filter water, causing shortages. Most of sub-Saharan Africa shows fairly low losses from degradation. That is not because its soils are healthier. Poor access to fertilizer, machinery, credit and markets holds yields down even more. Of the world's 570 million farms, 85% are under 2 hectares and work just 9% of farmland, which limits what farmers can do. Degradation sharpens competition for land. All but 3 conflicts inside African states since the 1990s are linked to it. It can also drive people to migrate.

  <!-- nature-gov-007 -->

- **The cycle of poverty**

  Children born into poverty depend on their guardians and are too young to work their own way out. That makes them the most vulnerable part of the cycle of poverty, also called a poverty trap. In this situation, poverty seems to pass down, and later generations cannot escape it. Self-reinforcing forces keep it going unless someone from outside steps in. Lack of money, education and social connections all hold families in place. Applied to whole developing countries, the idea is called a development trap. The cycle has an environmental edge. People living in degraded ecosystems may want sustainable options but cannot afford to let land and resources regenerate. The cycle also makes climate harms worse. Conditional cash transfers, payments tied to steps such as schooling or health checks, aim to help families now and break the cycle for the next generation.

  <!-- nature-gov-001 -->

- **Sustainable livelihoods**

  Poverty is not only a lack of money. The sustainable livelihoods idea widens the view to include vulnerability and social exclusion. It asks how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can bounce back from shocks. The Brundtland Commission introduced the idea. The 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development made sustainable livelihoods a broad goal for ending poverty. The approach favors development centered on people and shaped by their participation, linking environmental and economic concerns. The 17 Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 for 2030, are one example. The COVID-19 pandemic set back goals such as SDG 1, No Poverty.

  <!-- nature-gov-003 -->

- **Cheap water that misses the poor**

  Poor families without a piped connection often buy water from vendors at about 5 to 16 times the metered price. Meanwhile, subsidies that make piped water cheap flow mainly to households already connected, typically richer urban ones outside informal settlements. With heavy subsidies, water prices in developing countries cover on average only 30% of supply costs. Utilities then have little reason to maintain or extend their networks. Leaks lose enough water for 200 million people a year, and many poor homes stay unconnected. Subsidizing new connections has shown more promise.

  <!-- nature-gov-009 -->

- **Energy poverty and development**

  Businesses, schools, clinics and homes all run on energy, so lacking it holds development back. Poor energy access is linked to infant mortality, illiteracy and shorter lives, and can push people to move to cities. Energy use and economic growth have historically risen together, though it is unclear which drives the other. By the early 2000s, rich countries were growing without a matching rise in energy use. In developing countries the two stayed tightly linked. Energy-poor households often burn wood and dung, which release black carbon, a health hazard, when they burn incompletely.

  <!-- nature-gov-008 -->

- **Why whole countries stay poor**

  Some countries stay stuck in poverty as a whole, held back by lack of credit, degraded land, corruption, disease, war and poor infrastructure. Extreme environmental degradation is one cause, because it cuts what farmland can produce. Jeffrey Sachs argues that the extreme poor lack six kinds of capital, natural capital among them. When population grows faster than savings, capital per person can shrink each generation. Sachs argues that large, lasting foreign aid can lift households above subsistence. He wants public money spent on health, education, infrastructure and natural capital, such as conserving ecosystems, leaving business investment to private firms.

  <!-- nature-gov-002 -->

- **Five kinds of capital for a livelihood**

  The United Nations Development Programme sizes up how people make a living by the five kinds of capital they can draw on. Human capital is skills and health. Social capital is relationships. Natural capital is land, water and other resources. Physical capital is tools and infrastructure, and financial capital is money. How much people can reach of each shapes how the UNDP designs its projects. The framework also asks how people use these assets to cope with shocks. The UK's Department for International Development and the charity CARE use similar frameworks instead of sector-by-sector approaches.

  <!-- nature-gov-004 -->

### Business and nature

Firms make most of the goods people buy, and most of the harm that comes with them. This chapter asks what a business owes to nature and to the people around it. Some answers are voluntary, like corporate social responsibility, where companies run their main business so its overall effect on society is positive. Others are tools and rules: management systems, audits, emissions standards and an EU list of activities that count as sustainable. Buyers push too, choosing what to buy and what to boycott by how products affect people, animals and the environment.

- **Making money without wrecking the world around you**

  Before World War 1, start-ups were already selling organic food and wind and solar energy. The business historian Geoffrey Jones traces green business back to them. Sustainable business means running a firm so that it makes money while keeping its harm to the environment, local communities and society as small as possible. Such firms aim at the Triple bottom line: people, planet and profit: profit, people and planet, weighed together in every decision. The modern idea grew out of late-20th-century debates on Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later. The 1987 report Our Common Future: defining sustainable development shaped how private firms thought about managing the environment. A central aim is to cut the harm from making and using goods. Firms measure their carbon footprints, cut waste and redesign products to last longer. A green business offers products that cut demand for harmful ones, keeps its finances sound, respects human rights and supports inclusion of local and global communities. Sometimes tweaks are not enough. If a firm's whole model is unsustainable, becoming sustainable can mean rebuilding it, for example moving from selling cars to offering car sharing. In practice, firms often meet only the lowest standards. Real sustainability, its advocates say, needs a purpose that goes beyond simply obeying the law.

  <!-- nature-gov-059 -->

- **Nature-positive: halt the loss by 2030, recover by 2050**

  Over 90 world leaders signed the Leaders' Pledge for Nature, and the G7 committed to the goal at its 2021 summit. Nature-positive is a goal to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 and to achieve its full recovery by 2050. Progress is measured against a baseline of biodiversity in 2020. It was proposed as a single global goal for nature, to sit beside climate and development goals, aiming at an 'Equitable, Nature-Positive, Carbon Neutral world'. It matches the 2030 mission and 2050 vision of the The Kunming-Montreal framework: a Paris Agreement for nature, though that framework does not name it. What is new is its reach. Unlike earlier approaches, it covers a company's whole value chain, not just its direct impacts. It also aims for absolute gains, not merely doing less harm than before. The idea is contested. Critics call it vague and open to greenwashing, and warn of the 'financialization of nature', turning nature into something traded for money. Its 'net' approach is criticised for implying continued loss and for assuming that like-for-like compensation is possible. Supporters reply that business must be part of the solution. To keep the goal honest, the researcher Milner-Gulland proposed it needs a measured baseline, a timeframe, a target, clear actions, regular monitoring and disclosure.

  <!-- nature-gov-079 -->

- **The environmental management system: a firm's green rulebook**

  In March 1996 the ISO 14000 family of standards was first developed. Its member ISO 14001 is now the most widely used standard for an environmental management system, or EMS. An EMS is a set of policies, procedures and processes a firm uses to train staff and to monitor, summarize and report its environmental performance. Its goals are to obey legal standards more fully and to reduce waste, then to go beyond compliance. It helps an organization identify and control its impacts and set and track objectives. The system runs on a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, constantly reviewed and revised. Factories, service industries and government agencies can all use it. Independent bodies usually certify that a system conforms to ISO 14001. A good EMS also nudges contractors and suppliers to set up their own.

  <!-- nature-gov-100 -->

- **The environmental audit: checking a firm against the rules**

  Environmental audits do for environmental performance what financial audits do for accounts. An audit finds gaps in an organization's compliance with environmental rules and in its The environmental management system: a firm's green rulebook, then sets out corrective actions. There are two main types. Compliance audits check a site against the laws, regulations, permits and local codes that apply to it. Management system audits test the system itself. A multimedia audit covers all media, such as air, water and waste; a programmatic audit covers chosen areas, such as air alone. Certification to ISO 14001 does not by itself prove a firm obeys the law, though the standard requires firms to evaluate their compliance. Auditors work from a checklist called a protocol, and no standard protocol exists. Professionals still disagree whether detailed, prescriptive protocols beat flexible ones that rely on auditor expertise. Satellite imagery and digital mapping systems are an emerging audit tool.

  <!-- nature-gov-099 -->

- **The EU taxonomy: an official list of green activities**

  Early estimates put the average 'green asset ratio' of EU banks at just 2.23%. That ratio, which banks must disclose, comes from the EU taxonomy for sustainable activities. The taxonomy is a European Union classification system that defines which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable. It came into force in July 2020 as part of the The European Green Deal and its discontents, which aims for a carbon neutral economy by 2050. Its purpose is to prevent greenwashing, the practice of making things look greener than they are, and to help investors make informed sustainable choices. It covers six environmental objectives. They are climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, circular economy, pollution prevention, water and marine resources, and biodiversity and ecosystems. A Technical Expert Group set up in 2018 developed the technical screening criteria that judge whether an activity qualifies. The Environmental Delegated Act, published on 21 November 2023, set criteria for the remaining objectives, including protecting and restoring biodiversity and ecosystems. The taxonomy is spreading into other rules too. An EU green bond standard under development would require issuers to fund only activities aligned with it.

  <!-- nature-gov-096 -->

- **Design for the environment: cutting harm at the drawing board**

  Design for the environment cuts a product's or service's harm to health and the environment, counting impacts across its whole life. It has four parts: cleaner processing and manufacturing, greener packaging, design for disposal or reuse, and energy efficiency. Designers use Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave to compare options and pick the least harmful. Claimed benefits are cost savings, lower risk, new markets and meeting regulations. Leaders of Making money without wrecking the world around you treat it as part of their work, along with counting life-cycle costs.

  <!-- nature-gov-066 -->

- **Corporate sustainability strategies: profit from going green**

  A 2023 Swiss survey of 514 small and medium firms found 89% had never produced a sustainability report. These strategies, part of Corporate sustainability: the long game in strategy, are plans to win new revenue from sustainability while guarding against rising energy, regulation and resource costs and shifting customer views. Common strategies are innovation, collaboration, process improvement, reporting and greening the supply chain. The Sustainability Balanced Scorecard measures performance by balancing financial and non-financial, short- and long-term goals.

  <!-- nature-gov-062 -->

- **The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: counting a firm's emissions**

  Most of a company's emissions happen somewhere else. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the most common set of standards for measuring and tracking greenhouse gas emissions, makes that visible. The World Resources Institute: measuring the planet developed it with companies and published its first version in September 2001. It sorts an organization's emissions into Scope 1, 2 and 3. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from its activities. For most businesses the great majority are Scope 3, coming from the wider supply chain rather than the site or purchased energy. Scope 3 was estimated at 75% of all emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project, though it varies widely by sector. It is also hard to report accurately. In 2022 about 30% of US companies reported it, and double counting is a worry. The Science Based Targets initiative and the The TCFD: telling investors about climate risk both cite the protocol, and the ISO 14064 standard is based on it.

  <!-- nature-gov-109 -->

- **Stakeholder theory: who a company answers to**

  In 1968 Eric Rhenman coined the English word stakeholder in his book Industrial Democracy and Industrial Management. R. Edward Freeman later built it into a theory. Stakeholder theory holds that a firm answers not only to its shareholders, its owners, but to every group with a relationship to it: workers, customers, suppliers and communities. The idea runs through responsible business. A review of 14,523 articles found the stakeholder view to be the most common dimension of Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit. Satisfying stakeholders beyond shareholders is one reason firms take that path. The EU itself defines such responsibility as a firm being accountable for its impact on all relevant stakeholders. Critics say the stakeholder view ignores how complex the networks in partnerships between business, government and charities are.

  <!-- nature-gov-068 -->

- **Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit**

  In 1953 Howard Bowen published Social Responsibilities of the Businessman. He argued that business leaders' duties go beyond making profit, and the book is widely seen as the founding work of corporate social responsibility, or CSR. CSR means companies running their main business responsibly and sustainably, so their overall effect on society is positive. It is a form of private self-regulation that aims to help social and environmental goals by reducing harm, such as cutting a firm's carbon footprint. Since the 1960s it has gone by many names: Corporate sustainability: the long game in strategy, sustainable business, corporate citizenship, responsible business. There is little agreement on a definition. A business person may see it as strategy, an activist at a campaign group as greenwash, and a government official as voluntary regulation. Firms take it up for strategic, ethical or instrumental reasons. For companies listed on a stock market it often takes the form of ESG practices and reports, covering environmental, social and governance issues. Its scope has widened from a firm's own conduct to its suppliers, how its products are used and how they are thrown away. It has also been shifting from voluntary choices toward mandatory schemes at regional, national and international levels. Whether it works is contested. Supporters say it raises long-term profits; critics say it distracts from a firm's economic role or is mere window-dressing.

  <!-- nature-gov-067 -->

- **Sustainability reporting: telling outsiders how a firm behaves**

  Enron's collapse and the 2008 financial crisis helped drive a boom in a new kind of company report. Sustainability reporting is the disclosure, voluntary or required, of a company's non-financial performance to people outside it. It covers environmental, social, economic and governance issues, grouped under the acronym ESG. It also goes by ESG reporting, non-financial reporting, CSR reporting and social reporting. It grew from environmental reporting, popular in the 1970s, and has expanded greatly over the last twenty years, spurred by awareness of the ecological crisis. It rests on the stakeholder model of Stakeholder theory: who a company answers to. The Global Reporting Initiative standards are the most widely used benchmark worldwide. Critics say competing frameworks make reports hard to compare. Some firms hide negative or overstate positive environmental data, a practice linked to greenwashing.

  <!-- nature-gov-102 -->

- **Ethical consumerism: voting with your wallet**

  Every purchase is a small vote. Ethical consumerism means choosing what to buy, and what to boycott, by how products affect people, animals and the environment. It is a form of consumer activism based on this 'dollar voting'. Its rise over the last two decades is linked to the rise of Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit. Company ratings first made for shoppers are now common in business sustainability ratings, and ESG ratings reach stock traders' screens. More consumers demand sustainable goods, especially when they think firms neglect the environment. Two things hold it back: routine buying that leaves no room for reflection, and competing moral demands in daily life.

  <!-- nature-gov-077 -->

- **Profit for owners, or duties to society?**

  Milton Friedman gave the blunt answer. A firm's purpose, he argued, is to maximize returns to its shareholders, and obeying the law is socially responsible enough. People may spend their own money on causes, he said. But owners should not raise prices to fund social goals unrelated to profit, which he likened to a tax on consumers. This is one side of a long argument. Does a company exist only to earn returns for its owners, or does it also owe duties to society and the environment? The argument is older than Friedman. In the 1930s the legal scholars Berle and Dodd debated it. Should directors be bound by enforceable rules to serve labour, customers and the public as well as shareholders? The other side is Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit, backed by Stakeholder theory: who a company answers to, which holds that firms owe wider duties. The debate remains unsettled. Some argue better government regulation is the real alternative to voluntary CSR. Others reply that mandated programs distort how resources are allocated. Some studies even find CSR serves managers' interests at shareholders' cost. Economists call that an agency problem: hired managers acting for themselves rather than for the owners they work for.

  <!-- nature-gov-070 -->

- **The social license to operate: permission no law grants**

  A mine can hold every government permit and still be stopped by the people next door. The social license to operate is the ongoing support and approval that local communities and other stakeholders give a company's activities. The term was introduced in 1997, mostly in resource extraction industries such as mining, to describe company-community relations. Communities grant it, not governments. It can take a long time to win but be lost very quickly. Without it, local people may block projects, staff may leave and firms may face ongoing legal challenges. It rests on relationships and trust, so local firms tend to gain it more easily than outsiders. Showing commitment to Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit is one way to earn it, by improving a firm's reputation.

  <!-- nature-gov-071 -->

- **Corporate sustainability: the long game in strategy**

  Short-term thinking is described as the main enemy of corporate sustainability. The idea is a business approach that aims to create long-term value for stakeholders by building ethical, social, environmental, cultural and economic concerns into strategy. It is often confused with Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit. Scholars say the key difference is time: sustainability asks firms to make trade-offs across time to protect future generations. The idea grew out of sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission, and John Elkington's 1997 'triple bottom line'. Research usually treats it as three parts: social, environmental and economic. Its most widely accepted test is whether a firm uses Natural capital: nature as the stock behind the economy efficiently, keeping vital ecosystem services such as climate regulation and water purification. Firms often state their commitment through Corporate Sustainability Standards, policies meant to meet or beat legal minimums. Whether it can be measured at all remains disputed, because no accepted set of indicators separates sustainable from unsustainable operation.

  <!-- nature-gov-092 -->

- **The TCFD: telling investors about climate risk**

  In December 2015 the G20 and the Financial Stability Board set up a task force chaired by Michael Bloomberg. The Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, or TCFD, writes recommendations that tell investors how companies manage the risks of climate change and how they are governed. It was formed partly in response to the 2015 The Paris Agreement: every country pledges, whose national pledges were criticized for lacking transparent disclosure standards. Its aim is to give investors, lenders and insurers what they need to assess and price climate-related risks and opportunities. Its recommendations cover four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. It is described as the main framework used globally for climate disclosure. Ahead of COP26 in 2021, the UK became the first G20 country to require 1,300 of its largest companies to follow it. At COP26 the IFRS announced the International Sustainability Standards Board, into which the TCFD will converge.

  <!-- nature-gov-107 -->

- **Creating shared value: profit from solving social problems**

  Up to 90% of the ecological footprint in food processing comes from land management outside corporations' control. That gap is one test for creating shared value, a strategy in which a company seeks profit by solving social problems linked to its own operations. The aim is to improve its competitiveness and its communities' conditions at once. Michael Porter and Mark Kramer introduced the idea in a 2006 Harvard Business Review article and expanded it in January 2011. Firms can do it in three ways: reconceiving products and markets, redefining productivity in the value chain, and helping local clusters of businesses develop. Kramer says CSR is about responsibility, while shared value is about creating value. Porter presents it as a win-win, but critics disagree. The Economist called it 'undercooked', and a common complaint is that it plays down the trade-offs businesses must make. Reviewers found little rigorous evidence of its impact, mostly standalone case studies of mixed quality.

  <!-- nature-gov-094 -->

- **Supply chain sustainability: greening every link**

  For many companies, suppliers account for most of their total emissions. Supply chain sustainability means managing the environmental, social and economic effects of goods and services across their whole life. It runs from suppliers to customers and encourages good governance along the way. Traditional supply chain goals were lower costs, just-in-time delivery and faster transport. Rising environmental and social costs and consumer pressure added sustainability as a new measure. Many firms can measure only their own operations, so their true costs are hard to know. Buyers use their purchasing power to set standards for suppliers, treating sustainability like cost, quality and timeliness. Tools include supplier scorecards, Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave, surveys and rewards for suppliers that improve. A 2017 study found suppliers farther upstream, away from the end user, had the most to gain financially. After the COVID-19 disruptions, sustainable supply chains proved more resilient. A 2020 Boston Consulting Group survey found 70% of consumers willing to pay a 5% premium for more sustainably made products.

  <!-- nature-gov-082 -->

- **CSR as misdirection: good deeds as a smokescreen**

  The tobacco industry funded research in genetics, viruses and air pollution, drawing attention from the link between smoking and cancer. Critics say companies use social responsibility programs this way, to distract from harmful parts of their business. US firms convicted of bribery got lighter fines if seen to engage in CSR: a 20% rise in corporate giving went with a 40% lower fine. A review of 700 sources found firms engage in CSR mainly for expected financial gain. Supporters still see much of it as genuine responsibility.

  <!-- nature-gov-075 -->

- **The CSR-consumer paradox: saying green, buying cheap**

  Many shoppers say they will buy only from responsible companies. Yet ethical purchases are a small share of household spending. This gap is the CSR-consumer paradox. One explanation is the bystander effect: people act less when others seem not to care. Another is that ethical products cost more but give the buyer little extra in return. A Lisbon study found price, limited access and lack of education held back less engaged shoppers of sustainable fashion.

  <!-- nature-gov-078 -->

- **Carroll's pyramid: four layers of corporate duty**

  Archie Carroll began building his framework after a 1979 article on corporate social performance. It sorts what society expects of business into four responsibilities, often drawn as a pyramid. At the base are economic duties, then legal, then ethical, and at the top philanthropic ones, meaning charitable giving. The pyramid became a standard way to picture Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit.

  <!-- nature-gov-069 -->

- **The resource-based view: CSR as hard-to-copy advantage**

  Does CSR pay? One way to judge is to ask whether it gives a firm an advantage rivals cannot copy. Barney (1990) held that lasting advantage needs resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable. Reinhardt (1998) found a CSR-based strategy earns above-normal returns only if competitors cannot imitate it. Waddock and Graves (1997) linked social and financial performance. McWilliams and Siegel (2000) disagreed, saying innovation, not CSR, drove the gains, and argued managers can set CSR spending like any other investment.

  <!-- nature-gov-076 -->

- **Social accounting: a ledger for society**

  Ordinary accounts track money. Social accounting reports the social and environmental effects of a company's economic activity to interest groups and to society at large. It stresses that corporations should be accountable for their effects. There is no single fixed standard. Frameworks include AA1000, based on the Triple bottom line: people, planet and profit, the Global Reporting Initiative guidelines and ISO 14000.

  <!-- nature-gov-073 -->

- **Socially responsible investing: money as a message**

  Where investors put their money can reward or punish a company. Socially responsible investing uses that power to encourage behaviour investors consider responsible. What counts as ethical varies. Some religious investors withdraw money from firms that offend their views. Some secular investors divest, selling their holdings, from firms that impose religious views.

  <!-- nature-gov-074 -->

- **Six ways companies do good**

  Companies practise Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit through six kinds of activity. They are corporate philanthropy, community volunteering, socially responsible business practices, cause promotion, cause-related marketing and corporate social marketing, which runs behaviour-change campaigns. Philanthropy and volunteering usually have no profit motive. The rest can be cause marketing, which pursues profit and social good together.

  <!-- nature-gov-072 -->

- **Corporate environmental responsibility: a firm's duty to nature**

  Protecting the environment used to be seen as government's job, done through rules and penalties. Now the private sector shares it. Corporate environmental responsibility, or CER, is a company's duty to avoid damaging the natural environment. The term comes from Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit, but CER deals strictly with environmental effects inside company strategy, while CSR leans toward social matters. Its main elements are using resources efficiently and limiting activities that would spoil resources for future generations. Government rules drive it, backed by subsidies, tariffs and taxes, along with pressure from media, the public, shareholders and campaign groups. Obstacles include the cost of regulation, uncertain gains, expensive technology and rules that differ between countries. Much is contested. Sources disagree on whether firms must go beyond the law or first make profits for shareholders. It is also unclear which emissions a firm answers for when they are spread across suppliers. Should it answer for past emissions made before the harm was known?

  <!-- nature-gov-060 -->

- **How business responds to climate change**

  Many firms that once denied climate change, including major oil and car companies, changed position as scientific and political consensus grew. Business action on climate change covers everything from cutting a firm's own emissions to trying to influence regulation such as the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Business helps by investing in new energy technologies and energy efficiency. Firms act to improve their image, cut costs, align with owners, staff, suppliers and customers, and reduce exposure to costs they cannot control. But efficiency often pays off only in the medium to long term, while shareholders want short-term results, so regulation is often needed. By 2007 the Carbon Disclosure Project published emissions data for 2400 of the largest corporations, backed by investors with $41 trillion in assets. Small and medium firms account for around 13% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Physical risks of climate change top the list of concerns for US and EU firms. A 2025 PwC report found 84% of companies keeping or speeding up their climate targets.

  <!-- nature-gov-089 -->

- **Sustainable sourcing: buying responsibly from the start**

  A company is said to be only as sustainable as the start of its supply chain. Sustainable sourcing means getting the materials, products and services a firm needs in a way that is socially and environmentally responsible while still economically sound. Global supply chains and pressure to cut costs have harmed environments and communities, especially in developing nations. They harm nature mainly through resource depletion and pollution, which bring biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and soil degradation. Awareness has grown since the 1990s, when CSR took on environmental duties with Elkington's triple bottom line. Responsible sourcing means obeying ethical rules such as no child labour. Sustainable sourcing goes further and acts to improve conditions. Firms use supplier codes of conduct, supplier selection and assessment, and supplier development. The growing number of standards has raised costs for producers and confused people about their meaning. It relates directly to Sustainable Development Goal 12, responsible consumption and production.

  <!-- nature-gov-104 -->

- **Social sustainability: caring for workers and neighbors**

  A business also answers for the well-being of its employees, customers and community. That is social sustainability. Firms contribute by supporting education, encouraging staff to volunteer and giving to charity. It is often tied to environmental justice, because social fairness and environmental care affect each other.

  <!-- nature-gov-063 -->

- **Scope 3: the emissions a company does not make itself**

  In 2021, 61% of Chevron shareholders backed a resolution asking it to cut emissions, including those it does not make itself. These are Scope 3 emissions: the indirect greenhouse gas emissions in a company's value chain, such as its suppliers' and those from using its products. Scope 1 covers a firm's direct emissions from its own facilities, and Scope 2 the emissions from energy it buys. Scope 3 is especially hard to estimate. In 2020, 81% of S&P 500 companies reported Scope 1 and Scope 2. Rules are catching up. The EU's The CSRD: Europe's sustainability reporting law requires large and listed firms to disclose material Scope 3 emissions, starting with 2025 reports on 2024 data. The US SEC's 2024 rule requires Scope 3 reporting if emissions are material or part of corporate targets, though the regulator has signalled it may change this.

  <!-- nature-gov-085 -->

- **Science-based targets: emission cuts that match the climate goal**

  As of 2025, over 10,000 companies had set or committed to setting emission targets checked by one organization. Science-based targets are company goals for cutting greenhouse gas emissions, set in line with climate science and the The Paris Agreement: every country pledges. The Science Based Targets initiative, or SBTi, set up in 2015, helps firms set them and validates them. In October 2021 it launched the first net zero standard, for targets consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 °C. It says leftover emissions in most sectors should fall below 10% of an organization's baseline by 2050. Best practice includes transition plans covering scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, short-term milestones, board oversight and executive pay linked to those milestones. Offsets remain disputed, even inside the SBTi. A 2024 plan to let firms count environmental attribute certificates against Scope 3: the emissions a company does not make itself targets drew protest from its own staff, who argued offsets are incompatible with the Paris Agreement.

  <!-- nature-gov-087 -->

- **Does going green pay? The evidence is split**

  Do a company's environmental and social efforts raise its profits or lower them? The evidence points both ways. A positive link between environmental performance and economic performance has been reported. A 2026 study of Indian firms found that steady improvement in environmental performance went with better financial results. Other studies link sustainability practices to financial success and customer satisfaction. Gains can include attracting staff, tax breaks and new markets. There is a catch. Those positive links show up mostly at larger firms, which have more money to spend on such efforts. And not every study finds a win-win. A 2023 study of European listed firms found the opposite: stronger sustainability practices went with lower profitability, at least for a time. So the question remains open. The answer may depend on the firm, its size and how long one waits for results. For Making money without wrecking the world around you, that uncertainty matters, because the case for change often rests on the promise that it will pay.

  <!-- nature-gov-064 -->

- **Insetting: meeting targets without cutting your own emissions**

  Insetting is a business-coined way for a company to claim it has met emission targets by means other than cutting its own emissions. The private sector created the term, and international standards such as ISO 14050 and the IWA 42 Net Zero Guidelines do not define it. Still, the SBTi's forestry, land and agriculture guidance of September 2022 allows it. That broke with the initiative's long-held view that Science-based targets: emission cuts that match the climate goal be met only by emission cuts.

  <!-- nature-gov-088 -->

- **Eco-efficiency and socio-efficiency: value per unit of impact**

  Eco-efficiency compares the economic value a firm adds with its total ecological impact. Socio-efficiency compares that value with its social impact. Most corporate effects on the environment are assumed to be negative. Social effects can go either way: job creation is positive, work accidents negative. Both measures mainly aim at economic sustainability, treating natural and social capital as tools for win-win gains. Some authors argue sustainable development needs more: eco-effectiveness, socio-effectiveness, sufficiency and eco-equity.

  <!-- nature-gov-093 -->

- **Do no significant harm: green in one way, harmful in none**

  Helping one environmental goal is not enough. Under the The EU taxonomy: an official list of green activities, an activity counts as sustainable only if it contributes substantially to one objective without seriously harming any of the other five. It must meet four requirements: that substantial contribution, no significant harm to the others, minimum social safeguards, and the technical screening criteria. The rule bites. The Technical Expert Group held back from including nuclear energy because it could not settle whether nuclear passed this test.

  <!-- nature-gov-097 -->

- **Gas and nuclear: the EU taxonomy's hardest fight**

  Should fossil gas and nuclear power be labelled sustainable investments? The Complementary Climate Delegated Act, the most controversial part of the EU taxonomy, said certain gas and nuclear activities were transitional ones that help mitigate climate change. Expert advice split. The Technical Expert Group did not recommend nuclear, while the Joint Research Centre found its impact would stay below harmful levels. Some countries see gas as a bridge from coal to renewables; the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden and Denmark opposed it. On 6 July 2022 a resolution to reject the act failed: 278 MEPs backed it when 353 votes were needed.

  <!-- nature-gov-098 -->

- **Material flow cost accounting: pricing what goes to waste**

  Material flow cost accounting traces the physical flows of materials and energy through a company or supply chain and puts a cost on each. The point is to reveal hidden environmental and financial costs, and to cut both through better use of materials and energy. It was developed in Germany in the 1980s and became a huge success in Japan in the 2000s, where up to 300 companies had used it by 2010. In 2011 the International Organization for Standardization published a standard for it, ISO 14051.

  <!-- nature-eecon-021 -->

- **The bottom of the pyramid: doing business with the poor**

  Hindustan Unilever sold hygiene products in smaller package sizes that poor customers could afford. It is a classic inclusive business model. Such models create value by selling to the poor or buying from them, bringing poor people directly into companies' value chains. Prahalad and Hart wrote 'The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid'. Their paper argued that serving poor consumers offers commercial and social opportunities. Creating shared value: profit from solving social problems has focused on this group for the same reasons. Money is the snag: in an IFC survey, around 90% of 167 applicants named access to finance as a main obstacle.

  <!-- nature-gov-095 -->

- **Supplier audits: checking the factory floor**

  A supplier audit is a visit to a supplier's site to check that it meets social and environmental standards. The standard may be an outside one, such as SA8000 or ISO 14001, or the buyer's own supplier code of conduct. Buyers may audit suppliers themselves or send third-party auditors. The limit is reach. Buyers often deal with only one tier of suppliers, while their supply chain stretches through many tiers upstream.

  <!-- nature-gov-083 -->

- **Carbon bombs: the projects that could blow the budget**

  A carbon bomb is a new fossil fuel extraction project whose potential emissions exceed 1 billion tonnes of CO2. A 2022 study counted 425 such coal, oil and gas projects worldwide. Together their potential emissions are twice the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C The carbon budget: how much CO2 is left to burn, the total that can still be emitted. Studies say large amounts of fossil fuel must stay in the ground for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C. The researchers argue 'defusing' carbon bombs should be a priority for climate policy.

  <!-- nature-gov-091 -->

- **Why some firms lobby for tougher green rules**

  Some firms back new environmental rules because the rules will hurt their competitors more than themselves. Many find it pays to argue for such rules and prepare for them before they become law. One study found firms support climate laws to gain power over competitors. They accept short-term costs to come out ahead in the long run.

  <!-- nature-gov-065 -->

- **Voluntary sustainability standards: labels in place of laws**

  As regulation of global business shifted from governments to private actors, a new kind of rulebook appeared. Voluntary sustainability standards set requirements on human rights, worker safety and environmental impact that producers, traders and retailers may be asked to meet. Governments lead some, such as the USDA Organic label. Campaign groups create others, such as FairTrade and Rainforest Alliance. The FairTrade label aims to empower small producers mainly through a minimum price paid to them. Many companies write their own instead, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices.

  <!-- nature-gov-105 -->

- **Roundtables and councils: many parties, one product**

  The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil awards a certified label to companies meeting criteria meant to limit palm oil's harm to people and the environment. It is a multi-stakeholder sustainability initiative: a partnership of campaign groups, companies, suppliers and governments using voluntary, market-based approaches to make one product or sector more sustainable. Others include the Forest Stewardship Council and the Better Cotton Initiative. They develop standards, issue certifications and can act as learning platforms.

  <!-- nature-gov-106 -->

- **Double materiality: looking both ways**

  Something is material when it matters enough to report. Double materiality says a company should report both how sustainability issues affect its finances and how the company affects society and the environment. Some supply chain impacts are doubly material: the firm harms the environment, and the same issues bring risks or opportunities for the firm. The EU's The CSRD: Europe's sustainability reporting law uses this test. The Global Reporting Initiative's standards focus only on impact materiality, the firm's effects on the world.

  <!-- nature-gov-086 -->

- **The CSRD: Europe's sustainability reporting law**

  The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive is the EU law that sets uniform sustainability reporting rules, replacing the older Non-Financial Reporting Directive. It was adopted in December 2022, came into force on 5 January 2023 and applies in stages from 1 January 2024. It widens reporting to about 50.000 organizations, against roughly 11,600 companies under the older law by 2021. Firms exceeding two of three thresholds must report: 250 employees, a €25 million balance sheet, or €50 million net turnover. In February 2025 the Commission proposed an 'Omnibus' simplification and a two-year delay, to 2028, for later waves.

  <!-- nature-gov-103 -->

- **Mainstreaming nature: from site ecologists to the boardroom**

  Mainstreaming nature means building it into a company's decision-making, governance, strategy and risk management, rather than leaving it to site ecologists. This sets Nature-positive: halt the loss by 2030, recover by 2050 apart from older approaches such as no net loss and net positive impact, where ecological managers handle biodiversity at project sites. Since the Kunming-Montreal framework began, nature-positive has helped carry nature into businesses and governance systems.

  <!-- nature-gov-081 -->

- **Physical and transition risk: two ways climate hits balance sheets**

  In 2015 Bank of England governor Mark Carney gave a warning. Meeting the 2 °C limit could leave most fossil fuel reserves as stranded assets, worth little because they can never be used. That is transition risk: the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society, from changes in policy, technology and consumer behaviour, including carbon pricing. Physical risk comes from climate impacts such as extreme weather, which damage property, infrastructure and land. Physical risks top the list of business concerns for US and EU firms.

  <!-- nature-gov-108 -->

- **Supply chain transparency: seeing where goods come from**

  Forced labour often happens upstream, where buyers and end users can see little. Supply chain transparency means making it possible to see and trace where goods come from and how they were made. Consumers increasingly demand it, especially where forced or child labour may be involved. It shapes how they view and support companies. It also matters for global goals such as ending net deforestation.

  <!-- nature-gov-084 -->

## History, people and frontiers

In 1972 delegates from around the world met in Stockholm for the first global conference on environmental issues. The ideas they argued over were much older. In 18th-century France the physiocrats held that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land, and the British classical economists who followed thought hard about land, labor and limits. This last part of the course traces how those threads came together: in books like Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, in the Brundtland Report's definition of sustainable development, and in the summits from Rio de Janeiro to Johannesburg. It also meets the people and institutions, from the Club of Rome to the TEEB study, who tried to put a price on what nature does for us.

### How the field developed

Economists were thinking about nature long before anyone spoke of an environmental movement. Physiocracy, whose name means 'government of nature', was an 18th-century French theory that all wealth comes from land and farming. Two centuries later, the conservation movement, Silent Spring in 1962 and the first Earth Day in 1970 pushed nature onto the political agenda. The 1972 Stockholm conference, the 1987 Brundtland Report and the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio turned that pressure into a global project. This chapter follows that path, from the ideas of Adam Smith's era to the TEEB study's effort to show what losing biodiversity costs.

- **Stockholm 1972: the world's first environment summit**

  It took four years, 114 governments and over $30,000,000 just to prepare. Sweden had proposed the idea to the UN's Economic and Social Council in 1968. The result was the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, held in Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972, the first global conference on environmental issues. It is the moment when Environmental degradation: 70% of the land, already altered became a matter for diplomats. The meeting agreed a Declaration of 26 principles, an Action Plan of 109 recommendations and a Resolution. It also created UNEP: the UN's voice on the environment, the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country, in Nairobi. The meeting was not harmonious. Developing countries made up 70 of the 122 countries attending, and divisions between rich and poor surfaced quickly, while the Soviet bloc stayed away in protest. India's Indira Gandhi gave a speech linking the care of nature with relieving poverty, and that link became one of the conference's central themes. At home, the conference spurred countries to monitor their environments and set up environment ministries and agencies. Its long shadow is easy to trace. The 1992 Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties, the 2002 Johannesburg summit and Rio+20: the summit that called for new global goals in 2012 all took its The Stockholm Declaration's 26 principles as their starting point.

  <!-- nature-hist-002 -->

- **Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties**

  In June 1992, 108 heads of state and government gathered in Rio de Janeiro. The Earth Summit, formally the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, ran from 3 to 14 June. It built directly on Stockholm 1972: the world's first environment summit twenty years earlier, and it did more than any meeting before it to spread the idea of Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later. Its biggest achievement was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signed by 154 states, which later led to the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature there too. The summit also produced the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21, a plan of action. In all, 178 governments voted to adopt them, and a Commission on Sustainable Development was set up to oversee them. Rio helped spread three principles that run through later treaties. The precautionary principle says to act against serious threats even before the science is complete. Common but differentiated responsibilities means all countries share the duty but not equally. The polluter pays principle puts the cost of pollution on whoever causes it. Not everyone was impressed. Critics note that many Rio promises on poverty and cleanup were never kept, and some leaders called the whole effort green imperialism by the global North.

  <!-- nature-hist-003 -->

- **Classical economics: Smith, Ricardo, Malthus and Mill**

  In 1776 Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations, and a new way of thinking about the economy began. Classical economics is the school of thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century. Its leaders were Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill. These thinkers founded Economics: the science of running the world's household as we know it. They saw markets as largely self-regulating, a view summed up in Smith's image of the The invisible hand: self-interest serving the public. For Smith, a nation's wealth was its yearly income. Labor, land and capital produced it, and it was shared out as wages, rent and profits. Land, in other words, sat at the heart of the system. The classical economists favored free trade over the protectionism of the earlier mercantilists. Ricardo explained trade's gains through comparative advantage: each country does best by specializing in what it gives up least to produce. Mill went further than the others in a direction that sounds modern. He believed a future 'stationary state', with constant population and capital, was both inevitable and desirable, an idea now called a steady-state economy. Not everyone admired the school. Thomas Carlyle nicknamed it 'the dismal science', a jibe often linked to Malthus's gloomy analysis. From the 1870s it gave way to neoclassical economics, though many of its ideas remain fundamental.

  <!-- nature-hist-012 -->

- **Our Common Future: defining sustainable development**

  Nine hundred days of public hearings and expert testimony, held around the world, produced one famous sentence. Our Common Future, better known as the Brundtland Report, is the October 1987 report of the UN's World Commission on Environment and Development. Former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland chaired the work, which is why the body is often called the The Brundtland Commission. Its sentence defined Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The report treated environment and development as one single issue rather than two. It stressed that economic, environmental and social sides of human development lock together. Poverty, it argued, worsens pressure on the environment, and there are environmental limits to economic growth. Fifteen years after Stockholm 1972: the world's first environment summit, it laid the groundwork for the 1992 Earth Summit, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration. Its reception was not universal applause. In 1988 the scholar Helge Ole Bergesen wrote that Third World elites saw the report as green imperialism.

  <!-- nature-hist-004 -->

- **The conservation movement: saving resources for later**

  In 1662 John Evelyn's book Sylva urged England to slow the felling of its trees and replant the ones it cut. The conservation movement is often traced to that plea. It is an environmental, social and political movement that seeks to manage and protect Natural resources: where every product beginss, wild species and their habitats for the future. It grew from practical need: people wanted to keep their fisheries, wildlife, water, soil and forests going. By the 19th century it had an ethic. Human activity harms the environment, people have a civic duty to keep it for future generations, and science should guide that duty. The first practical use of scientific conservation came in the forests of India in the mid-19th century. Over time the goals widened. Conservation moved from steady yields of resources and the preservation of wilderness to the protection of biodiversity, the whole variety of living things. Its history has a darker side. Scholars note that early conservation often protected game for elite white hunters while policing hunting by Indigenous and poor people.

  <!-- nature-hist-014 -->

- **Silent Spring: the book that turned the US against DDT**

  Rachel Carson thought the word pesticide was too kind. In Silent Spring, her 1962 book, she argued that these chemicals should be called 'biocides', because their effects rarely stop at the target pests. The book documented the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT and its spread through the wider environment as Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill. Carson accused the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its claims without question. Chemical companies fought back hard. They lost the argument with the public. Silent Spring shifted opinion, reversed US pesticide policy and led to a national ban on DDT for farm use. It also fed the movement that created the US Environmental Protection Agency. The book became a rallying point for the new social movement of the 1960s and is seen as the start of the deep ecology movement. As one scholar put it, after Carson no one could so easily sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress. A dispute still clings to it. Some anti-environmentalist groups blame Carson for malaria deaths after DDT was restricted. Scientists and journalists have dismissed that claim as a myth, but it has not gone away.

  <!-- nature-hist-006 -->

- **Rio+20: the summit that called for new global goals**

  Twenty years after the Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties, the world came back to the same city. Rio+20, the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, ran from 13 to 22 June 2012 and tried to reconcile economic and environmental goals. It had two themes: a green economy that lifts people out of poverty, and an institutional framework for sustainable development. Its 49-page outcome document, 'The Future We Want', was nonbinding. It called for the Sustainable Development Goals, a set of measurable targets. Nations agreed to explore alternatives to GDP that count things like nature's carbon storage, and reaffirmed promises to phase out fossil fuel subsidies. The summit also popularized the term blue economy. Yet Obama, Merkel and Cameron stayed away, a sign that sustainability was not their priority.

  <!-- nature-hist-008 -->

- **The Club of Rome and The Limits to Growth**

  Its first report sold 30 million copies in more than 30 languages, the best-selling environmental book in history. The Club of Rome is an informal non-profit group of intellectuals and business leaders, founded in Rome in 1968. Italian industrialist Aurelio Peccei and British scientist Alexander King started it because they doubted that technology and development alone could solve the world's problems. That 1972 report was The Limits to Growth: a computer model meets a finite planet. Its computer simulations suggested that growth in production and consumption could not go on forever, because resources would run out or pollution would build up. The OECD, committed to unfettered growth, reacted with hostility. Critics remain divided. Economist Robert Solow called the scenarios 'simplistic', and a 1973 Sussex University study, Models of Doom, found the forecasts hinged on a few unduly pessimistic assumptions. Yet in 2009 Solow allowed that rapid growth in India and China might change the picture. The club has issued 55 reports, including 'Earth for All' in 2022.

  <!-- nature-hist-026 -->

- **Earth Day: a teach-in that became a global event**

  In 1969 an oil spill off Santa Barbara released over 3 million US gallons of oil and killed more than 10,000 seabirds and sea mammals. US Senator Gaylord Nelson was moved to act. He proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in for April 22, 1970, and hired a young activist, Denis Hayes, to run it. That was the first Earth Day, now an annual event in support of environmental protection. The decade that followed brought the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts, the EPA, and bans on DDT and leaded gasoline. In 1990 Earth Day went global, mobilizing 200 million people in 141 countries. In 2016, leaders of 175 nations signed the Paris Agreement on Earth Day. Nelson summed up its view: 'The economy is a wholly owned subsidiary of the environment, not the other way around.'

  <!-- nature-hist-016 -->

- **Physiocracy: when wealth came only from the land**

  Its name, from the Greek, means 'government of nature'. Physiocracy was an 18th-century French theory holding that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land and farming. Led by François Quesnay, the Marquis de Mirabeau and Turgot, it was one of the first well-developed theories in Economics: the science of running the world's household, just before Adam Smith. Unlike the mercantilists, who counted a ruler's gold, the physiocrats saw productive work as the source of wealth. But only farm labor created value; industry was an 'unproductive appendage' to agriculture. They trusted a 'natural order' and laissez-faire, the idea that self-interest and free trade make an economy work.
